uni-bsc-bio-plant-physiology-biochemistr.title: Plant Physiology & Biochemistry
uni-bsc-bio-plant-physiology-biochemistr.description: Water relations, mineral nutrition, photosynthesis, respiration, nitrogen metabolism, biomolecules and enzymes, growth regulators and photomorphogenesis, with worked numericals and standard physiology experiments. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. (Botany/Biology) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Plant water relations and mineral nutrition
courses.summary: Water potential and its components, osmosis and plasmolysis, absorption and ascent of sap, transpiration and stomatal regulation, essential elements, deficiency symptoms and mechanisms of ion uptake.
outcomes: Calculate water potential and solute potential
Explain absorption of water and the cohesion–tension theory
Describe the mechanism of stomatal opening and factors affecting transpiration
List essential macro- and micronutrients with roles and deficiency symptoms
Distinguish passive and active ion uptake

scenes.text: Cucumber slices sprinkled with salt go limp and release water — osmosis down a water-potential gradient.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Water potential
steps.body: Water potential (Ψw) is the chemical potential of water per unit molar volume relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure (Ψw of pure water = 0 MPa). For a plant cell: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp (+ Ψm, matric, important in soils and dry seeds). Solute potential Ψs is always negative; pressure potential Ψp is usually positive in turgid cells (turgor), zero at incipient plasmolysis, and negative in xylem under tension. Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) Ψw.

steps.title: Van't Hoff equation
steps.body: Ψs = −iCRT, where i = ionisation constant (1 for sucrose), C = molar concentration (mol L⁻¹), R = 0.00831 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T = absolute temperature (K).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Solute potential of 0.2 M sucrose at 27 °C: T = 300 K. Ψs = −1 × 0.2 × 0.00831 × 300 = −0.4986 ≈ −0.50 MPa.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Cell A: Ψs = −0.8 MPa, Ψp = +0.3 MPa → ΨA = −0.5 MPa. Cell B: Ψs = −0.6 MPa, Ψp = +0.3 MPa → ΨB = −0.3 MPa. Water flows from B (−0.3) to A (−0.5).

steps.title: Plasmolysis and imbibition
steps.body: In a hypertonic solution protoplast shrinks from the wall (plasmolysis): incipient → evident → final. Deplasmolysis when returned to water. Imbibition: adsorption of water by hydrophilic colloids (dry seeds, wood) creating large imbibition pressure; matric potential is very negative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: A more concentrated solution has a more negative Ψs, i.e. lower water potential. Remember Kelvin = °C + 273.

activity.prompt: Calculate the solute potential (MPa) of 0.1 M sucrose at 27 °C (R = 0.00831 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Enter a negative number to 2 decimals.

quiz.why: Pure water at atmospheric pressure is the reference state with Ψw defined as zero.

quiz.q: Cell X Ψ = −0.4 MPa, cell Y Ψ = −0.7 MPa. Water moves

quiz.q: Dry seeds swell in water mainly by

story.title: Water to the top of a eucalyptus

scenes.text: A 60 m tall eucalyptus lifts water without a pump — the leaves pull it.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Absorption pathways
steps.body: Root hairs absorb water. Pathways across cortex: apoplast (cell walls, intercellular spaces), symplast (through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata) and transmembrane. At the endodermis the Casparian strip blocks apoplast, forcing water into the symplast — letting the root control solute entry. Active absorption (root pressure, osmotic) vs passive absorption (transpiration pull, the main route).

steps.title: Theories of ascent
steps.body: Vital theories (Bose's pulsation theory) and root pressure theory are inadequate: root pressure is usually only a few tenths of a MPa and absent in many tall trees. Capillarity is too weak. Cohesion–tension theory (Dixon and Joly, 1894): transpiration lowers Ψw in leaf mesophyll, creating tension; water columns in xylem stay continuous due to cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls; tension is transmitted to roots. Evidence: negative pressure measured by Scholander pressure bomb; diurnal shrinkage of tree trunks.

steps.title: Root pressure and guttation
steps.body: Root pressure arises from active ion accumulation in xylem; seen as exudation from cut stumps and as guttation from hydathodes at night (grasses, tomato).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Cohesion–tension does not require living cells in xylem; it works in dead vessels. Embolism (air bubbles) breaks columns, which is why multiple vessels and pits matter.

items: Substomatal cavity as vapour, out through stoma

quiz.why: Tension generated by transpiration pulls cohesive water columns up the xylem.

scenes.text: On a hot afternoon, a wheat field's stomata partly close — saving water but cutting CO₂ uptake.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Types and factors
steps.body: Stomatal (about 90% or more), cuticular and lenticular transpiration. External factors: light, temperature, humidity (vapour pressure deficit), wind, soil water. Internal: stomatal density and size, leaf area, cuticle, root–shoot ratio. Antitranspirants: phenyl mercuric acetate, abscisic acid, CO₂, wax emulsions.

steps.title: Mechanism of stomatal movement
steps.body: Classical starch–sugar hypothesis (Sayre; Steward) — starch converts to glucose in light due to pH rise. Modern K⁺ ion pump hypothesis (Levitt; Fischer and Hsiao): blue light activates H⁺-ATPase in guard cell plasma membrane → H⁺ pumped out → membrane hyperpolarised → K⁺ enters via channels, balanced by Cl⁻ uptake and malate synthesis → Ψs falls, water enters, guard cells swell; radial micellation of cellulose and thicker inner walls make them bow apart → pore opens. ABA (water stress) triggers K⁺ efflux and closure.

steps.title: Transpiration — necessary evil (Curtis)
steps.body: Benefits: cooling, mineral transport, ascent of sap. Cost: water loss and wilting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Stomata open because guard cells gain K⁺ and water, not because they lose turgor. CAM plants open stomata at night.

activity.prompt: Order the events in stomatal opening (K⁺ pump model).
items: Blue light is perceived by guard cells
Plasma membrane H⁺-ATPase pumps protons out
K⁺ enters through channels, with Cl⁻ and malate as counter-ions
Guard cell solute potential falls and water enters
Guard cells become turgid and the pore opens

quiz.q: Ion mainly responsible for stomatal opening
quiz.why: Large K⁺ influx into guard cells lowers their water potential.

quiz.q: Hormone that closes stomata under stress
quiz.why: ABA triggers ion efflux from guard cells, causing closure.

quiz.q: Transpiration is called a necessary evil by
quiz.why: Curtis emphasised that it is both harmful and useful to plants.

quiz.q: High humidity transpiration
quiz.why: It lowers the vapour pressure gradient between leaf and air.

scenes.text: Older leaves of a paddy crop yellow first — the farmer suspects nitrogen deficiency, a mobile element.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Essential elements
steps.body: Criteria of essentiality (Arnon and Stout, 1939): without it the plant cannot complete its life cycle; it cannot be replaced by another element; it is directly involved in metabolism. Macronutrients (>10 mmol kg⁻¹ dry matter): C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S. Micronutrients: Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, Mo, Cl, Ni. Studied by hydroponics (Sachs, Knop).

steps.title: Roles and deficiency
steps.body: N: proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll — chlorosis of older leaves. P: ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids — purple leaves, poor roots. K: enzyme activation, stomata — marginal scorching of older leaves. Mg: chlorophyll centre — interveinal chlorosis of old leaves. Ca: middle lamella, membranes — young leaf and tip necrosis. Fe: cytochromes, ferredoxin — young leaf chlorosis. Zn: auxin synthesis — little leaf, khaira disease of rice. B: pollen germination — heart rot of beet. Mo: nitrate reductase, nitrogenase — whiptail of cauliflower. Mn: water splitting — grey speck of oats. Mobile elements (N, P, K, Mg) show symptoms first in older leaves; immobile (Ca, Fe, B, S) in young leaves.

steps.title: Ion uptake
steps.body: Passive: diffusion, ion exchange, Donnan equilibrium, mass flow into free space (apparent free space). Active: against concentration gradient, needs ATP — carrier concept (Epstein's dual mechanism), H⁺-ATPase-driven symports/antiports, ion channels. Evidence for active uptake: inhibited by low O₂, low temperature and respiratory inhibitors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Khaira disease of rice is zinc deficiency, not iron. Chlorine and nickel are micronutrients, not macronutrients.

quiz.why: It depends on respiration for ATP, which needs oxygen.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Photosynthesis
courses.summary: Photosynthetic pigments and absorption spectra, light reactions (Z-scheme, photophosphorylation), Calvin cycle, photorespiration, C4 and CAM pathways and factors affecting photosynthesis.
outcomes: Describe pigments, absorption and action spectra and Emerson effects
Explain the Z-scheme and cyclic vs non-cyclic photophosphorylation
Work out ATP and NADPH budgets of the Calvin cycle
Compare C3, C4 and CAM plants
Apply Blackman's law of limiting factors

lessons.title: Pigments, light and the two photosystems

scenes.text: Robert Emerson saw photosynthesis efficiency fall sharply beyond 680 nm — and recover when shorter red light was added.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pigments
steps.body: Chlorophyll a (universal primary pigment, blue-green, absorbs ~430 and ~662 nm), chlorophyll b (yellow-green, accessory), carotenoids (carotenes and xanthophylls — accessory and photoprotective), phycobilins in algae. Absorption spectrum: light absorbed by a pigment vs wavelength. Action spectrum: rate of photosynthesis vs wavelength (Engelmann's experiment with Cladophora and aerobic bacteria).

steps.title: Emerson effects
steps.body: Red drop: quantum yield falls above 680 nm. Enhancement effect: far-red (>680 nm) plus shorter red light together give more photosynthesis than the sum of each alone — evidence for two photosystems. PS I reaction centre P700, PS II reaction centre P680. Located in thylakoid membranes; PS II mostly in grana (appressed) and PS I in stroma lamellae.

steps.title: Quantum requirement
steps.body: About 8 photons are needed per O₂ evolved (4 electrons × 2 photosystems), so maximum quantum yield ≈ 1/8 = 0.125.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Absorption spectrum belongs to a pigment; action spectrum belongs to the process. Chlorophyll reflects green light — it absorbs blue and red.

activity.prompt: If 8 photons are needed per O₂ molecule, how many photons are needed to evolve 6 O₂ (one glucose equivalent)?

quiz.q: Reaction centre of PS II is
quiz.why: PS II's special chlorophyll pair absorbs maximally at 680 nm.

quiz.q: Enhancement effect indicates
quiz.why: Synergy between far-red and red light shows two cooperating photosystems.

quiz.q: Engelmann used
quiz.why: Bacteria clustered where the alga evolved most oxygen under a spectrum.

quiz.q: Maximum quantum yield of O₂ evolution is about
quiz.why: One O₂ per 8 photons gives a yield of 1/8.

scenes.text: The oxygen you breathe comes from water split by PS II, as shown with ¹⁸O by Ruben and Kamen.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Non-cyclic electron flow (Z-scheme)
steps.body: Light excites P680 → electron to pheophytin → plastoquinone (PQ) → cytochrome b6f complex → plastocyanin (PC) → P700 (excited by light) → ferredoxin (Fd) → Fd-NADP⁺ reductase → NADPH. P680⁺ is reduced by electrons from water via the oxygen-evolving complex (Mn₄CaO₅ cluster): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. Products: ATP, NADPH, O₂.

steps.title: Cyclic photophosphorylation
steps.body: Only PS I: electrons from Fd return via cytochrome b6f and PC to P700. Produces ATP only (no NADPH, no O₂). Helps balance ATP:NADPH demand (Calvin cycle needs 3:2).

steps.title: Chemiosmosis
steps.body: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis: proton gradient across thylakoid membrane (lumen acidic) from water splitting and PQ shuttle drives ATP synthase (CF0–CF1) as protons flow back to stroma.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: O₂ comes from water, not CO₂. NADPH is formed on the stromal side, ATP also released into stroma.

quiz.why: Electrons cycle back to PS I so no NADP⁺ is reduced and no water is split.

quiz.q: Source of O₂ in photosynthesis
quiz.why: Isotope labelling showed that evolved oxygen comes from water.

quiz.q: Mobile carrier between PS II and cytochrome b6f
quiz.why: Plastoquinone shuttles electrons and protons within the membrane.

quiz.q: Chemiosmotic hypothesis was given by
quiz.why: Peter Mitchell proposed that a proton gradient drives ATP synthesis.

scenes.text: Melvin Calvin fed ¹⁴CO₂ to Chlorella and found the first stable product within seconds: 3-phosphoglycerate.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Three phases
steps.body: 1) Carboxylation: RuBP (5C) + CO₂ → 2 × 3-PGA, by Rubisco. 2) Reduction: 3-PGA + ATP → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; + NADPH → glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). 3) Regeneration: G3P → RuBP using ATP (ribulose-5-phosphate kinase).

steps.title: Worked example: energy budget
steps.body: Per CO₂ fixed: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH. For 3 CO₂ (one net G3P): 9 ATP + 6 NADPH. For one hexose (6 CO₂): 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.

steps.title: Photorespiration (C2 cycle)
steps.body: Rubisco also acts as oxygenase: RuBP + O₂ → 3-PGA + 2-phosphoglycolate. Glycolate goes to peroxisome → glyoxylate → glycine; in mitochondria 2 glycine → serine + CO₂ + NH₃; serine returns to chloroplast as glycerate. Three organelles: chloroplast, peroxisome, mitochondrion. It wastes fixed carbon and energy, increasing with high temperature and high O₂:CO₂ ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: CO₂ is released in mitochondria during photorespiration, not in the peroxisome. The Calvin cycle is light-independent but runs in light because it needs ATP/NADPH and light-activated enzymes.

activity.prompt: How many ATP molecules does the Calvin cycle use to fix 12 molecules of CO₂?

quiz.q: First stable product of the Calvin cycle
quiz.why: Carboxylation of RuBP produces two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

quiz.q: Rubisco stands for
quiz.why: Its name reflects both carboxylase and oxygenase activities.

quiz.q: Organelles involved in photorespiration
quiz.why: Glycolate pathway passes through these three organelles.

quiz.q: NADPH needed per CO₂ fixed
quiz.why: Two NADPH reduce two 1,3-BPG molecules formed per CO₂.

scenes.text: Sugarcane outgrows wheat in hot Indian summers because it concentrates CO₂ around Rubisco.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: C4 (Hatch–Slack) pathway
steps.body: In mesophyll: PEP + HCO₃⁻ → oxaloacetate (OAA) by PEP carboxylase (no affinity for O₂) → malate/aspartate. In bundle sheath (Kranz anatomy): decarboxylation releases CO₂ for Rubisco → Calvin cycle; pyruvate returns to mesophyll and is regenerated to PEP using ATP (pyruvate phosphate dikinase). Cost: 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂. Examples: maize, sugarcane, sorghum, Amaranthus. Little photorespiration, high water-use efficiency.

steps.title: CAM
steps.body: Crassulacean acid metabolism (Bryophyllum, pineapple, Opuntia): stomata open at night; CO₂ fixed by PEPC into malate stored in vacuole (acidity rises at night); by day stomata close, malate is decarboxylated and CO₂ enters Calvin cycle in the same cell — temporal separation.

steps.title: Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905)
steps.body: When a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor nearest its minimum value. Example: in bright light, raising CO₂ increases rate until light becomes limiting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: C4 separates steps spatially (two cell types); CAM separates them temporally (night/day). The first product of C4 is OAA (4C).

quiz.why: F. F. Blackman proposed it in 1905 for photosynthesis.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Respiration and nitrogen metabolism
courses.summary: Glycolysis, fermentation, Krebs cycle, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation, ATP accounting, respiratory quotient, pentose phosphate pathway, biological nitrogen fixation, nitrate assimilation and amino acid synthesis.
outcomes: Trace glycolysis, Krebs cycle and ETS with key enzymes
Compute ATP yield and respiratory quotient
Explain the pentose phosphate pathway and alternative oxidase
Describe symbiotic nitrogen fixation and nitrogenase
Explain nitrate reduction and ammonia assimilation (GS–GOGAT)

scenes.text: Overnight idli batter rises with CO₂ from fermentation — glycolysis without oxygen.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Glycolysis (EMP pathway, cytosol)
steps.body: Glucose → (hexokinase, ATP) glucose-6-P → fructose-6-P → (phosphofructokinase, ATP; key regulatory step) fructose-1,6-bisP → (aldolase) DHAP + G3P → 2 G3P → (G3P dehydrogenase) 2 × 1,3-BPG + 2 NADH → (substrate-level) 2 × 3-PGA + 2 ATP → 2-PGA → PEP → (pyruvate kinase) 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP. Net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 pyruvate per glucose.

steps.title: Fermentation
steps.body: Alcoholic (yeast, plant tissues under flooding): pyruvate → (pyruvate decarboxylase) acetaldehyde + CO₂ → (alcohol dehydrogenase) ethanol, regenerating NAD⁺. Lactic acid (bacteria, muscle): pyruvate + NADH → lactate (lactate dehydrogenase). Net energy only 2 ATP per glucose.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 — net 2. It occurs in cytosol, not mitochondria.

activity.prompt: Order the glycolysis intermediates.

quiz.q: Key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis
quiz.why: PFK catalyses the committed step and is allosterically regulated by ATP and citrate.

quiz.q: Net ATP from glycolysis per glucose
quiz.why: Four ATP are formed but two are used in the preparatory phase.

quiz.q: Alcoholic fermentation products
quiz.why: Pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, then reduced to ethanol.

quiz.q: Glycolysis occurs in
quiz.why: All glycolytic enzymes are cytosolic.

lessons.title: Krebs cycle, ETS and ATP accounting

scenes.text: Inside mitochondria, the Krebs cycle strips electrons from acetyl-CoA and the ETS turns them into ATP.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Link reaction and Krebs cycle (matrix)
steps.body: Pyruvate dehydrogenase: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. TCA: acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate → isocitrate → (NADH, CO₂) α-ketoglutarate → (NADH, CO₂) succinyl-CoA → (GTP/ATP) succinate → (FADH₂, succinate dehydrogenase on inner membrane) fumarate → malate → (NADH) OAA. Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP, 2 CO₂.

steps.title: Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation
steps.body: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) → ubiquinone → Complex III (cyt bc1) → cytochrome c → Complex IV (cytochrome oxidase, reduces O₂ to H₂O). FADH₂ enters via Complex II. Proton gradient drives Complex V (ATP synthase). Plants also have rotenone-insensitive NAD(P)H dehydrogenases and a cyanide-resistant alternative oxidase that produces heat (thermogenesis in Arum spadix).

steps.title: Worked example: ATP per glucose
steps.body: NADH: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (link) + 6 (TCA) = 10; FADH₂ = 2; substrate-level ATP = 2 + 2 = 4. Classical (NADH = 3, FADH₂ = 2): 30 + 4 + 4 = 38 ATP (36 in eukaryotes if glycolytic NADH uses the glycerol-phosphate shuttle). Modern P/O ratios (2.5 and 1.5): 25 + 3 + 4 = 32 (or 30).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only TCA enzyme bound to the inner membrane. State which P/O ratios you used when quoting an ATP total.

activity.prompt: Using classical values (NADH = 3 ATP, FADH₂ = 2 ATP), how many ATP are produced from ONE acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle and ETS (include the 1 substrate-level ATP)?

quiz.q: CO₂ molecules released per pyruvate fully oxidised
quiz.why: One in the link reaction and two in the Krebs cycle.

quiz.q: Terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration
quiz.why: Cytochrome oxidase transfers electrons to oxygen, forming water.

quiz.q: Cyanide-resistant respiration is due to
quiz.why: Alternative oxidase bypasses complexes III and IV and is not inhibited by cyanide.

quiz.q: Total NADH formed per glucose (glycolysis + link + TCA)

lessons.title: Respiratory quotient and pentose phosphate pathway

scenes.text: Oily castor seeds take up more O₂ than they release CO₂ when germinating — RQ less than 1.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Respiratory quotient
steps.body: RQ = volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ absorbed. Carbohydrate: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, RQ = 1. Fat (tripalmitin): 2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O, RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.70. Organic acid (oxalic): 2(COOH)₂ + O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O, RQ = 4. Proteins ≈ 0.8–0.9. Anaerobic respiration: RQ is infinite (no O₂ used). CAM succulents at night: RQ near 0 (CO₂ fixed).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Germinating seeds absorb 50 mL O₂ and release 35 mL CO₂. RQ = 35 ÷ 50 = 0.70 → fat is the substrate.

steps.title: Pentose phosphate pathway
steps.body: Cytosol/plastids. Oxidative phase: glucose-6-P → (G6P dehydrogenase) 6-phosphogluconate → ribulose-5-P + CO₂, producing 2 NADPH. Non-oxidative phase interconverts sugars (transketolase, transaldolase). Supplies NADPH for biosynthesis and ribose-5-P for nucleotides, erythrose-4-P for shikimate pathway (aromatic amino acids, lignin).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: RQ < 1 means more O₂ used, typical of fats; RQ > 1 typical of organic acids.

activity.prompt: A tissue absorbs 40 mL O₂ and releases 52 mL CO₂. Calculate RQ (2 decimals).

quiz.q: RQ of glucose
quiz.why: Six CO₂ are released for six O₂ consumed.

quiz.q: RQ of fats is about
quiz.why: Fats are highly reduced and need more oxygen per CO₂ released.

quiz.q: Pentose phosphate pathway mainly produces
quiz.why: Its oxidative phase yields NADPH and ribulose-5-phosphate.

quiz.q: RQ of anaerobic respiration
quiz.why: CO₂ is released while no O₂ is consumed, so the ratio is undefined/infinite.

scenes.text: Splitting a gram root nodule shows pink tissue — leghaemoglobin protecting nitrogenase from oxygen.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Biological nitrogen fixation
steps.body: Free-living: Azotobacter, Clostridium, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc). Symbiotic: Rhizobium with legumes, Frankia with non-legumes (Casuarina, Alnus), Anabaena with Azolla. Nitrogenase (Fe protein + MoFe protein) reaction: N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂. Requires anaerobic conditions — provided by leghaemoglobin in nodules and heterocysts in cyanobacteria.

steps.title: Nodule formation
steps.body: Root secretes flavonoids → Rhizobium nod genes → Nod factors → root hair curling → infection thread → cortical cell division → bacteroids in symbiosomes → nodule with leghaemoglobin. Plant nodulin genes and bacterial nif genes are involved.

steps.title: Nitrate and ammonia assimilation
steps.body: Nitrate reductase (cytosol, Mo-containing): NO₃⁻ → NO₂⁻. Nitrite reductase (plastid, ferredoxin): NO₂⁻ → NH₄⁺. Ammonia assimilation: GS–GOGAT — glutamine synthetase: glutamate + NH₄⁺ + ATP → glutamine; GOGAT: glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate → 2 glutamate. Transamination transfers amino groups to keto acids to make other amino acids. Reductive amination by glutamate dehydrogenase is a minor route.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Biomolecules and enzymes
courses.summary: Carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids and proteins of plants, enzyme classification, mechanism and kinetics (Michaelis–Menten, Lineweaver–Burk), inhibition and regulation.
outcomes: Classify carbohydrates and describe storage and structural polysaccharides
Describe lipid classes and fatty acids of plants

scenes.text: Cotton fibre is almost pure cellulose; rice grain is mostly starch — both are glucose polymers, linked differently.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Carbohydrates
steps.body: Monosaccharides: trioses (glyceraldehyde), pentoses (ribose), hexoses (glucose — aldose; fructose — ketose). Disaccharides: sucrose (glucose α1→β2 fructose, non-reducing, main transport sugar in phloem), maltose (α1→4, reducing). Polysaccharides: starch = amylose (linear α1→4) + amylopectin (branched α1→6 every 24–30 residues); cellulose (β1→4 glucose, H-bonded microfibrils); hemicellulose (xyloglucans); pectin (galacturonic acid, middle lamella); inulin (fructan, dahlia tubers); callose (β1→3 glucan).

steps.title: Lipids
steps.body: Fatty acids: saturated (palmitic C16:0, stearic C18:0) and unsaturated (oleic 18:1, linoleic 18:2, linolenic 18:3). Triacylglycerols store energy in oilseeds (oil bodies). Phospholipids and galactolipids (MGDG, DGDG — dominant in thylakoids) form membranes. Waxes, cutin and suberin form protective barriers. Sterols (sitosterol, stigmasterol).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are in the glycosidic bond. Cellulose is β-linked; starch α-linked.

activity.prompt: Classify each biomolecule.

quiz.why: Sucrose is non-reducing and stable, ideal for long-distance transport.

quiz.why: β1→4 glucose chains form straight hydrogen-bonded microfibrils.

quiz.why: α1→6 links create branches on the α1→4 backbone.

scenes.text: Rubisco makes up a large share of soluble leaf protein — perhaps the most abundant protein on Earth.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Amino acids
steps.body: 20 standard α-amino acids with an amino group, carboxyl group, H and R group on α-carbon; zwitterions at isoelectric point. Classified by R group: non-polar (glycine, alanine, valine, leucine), polar uncharged (serine, threonine), acidic (aspartate, glutamate), basic (lysine, arginine, histidine), aromatic (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan). Peptide bond forms by condensation between –COOH and –NH₂.

steps.title: Protein structure
steps.body: Primary: amino-acid sequence. Secondary: α-helix and β-pleated sheet stabilised by backbone H-bonds. Tertiary: 3D fold by hydrophobic interactions, H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bridges. Quaternary: assembly of subunits (Rubisco: 8 large + 8 small subunits). Denaturation by heat, pH, urea destroys higher structure.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A tripeptide is made from 3 amino acids. Number of peptide bonds = 3 − 1 = 2, water molecules released = 2. For a protein of 150 residues: 149 peptide bonds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Glycine is not optically active (R = H). Rubisco small subunits are encoded in the nucleus, large subunits in the chloroplast genome.

scenes.text: Emil Fischer imagined enzymes as locks; Koshland later showed the lock changes shape as the key enters.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: IUBMB classes
steps.body: EC 1 Oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases, oxidases), EC 2 Transferases (kinases, transaminases), EC 3 Hydrolases (amylase, lipase, protease), EC 4 Lyases (aldolase, decarboxylases, fumarase), EC 5 Isomerases (phosphohexose isomerase), EC 6 Ligases (synthetases, e.g. glutamine synthetase, DNA ligase).

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Enzymes lower activation energy by forming an enzyme–substrate complex at the active site. Models: lock-and-key (Fischer 1894) and induced fit (Koshland 1958). Cofactors: metal ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺), coenzymes (NAD⁺, FAD, CoA), prosthetic groups (haem). Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme. Isozymes: different forms catalysing the same reaction (lactate dehydrogenase).

steps.title: Factors
steps.body: Temperature (optimum, then denaturation), pH (optimum), substrate concentration (saturation), enzyme concentration (linear), inhibitors, activators.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Enzymes do not change ΔG or equilibrium; they only speed attainment of equilibrium. Aldolase is a lyase, not a hydrolase.

activity.prompt: Assign each enzyme to its class.

quiz.why: The complete catalytically active enzyme is the holoenzyme.

quiz.why: They speed reactions by lowering the activation energy barrier.

scenes.text: Plotting reaction rate against substrate gives a hyperbola that levels off at Vmax.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Michaelis–Menten equation
steps.body: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Km is the substrate concentration at which v = Vmax/2; low Km = high affinity. Lineweaver–Burk double reciprocal: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Vmax = 100 µmol min⁻¹, Km = 2 mM. At [S] = 2 mM: v = 100 × 2 ÷ (2 + 2) = 50. At [S] = 6 mM: v = 600 ÷ 8 = 75 µmol min⁻¹.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: At what [S] is v = 80% of Vmax? 0.8 = [S]/(Km + [S]) → 0.8Km = 0.2[S] → [S] = 4Km. With Km = 2 mM, [S] = 8 mM.

steps.title: Inhibition
steps.body: Competitive (inhibitor resembles substrate, binds active site; Km increases, Vmax unchanged; overcome by excess substrate — malonate on succinate dehydrogenase). Non-competitive (binds elsewhere; Vmax decreases, Km unchanged — heavy metals). Uncompetitive (binds ES complex; both decrease). Allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition (end product inhibits first enzyme).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In competitive inhibition lines on a Lineweaver–Burk plot meet at the y-axis (same 1/Vmax); in non-competitive they meet on the x-axis.

activity.prompt: An enzyme has Vmax = 120 µmol/min and Km = 4 mM. Find v (µmol/min) at [S] = 12 mM.

quiz.why: Substituting v = Vmax/2 into the equation gives [S] = Km.

quiz.q: Competitive inhibitor changes
quiz.why: It raises apparent Km; enough substrate still reaches the same Vmax.

quiz.q: Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase
quiz.why: Malonate resembles succinate and competes for the active site.

quiz.q: x-intercept of Lineweaver–Burk plot
quiz.why: Setting 1/v = 0 gives 1/[S] = −1/Km.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Translocation, growth regulators and photomorphogenesis
courses.summary: Phloem translocation (pressure-flow), growth kinetics, discovery and roles of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid, phytochrome, photoperiodism, vernalisation, seed dormancy and plant movements.
outcomes: Explain Münch's pressure-flow hypothesis
Calculate growth rates and describe the sigmoid growth curve
Relate each major phytohormone to its physiological effects and uses
Explain phytochrome, photoperiodism and florigen
Describe vernalisation and seed dormancy

scenes.text: Researchers cut feeding aphids off their stylets and collected pure sieve-tube sap oozing under pressure.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pressure-flow (mass flow) hypothesis — Münch 1930
steps.body: At the source (leaf), sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes (apoplastic loading via H⁺–sucrose symport, or symplastic polymer trapping). Ψs falls, water enters from xylem, turgor rises. At the sink (root, fruit), sucrose is unloaded, water leaves, turgor falls. Sap moves by bulk flow from high to low pressure. Evidence: aphid stylet exudate under pressure, ringing (girdling) experiments, radioactive tracers. Speed often around 0.5–1 m h⁻¹.

steps.title: Growth
steps.body: Irreversible increase in size. Phases: cell division, elongation, maturation. Sigmoid (S-shaped) curve: lag, log (exponential), deceleration, stationary. Arithmetic growth: Lt = L0 + rt (root elongation). Geometric growth: W1 = W0 e^(rt) (early embryo). Absolute growth rate = increase per unit time; relative growth rate = increase per unit time per unit initial size.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Leaf A grows from 5 cm² to 10 cm² and leaf B from 50 cm² to 55 cm² in one day. Absolute growth for both = 5 cm² day⁻¹. Relative growth: A = 5/5 = 100%, B = 5/50 = 10% per day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Translocation in phloem can go up or down depending on source and sink; xylem flow is mainly upward.

activity.prompt: A seedling's dry mass rises from 20 g to 26 g in a week. What is its relative growth over the week as a percentage of initial mass?

quiz.q: Pressure-flow hypothesis was proposed by
quiz.why: Ernst Münch proposed mass flow from source to sink in 1930.

quiz.q: Girdling a stem first stops
quiz.why: Removing bark removes phloem, so sugars accumulate above the ring.

quiz.q: Exponential phase of the sigmoid curve is
quiz.why: Growth rate is maximal and proportional to size during the log phase.

quiz.q: Absolute growth of two leaves is equal but relative growth differs because
quiz.why: Relative growth divides the increase by the starting size.

scenes.text: Japanese farmers saw rice seedlings grow absurdly tall and fall over — 'bakanae' — caused by gibberellin from the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Auxins
steps.body: Discovery: Darwins' phototropism experiments (1880), Boysen-Jensen, Paál, F. W. Went (1928, Avena coleoptile curvature test; agar block). Natural: indole-3-acetic acid (IAA); synthetic: 2,4-D, NAA, IBA. Effects: cell elongation (acid growth), apical dominance, rooting of cuttings (IBA, NAA), parthenocarpy, prevention of premature fruit drop, xylem differentiation; 2,4-D as selective weedicide against dicot weeds. Polar transport (basipetal in stems).

steps.title: Gibberellins
steps.body: Over 100 GAs; GA₃ most used. Effects: stem elongation (bolting in rosette plants like cabbage), breaking seed dormancy, induction of α-amylase in aleurone of cereal grains (malting), seedless/bigger grapes, overcoming genetic dwarfism, substituting long days/cold in some plants.

steps.title: Cytokinins
steps.body: Kinetin discovered by Skoog and Miller from autoclaved herring sperm DNA (1955); zeatin from maize kernels; coconut milk is rich in cytokinins. Effects: cell division, shoot formation in tissue culture (high cytokinin:auxin → shoots, low → roots), delay of senescence (Richmond–Lang effect), release of lateral buds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Kinetin is not naturally found in plants — it is a DNA degradation product; zeatin is the natural cytokinin. 2,4-D kills broad-leaved (dicot) weeds, not grasses.

quiz.q: Selective weedicide

scenes.text: A single ripe banana in a box speeds the ripening of all the others — ethylene gas at work.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Ethylene
steps.body: Gaseous hormone synthesised from methionine → SAM → ACC (ACC synthase) → ethylene (ACC oxidase). Effects: fruit ripening of climacteric fruits (banana, mango, tomato — burst of respiration), triple response in etiolated pea seedlings (reduced elongation, swelling, horizontal growth), leaf and flower abscission, epinasty, flowering in pineapple. Ethephon releases ethylene commercially.

steps.title: Abscisic acid
steps.body: Stress hormone (Addicott; Wareing named dormin). Effects: stomatal closure under water stress, induction and maintenance of seed and bud dormancy, inhibition of germination, promotes storage protein synthesis, antagonises GA.

steps.title: Seed dormancy
steps.body: Causes: hard impermeable seed coat, immature embryo, inhibitors (ABA, phenolics), light requirement. Breaking: scarification (mechanical/acid), stratification (moist chilling), GA treatment, removal of inhibitors by leaching, light (phytochrome).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Non-climacteric fruits (grapes, citrus) do not show the ethylene-linked respiratory burst. ABA promotes, not breaks, dormancy.

scenes.text: Garner and Allard (1920) noticed a tobacco variety that flowered only as days shortened in winter.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Phytochrome
steps.body: Blue-green chromoprotein existing as Pr (absorbs red, 660 nm) and Pfr (absorbs far-red, 730 nm). Red converts Pr → Pfr (active); far-red reverses. Discovered via lettuce seed germination (Borthwick and Hendricks): last exposure decides — R promotes, FR inhibits.

steps.title: Photoperiodism
steps.body: Short-day plants flower when night exceeds a critical length (tobacco Maryland Mammoth, Xanthium, soybean, chrysanthemum); long-day plants when night is shorter than critical (wheat, spinach, radish, Hyoscyamus); day-neutral (tomato, sunflower, cucumber). Critical factor is the uninterrupted dark period — a flash of red light during the night prevents flowering of SDP. Stimulus perceived by leaves; florigen (now identified with FT protein) moves through phloem to the apex (Chailakhyan's grafting experiments).

steps.title: Vernalisation and movements
steps.body: Vernalisation: cold treatment (about 0–10 °C for weeks) of seeds/young plants to induce flowering in winter annuals and biennials (winter wheat, cabbage, sugar beet); perceived by the shoot apex; devernalisation by high temperature. Movements: tropisms (photo-, geo-, thigmo-), nastic movements (seismonasty in Mimosa pudica by pulvinus turgor change, nyctinasty).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Short-day plants are really long-night plants. Leaves perceive photoperiod; shoot apex perceives vernalisation.

courses.summary: Formula sheet for plant physiology and biochemistry, standard experiments (osmotic potential by plasmolysis, pigment chromatography, transpiration, RQ) and previous-year-style questions.

scenes.text: Every numerical in this subject uses fewer than ten formulas — learn them cold.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp (+ Ψm). Ψs = −iCRT (R = 0.00831 L MPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). RQ = CO₂ evolved ÷ O₂ absorbed. Calvin: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂; C4: 5 ATP + 2 NADPH. Quantum requirement ≈ 8 photons per O₂. Nitrogenase: N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂. Michaelis–Menten: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Stomatal index = S/(S+E) × 100.

steps.title: Key numbers
steps.body: Glucose: classical 38 ATP (36 in eukaryotes), modern ~30–32. RQ: carbohydrate 1, fat ≈ 0.7, protein ≈ 0.8–0.9, oxalic acid 4. Chlorophyll a peaks ≈ 430 and 662 nm. P680, P700. Pr 660 nm, Pfr 730 nm.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: In numericals write formula → substitution with units → answer with unit and sign. Examiners award marks for each step.

lessons.title: Lab: Osmotic potential by incipient plasmolysis

scenes.text: Purple Rhoeo epidermal cells make plasmolysis easy to see as the coloured protoplast pulls away.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Prepare sucrose solutions 0.1–0.8 M. Place Rhoeo (Tradescantia) leaf peels in each for 20–30 min. Mount in the same solution; count plasmolysed and total cells in a field. Plot % plasmolysis vs concentration; the concentration giving 50% plasmolysis is taken as incipient plasmolysis, where Ψp = 0 and cell Ψs = Ψs of solution.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why 50%? Cells differ slightly; the mean cell is at incipient plasmolysis. Why sucrose? It does not easily cross membranes. Why Rhoeo? Coloured vacuolar sap (anthocyanin) shows the protoplast clearly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mount peels in the same solution, not water, otherwise deplasmolysis occurs during observation.

activity.prompt: 50% plasmolysis occurs at 0.35 M sucrose at 27 °C (T = 300 K). Calculate the cell's osmotic (solute) potential in MPa (2 decimals, negative).

quiz.q: At incipient plasmolysis
quiz.why: The protoplast just leaves the wall, so turgor is zero.

quiz.q: Rhoeo is chosen because
quiz.why: Anthocyanin in the vacuole makes plasmolysis easy to see.

quiz.q: Peels are mounted in
quiz.why: Water would reverse plasmolysis before observation.

quiz.q: Percentage plasmolysis considered incipient
quiz.why: The average cell is at the point of plasmolysis when half are plasmolysed.

lessons.title: Lab: Paper chromatography of chloroplast pigments

scenes.text: Spinach extract spotted on Whatman paper separates into yellow, yellow-orange, blue-green and yellow-green bands.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Grind spinach leaves in 80% acetone, filter. Spot repeatedly on a line 2 cm from the bottom of Whatman No. 1 strip, drying between spots. Develop in a closed jar with solvent (petroleum ether : acetone, 9:1). Remove when solvent front nears top; mark front. Order from top: carotene (orange-yellow), xanthophyll (yellow), chlorophyll a (blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green).

steps.title: Worked example: Rf
steps.body: Solvent front 12.0 cm; carotene 11.4 cm → Rf 0.95; xanthophyll 8.4 cm → 0.70; chlorophyll a 6.0 cm → 0.50; chlorophyll b 4.8 cm → 0.40 (values depend on solvent; order matters).

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why closed jar? To saturate the atmosphere with solvent. Why spot line above solvent level? So pigment does not dissolve into the solvent pool. Why does carotene move farthest? It is the least polar and most soluble in the non-polar solvent.

activity.prompt: Solvent front moved 10 cm; xanthophyll band moved 7.2 cm. Calculate the Rf value.

quiz.q: Pigment moving farthest in non-polar solvent
quiz.why: Carotene is least polar and travels with the solvent front.

quiz.q: Chlorophyll b colour
quiz.why: Chlorophyll b appears yellow-green; chlorophyll a blue-green.

quiz.q: Rf if pigment 3 cm and solvent 12 cm
Jar is kept closed to
quiz.why: A saturated chamber gives even solvent movement and sharp bands.

lessons.title: Lab: Transpiration and RQ; previous-year-style questions

scenes.text: In Ganong's potometer, an air bubble creeps along the capillary as the twig drinks.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Ganong's potometer
steps.body: Cut a leafy twig under water, fix airtight, introduce an air bubble; time its movement over a fixed distance under different conditions (light, fan, humidity). It measures water absorption, which approximates transpiration. Rate = volume moved per unit time (bubble distance × capillary cross-section).

steps.title: Ganong's respiroscope (RQ)
steps.body: Germinating seeds in bulb, KOH tube to absorb CO₂, mercury/water level changes. If level unchanged with carbohydrate substrate → RQ 1; with oilseeds (castor) level rises (O₂ consumed > CO₂) → RQ < 1.

steps.title: Long answers
steps.body: 1) Cohesion–tension theory. 2) Mechanism of stomatal movement. 3) Z-scheme and photophosphorylation. 4) C4 pathway with Kranz anatomy. 5) Krebs cycle and ATP accounting. 6) Biological nitrogen fixation. 7) Phytochrome and photoperiodism. 8) Michaelis–Menten kinetics and inhibition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Cut the twig under water — an air embolism in xylem stops uptake. The potometer measures absorption, not true transpiration.

activity.prompt: A potometer bubble moves 6 cm in 3 minutes; the capillary cross-section is 0.02 cm². Rate of water uptake in cm³ per minute?

quiz.q: Ganong's potometer actually measures
quiz.why: Bubble movement reflects uptake, which approximates transpiration loss.

quiz.q: Twig is cut under water to

uni-bsc-chem-analytical-spectroscopy.title: Analytical Chemistry & Spectroscopy — Data, UV-Vis, IR, NMR, MS
uni-bsc-chem-analytical-spectroscopy.description: Errors and statistics of analytical data, electromagnetic radiation and the Beer–Lambert law, UV-Visible, infrared, ¹H/¹³C NMR and mass spectrometry, combined structure elucidation, and standard instrumental practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Analytical data, radiation and the Beer–Lambert law
courses.summary: Types of error, accuracy and precision, mean, standard deviation, Q-test and significant figures; the electromagnetic spectrum and energy of radiation; the Beer–Lambert law, its deviations and its use in colorimetry; and the components of a spectrophotometer.
outcomes: Classify errors and compute mean, standard deviation and RSD
Apply the Q-test to reject an outlier
Convert between wavelength, frequency, wavenumber and energy
Use A = εbc and %T in quantitative analysis
Describe sources, monochromators, cells and detectors of a spectrophotometer

scenes.text: Nisha's five burette readings differ by a few hundredths of a millilitre. Which value should she report?
Statistics turns scattered readings into a mean with an honest uncertainty.

steps.title: Types of error
steps.body:
- **Determinate (systematic)** errors have a definite cause and direction: instrumental (uncalibrated pipette), method (indicator end point ≠ equivalence point), personal (parallax). They affect **accuracy** and can be corrected (calibration, blanks, standards).
- **Indeterminate (random)** errors fluctuate either way; they affect **precision** and follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution.
- **Accuracy**: closeness to the true value (absolute error = x − μ; relative error = (x − μ)/μ).
- **Precision**: closeness of repeated results to each other.

steps.title: Statistics
steps.body:
- Mean x̄ = Σxᵢ/n
- Standard deviation **s = √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1)]**
- Relative standard deviation RSD = (s/x̄) × 100%
- **Q-test** for an outlier: Q = |suspect − nearest|/range; reject if Q > Q_crit (90%: n = 3: 0.94; 4: 0.76; 5: 0.64; 6: 0.56).
- Significant figures: in multiplication/division keep the fewest significant figures; in addition/subtraction keep the fewest decimal places.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by n instead of n − 1 for a sample standard deviation.
- Thinking high precision guarantees accuracy (a systematic error can shift all results).
- Rejecting a reading just because it 'looks wrong' without a test.

activity.prompt: Match each error source to its type.
pairs: Small random fluctuations in balance readings

quiz.q: Precision describes:
quiz.why: Precision is about reproducibility — how close replicate results are to each other, regardless of the true value.

quiz.q: Standard deviation of 2.0, 4.0, 6.0:
quiz.why: Mean = 4.0; squared deviations sum to 8; s = √(8/2) = 2.0.

quiz.q: Q for data 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 6.0 (suspect 6.0):
Systematic errors can be detected by:
options: Analysing a certified standard or blank
quiz.why: Repeating only reduces random error; comparing with a known standard reveals a consistent bias.

scenes.text: A prism splits sunlight into colours, but visible light is a tiny slice of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Each slice excites a different molecular motion — electrons, vibrations, nuclear spins.

steps.title: Wave and particle relations
steps.body:
- c = λν (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
- Wavenumber ν̄ = 1/λ (cm⁻¹)
- **E = hν = hc/λ = hc ν̄**, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
- Molar energy = E × N_A

Shorter λ means higher energy.

steps.title: Regions and what they probe
steps.body:
- X-ray (0.01–10 nm): inner-shell electrons, crystal structure
- UV (200–400 nm) and visible (400–800 nm): valence electronic transitions
- IR (2.5–25 µm, 4000–400 cm⁻¹): molecular vibrations
- Microwave: rotations (and ESR in a magnetic field)
- Radiofrequency: nuclear spin transitions (NMR)

Energy order: electronic > vibrational > rotational > nuclear spin.

steps.title: Solved: energy of a 500 nm photon
Solved: IR wavenumber to wavelength
steps.body:
A C=O stretch at 1715 cm⁻¹:
- λ = 1/1715 cm = 5.83 × 10⁻⁴ cm = **5.83 µm**
- E = hc ν̄ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10¹⁰ cm s⁻¹ × 1715 = 3.41 × 10⁻²⁰ J → **20.5 kJ mol⁻¹** (much smaller than electronic energies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing c in m s⁻¹ with ν̄ in cm⁻¹ (use c = 3.00 × 10¹⁰ cm s⁻¹).
- Forgetting nm → m conversion (× 10⁻⁹).
- Saying wavenumber is inversely proportional to energy — it is directly proportional.

activity.prompt: Match each region to the molecular process it excites.

quiz.why: E = hc ν̄, so energy rises linearly with wavenumber (and inversely with wavelength).

quiz.q: Wavenumber of 250 nm radiation:
Which transitions need the least energy?
quiz.why: Nuclear spin levels in a magnetic field are separated by radiofrequency energies, the smallest of these.

scenes.text: A municipal lab adds 1,10-phenanthroline to a water sample, and an orange-red colour develops.
The deeper the colour, the more iron. The Beer–Lambert law turns colour into concentration.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
- Transmittance T = I/I₀; %T = 100T
- **Absorbance A = −log T = log(I₀/I) = εbc**
- ε = molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), b = path length (cm), c = mol L⁻¹
- For mixtures, absorbances add: A = Σεᵢbcᵢ.
- Measure at **λ_max** for maximum sensitivity and minimum error from small λ shifts; best accuracy for A ≈ 0.2–0.8.

steps.title: Deviations
steps.body:
- **Real**: at high concentration (> ~0.01 M), solute interactions and refractive-index change.
- **Chemical**: association, dissociation or reaction with solvent (e.g. Cr₂O₇²⁻ ⇌ CrO₄²⁻ with pH).
- **Instrumental**: polychromatic light, stray light, mismatched cells.

Always use a calibration curve of standards rather than relying on one standard.

steps.title: Solved: calibration curve
steps.body:
Fe–phenanthroline standards (ppm Fe, A at 510 nm): 1.0 → 0.198; 2.0 → 0.395; 3.0 → 0.594; 4.0 → 0.790. Slope ≈ 0.198 A per ppm.

Sample A = 0.475 → c = 0.475/0.198 = **2.40 ppm Fe**. (Limit in Indian drinking-water guidelines is often cited as 0.3 mg/L acceptable, so the sample is high.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using %T in A = εbc instead of A.
- Forgetting the blank (reagents + solvent) to set A = 0.
- Measuring off-peak, where small wavelength errors give large absorbance errors.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a colorimetric determination.
items: Prepare a series of standard solutions and a blank
Develop the colour with the complexing reagent
Find λ_max from the spectrum of one standard
Zero the instrument with the blank at λ_max
Measure absorbance of standards and plot the calibration curve
Measure the sample and read its concentration

quiz.why: A = εbc is directly proportional to b.

quiz.q: Molar absorptivity units:
quiz.why: ε = A/(bc) and A is dimensionless, so ε has units L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: Measurements are made at λ_max because:
options: Sensitivity is highest and absorbance changes least with small λ errors
quiz.why: At the peak dA/dλ ≈ 0 and ε is largest, giving maximum sensitivity and robustness.

scenes.text: The UV-Vis spectrophotometer in the department looks like a simple box with a lid.
Inside: a lamp, a grating, a sample cell and a detector, each chosen for a reason.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Sources**: deuterium (D₂) lamp for UV (190–350 nm); tungsten-halogen for visible/near-IR (350–2500 nm). IR uses a Nernst glower or globar.
- **Wavelength selector**: filters (colorimeter) or monochromator with a diffraction grating or prism.
- **Cells (cuvettes)**: quartz/fused silica for UV; glass or plastic only in the visible; NaCl/KBr windows for IR.
- **Detectors**: phototube, photomultiplier tube (PMT, very sensitive), photodiode array (whole spectrum at once). IR: thermocouple, DTGS, MCT.

steps.title: Single vs double beam
steps.body:
- Single beam: blank and sample measured one after the other; source drift causes error.
- **Double beam**: a chopper alternates the beam between reference and sample cells; the ratio compensates for lamp fluctuations — preferred for scanning spectra.
- FT-IR uses a Michelson interferometer and Fourier transform (all wavelengths simultaneously; faster, better signal-to-noise).

steps.title: Solved: choosing the setup
steps.body:
1. Measuring benzene at 254 nm → D₂ lamp + **quartz cuvette** (glass absorbs below ~340 nm).
2. KMnO₄ at 525 nm → tungsten lamp; glass or plastic cuvette is fine.
3. Recording a full UV spectrum of a drug quickly → **photodiode array** instrument.
4. Solvent for 210 nm work → water, acetonitrile or hexane (low UV cut-off); not acetone (cut-off ≈ 330 nm).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using plastic or glass cuvettes for UV measurements.
- Handling cuvettes on the optical faces (fingerprints absorb and scatter).
- Choosing a solvent whose UV cut-off is above the analysis wavelength.

quiz.why: The interferometer collects every wavelength at once (multiplex advantage), so spectra are faster and less noisy.

questions.why: Systematic errors shift results consistently away from the true value, reducing accuracy.

questions.why: Leading zeros are not significant; 4, 0, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal are, giving 4.

courses.title: Unit 2 · UV-Visible spectroscopy
courses.summary: Electronic transitions, chromophores and auxochromes, bathochromic and hypsochromic shifts, solvent effects, the Woodward–Fieser rules for dienes and enones, and applications in structure determination and quantitative assay.
outcomes: Identify σ→σ*, n→σ*, π→π* and n→π* transitions and their typical λ and ε
Explain spectral shifts caused by conjugation, auxochromes and solvent
Calculate λ_max of dienes and enones by Woodward–Fieser rules
Use UV data to distinguish isomers and follow conjugation
Assay a drug by UV absorbance using A(1%, 1 cm)

scenes.text: β-carotene has eleven conjugated C=C bonds and absorbs blue light near 450 nm, so we see orange.
Ethene, with a single C=C, absorbs only in the far UV at about 171 nm. Conjugation shifts absorption to longer wavelength.

steps.title: Types of transitions
steps.body:
Energy order: σ→σ* > n→σ* > π→π* > n→π*.

- **σ→σ***: alkanes, < 150 nm (vacuum UV)
- **n→σ***: alcohols, amines, halides, ~175–220 nm (CH₃OH ≈ 183 nm)
- **π→π***: alkenes, aromatics; strong (ε ≈ 10³–10⁵); ethene 171 nm, buta-1,3-diene 217 nm
- **n→π***: C=O, N=O; weak, symmetry-forbidden (ε ≈ 10–100); acetone ≈ 280 nm

**Chromophore**: group responsible for absorption (C=C, C=O, N=N, NO₂). **Auxochrome**: group with lone pairs (–OH, –NH₂, –OR) that extends conjugation and shifts λ_max to longer wavelength.

steps.title: Shifts
steps.body:
- **Bathochromic (red) shift**: to longer λ (more conjugation, auxochromes)
- **Hypsochromic (blue) shift**: to shorter λ
- **Hyperchromic**: ε increases; **hypochromic**: ε decreases
- **Solvent effect**: polar solvents shift n→π* to shorter λ (lone pair stabilised by H-bonding) and π→π* slightly to longer λ.
- Example: phenol 270 nm → phenoxide 287 nm (bathochromic, hyperchromic) in base; aniline 280 nm → anilinium 254 nm (lone pair lost, hypsochromic) in acid.

steps.title: Solved: assigning bands
steps.body: Acetone in hexane: strong band 188 nm (π→π*, ε ≈ 900) and weak band 279 nm (n→π*, ε ≈ 15). In water the weak band moves to ~265 nm — a hypsochromic shift because H-bonding lowers the n orbital.

steps.title: Solved: effect of conjugation
steps.body: λ_max of π→π*: ethene 171 nm; buta-1,3-diene 217 nm; hexa-1,3,5-triene 258 nm; β-carotene ≈ 450 nm. Each added conjugated C=C narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap, moving absorption toward and eventually into the visible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling n→π* the strongest band — it is the weakest.
- Mixing up bathochromic (wavelength) with hyperchromic (intensity).
- Using acetone or benzene as solvent for work below ~280 nm.

activity.prompt: Match each transition with a typical example.

quiz.q: The weakest UV band of a ketone is due to:
quiz.why: The n→π* transition is symmetry-forbidden, so its molar absorptivity is very low (10–100).

quiz.q: Adding NaOH to phenol causes:
quiz.why: Phenoxide's extra lone-pair density extends conjugation, moving λ_max to longer wavelength with higher intensity.

quiz.q: An auxochrome is a group that:
options: Has lone pairs and modifies a chromophore's absorption
Absorbs on its own in the visible
quiz.why: Groups like –OH and –NH₂ do not absorb strongly alone but extend conjugation with a chromophore, shifting λ_max.

quiz.q: In polar solvents the n→π* band of acetone shifts to:
quiz.why: Hydrogen bonding stabilises the non-bonding electrons, widening the gap to π*, so absorption moves to shorter λ.

scenes.text: In the 1940s Woodward noticed that λ_max of conjugated dienes followed simple additive rules.
With a few increments you can predict λ_max within about 5 nm — useful for choosing between candidate structures.

steps.title: Diene rules (hexane/ethanol)
steps.body:
Base values:
- Acyclic or **heteroannular** diene (double bonds in different rings): **214 nm**
- **Homoannular** diene (both C=C in one ring): **253 nm**

Increments:
- Each alkyl substituent or ring residue on the diene: **+5**
- Each **exocyclic** C=C (to any ring): **+5**
- Each extra conjugated C=C: **+30**
- –OR +6, –SR +30, –Cl/–Br +5, –NR₂ +60, –OCOR 0

steps.title: Solved: simple dienes
steps.body:
1. **2,3-dimethylbuta-1,3-diene**: base 214 + 2 alkyl (10) = **224 nm** (obs. 226)
2. **Penta-1,3-diene**: 214 + 1 alkyl (5) = **219 nm** (obs. 223)
3. **Cyclohexa-1,3-diene** (homoannular): 253 + 2 ring residues (10) = **263 nm** (obs. 256)

steps.title: Solved: a steroidal heteroannular diene
steps.body:
A heteroannular diene with 3 ring residues and 1 exocyclic C=C (typical of cholesta-3,5-diene):

- Base 214
- 3 ring residues: +15
- 1 exocyclic double bond: +5
- **Calculated 234 nm** (observed ≈ 235 nm)

steps.title: How to count
steps.body: Draw the diene (four carbons). Count every carbon attached to those four atoms that is not part of the diene itself — each is an alkyl substituent or ring residue. An exocyclic C=C is a ring double bond with one carbon outside that particular ring; one C=C can be exocyclic to two rings (count twice).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the homoannular base when the double bonds are in different rings.
- Counting carbons of the diene itself as substituents.
- Applying diene rules to α,β-unsaturated ketones (separate rules).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to calculate λ_max of a diene.
items: Decide homoannular (253) or heteroannular/acyclic (214) base value
Add 5 nm for each alkyl substituent or ring residue
Add 5 nm for each exocyclic double bond
Add 30 nm for each extended conjugated C=C and any polar group increments

quiz.q: Base value for a homoannular diene:
quiz.why: Both double bonds in one ring are held cisoid, which gives a higher base value of 253 nm.

quiz.q: λ_max of 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene (isoprene) by Woodward–Fieser:
quiz.why: Acyclic base 214 + one methyl substituent (5) = 219 nm (observed ≈ 220 nm).

quiz.q: Increment for each extra conjugated double bond:
quiz.why: Extending conjugation by one C=C adds 30 nm in the Woodward–Fieser scheme.

quiz.q: A homoannular diene with 3 ring residues and 2 exocyclic C=C bonds has calculated λ_max:
quiz.why: 253 + 3 × 5 (ring residues) + 2 × 5 (exocyclic bonds) = 253 + 15 + 10 = 278 nm.

lessons.title: Woodward–Fieser rules for enones and applications

scenes.text: A student has two isomeric unsaturated ketones and only a UV spectrometer.
The conjugated enone absorbs strongly near 230–240 nm; the non-conjugated one does not.

steps.title: Enone rules (ethanol)
steps.body:
Base: acyclic or six-membered ring α,β-unsaturated ketone **215 nm**; five-membered ring ketone **202 nm**; aldehyde **210 nm**; acid/ester **195 nm**.

Increments:
- Alkyl or ring residue at **α +10**, **β +12**, **γ and beyond +18**
- Exocyclic C=C **+5**; homoannular diene component **+39**
- Extended conjugation **+30**
- α-OH +35, β-OR +30, α-Br +25

steps.title: Solved: enones
steps.body:
1. **Mesityl oxide** (CH₃)₂C=CH–CO–CH₃: 215 + 2 β-alkyl (2 × 12) = **239 nm** (obs. ≈ 236)
2. **Cyclohex-2-enone**: 215 + 1 β ring residue (12) = **227 nm** (obs. ≈ 225)
3. **3-Methylcyclohex-2-enone**: 215 + 2 β substituents (24) = **239 nm**
4. **2-Methylcyclopent-2-enone**: 202 + α-methyl (10) + β ring residue (12) = **224 nm**

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- **Detecting conjugation**: but-3-en-2-one shows a strong band (~219 nm), the non-conjugated pent-4-en-2-one only weak n→π*.
- **Geometric isomers**: trans-stilbene λ_max ≈ 295 nm (ε ≈ 27 000); cis-stilbene ≈ 280 nm (ε ≈ 10 500) — steric twisting reduces conjugation.
- **Keto–enol tautomerism**: ethyl acetoacetate enol shows a strong band absent in the keto form; the ratio depends on solvent.
- **Quantitative assay**: drugs, vitamins, metal complexes; kinetic studies by following A vs time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the carbonyl's own alkyl group (on C=O) as an α-substituent — it is not on the C=C.
- Using 215 for a cyclopentenone (base is 202).
- Forgetting that rules work only for π→π* bands, not n→π*.

activity.prompt: Match each enone position or feature to its increment.

quiz.q: Calculated λ_max of pent-3-en-2-one CH₃CH=CHCOCH₃:
quiz.why: Base 215 + one β-methyl (12) = 227 nm (observed ≈ 224 nm).

quiz.q: trans-Stilbene absorbs at longer λ than cis-stilbene because:
options: It is planar, allowing better conjugation
quiz.why: In the cis isomer the phenyl rings clash and twist out of plane, reducing π overlap and shifting absorption to shorter λ.

quiz.q: Base value for a cyclopentenone:
quiz.why: Five-membered ring enones have a lower base value of 202 nm in Woodward's rules.

quiz.q: Calculated λ_max of 2,3-dimethylcyclohex-2-enone:
quiz.why: 215 + α-methyl (10) + β substituents: methyl (12) and ring residue (12) = 215 + 10 + 24 = 249 nm.

lessons.title: Lab: UV assay of paracetamol tablets

story.title: Does the tablet contain what the label says?

scenes.text: A quality-control analyst at a pharma unit receives a batch of 500 mg paracetamol tablets.
A UV absorbance reading tells her, within minutes, whether the content is within limits.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Paracetamol in dilute NaOH absorbs at **λ_max ≈ 257 nm**; in 0.1 M HCl or water/methanol near **249 nm**. Pharmacopoeial assays use a specific absorbance **A(1%, 1 cm)** — the absorbance of a 1 g/100 mL solution in a 1 cm cell. A commonly used value for paracetamol in 0.1 M NaOH at 257 nm is 715.

c (g/100 mL) = A/A(1%, 1 cm).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Weigh and powder 20 tablets; find the average tablet weight.
2. Weigh powder equivalent to 100 mg paracetamol; dissolve in 0.1 M NaOH, make up to 100 mL; filter.
3. Dilute 1.0 mL of filtrate to 100 mL with 0.1 M NaOH (expected 10 µg/mL).
4. Measure A at 257 nm against a 0.1 M NaOH blank in a quartz cell.
5. Calculate content and compare with the label (e.g. 95–105%).

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why NaOH medium? — Gives a stable phenoxide band and dissolves the drug well.
- Why dilute so much? — To bring A into the linear, accurate range (0.2–0.8).
- Why a quartz cell? — Glass absorbs at 257 nm.
- What is A(1%, 1 cm)? — Specific absorbance; ε = A(1%, 1 cm) × M/10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the dilution factor in the final calculation.
- Using a blank different from the solvent used for the sample.
- Not filtering, so insoluble excipients scatter light and raise A.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the tablet assay.
items: Weigh powder equivalent to 100 mg drug and dissolve in 0.1 M NaOH
Make up to 100 mL and filter
Dilute 1 mL of filtrate to 100 mL
Measure absorbance at 257 nm against the blank

quiz.q: If A = 0.680 in the same assay, content is:
quiz.why: c = 0.680/715 = 9.51 µg/mL, which is 95.1% of the expected 10.0 µg/mL.

quiz.q: ε of paracetamol (M = 151.2) from A(1%, 1 cm) = 715:
The sample is diluted so that absorbance is about:
quiz.why: Photometric error is smallest at moderate absorbance; very high or very low A gives poor accuracy.

questions.q: Highest-energy transition:
questions.why: σ→σ* involves the most strongly bound bonding electrons and the highest antibonding orbital, so it needs the most energy.

questions.q: A hypsochromic shift is a shift to:
questions.why: Hypsochromic means blue shift — absorption moves to shorter wavelength.

questions.q: Aniline in acid shows a blue shift because:
options: N lone pair is protonated and no longer conjugated with the ring

questions.why: Being symmetry-forbidden, n→π* bands are weak with ε usually below 100.

questions.q: Colour of a compound absorbing at 450 nm (blue):
questions.why: We see the complementary colour of the absorbed light; blue absorption appears orange-yellow.

questions.q: Solvent suitable for UV work at 210 nm:
questions.why: Acetonitrile is transparent down to about 190 nm; acetone, benzene and chloroform absorb above 240 nm.

questions.q: β-Carotene is coloured because:

questions.why: In both diene and enone Woodward–Fieser rules each exocyclic C=C adds 5 nm.

Hyperchromic effect is an increase in:
questions.why: Hyperchromic refers to greater absorption intensity, not a wavelength change.
