uni-bsc-chem-inorganic-1.description: Atomic structure and quantum mechanics basics, periodic properties, ionic and covalent bonding (VSEPR, VBT, MOT), weak forces and metallic bonding, plus revision and lab practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Atomic structure
courses.summary: From Bohr's model and the hydrogen spectrum to de Broglie waves, the uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, quantum numbers, orbital shapes and nodes, and electronic configurations with Slater's rules.
outcomes: Calculate energies, radii and wavelengths for hydrogen-like species using Bohr's model and the Rydberg equation
Apply de Broglie and Heisenberg relations to particles of different mass
State the meaning of ψ and ψ², and count radial and angular nodes
Write ground-state configurations including Cr/Cu exceptions and ions
Compute effective nuclear charge with Slater's rules

lessons.title: Bohr's model and the hydrogen spectrum

story.title: The red line in a discharge tube

scenes.text: Aditi looks at a hydrogen discharge tube through a hand spectroscope and sees sharp coloured lines instead of a rainbow.
Her teacher says the red line at 656 nm can be calculated with one formula — and that is where quantum chemistry began.

steps.title: Bohr's postulates
steps.body:
1. Electrons move in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) without radiating.
2. Angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh/2π (n = 1, 2, 3…).
3. Energy is absorbed or emitted only when an electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = hν.

Results for a hydrogen-like species (nuclear charge Z):
- Radius: rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å
- Energy: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ Z²/n² J
- Velocity: vₙ = 2.18 × 10⁶ Z/n m s⁻¹

steps.title: Spectral series
steps.body:
Rydberg equation: 1/λ = R_H Z² (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

- Lyman (n₁ = 1): ultraviolet
- Balmer (n₁ = 2): visible
- Paschen (n₁ = 3), Brackett (4), Pfund (5): infrared

Number of lines when electrons fall from level n to the ground state (many atoms): n(n − 1)/2.

steps.title: Solved: radius and ionisation energy of He⁺
steps.body:
- r₂ for He⁺ (Z = 2): 0.529 × 2²/2 = **1.058 Å**
- Ionisation energy of He⁺ from n = 1: 13.6 × 2² = **54.4 eV**
- Lines from n = 5 to ground state: 5 × 4/2 = **10 lines**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting Z² for He⁺, Li²⁺ (Bohr applies only to one-electron species).
- Putting the larger n as n₁ — n₁ is always the lower level.
- Mixing eV and J: 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
- Claiming Bohr's model explains multi-electron spectra or the Zeeman effect — it does not.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body: Bohr's model fails for multi-electron atoms, cannot explain fine structure or relative line intensities, and violates the uncertainty principle by giving exact orbits.

activity.prompt: Match each hydrogen spectral series to its lower level and region.

quiz.q: Energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of H:
quiz.why: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so for n = 2 the energy is −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV.

quiz.q: Which series lies in the visible region?
quiz.why: Balmer lines end at n = 2, and their wavelengths fall between about 365 and 656 nm, mostly visible light.

quiz.q: Radius of the first Bohr orbit of Li²⁺ (Z = 3):
quiz.why: rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å, so r₁ = 0.529/3 = 0.176 Å because a larger nuclear charge pulls the electron closer.

quiz.q: Maximum spectral lines when electrons fall from n = 4 to n = 1:
quiz.why: The number of possible lines is n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.

lessons.title: Wave–particle duality and the uncertainty principle

story.title: Why a cricket ball doesn't diffract

scenes.text: Rohan asks: if electrons are waves, why don't cricket balls bend around the stumps?
A quick de Broglie calculation shows the ball's wavelength is about 10⁻³⁴ m — far too small to notice.

steps.title: de Broglie relation
steps.body:
Every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/mv = h/p (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).

For an electron accelerated through V volts: λ = h/√(2meV), which simplifies to λ ≈ 1.226/√V nm.

Experimental proof: Davisson–Germer electron diffraction from a nickel crystal (1927). Bohr's quantisation follows if a whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit: 2πr = nλ.

steps.title: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
steps.body:
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly at the same time:

Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π (= 5.27 × 10⁻³⁵ J s)

Also ΔE · Δt ≥ h/4π. Consequence: exact electron orbits are meaningless; we use probability (orbitals) instead.

steps.title: Solved: de Broglie wavelengths
steps.body:
- Ball, m = 0.1 kg, v = 10 m s⁻¹: λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.1 × 10) = **6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ m** (undetectable)
- Electron accelerated through 100 V: λ = 1.226/√100 = **0.123 nm**, comparable to atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons.

steps.title: Solved: uncertainty in velocity
steps.body:
Electron confined to Δx = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (atom size).
- Δp ≥ 5.27 × 10⁻³⁵/1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 5.27 × 10⁻²⁵ kg m s⁻¹
- Δv = Δp/m = 5.27 × 10⁻²⁵/9.109 × 10⁻³¹ = **5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹**

The uncertainty is comparable to the electron's speed itself — a fixed orbit cannot be defined.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mass in grams instead of kg in λ = h/mv.
- Writing h/2π instead of h/4π in the uncertainty relation (h/4π = ħ/2).
- Thinking uncertainty is due to poor instruments — it is a fundamental property of nature.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to compute the uncertainty in velocity of a confined electron.
items: Substitute h/4π = 5.27 × 10⁻³⁵ J s and Δx in metres
Divide by the electron mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg
Report Δv in m s⁻¹ and compare with typical speeds

quiz.q: de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to:
quiz.why: λ = h/p, so doubling the momentum halves the wavelength.

quiz.q: The experiment that confirmed electron waves:
quiz.why: Davisson and Germer observed diffraction peaks when electrons scattered from a nickel crystal, proving their wave nature.

quiz.q: Wavelength of an electron accelerated through 400 V is about:
Heisenberg's principle makes which idea invalid?
quiz.why: An exact orbit requires knowing position and momentum precisely at once, which the uncertainty principle forbids.

lessons.title: Schrödinger equation, quantum numbers and orbitals

scenes.text: Neha's textbook shows a dumbbell for a 2p orbital, but her professor calls it a 'boundary surface enclosing 90% probability'.
The shapes come from solving one equation — and the integers that appear are the quantum numbers.

steps.title: The Schrödinger wave equation
steps.body:
Time-independent form: Ĥψ = Eψ, or
∂²ψ/∂x² + ∂²ψ/∂y² + ∂²ψ/∂z² + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0

- ψ (wave function) has no direct physical meaning; it can be positive or negative.
- ψ² (Born interpretation) is the probability density of finding the electron.
- Acceptable ψ must be single-valued, finite, continuous and normalised (∫ψ²dτ = 1).
- In spherical polar coordinates ψ(r, θ, φ) = R(r) · Y(θ, φ): the radial part sets size and radial nodes; the angular part sets shape.

steps.title: Quantum numbers
steps.body:
- **n** (1, 2, 3…): shell, energy and size
- **l** (0 … n − 1): subshell/shape (s, p, d, f = 0, 1, 2, 3); orbital angular momentum = √[l(l + 1)] h/2π
- **mₗ** (−l … +l): orientation; 2l + 1 orbitals per subshell
- **mₛ** (±½): spin

Orbitals in shell n = n²; electrons = 2n².

steps.title: Nodes and shapes
steps.body:
- Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l; total = n − 1.
- Radial distribution function 4πr²R² gives the probability of finding the electron at distance r; for 1s H the maximum is at 0.529 Å.
- s: spherical; p: two lobes along an axis with a nodal plane; d: four-lobed (dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y²) and dz² (two lobes + a ring).

steps.title: Solved: nodes
steps.body:
- 3s: radial = 3 − 0 − 1 = **2**, angular = 0
- 4p: radial = 4 − 1 − 1 = **2**, angular = 1
- 3d: radial = **0**, angular = 2
- 5f: radial = 5 − 3 − 1 = **1**, angular = 3

steps.title: Solved: allowed sets
steps.body:
Is (n = 2, l = 2, mₗ = 0) allowed? No — l must be ≤ n − 1 = 1.
Is (n = 3, l = 1, mₗ = −1, mₛ = +½) allowed? Yes — a 3p electron.
Orbital angular momentum of a 3d electron: √[2 × 3] h/2π = **√6 h/2π**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ψ is the probability — ψ² is.
- Confusing the dz² ring with an extra orbital; dz² is one orbital.
- Thinking a node is where the electron 'cannot pass' — it is simply zero probability density at that surface.

activity.prompt: Match each orbital with its radial node count.

quiz.q: Physical significance is attached to:
quiz.why: Born's interpretation says ψ² gives the probability density of finding the electron in a region.

quiz.q: Number of orbitals in the n = 4 shell:
quiz.why: A shell holds n² orbitals, so n = 4 has 16 orbitals (and up to 32 electrons).

quiz.q: Angular nodes in a 4f orbital:
quiz.why: Angular nodes equal l, and l = 3 for f orbitals.

quiz.q: Which set is NOT allowed?
quiz.why: For n = 1, l can only be 0, so l = 1 is forbidden.

scenes.text: Arjun writes Fe²⁺ as [Ar]3d⁴4s² and his answer on magnetism goes wrong.
Once 3d is occupied it lies below 4s in energy, so ions lose 4s electrons first — a point Slater's rules help explain.

steps.title: Filling rules
steps.body:
- **Aufbau**: fill in order of increasing (n + l); for equal (n + l), lower n first: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p…
- **Pauli exclusion**: no two electrons have all four quantum numbers the same → max 2 per orbital.
- **Hund's rule**: in degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy singly with parallel spin first (maximum multiplicity).
- Exceptions: Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ — half-filled and filled subshells are stabilised by exchange energy.

steps.title: Slater's rules for Zeff
steps.body:
Zeff = Z − S. Group as (1s)(2s,2p)(3s,3p)(3d)(4s,4p)(4d)(4f)(5s,5p)…
For an ns/np electron:
- Others in the same group: 0.35 each (0.30 within 1s)
- Electrons in shell n − 1: 0.85 each
- Electrons in n − 2 and lower: 1.00 each
For an nd or nf electron: same group 0.35; everything to the left 1.00.

steps.title: Solved: Zeff of a 2p electron of N
Solved: Zeff of a 4s electron of Zn
steps.body:
Zn (Z = 30): (1s²)(2s²2p⁶)(3s²3p⁶)(3d¹⁰)(4s²)
- Same group: 1 × 0.35 = 0.35
- n − 1 shell (3s, 3p, 3d = 18 electrons): 18 × 0.85 = 15.30
- n − 2 and lower (10 electrons): 10 × 1.00 = 10.00
- S = 25.65 → Zeff = **4.35**

steps.title: Solved: ions and magnetism
steps.body:
- Fe²⁺: [Ar]3d⁶ → 4 unpaired; μ = √[n(n + 2)] = √24 = **4.90 BM**
- Cu²⁺: [Ar]3d⁹ → 1 unpaired; μ = √3 = **1.73 BM**
- Zn²⁺: 3d¹⁰ → diamagnetic

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming cations.
- Using 0.85 for electrons in the same group.
- Applying the 0.85 rule to d/f electrons (they use 1.00 for all inner electrons).

activity.prompt: Order the subshells in the Aufbau filling sequence.

quiz.q: Ground-state configuration of Cu⁺:
quiz.why: Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; removing the 4s electron leaves [Ar]3d¹⁰.

quiz.q: Shielding contribution of each (n − 1)-shell electron when finding Zeff of a 3p electron:
quiz.why: For s and p electrons, each electron in the (n − 1) shell contributes 0.85 to the shielding constant.

quiz.q: Spin-only magnetic moment of Mn²⁺:
quiz.why: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons, so μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM.

quiz.q: Hund's rule concerns:
options: Single occupancy of degenerate orbitals first
quiz.why: Hund's rule states that degenerate orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing, giving maximum multiplicity.

questions.q: Energy of He⁺ in n = 1:
questions.why: Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n², so with Z = 2 and n = 1 the energy is −54.4 eV.

questions.q: Shortest-wavelength line of the Balmer series corresponds to:
questions.why: The largest energy gap within the Balmer series is from n = ∞ to n = 2, which gives the shortest wavelength (series limit, about 365 nm).

questions.q: Wavelength of a 6.6 × 10⁻²⁶ kg particle at 100 m s⁻¹ (h ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s):
Heisenberg's relation for position and momentum is:
questions.why: The product of uncertainties in position and momentum must be at least h/4π.

questions.q: Total nodes in a 4d orbital:
questions.why: Total nodes are n − 1 = 3 (one radial and two angular).

questions.q: Maximum electrons with n = 3 and mₛ = +½:
questions.why: The n = 3 shell has 9 orbitals, and each can hold exactly one electron with spin +½.

questions.q: Orbital angular momentum of a p electron:
questions.why: Orbital angular momentum is √[l(l + 1)] h/2π; with l = 1 this is √2 h/2π.

questions.q: Configuration of Cr³⁺:
questions.why: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; removing the 4s electron and two 3d electrons leaves [Ar]3d³.

questions.q: Zeff for the 3s electron of Na (Z = 11):
questions.why: S = 8 × 0.85 for the n − 1 shell plus 2 × 1.00 for 1s = 8.80, so Zeff = 11 − 8.80 = 2.20.

questions.q: Which statement about ψ is correct?
options: It must be infinite at the nucleus
It must be finite, single-valued and continuous
questions.why: An acceptable wave function must be finite, single-valued and continuous so that ψ² is a sensible probability density.

questions.q: Bohr's model successfully explains the spectrum of:
questions.why: Bohr's model works only for one-electron species such as H, He⁺ and Li²⁺.

questions.q: Spin-only moment 3.87 BM corresponds to how many unpaired electrons?
questions.why: √[n(n + 2)] = 3.87 gives n(n + 2) = 15, so n = 3 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Radial nodes in a 3p orbital:
questions.why: Radial nodes are n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Periodic properties
courses.summary: Trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity (Pauling, Mulliken, Allred–Rochow), with special effects: lanthanide contraction, inert pair effect and diagonal relationships.
outcomes: Explain radius and ionisation enthalpy trends using effective nuclear charge
Account for irregularities such as IE(N) > IE(O) and EA(F) < EA(Cl)
Calculate Pauling electronegativity difference from bond energies
Explain lanthanide contraction, inert pair effect and diagonal relationships with examples

scenes.text: Kavya notices that O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have 10 electrons, yet their radii range from 140 pm down to 72 pm.
The difference is nuclear charge: more protons pull the same electron cloud tighter.

steps.title: Types of radius
steps.body:
- **Covalent radius**: half the internuclear distance in a homonuclear single bond (Cl₂: 198 pm → 99 pm).
- **Metallic radius**: half the distance between neighbouring atoms in a metal crystal.
- **van der Waals radius**: half the distance between non-bonded atoms of neighbouring molecules — always larger than covalent radius.
- **Ionic radius**: from internuclear distances in ionic crystals (e.g. Pauling's method, r ∝ 1/Zeff).

steps.title: Trends
steps.body:
- Across a period: radius decreases because Zeff increases while electrons enter the same shell.
- Down a group: radius increases as new shells are added.
- Cations are smaller than parent atoms; anions are larger.
- Isoelectronic series: radius falls as Z rises: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
- Noble gases are compared using van der Waals radii, so they appear 'large'.

steps.title: Solved: Pauling ionic radii of NaCl? (isoelectronic pair Na⁺/F⁻)
steps.body:
In NaF, r(Na⁺) + r(F⁻) = 231 pm. Both have the neon configuration.
Slater: for a 2p electron in Na⁺, S = 7 × 0.35 + 2 × 0.85 = 4.15 → Zeff = 11 − 4.15 = 6.85; for F⁻, Zeff = 9 − 4.15 = 4.85.
Pauling: r ∝ 1/Zeff → r(Na⁺)/r(F⁻) = 4.85/6.85 = 0.708.
- r(F⁻) = 231/1.708 = **135 pm**
- r(Na⁺) = 231 − 135 = **96 pm**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing a covalent radius with a van der Waals radius across a period.
- Saying Ga is larger than Al — they are nearly equal (Ga ≈ 135 pm, Al ≈ 143 pm) because of poor shielding by the 3d electrons.
- Forgetting that a higher cation charge means a smaller ion: Fe³⁺ < Fe²⁺.

activity.prompt: Arrange the isoelectronic ions from largest to smallest.

quiz.q: Which is the largest?
quiz.why: In an isoelectronic series the species with the lowest nuclear charge is largest, and O²⁻ has only 8 protons for 10 electrons.

quiz.q: van der Waals radius compared to covalent radius is:
quiz.why: van der Waals radii are measured between non-bonded atoms that do not share electrons, so they are always larger than covalent radii.

quiz.q: Al and Ga have similar radii because of:
quiz.why: Ga has ten 3d electrons that shield poorly, so the extra nuclear charge contracts it to roughly the size of Al.

story.title: Why sodium is stored in kerosene

scenes.text: In the lab, sodium sits under kerosene while magnesium ribbon lies in an open box.
Sodium's first ionisation enthalpy is only 496 kJ mol⁻¹ — it gives up its electron to air and water very easily.

steps.title: Definition and factors
steps.body:
First ionisation enthalpy (IE₁): energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from one mole of isolated gaseous atoms: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻.

IE increases with: higher Zeff, smaller size, more penetrating orbital (s > p > d > f), stable half-filled/filled configurations. IE₂ > IE₁ always because the electron is removed from a cation.

steps.title: Trends and irregularities
steps.body:
- Increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Be > B** (899 vs 801 kJ mol⁻¹): B loses a 2p electron, which is higher in energy and shielded by 2s.
- **N > O** (1402 vs 1314): N has a stable half-filled 2p³; O's paired 2p electron suffers repulsion.
- Large jump in successive IE shows a change of shell — used to find group number.

steps.title: Solved: group from successive IEs
steps.body:
An element has IE₁ to IE₄ = 738, 1451, 7733, 10540 kJ mol⁻¹.
- Ratios: IE₂/IE₁ ≈ 2.0; IE₃/IE₂ ≈ 5.3 → large jump after the 2nd electron.
- So it has **2 valence electrons → group 2** (this is Mg).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying IE always increases across a period without noting the B and O dips.
- Confusing IE (always endothermic, positive) with electron gain enthalpy (often negative).
- Treating IE values of atoms in solids — IE refers to gaseous atoms.

activity.prompt: Arrange period 2 elements by increasing first ionisation enthalpy.

quiz.q: Which has higher IE₁?
quiz.why: N has a smaller size than S and Se and a stable half-filled 2p³ subshell, giving it a higher IE₁ than O as well.

quiz.q: A big jump between IE₁ and IE₂ suggests the element is in group:
quiz.why: If the second electron must come from an inner noble-gas shell, the atom had just one valence electron, as in group 1.

quiz.q: IE₁ of B is less than that of Be because:
options: B's 2p electron is higher in energy and shielded by 2s
quiz.why: The 2p electron of boron penetrates less than 2s and is shielded by the 2s pair, so it is easier to remove.

lessons.title: Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity scales

scenes.text: Meera reads that fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and wonders why F is the most electronegative element — yet Cl releases more energy on gaining an electron.
Different scales answer different questions; let's compute one from bond energies.

steps.title: Electron gain enthalpy
steps.body:
ΔegH: enthalpy change for X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). Electron affinity (EA) is the energy released (= −ΔegH).

- Becomes more negative across a period; less negative down a group.
- **Cl (−349) is more negative than F (−328 kJ mol⁻¹)**: the small, crowded 2p shell of F repels the incoming electron.
- Noble gases, Be, Mg and N have positive or near-zero values (stable configurations).
- Second electron gain (O⁻ → O²⁻) is always positive (repulsion).

steps.title: Electronegativity scales
steps.body:
Electronegativity: the tendency of a bonded atom to attract shared electrons.
- **Pauling**: (χA − χB) = 0.102 √Δ, where Δ = D(A–B) − √[D(A–A) × D(B–B)] in kJ mol⁻¹.
- **Mulliken**: χ = (IE + EA)/2 (both in eV).
- **Allred–Rochow**: χ = 0.359 Zeff/r² + 0.744 (r = covalent radius in Å).
F = 4.0 (Pauling) is the highest; Cs/Fr the lowest (≈ 0.7).

steps.title: Solved: Mulliken χ
steps.body: For an element with IE = 13.0 eV and EA = 3.6 eV: χM = (13.0 + 3.6)/2 = **8.3 eV**. (These are roughly chlorine's values; Mulliken values in eV are about 2.8 times Pauling values.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating electronegativity as an isolated-atom energy — it is a property of a bonded atom and has no units on the Pauling scale.
- Using arithmetic instead of geometric mean in the Pauling formula (Pauling used both; the 0.102 factor goes with kJ mol⁻¹ and the geometric mean).
- Saying F has the most negative ΔegH.

activity.prompt: Match each electronegativity scale to its basis.
pairs: Extra bond energy of A–B over the mean of A–A and B–B
Average of ionisation energy and electron affinity
Electrostatic force Zeff/r² at the covalent radius
Electron density compared with an inert-gas atom

quiz.q: Most negative electron gain enthalpy:
quiz.why: Chlorine's larger 3p shell has less electron–electron repulsion than fluorine's compact 2p shell, so Cl releases the most energy.

quiz.q: On the Mulliken scale electronegativity equals:
quiz.why: Mulliken defined electronegativity as the average of ionisation energy and electron affinity.

quiz.q: Δ for H–F (D: H–H 436, F–F 158, H–F 568 kJ mol⁻¹) is about:
Second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is:
quiz.why: Adding an electron to the already negative O⁻ ion must overcome repulsion, so energy is absorbed and the value is positive.

lessons.title: Lanthanide contraction, inert pair effect and diagonal relationship

scenes.text: Zirconium and hafnium are so alike that separating them for nuclear reactors is a major industrial challenge.
The 14 lanthanides squeezed in between shrink Hf to almost exactly the size of Zr.

steps.title: Lanthanide contraction
steps.body:
Steady decrease in size from La to Lu because 4f electrons shield poorly. Consequences:
- Zr (160 pm) ≈ Hf (159 pm); Nb ≈ Ta; Mo ≈ W — 4d and 5d pairs are very similar.
- Basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases from La to Lu.
- 5d metals have higher IE and density than expected; Au and Pt are noble.

steps.title: Inert pair effect
steps.body:
In heavier p-block elements (Tl, Pb, Bi), the ns² pair resists bonding because of poor shielding by d and f electrons and relativistic stabilisation of 6s.
- Tl⁺ more stable than Tl³⁺; Pb²⁺ more stable than Pb⁴⁺ (PbO₂ is a strong oxidant); Bi³⁺ more stable than Bi⁵⁺ (NaBiO₃ oxidises Mn²⁺ to MnO₄⁻).

steps.title: Diagonal relationship
steps.body:
First members of groups 1, 2 and 13 resemble the element diagonally below-right, because size and charge/size ratio (polarising power) are similar.
- **Li–Mg**: both form normal oxides (Li₂O, MgO), nitrides (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂), carbonates decompose on heating, chlorides are deliquescent and soluble in ethanol.
- **Be–Al**: amphoteric oxides/hydroxides, covalent chlorides that act as Lewis acids, passivation by conc. HNO₃.
- **B–Si**: acidic oxides, covalent hydrides, semiconducting/metalloid character.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking lanthanide contraction affects only lanthanides — its biggest effect is on the 5d series.
- Saying the inert pair is 'unreactive' — it is reluctant to be used in bonding, giving lower oxidation states.
- Extending the diagonal relationship beyond period 2–3.

activity.prompt: Match the observation to its cause.
pairs: Zr and Hf have nearly equal radii
PbO₂ is a strong oxidising agent
Li₃N forms on direct reaction with N₂

quiz.q: Lanthanide contraction is due to:
quiz.why: 4f orbitals are diffuse and shield the outer electrons poorly, so the increasing nuclear charge contracts the atoms.

quiz.q: Which pair shows a diagonal relationship?
quiz.why: Li and Mg have similar sizes and polarising power, so lithium chemistry resembles magnesium's.

quiz.q: Most stable oxidation state of bismuth:
quiz.why: Because of the inert pair effect, Bi keeps its 6s² pair and is most stable in the +3 state.

questions.q: Across a period, atomic radius generally:
questions.why: Zeff increases across a period while electrons enter the same shell, so atoms contract.

questions.q: Correct order of size:
questions.why: Removing electrons increases the effective pull on the rest, so each higher positive charge gives a smaller species.

questions.q: IE₁ of N exceeds that of O because:
questions.why: N's half-filled 2p³ is extra stable while O's paired 2p electron is easier to remove due to repulsion.

questions.q: Successive IEs 577, 1817, 2745, 11577 kJ mol⁻¹ indicate group:
questions.why: The large jump comes after the third electron, so the element has three valence electrons (this is Al, group 13).

questions.q: The Pauling factor 0.102 is used when Δ is in:
questions.why: χA − χB = 0.102√Δ applies with Δ in kJ mol⁻¹ (the older form 0.208√Δ uses kcal mol⁻¹).

questions.q: Allred–Rochow electronegativity depends on:
questions.why: Allred and Rochow took electronegativity as proportional to the electrostatic force Zeff e²/r² at the covalent radius.

questions.q: Positive electron gain enthalpy is expected for:
questions.why: Neon's filled shell means an added electron must enter the next shell, so energy is absorbed.

questions.q: Similar properties of Nb and Ta are due to:
questions.why: Lanthanide contraction makes the 5d element Ta almost the same size as the 4d element Nb.

questions.q: Which pair is isoelectronic and has the smaller radius first?
questions.why: Na⁺ and F⁻ both have 10 electrons, and Na⁺ is smaller because it has 11 protons versus 9.

questions.q: Be resembles Al because both:
questions.why: BeO and Al₂O₃ both dissolve in acids and in alkalis, a hallmark of the Be–Al diagonal relationship.

questions.q: Mulliken χ for IE = 17.4 eV and EA = 3.4 eV is:
questions.why: χ = (17.4 + 3.4)/2 = 20.8/2 = 10.4 eV (roughly fluorine's values).

questions.q: Stability of +1 state increases down group 13 because of:
questions.why: Down the group the ns² pair becomes reluctant to bond, so the +1 state (as in Tl⁺) becomes more stable.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Ionic bonding and ionic solids
courses.summary: Ionic bond formation, lattice energy by the Born–Landé and Kapustinskii equations, Born–Haber cycles, radius-ratio rules and common crystal structures, polarisation and Fajans' rules, and solubility of ionic compounds.
outcomes: Calculate lattice energy with the Born–Landé and Kapustinskii equations
Construct a Born–Haber cycle and solve for any unknown term
Predict coordination number and structure from the radius ratio
Use Fajans' rules to compare covalent character, melting points and solubility

story.title: Counting the glue in a salt crystal

scenes.text: Imran wonders why NaCl melts at 801 °C while ice melts at 0 °C.
A pencil-and-paper Born–Landé calculation shows over 750 kJ is needed to pull one mole of NaCl apart into gaseous ions.

steps.title: Born–Landé equation
steps.body:
U = −(N_A · A · z⁺z⁻ · e²)/(4πε₀ r₀) × (1 − 1/n)

- A = Madelung constant (geometry): NaCl 1.748, CsCl 1.763, zinc blende 1.638, fluorite 2.519
- r₀ = shortest cation–anion distance
- n = Born exponent (repulsion), from the ion's electron configuration: He 5, Ne 7, Ar 9, Kr 10, Xe 12 (average for the two ions)
- Useful constant: N_A e²/(4πε₀) = 1.389 × 10⁻⁴ J m mol⁻¹

steps.title: Kapustinskii equation
steps.body:
When the structure (and so A) is unknown:
U = −(1.202 × 10⁵ · ν · |z⁺z⁻|/d) × (1 − 34.5/d) kJ mol⁻¹
where ν = ions per formula unit and d = r⁺ + r⁻ in pm.

steps.title: Solved: Kapustinskii for NaCl
steps.body:
ν = 2, d = 102 + 179 ≈ 281 pm.
- 1.202 × 10⁵ × 2/281 = 855.5
- × (1 − 34.5/281) = × 0.877 → **U ≈ −750 kJ mol⁻¹**
Close to Born–Landé, despite not using a Madelung constant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r₀ in Å or pm in the Born–Landé formula (must be metres with the SI constant).
- Forgetting that doubling both charges multiplies U by four (MgO ≈ −3800 kJ mol⁻¹).
- Mixing sign conventions: lattice formation energy is negative; lattice dissociation enthalpy is positive.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to evaluate the Born–Landé lattice energy.
items: Identify the structure and its Madelung constant A
Find r₀ = r⁺ + r⁻ and convert to metres
Average the Born exponents of the two ions
Multiply 1.389 × 10⁻⁴ J m mol⁻¹ by A z⁺z⁻ and divide by r₀
Multiply by (1 − 1/n) and convert to kJ mol⁻¹

quiz.q: Madelung constant depends on:
quiz.why: The Madelung constant sums the geometric arrangement of all ions in the lattice, so it depends only on the structure type.

quiz.q: Born exponent for a Na⁺/F⁻ pair (both Ne-like):
quiz.why: Ions with the neon configuration have a Born exponent of 7, so the average for NaF is 7.

quiz.q: Largest lattice energy magnitude:
quiz.why: MgO has doubly charged ions and a short interionic distance, giving roughly four times the lattice energy of NaCl.

quiz.q: Kapustinskii's equation is useful because it needs no:
quiz.why: Kapustinskii absorbed the geometric factor into a constant, so the structure and its Madelung constant need not be known.

scenes.text: Pooja asks why magnesium forms MgCl₂ and never MgCl, even though removing one electron costs less energy.
The Born–Haber cycle shows the huge lattice energy of Mg²⁺ salts pays back the second ionisation cost.

steps.title: The cycle
steps.body:
By Hess's law, for MX(s) formed from M(s) and ½X₂(g):
ΔfH = ΔsubH(M) + IE(M) + ½D(X₂) + ΔegH(X) + U

Uses: find U (experimentally inaccessible), find EA, and test whether a hypothetical compound (NeCl, MgCl) is stable.

steps.title: Solved: lattice energy of KCl
steps.body:
Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔsubH(K) = 89, IE(K) = 419, ½D(Cl₂) = 122, ΔegH(Cl) = −349, ΔfH(KCl) = −437.
- Sum of steps before U: 89 + 419 + 122 − 349 = 281
- −437 = 281 + U → **U = −718 kJ mol⁻¹**

steps.title: Solved: finding electron gain enthalpy
steps.body:
For NaBr: ΔfH = −361, ΔsubH(Na) = 108, IE = 496, ½ΔH for Br₂(l) → Br(g) = 112, U = −747 kJ mol⁻¹.
- −361 = 108 + 496 + 112 + ΔegH − 747
- −361 = −31 + ΔegH → **ΔegH(Br) = −330 kJ mol⁻¹** (tabulated ≈ −325)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- For bromine, forgetting vaporisation of liquid Br₂ before dissociation.
- For MX₂ salts, not doubling the halogen atomisation and electron gain terms, and not adding IE₂.
- Sign errors: write every step as formation from elements, then solve.

activity.prompt: Match each Born–Haber step for KCl with its sign.

quiz.q: In a Born–Haber cycle for CaCl₂ the ionisation term is:
quiz.why: Forming Ca²⁺ requires removing two electrons, so both the first and second ionisation enthalpies are added.

quiz.q: The cycle is an application of:
quiz.why: Enthalpy is a state function, so the direct formation enthalpy equals the sum of the stepwise path (Hess's law).

quiz.q: Using ΔfH = −411, steps sum = +376 kJ mol⁻¹, U is:
quiz.why: U = ΔfH − (sum of other steps) = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol⁻¹.

lessons.title: Radius ratio and ionic crystal structures

scenes.text: A fruit seller stacks big oranges and tucks grapes into the gaps — small grapes fit tetrahedral holes, bigger ones need octahedral holes.
Ionic crystals choose their structures the same way: by the ratio r⁺/r⁻.

steps.title: Radius-ratio rules
steps.body:
| r⁺/r⁻ | CN | Geometry | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.155–0.225 | 3 | Trigonal | B₂O₃ |
| 0.225–0.414 | 4 | Tetrahedral | ZnS |
| 0.414–0.732 | 6 | Octahedral | NaCl |
| 0.732–1.0 | 8 | Cubic | CsCl |

A cation must touch its anion neighbours; if it is too small it 'rattles' and a lower CN results.

steps.title: Derivation: octahedral limit 0.414
steps.body:
In a square plane of four anions touching each other around a cation:
- Diagonal of square = 2(r⁺ + r⁻); side = 2r⁻
- Diagonal = √2 × side → r⁺ + r⁻ = √2 r⁻
- r⁺/r⁻ = √2 − 1 = **0.414**
Similarly, the cubic limit is √3 − 1 = **0.732**.

steps.title: Solved: predicting structures
steps.body:
- NaCl: 102/181 = **0.564** → CN 6, rock salt
- CsCl: 167/181 = **0.923** → CN 8, CsCl structure
- ZnS: 74/184 = **0.402** → CN 4, zinc blende/wurtzite
- CaF₂: Ca²⁺ CN 8, F⁻ CN 4 (fluorite); Na₂O adopts the antifluorite structure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating radius-ratio rules as strict laws — many salts (e.g. LiI) deviate because of covalency.
- Dividing r⁻ by r⁺.
- Forgetting that in fluorite the two ions have different coordination numbers (8:4).

activity.prompt: Match the compound to its coordination numbers.

quiz.q: Radius ratio 0.30 suggests:
quiz.why: A ratio of 0.225–0.414 fits a cation in a tetrahedral hole, giving coordination number 4.

quiz.q: Limiting radius ratio for cubic (CN 8):
quiz.why: Geometry of a cube's body diagonal gives r⁺/r⁻ = √3 − 1 = 0.732 as the minimum for eight-fold coordination.

quiz.q: In CsCl each Cs⁺ is surrounded by:
quiz.why: In the CsCl structure the cation sits at the body centre of a cube of eight chloride ions.

scenes.text: In the lab, AgF dissolves easily in water while AgI does not — yet both are 'ionic silver salts'.
Ag⁺ distorts the big iodide cloud, giving AgI significant covalent character.

steps.title: Fajans' rules
steps.body:
Covalent character in an ionic bond increases when:
1. The cation is small and highly charged (high polarising power, ∝ charge/size).
2. The anion is large and highly charged (high polarisability).
3. The cation has an 18-electron (pseudo-noble-gas) or 18+2 shell (Cu⁺, Ag⁺, Zn²⁺, Hg²⁺) rather than a noble-gas shell — d electrons shield poorly.

steps.title: Solved: applying Fajans' rules
steps.body:
- Melting point NaCl (801 °C) > MgCl₂ (714 °C) > AlCl₃ (sublimes ≈ 180 °C): covalency increases as cation charge rises.
- LiF > LiCl > LiBr > LiI in ionic character (anion size rises).
- CuCl is more covalent than NaCl although Cu⁺ (77 pm) and Na⁺ (102 pm) — 18-electron shell.
- Solubility in water: AgF > AgCl > AgBr > AgI; colour deepens (AgI yellow) with covalency.

steps.title: Solubility of ionic compounds
steps.body:
Dissolution: ΔsolH = U(dissociation) + ΣΔhydH. A salt dissolves well when hydration enthalpy compensates lattice energy (and entropy helps).
- Group 2 sulphates: solubility falls down the group (BeSO₄ ≫ BaSO₄) — hydration enthalpy of the cation falls faster than lattice energy, since the large SO₄²⁻ keeps U nearly constant.
- Group 2 hydroxides: solubility rises down the group — lattice energy falls faster with the small OH⁻.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all ionic compounds are water soluble.
- Ignoring the 18-electron rule when comparing Cu⁺/Ag⁺ salts with alkali-metal salts.
- Explaining solubility using lattice energy alone without hydration enthalpy.

activity.prompt: Arrange the chlorides from most ionic to most covalent.

quiz.q: Most covalent halide:
quiz.why: Iodide is the largest and most polarisable anion, so Li⁺ distorts it most, giving LiI the greatest covalent character.

quiz.q: CuCl is more covalent than NaCl because Cu⁺:
quiz.why: The 3d¹⁰ shell of Cu⁺ shields nuclear charge poorly, making it far more polarising than the noble-gas-like Na⁺.

quiz.q: Solubility trend of group 2 sulphates down the group:
quiz.why: Lattice energy stays nearly constant with the large sulphate ion while cation hydration enthalpy falls, so solubility decreases.

questions.q: Madelung constant of the NaCl structure:
questions.why: The rock-salt geometry gives a Madelung constant of 1.748.

questions.q: Lattice energy is proportional to:
questions.why: Coulombic attraction scales with the product of charges divided by the interionic distance.

questions.q: (1 − 1/n) with n = 9 equals:
questions.why: 1 − 1/9 = 8/9 = 0.889, which is the repulsion correction for Ar-like ion pairs.

questions.q: Kapustinskii lattice energy for KCl (d = 314 pm, ν = 2):
questions.why: 1.202 × 10⁵ × 2/314 = 765.6, and multiplying by (1 − 34.5/314) = 0.890 gives about 681 kJ mol⁻¹, so U ≈ −680 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle, which step is exothermic?
questions.why: Chlorine releases energy when it captures an electron, so ΔegH is negative.

questions.q: Radius ratio of 0.80 predicts:
questions.why: Ratios above 0.732 allow eight anions around the cation in a cubic arrangement.

questions.q: Coordination of F⁻ in fluorite is:
questions.why: In CaF₂ each Ca²⁺ has 8 fluorides, and to keep the 1:2 ratio each F⁻ has 4 calcium neighbours.

questions.q: AlCl₃ is more covalent than NaCl because Al³⁺:
options: Has high charge and small size
questions.why: High charge and small size make Al³⁺ strongly polarising, so it distorts the chloride electron cloud.

questions.q: Hypothetical MgCl is not formed mainly because:
options: MgCl₂ has a much larger lattice energy that outweighs IE₂
questions.why: Although IE₂ costs energy, the far larger lattice energy of Mg²⁺ salts makes MgCl₂ formation much more exothermic, so MgCl would disproportionate.

questions.q: AgI is less soluble than AgF because:
questions.why: Large, polarisable I⁻ is distorted by Ag⁺, giving covalent character that lowers solubility in water.

questions.q: Limiting radius ratio derivation for CN 6 gives:
questions.why: Four anions touching in a square around the cation give r⁺ + r⁻ = √2 r⁻, so r⁺/r⁻ = √2 − 1 = 0.414.

questions.q: Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group because:
options: Lattice energy falls faster than hydration enthalpy
questions.why: With the small OH⁻ ion, lattice energy depends strongly on cation size and falls faster than hydration enthalpy as the cation grows.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Covalent bonding: VSEPR, VBT and MOT
courses.summary: Lewis structures and formal charge, VSEPR shapes, valence bond theory with hybridisation and Bent's rule, molecular orbital theory for homonuclear and heteronuclear diatomics, and bond polarity with dipole moments.
outcomes: Predict shapes and bond angles of molecules and ions using VSEPR
Assign hybridisation and apply Bent's rule
Draw MO diagrams for B₂–Ne₂, CO and NO and derive bond order and magnetism
Estimate percentage ionic character from dipole moments

scenes.text: Sanjay draws H₂O as a straight line, like CO₂. His mentor asks: where are oxygen's two lone pairs?
Lone pairs push harder than bonding pairs, folding water to 104.5°.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
1. Count electron domains on the central atom: steric number (SN) = bonded atoms + lone pairs (a multiple bond counts once).
2. Domains arrange to minimise repulsion: SN 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, 5 trigonal bipyramidal, 6 octahedral, 7 pentagonal bipyramidal.
3. Repulsion order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp. Lone pairs compress bond angles.
4. In trigonal bipyramids, lone pairs and less electronegative/double-bonded groups go equatorial.

steps.title: Solved: counting domains
steps.body:
Lone pairs on centre = (valence e⁻ − bonds formed − charge adjustments)/2.
- **ClF₃**: Cl has 7 e⁻, uses 3 → 4 left = 2 lp; SN 5 → **T-shaped**
- **XeF₄**: Xe 8 e⁻, uses 4 → 2 lp; SN 6 → **square planar**
- **SF₄**: S 6, uses 4 → 1 lp; SN 5 → **see-saw**
- **I₃⁻**: central I has 7 + 1 = 8, uses 2 → 3 lp; SN 5 → **linear**
- **NH₄⁺**: SN 4, 0 lp → tetrahedral 109.5°

steps.title: Solved: bond-angle trends
steps.body:
- CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5° (more lone pairs).
- NH₃ 107° > PH₃ 93.5°: P is larger and less electronegative, so bond pairs are farther apart and repel less.
- NF₃ (102°) < NH₃: electronegative F pulls bond pairs away from N.

steps.title: Formal charge
steps.body: FC = valence e⁻ − non-bonding e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻). Prefer structures with the smallest formal charges and negative charge on the more electronegative atom. Example: in CO₂ (O=C=O) every atom has FC = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming the shape from the electron geometry (H₂O is bent, not tetrahedral).
- Putting lone pairs axial in a trigonal bipyramid.
- Forgetting the ionic charge when counting electrons (I₃⁻, ICl₄⁻).

activity.prompt: Match each species to its VSEPR shape.

quiz.q: Shape of XeF₂:
quiz.why: Xe has 3 lone pairs and 2 bonds (SN 5); the lone pairs take equatorial positions, leaving the two F atoms linear.

quiz.q: Bond angle order:
quiz.why: Each added lone pair repels the bond pairs more strongly, compressing the angle from 109.5° to 107° to 104.5°.

quiz.q: Lone pairs on Cl in ClF₃:
quiz.why: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons and uses 3 in bonds, leaving 4 electrons, i.e. 2 lone pairs.

quiz.q: Shape of SF₄:
quiz.why: SF₄ has four bonds and one equatorial lone pair on a trigonal bipyramid, which gives a see-saw shape.

lessons.title: Valence bond theory, hybridisation and Bent's rule

story.title: Four equal bonds from unequal orbitals

scenes.text: Carbon has one 2s and three 2p orbitals, yet the four C–H bonds of methane are identical.
Hybridisation mixes them into four equivalent sp³ orbitals.

steps.title: Valence bond theory
steps.body:
A covalent bond forms by overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals with opposite spins; greater overlap means a stronger bond.
- σ bond: head-on overlap along the axis (s–s, s–p, p–p, hybrid).
- π bond: sideways p–p overlap; weaker, prevents rotation.
- Hybridisation from steric number: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³, 5 sp³d, 6 sp³d².

steps.title: s-character and Bent's rule
steps.body:
- s-character: sp 50%, sp² 33%, sp³ 25%. More s-character → shorter, stronger bonds and more electronegative carbon (acidity HC≡CH > H₂C=CH₂ > CH₄).
- Bond angle from hybridisation: cos θ = −s/(1 − s) where s = fractional s-character (s = 0.25 gives 109.5°).
- **Bent's rule**: atomic s-character concentrates in orbitals directed towards electropositive substituents; more electronegative substituents get orbitals with more p-character. Example: in CH₂F₂ the F–C–F angle (≈ 108°) is smaller than H–C–H (≈ 112°).

steps.title: Solved: hybridisation
steps.body:
- PCl₅: SN 5 → **sp³d**, trigonal bipyramidal; axial bonds (≈ 214 pm) longer than equatorial (≈ 202 pm).
- SF₆: SN 6 → **sp³d²**, octahedral.
- [NH₄]⁺ sp³; BF₃ sp² (planar 120°); BeCl₂ (gas) sp, linear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking hybridisation is a physical process that 'causes' shape — it is a model consistent with the observed shape.
- Calling π bonds stronger than σ bonds.
- Forgetting that VBT cannot explain the paramagnetism of O₂.

activity.prompt: Match each species to the hybridisation of its central atom.

quiz.q: Percentage s-character in sp² hybrids:
quiz.why: One s orbital mixes with two p orbitals, so each sp² hybrid has one-third s-character.

quiz.q: In PCl₅ the axial bonds are:
quiz.why: Axial bonds experience three 90° repulsions from equatorial bonds, so they are longer and weaker.

quiz.q: Bent's rule says electronegative substituents prefer hybrids with:
quiz.why: Electronegative groups draw electron density, and directing p-rich orbitals to them keeps s-character where it stabilises electrons best.

story.title: Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet

scenes.text: In a famous demonstration, liquid O₂ poured between magnet poles hangs there, while liquid N₂ falls straight through.
Only MO theory predicts two unpaired electrons in O₂.

steps.title: LCAO principles
steps.body:
- Atomic orbitals of similar energy and symmetry combine: ψ_b = ψA + ψB (bonding), ψ* = ψA − ψB (antibonding).
- n atomic orbitals → n MOs. Antibonding orbitals are raised slightly more than bonding orbitals are lowered.
- Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a); BO 0 → molecule does not exist.
- Unpaired electrons → paramagnetic.

steps.title: Energy order
steps.body:
- **B₂, C₂, N₂** (s–p mixing): σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < π2p(x,y) < σ2p(z) < π*2p < σ*2p
- **O₂, F₂, Ne₂**: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p(z) < π2p(x,y) < π*2p < σ*2p
The switch happens because the 2s–2p gap widens across the period, reducing s–p mixing.

steps.title: Solved: O₂ and its ions
steps.body:
O₂ (16 e⁻, 12 valence): σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p²
- BO = ½(8 − 4) = **2**, two unpaired electrons in π* → paramagnetic
- O₂⁺: remove one π* → BO **2.5**
- O₂⁻ (superoxide): BO **1.5**; O₂²⁻ (peroxide): BO **1**, diamagnetic
Bond length order: O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻.

steps.title: Solved: B₂, C₂, N₂
steps.body:
- B₂ (6 valence e⁻): σ2s² σ*2s² π2p² → BO 1, **paramagnetic** (proof of s–p mixing)
- C₂ (8): … π2p⁴ → BO 2, diamagnetic
- N₂ (10): … π2p⁴ σ2p² → BO **3**, diamagnetic, very strong bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹)
- N₂⁺: loses a σ2p electron → BO 2.5

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the O₂ order for N₂ or B₂ (B₂ would wrongly come out diamagnetic).
- Counting core 1s electrons inconsistently (they cancel; including them does not change BO).
- Saying higher BO means longer bond — it means shorter and stronger.

activity.prompt: Arrange the species by increasing bond order.

quiz.q: Bond order of N₂⁺:
quiz.why: N₂⁺ has 9 valence electrons: 7 bonding and 2 antibonding, giving BO = ½(7 − 2) = 2.5.

quiz.q: Which is paramagnetic?
quiz.why: In B₂ the two highest electrons occupy the degenerate π2p orbitals singly, so it has two unpaired electrons.

quiz.q: Bond order of He₂:
quiz.why: He₂ would have two bonding and two antibonding electrons, so BO = 0 and the molecule is not stable.

quiz.q: Longest O–O bond:
quiz.why: Peroxide O₂²⁻ has the lowest bond order (1), so its O–O bond is the longest.

lessons.title: Heteronuclear diatomics, polarity and dipole moment

scenes.text: Carbon monoxide from car exhaust binds haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than O₂.
MO theory shows CO's HOMO is a carbon-centred lone pair, ready to donate to iron.

steps.title: Heteronuclear MOs
steps.body:
The more electronegative atom has lower-energy AOs, so bonding MOs have more of its character and antibonding MOs more of the other atom's.
- **CO** (10 valence e⁻, isoelectronic with N₂): BO 3; HOMO (3σ) is mainly on C → CO binds metals through carbon; LUMO π* allows back-bonding.
- **NO** (11 e⁻): BO 2.5, one unpaired electron in π* → paramagnetic; NO⁺ has BO 3.
- **HF**: H 1s combines with F 2pz; F 2px, 2py remain non-bonding lone pairs.

steps.title: Dipole moment
steps.body:
μ = q × d (unit: debye, 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). For a full electron charge separated by 1 Å, μ = 4.80 D.
% ionic character = (μ_observed/μ_ionic) × 100.
Hannay–Smyth estimate: % ionic = 16Δχ + 3.5(Δχ)².
Symmetric molecules (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄, XeF₄) have μ = 0 because bond dipoles cancel.

steps.title: Solved: NH₃ vs NF₃
steps.body: NH₃ μ = 1.47 D but NF₃ only 0.23 D. In NH₃ the N–H bond dipoles point towards N, adding to the lone-pair moment; in NF₃ the N–F dipoles point away from N and largely cancel the lone-pair moment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using N₂'s order but forgetting CO's HOMO is carbon-centred.
- Assuming any molecule with polar bonds is polar.
- Forgetting to convert Å to the 4.80 D per Å relation correctly.

activity.prompt: Match the species with its bond order.

quiz.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
quiz.why: BF₃ is trigonal planar, so its three equal B–F bond dipoles cancel.

quiz.q: NO is paramagnetic because:
options: It has an unpaired electron in π*
quiz.why: NO has 11 valence electrons, so one electron sits alone in a π* orbital.

quiz.q: A bond with μ = 2.4 D and length 1.0 Å has ionic character:

questions.q: Shape of BrF₅:
questions.why: Br has 5 bonds and 1 lone pair (SN 6), so the octahedral arrangement minus one position is square pyramidal.

questions.q: Shape of ICl₄⁻:
questions.why: Iodine has 8 electrons (7 + 1), uses 4 in bonds and keeps 2 lone pairs trans to each other, giving a square planar ion.

questions.q: Hybridisation of Xe in XeF₄:
questions.why: Steric number 6 (4 bonds + 2 lone pairs) corresponds to sp³d² hybridisation.

questions.q: Bond angle for hybrids of s = 0.5:
questions.why: cos θ = −0.5/0.5 = −1, so θ = 180°, as expected for sp hybrids.

questions.q: Bond order of O₂⁻:
questions.why: O₂⁻ has 8 bonding and 5 antibonding valence electrons, so BO = ½(8 − 5) = 1.5.

questions.q: s–p mixing explains the paramagnetism of:
questions.why: s–p mixing pushes σ2p above π2p, so B₂'s last two electrons go singly into π orbitals, making it paramagnetic.

questions.q: CO binds to metals mainly through:
questions.why: CO's HOMO is a σ orbital concentrated on carbon, so carbon donates the lone pair to the metal.

questions.q: Which is isoelectronic with N₂?
questions.why: CO has 14 electrons in total, the same as N₂, and both have bond order 3.

questions.q: Dipole moment of NF₃ is smaller than NH₃ because:
options: Bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair moment in NF₃
questions.why: In NF₃ the N–F bond dipoles point away from N and cancel much of the lone-pair contribution, while in NH₃ they reinforce it.

questions.q: Hannay–Smyth % ionic for Δχ = 2.0:
Formal charge on N in NH₄⁺:
questions.why: FC = 5 − 0 − ½(8) = +1, which is the charge of the ammonium ion.

questions.q: The weakest repulsion in VSEPR is:
questions.why: Bond pairs are held between two nuclei and are less spread out, so bond-pair–bond-pair repulsion is the weakest.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Metallic bonding, weak forces, revision & practicals
courses.summary: Metallic bonding and band theory, hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces, two standard volumetric practicals (acid–base and permanganometry), and a full formula sheet with an exam covering the whole paper.
outcomes: Explain conductors, semiconductors and insulators with band theory
Distinguish intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding and their effects on properties
Perform and calculate acid–base and KMnO₄ titrations
Revise all key formulas of the paper

story.title: Why copper wires and silicon chips

scenes.text: Riya's phone charger uses copper; its processor uses silicon. Both conduct — but in very different ways.
Band theory explains the difference through the gap between filled and empty energy levels.

steps.title: Models of metallic bonding
steps.body:
- **Electron sea (Drude–Lorentz)**: cations in a sea of delocalised electrons — explains conductivity, lustre, malleability and ductility.
- **Band theory**: N atomic orbitals combine into N closely spaced MOs forming a band. The filled band is the valence band; the next empty band is the conduction band; between them is the band gap (Eg).

steps.title: Conductors, semiconductors, insulators
steps.body:
- Metals: partly filled band or overlapping bands (Mg: 3s and 3p overlap) → conduct; conductivity falls with temperature (more lattice vibration).
- Semiconductors: small gap (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.67 eV); conductivity rises with temperature.
- Insulators: large gap (diamond ≈ 5.5 eV).
- Doping: n-type (Si + P/As, extra electrons); p-type (Si + B/Ga, holes).

steps.title: Solved: photon to cross the Si gap
steps.body: Eg = 1.1 eV → λ = 1240/1.1 = **1127 nm** (near-IR). Photons with λ shorter than this can create electron–hole pairs — the basis of silicon solar cells.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying semiconductors conduct less when heated — they conduct more.
- Calling B-doped Si n-type (boron has 3 valence electrons → holes → p-type).
- Thinking Mg should be an insulator because 3s is full — band overlap makes it a metal.

activity.prompt: Match the material to its classification.

quiz.q: Conductivity of a metal on heating:
quiz.why: Higher temperature increases lattice vibrations that scatter electrons, so a metal's conductivity decreases.

quiz.q: Ge doped with Ga is:
quiz.why: Gallium has three valence electrons, creating holes in the germanium lattice, which makes a p-type semiconductor.

quiz.q: Mg is a conductor because:
options: It has no band gap due to doping
quiz.why: The full 3s band overlaps the empty 3p band, so electrons can move into empty levels and conduct.

lessons.title: Hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces

scenes.text: Lakes freeze from the top, letting fish survive winter beneath.
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open tetrahedral network less dense than liquid water.

steps.title: Hydrogen bonding
steps.body:
A–H···B where A and B are small, highly electronegative atoms (F, O, N). Energy ≈ 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹ (stronger than van der Waals, weaker than covalent).
- **Intermolecular**: raises boiling point (H₂O 100 °C vs H₂S −60 °C; HF 19.5 °C vs HCl −85 °C); explains association of acetic acid as dimers and the open structure of ice.
- **Intramolecular** (chelation): o-nitrophenol — lowers boiling point and water solubility, makes it steam-volatile; p-nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds and is not steam-volatile.

steps.title: van der Waals forces
steps.body:
- **Dipole–dipole (Keesom)**: between permanent dipoles (HCl···HCl).
- **Dipole–induced dipole (Debye)**.
- **London dispersion**: instantaneous dipoles; present in all molecules; increase with polarisability (size, surface area). Explains boiling point order F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ and n-pentane (36 °C) > neopentane (9.5 °C).
- Potential energy falls as 1/r⁶ for these attractions.

steps.title: Solved: explaining boiling points
steps.body:
Group 16 hydrides: H₂O (100) ≫ H₂Te (−2) > H₂Se (−41) > H₂S (−60 °C).
- From H₂S to H₂Te, boiling point rises with size (dispersion forces).
- H₂O is anomalous because of extensive hydrogen bonding.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming H-bonding in HCl — Cl is too large for significant H-bonding.
- Confusing intramolecular H-bonding (lowers b.p.) with intermolecular (raises b.p.).
- Ignoring dispersion forces in polar molecules — they are often the largest contribution.

activity.prompt: Match the observation to the interaction responsible.
pairs: Ice is less dense than water
I₂ is solid, F₂ is gas
Acetic acid has molar mass ≈ 120 in benzene

quiz.q: Which has the highest boiling point?
quiz.why: HF forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which outweigh the larger dispersion forces in HI.

quiz.q: o-Nitrophenol is more volatile than p-nitrophenol because:
quiz.why: The OH of o-nitrophenol bonds internally to the nitro group, so molecules do not associate with each other.

quiz.q: London forces increase with:
quiz.why: Larger, more polarisable electron clouds form bigger instantaneous dipoles, which strengthens dispersion attractions.

scenes.text: The lab's bottle of 'approximately 0.1 M HCl' must be standardised before anyone can use it for analysis.
Anhydrous sodium carbonate is a primary standard: weigh it accurately, dissolve, and titrate.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. With methyl orange (yellow → orange-red at end point, pH ≈ 4), both stages of neutralisation are complete.
M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ → M(HCl) = 2 × M(Na₂CO₃) × V(Na₂CO₃)/V(HCl).

steps.title: Preparing 250 mL of 0.05 M Na₂CO₃
steps.body:
Molar mass Na₂CO₃ = 105.99 g mol⁻¹.
Mass = 0.05 × 0.250 × 105.99 = **1.325 g**. Weigh by difference into a beaker, dissolve, transfer quantitatively into a 250 mL volumetric flask and make up to the mark.

steps.title: Solved: observation table
steps.body:
10.0 mL of 0.05 M Na₂CO₃ pipetted; burette readings for HCl:
| Trial | Initial | Final | Volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0 | 9.9 | 9.9 |
| 2 | 10.0 | 19.8 | 9.8 |
| 3 | 20.0 | 29.8 | 9.8 |
Concordant = 9.8 mL. M(HCl) = 2 × 0.05 × 10.0/9.8 = **0.102 M**.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body:
- Why methyl orange, not phenolphthalein? Phenolphthalein changes near pH 8.3 and detects only the first stage (CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻).
- Why rinse the burette with HCl but not the conical flask with Na₂CO₃? Rinsing the flask would add extra solute.
- Primary standard requirements: high purity, stable, non-hygroscopic, high molar mass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the burette at the top of the meniscus (read the bottom for colourless solutions).
- Using the rough titre in the average.
- Forgetting the 2 : 1 stoichiometry.

activity.prompt: Order the procedure for standardising HCl.
items: Weigh 1.325 g anhydrous Na₂CO₃ and make up to 250 mL
Rinse and fill the burette with HCl, removing air bubbles
Pipette 10.0 mL Na₂CO₃ into a clean conical flask
Titrate until yellow just turns orange-red
Repeat to get concordant readings and calculate molarity

quiz.q: Mass of Na₂CO₃ for 100 mL of 0.1 M solution:
If 10 mL of 0.05 M Na₂CO₃ needs 10 mL HCl, M(HCl) is:
quiz.why: Each carbonate needs two HCl, so M(HCl) = 2 × 0.05 × 10/10 = 0.10 M.

quiz.q: Phenolphthalein in this titration shows the end point of:
quiz.why: Phenolphthalein turns colourless near pH 8.3, which corresponds to conversion of carbonate to bicarbonate only.

scenes.text: Permanganate is so intensely purple that one extra drop colours the whole flask pink — no indicator needed.
After the lab, Sneha compiles one revision sheet for the whole Inorganic I paper.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
In acid (dil. H₂SO₄): MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
With oxalate: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O.
Warm oxalic acid to 60–70 °C; the reaction is autocatalysed by Mn²⁺. End point: permanent pale pink.
With Mohr's salt (Fe²⁺): MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O (no heating — Fe²⁺ oxidises in air).

steps.title: Solved: molarity of KMnO₄
steps.body:
10.0 mL of 0.05 M oxalic acid needs 10.0 mL KMnO₄.
- Moles oxalate = 0.05 × 0.010 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴
- Moles MnO₄⁻ = (2/5) × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴
- M = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴/0.010 = **0.020 M**
Oxalic acid (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O, 126.07 g mol⁻¹): 250 mL of 0.05 M needs **1.576 g**.

steps.title: Formula sheet — Inorganic I
steps.body:
- Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV; rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å; 1/λ = R Z²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
- λ = h/mv; Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π
- Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l
- Zeff = Z − S (0.35 / 0.85 / 1.00)
- μ_spin = √[n(n + 2)] BM
- χA − χB = 0.102√Δ; χM = (IE + EA)/2; χAR = 0.359 Zeff/r² + 0.744
- U = −N_A A z⁺z⁻e²/(4πε₀r₀) (1 − 1/n); Kapustinskii U = −1.202 × 10⁵ νz⁺z⁻/d (1 − 34.5/d)
- Radius ratio limits 0.155, 0.225, 0.414, 0.732
- BO = ½(N_b − N_a); % ionic = μ_obs/μ_ionic × 100

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using HCl instead of H₂SO₄ to acidify (Cl⁻ is oxidised by MnO₄⁻).
- Titrating oxalic acid cold (very slow at the start).
- Taking 1 : 1 stoichiometry instead of 2 : 5.

activity.prompt: Order the procedure for the KMnO₄ vs oxalic acid titration.
items: Fill the burette with KMnO₄ and read the upper meniscus
Pipette 10.0 mL oxalic acid into a conical flask
Titrate until a pale pink colour persists for 30 s
Repeat for concordant readings and calculate molarity

quiz.q: KMnO₄ is read at the upper meniscus because:
quiz.why: The deep purple colour hides the bottom of the meniscus, so the upper edge is read instead.

quiz.q: Electrons gained per MnO₄⁻ in acid:
quiz.why: Manganese goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a gain of 5 electrons.

quiz.q: HCl is not used to acidify because:
options: It is oxidised to Cl₂ by MnO₄⁻
quiz.why: Permanganate oxidises chloride to chlorine, which consumes titrant and gives a high, wrong result.

questions.q: Energy of the n = 3 level of H:
Radial nodes in 5s:
questions.why: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 5 − 0 − 1 = 4.

questions.q: Spin-only moment of Fe³⁺:
questions.why: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons, so μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM.

questions.q: Which has the largest first IE?
questions.why: Si has the highest Zeff and smallest radius of these, so its IE₁ (786 kJ mol⁻¹) is the largest; Al dips below Mg.

questions.q: Inert pair effect is most marked in:
questions.why: Thallium's 6s² pair is poorly shielded and relativistically stabilised, so Tl⁺ is its most stable state.

questions.q: Coordination number in rock salt:
questions.why: Each ion in NaCl sits in an octahedron of six counter-ions.

questions.q: Shape of ClF₃:
questions.why: Two lone pairs occupy equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid, leaving the three F atoms in a T shape.

questions.q: Bond order of CN⁻:
questions.why: CN⁻ is isoelectronic with N₂ (10 valence electrons), so its bond order is 3.

questions.q: Band gap of silicon is about:
questions.why: Silicon is a semiconductor with a band gap of about 1.1 eV at room temperature.

questions.q: Highest boiling point:
questions.why: Extensive hydrogen bonding gives water an anomalously high boiling point of 100 °C.

questions.q: 0.10 M HCl needed for 20 mL of 0.05 M Na₂CO₃ (methyl orange):
questions.why: Moles CO₃²⁻ = 1.0 × 10⁻³, which needs 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol HCl, i.e. 20 mL of 0.10 M.

questions.q: KMnO₄ titre 12.5 mL for 10 mL of 0.05 M oxalic acid gives M(KMnO₄):
Pauling χ difference for Δ = 100 kJ mol⁻¹:
Which compound is most covalent?
questions.why: Al³⁺ has the highest charge and smallest size, giving the greatest polarising power and covalent character.

questions.q: Lattice energy of KCl from ΔfH = −437 and other steps summing to +281 kJ mol⁻¹:
questions.why: U = −437 − 281 = −718 kJ mol⁻¹ by Hess's law.

uni-bsc-chem-inorganic-2.title: B.Sc Chemistry · Inorganic Chemistry II (s- and p-block, coordination chemistry)
uni-bsc-chem-inorganic-2.description: Chemistry of s-block elements, groups 13–18 with key compounds (boranes, silicates, oxoacids, interhalogens, xenon compounds), and coordination chemistry: nomenclature, isomerism, VBT, crystal field theory, colour and magnetism, plus EDTA and qualitative-analysis practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · s-Block elements
courses.summary: Alkali and alkaline earth metals: general trends, flame colours, solutions in liquid ammonia, oxides, peroxides and superoxides, thermal stability and solubility of salts, anomalous behaviour of Li and Be, complexation by crown ethers and cryptands, and key industrial compounds.
outcomes: Explain trends in reactivity, reducing power and flame colours of groups 1 and 2
Describe the blue solutions of alkali metals in liquid ammonia
Predict thermal stability and solubility trends of carbonates, nitrates, sulphates and hydroxides
Explain anomalous properties of Li and Be and the role of crown ethers
Outline the Solvay process and chlor-alkali manufacture

lessons.title: General properties and solutions in liquid ammonia

scenes.text: Crimson, golden-yellow and apple-green sparks light up the Diwali sky.
The colours come from Sr, Na and Ba salts — electrons excited by heat and falling back.

steps.title: Group trends
steps.body:
- Configuration: group 1 ns¹, group 2 ns².
- Down the group: radius ↑, IE ↓, electropositivity and reactivity ↑; melting points fall in group 1 (weaker metallic bonding).
- Reducing power in water (E°): Li is the strongest (E° Li⁺/Li = −3.04 V) despite having the highest IE, because of the very large hydration enthalpy of the small Li⁺.
- Flame colours: Li crimson, Na golden yellow (589 nm), K lilac, Rb red-violet, Cs blue; Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green. Be and Mg give no colour (electrons too tightly held).

steps.title: Solutions in liquid ammonia
steps.body:
M + (x + y)NH₃ → [M(NH₃)ₓ]⁺ + [e(NH₃)ᵧ]⁻
- Dilute: deep blue (solvated electrons absorb in the red/near-IR), paramagnetic, highly conducting.
- Concentrated (> 3 M): bronze/copper coloured, diamagnetic as electrons pair, metallic lustre.
- On standing / with catalyst (Fe): M + NH₃ → MNH₂ + ½H₂.
- Used as a powerful reducing agent (Birch reduction of benzene to 1,4-cyclohexadiene).

steps.title: Solved: why Li is the best reductant in water
steps.body:
Consider M(s) → M⁺(aq) + e⁻ as sublimation + ionisation + hydration (kJ mol⁻¹, approximate):
- Li: 161 + 520 − 520 = **+161**
- Na: 108 + 496 − 406 = **+198**
- K: 89 + 419 − 322 = **+186**
Li has the smallest net energy cost, so it is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution (although K reacts faster).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Li reacts most vigorously with water — it is the strongest reductant thermodynamically, but K and Cs react faster (kinetics).
- Thinking concentrated metal–ammonia solutions are still paramagnetic.
- Claiming Be and Mg give flame colours.

activity.prompt: Match each element to its flame colour.

quiz.q: Blue colour of Na in liquid NH₃ is due to:
quiz.why: Solvated electrons absorb light in the red/near-infrared region, so the transmitted light looks blue.

quiz.q: Strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution:
quiz.why: Li⁺ has an exceptionally large hydration enthalpy, giving Li the most negative standard reduction potential.

quiz.q: Which gives no flame colour?
quiz.why: Magnesium's electrons are held too tightly for flame temperatures to excite visible transitions.

lessons.title: Oxides, hydroxides and salts: stability and solubility

scenes.text: Emergency breathing sets use potassium superoxide, KO₂.
It absorbs exhaled CO₂ and releases O₂: 4KO₂ + 2CO₂ → 2K₂CO₃ + 3O₂.

steps.title: Oxides formed on burning in air
steps.body:
- Li → Li₂O (normal oxide, O²⁻)
- Na → Na₂O₂ (peroxide, O₂²⁻, diamagnetic)
- K, Rb, Cs → MO₂ (superoxide, O₂⁻, paramagnetic, yellow/orange)
Large cations stabilise large anions (lattice energy matching). Group 2 mainly forms MO; Ba gives BaO₂.

steps.title: Thermal stability
steps.body:
- Carbonates: group 2 decomposition temperature rises down the group (MgCO₃ ≈ 540 °C, BaCO₃ ≈ 1360 °C). Small, polarising cations distort CO₃²⁻ and favour MO + CO₂.
- Li₂CO₃ decomposes (Li₂O + CO₂); other alkali carbonates are stable.
- Nitrates: LiNO₃ and group 2 → oxide + NO₂ + O₂; NaNO₃/KNO₃ → nitrite + O₂.
- Bicarbonates of Na, K exist as solids; those of group 2 only in solution (temporary hardness).

steps.title: Solubility (group 2)
steps.body:
- Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group (Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ fairly soluble).
- Sulphates: solubility decreases (BeSO₄, MgSO₄ soluble; BaSO₄ insoluble, used as X-ray contrast meal).
Reason: hydration enthalpy vs lattice energy — with large SO₄²⁻, U changes little, hydration falls; with small OH⁻, U falls faster.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Na₂O as the product of burning sodium in excess air.
- Assuming thermal stability decreases down group 2.
- Mixing up hydroxide and sulphate solubility trends.

activity.prompt: Match the metal to the main product of burning in excess air.

quiz.q: Most thermally stable carbonate:
quiz.why: Ba²⁺ is the largest and least polarising cation, so it distorts the carbonate ion least and BaCO₃ decomposes at the highest temperature.

quiz.q: Superoxide ion O₂⁻ is paramagnetic because:
quiz.why: O₂⁻ has 13 valence electrons, leaving one unpaired electron in a π* orbital.

quiz.q: Heating NaNO₃ gives:
quiz.why: Sodium nitrate loses only oxygen on heating, forming sodium nitrite, unlike LiNO₃ which gives the oxide.

lessons.title: Anomalous Li and Be; crown ethers and cryptands

scenes.text: Potassium permanganate does not dissolve in benzene — until 18-crown-6 is added. Then the benzene turns purple ('purple benzene').
The crown ether wraps K⁺ in a hydrophobic coat, dragging MnO₄⁻ along.

steps.title: Why Li and Be are different
steps.body:
Small size, high charge density (polarising power), high IE and no d orbitals in the valence shell (maximum covalency 4).
- Li: forms Li₃N directly; LiCl is covalent-ish, deliquescent, soluble in ethanol; Li₂CO₃ decomposes; resembles Mg (diagonal).
- Be: BeCl₂ is covalent — polymeric chains in the solid, linear monomer in vapour above ≈ 900 °C; Be(OH)₂ amphoteric; BeO covalent with high m.p.; resembles Al.

steps.title: Crown ethers and cryptands
steps.body:
- Crown ethers: cyclic polyethers. Cavity size selects the ion: 12-crown-4 ↔ Li⁺, 15-crown-5 ↔ Na⁺, 18-crown-6 ↔ K⁺.
- Cryptands ([2.2.2]-cryptand): 3-D cages giving even stronger complexes (cryptate effect).
- Uses: phase-transfer catalysis, dissolving salts in organic solvents, making alkalides (Na⁻ salts such as [Na(2.2.2)]⁺Na⁻).

steps.title: Solved: which crown for which ion?
steps.body:
Ionic radii: Li⁺ 76, Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138 pm. Approximate cavity diameters: 12-crown-4 ≈ 120–150 pm, 15-crown-5 ≈ 170–220 pm, 18-crown-6 ≈ 260–320 pm.
K⁺ (diameter ≈ 276 pm) fits 18-crown-6 best, so 18-crown-6 binds K⁺ selectively over Na⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Be forms BeCl₄²⁻ via d orbitals — Be uses sp³ and maximum covalency is 4.
- Thinking crown ethers bind anions (they bind cations; the anion follows as 'naked', highly reactive).
- Forgetting Li's diagonal similarity with Mg.

activity.prompt: Match the crown ether with the cation it binds best.

quiz.q: Solid BeCl₂ has:
quiz.why: In the solid each Be is tetrahedrally surrounded by bridging chlorides, giving polymeric chains.

quiz.q: 'Purple benzene' is produced by KMnO₄ with:
quiz.why: 18-crown-6 complexes K⁺, letting the ion pair dissolve in benzene and colour it purple.

quiz.q: Maximum covalency of Be is 4 because:
quiz.why: Be has only 2s and 2p valence orbitals, which can form at most four bonds.

lessons.title: Industrial compounds: Solvay process and chlor-alkali

scenes.text: Gujarat's coastal plants turn sea salt and limestone into washing soda for detergents and glass.
The Solvay process recycles its ammonia; the chlor-alkali plant next door makes NaOH and Cl₂.

steps.title: Solvay (ammonia–soda) process
steps.body:
1. Brine saturated with NH₃, then carbonated:
   NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl
2. NaHCO₃ is filtered (least soluble) and calcined: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O
3. CO₂ from CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
4. NH₃ recovered: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O
Overall: CaCO₃ + 2NaCl → Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂. K₂CO₃ cannot be made this way because KHCO₃ is too soluble.

steps.title: Chlor-alkali (membrane cell)
steps.body:
Electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂
- Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
- Cathode: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻
A cation-exchange membrane lets Na⁺ through but keeps Cl₂ away from OH⁻ (which would form hypochlorite). Older mercury cells are being phased out (mercury pollution).

steps.title: Solved: yield calculation
steps.body:
How much Na₂CO₃ from 1.00 tonne NaCl (100% yield)?
- 2 NaCl (2 × 58.44 = 116.9 g) → 1 Na₂CO₃ (106.0 g)
- Mass = 1.00 × 106.0/116.9 = **0.907 t**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Na₂CO₃ as the precipitate in the carbonating tower (it is NaHCO₃).
- Forgetting that the overall reaction is not thermodynamically favourable directly — it works through NH₃.
- Placing Cl₂ at the cathode.

activity.prompt: Order the main steps of the Solvay process.
items: Recover NH₃ from NH₄Cl using slaked lime

quiz.q: In the Solvay process the precipitate is:
quiz.why: Sodium bicarbonate is the least soluble salt in the ammoniacal brine, so it crystallises out.

quiz.q: By-product of the Solvay process:
quiz.why: Recovery of ammonia with lime leaves calcium chloride as the main waste product.

quiz.q: Product at the cathode in a membrane cell:
quiz.why: Water is reduced at the cathode to H₂ gas and OH⁻, which combine with Na⁺ to give NaOH.

questions.q: Ionisation enthalpy down group 1:
questions.why: The valence electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so it is easier to remove.

questions.q: Concentrated Na–NH₃ solutions are:
questions.why: At high concentration the solvated electrons pair up and the solution becomes bronze-coloured and less paramagnetic, with metallic lustre.

questions.q: Hydration enthalpy is largest for:
questions.why: Li⁺ is the smallest alkali ion with the highest charge density, so water binds to it most strongly.

questions.q: Peroxide ion is:
questions.why: Peroxide is O₂²⁻ with an O–O single bond (bond order 1).

questions.q: Least soluble sulphate:
questions.why: Ba²⁺ has the lowest hydration enthalpy in group 2, so BaSO₄ is the least soluble sulphate.

questions.q: LiNO₃ on heating gives:
questions.why: Like magnesium nitrate, LiNO₃ decomposes fully to the oxide, NO₂ and O₂ because Li⁺ is strongly polarising.

questions.q: BeO differs from other group 2 oxides as it is:
questions.why: BeO dissolves in both acids and bases, showing amphoteric behaviour like Al₂O₃.

questions.q: 18-crown-6 is selective for:
questions.why: The 18-crown-6 cavity matches the diameter of K⁺, giving the most stable complex.

questions.q: K₂CO₃ cannot be made by the Solvay process because:
options: KHCO₃ is too soluble to precipitate
questions.why: The process depends on bicarbonate crystallising out, and KHCO₃ remains in solution.

questions.q: Mass of Na₂CO₃ from 117 g NaCl:
questions.why: 117 g NaCl is 2 mol, and 2 mol NaCl gives 1 mol (106 g) Na₂CO₃.

questions.q: KO₂ in breathing apparatus works because it:
questions.why: 4KO₂ + 2CO₂ → 2K₂CO₃ + 3O₂ removes exhaled CO₂ and supplies oxygen.

questions.q: Vapour-phase BeCl₂ at high temperature is:
questions.why: Above about 900 °C BeCl₂ exists as linear sp-hybridised monomers; at lower vapour temperatures a dimer is also present.

courses.title: Unit 2 · p-Block I: groups 13 and 14
courses.summary: Boron chemistry (diborane and 3c–2e bonding, Wade's rules, borazine, boric acid), aluminium halides and Lewis acidity, carbon allotropes, silicates and silicones.
outcomes: Describe the structure and bonding of diborane and classify boranes with Wade's rules
Compare borazine with benzene and explain boric acid as a Lewis acid

story.title: A molecule that breaks the octet

scenes.text: In the 1950s boranes were studied as high-energy rocket fuels.
Diborane, B₂H₆, has too few electrons for normal bonds — it uses banana-shaped three-centre bonds.

steps.title: Structure of diborane
steps.body:
- B₂H₆ has 12 valence electrons: not enough for 8 two-centre bonds.
- Each B is roughly sp³: four terminal B–H bonds (2c–2e, 119 pm) lie in one plane; two bridging H atoms (above and below the plane) form two **B–H–B 3c–2e 'banana' bonds** (133 pm).
- Terminal H–B–H angle ≈ 122°; bridge angle B–H–B ≈ 97°.
- Preparation: 4BF₃ + 3LiAlH₄ → 2B₂H₆ + 3LiF + 3AlF₃ (in ether), or NaBH₄ + I₂ in diglyme.
- Reactions: burns (ΔH ≈ −2030 kJ mol⁻¹), hydrolyses to B(OH)₃ + H₂, hydroboration of alkenes, cleaved by NH₃ (to [BH₂(NH₃)₂]⁺[BH₄]⁻).

steps.title: Wade's rules (skeletal electron pairs)
steps.body:
For a borane BₙHₘ: skeletal electron pairs (SEP) = [n(3 − 1)... simplest form: count total valence electrons, subtract 2 per B–H(terminal) unit, divide by 2.
- SEP = n + 1 → **closo** (closed polyhedron), e.g. [B₆H₆]²⁻
- SEP = n + 2 → **nido** (one vertex missing), e.g. B₅H₉
- SEP = n + 3 → **arachno** (two vertices missing), e.g. B₄H₁₀
Formula shortcut: BₙHₙ₊₄ = nido, BₙHₙ₊₆ = arachno, [BₙHₙ]²⁻ = closo.

steps.title: Solved: classify B₅H₉
steps.body:
- Valence electrons: 5 × 3 + 9 × 1 = 24
- Subtract 2 for each of 5 B–H units: 24 − 10 = 14 electrons = **7 SEP**
- n + 2 = 7 → **nido** (octahedron with one vertex missing → square pyramid)

steps.title: Solved: classify [B₁₂H₁₂]²⁻
steps.body: - Electrons: 12 × 3 + 12 + 2 = 50; minus 24 → 26 = **13 SEP** = n + 1 → **closo** (icosahedron). It is exceptionally stable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing B=B double bonds or ethane-like B–B bonds in diborane.
- Forgetting the ionic charge when counting skeletal electrons.
- Thinking the bridging and terminal hydrogens are equivalent (they differ in bond length and NMR).

activity.prompt: Match each borane with its Wade structural type.

quiz.q: Number of 3c–2e bonds in B₂H₆:
quiz.why: Two bridging hydrogens each hold one three-centre two-electron B–H–B bond.

quiz.q: B₄H₁₀ is classified as:
quiz.why: B₄H₁₀ fits BₙHₙ₊₆, which corresponds to n + 3 skeletal electron pairs, the arachno type.

quiz.q: Diborane on hydrolysis gives:
quiz.why: B₂H₆ + 6H₂O → 2B(OH)₃ + 6H₂, releasing hydrogen gas.

lessons.title: Borazine, boric acid and Lewis acidity of BX₃

scenes.text: Borazine, B₃N₃H₆, looks just like benzene on paper.
But it adds HCl readily — its polar B–N bonds make it far more reactive than benzene.

steps.title: Borazine
steps.body:
- Prepared: 3B₂H₆ + 6NH₃ → 3[BH₂(NH₃)₂]⁺[BH₄]⁻ → (heat) 2B₃N₃H₆ + 12H₂; or from BCl₃ + NH₄Cl, then NaBH₄.
- Planar hexagon, B–N 144 pm (between single and double), isoelectronic with benzene.
- Unlike benzene, it undergoes **addition**: B₃N₃H₆ + 3HCl → B₃N₃H₉Cl₃ (Cl on B, H on N) because N is electron-rich and B electron-poor.

steps.title: Boric acid
steps.body:
- B(OH)₃: layered structure held by hydrogen bonds (soft, slippery flakes).
- A **monobasic Lewis acid**, not a proton donor: B(OH)₃ + H₂O → [B(OH)₄]⁻ + H⁺ (pKa ≈ 9.2).
- Too weak to titrate with NaOH directly; adding a cis-diol (glycerol, mannitol) forms a chelate complex, making it a strong enough acid to titrate with phenolphthalein.

steps.title: Lewis acidity of boron trihalides
steps.body:
Order: BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ < BI₃ — opposite to electronegativity!
Reason: pπ–pπ back-bonding from filled halogen p orbitals into the empty B 2p orbital is strongest for F (similar 2p size), partly filling boron's vacancy and reducing acidity. Reorganisation energy to pyramidalise BF₃ is also largest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling boric acid a tribasic protic acid.
- Ranking BF₃ as the strongest Lewis acid because F is most electronegative.
- Saying borazine is as aromatic and unreactive as benzene.

activity.prompt: Arrange boron trihalides from weakest to strongest Lewis acid.

quiz.q: Boric acid behaves as:
quiz.why: B(OH)₃ accepts OH⁻ from water to form [B(OH)₄]⁻, releasing one H⁺, so it is a monobasic Lewis acid.

quiz.q: Why is glycerol added in the titration of boric acid?
options: To form a stronger acid complex
quiz.why: Glycerol chelates boron and shifts the equilibrium, making the boric acid complex acidic enough to titrate sharply.

quiz.q: Borazine reacts with HCl by:
quiz.why: The polar B–N bonds allow HCl to add across them, with Cl going to boron and H to nitrogen.

story.title: The catalyst in every organic lab

scenes.text: Friedel–Crafts reactions need anhydrous AlCl₃ — a few drops of water ruin it.
Meanwhile the carbon in the same flask could be diamond, graphite, a fullerene or graphene.

steps.title: Aluminium halides
steps.body:
- AlF₃: ionic, high m.p. (sublimes ≈ 1290 °C).
- AlCl₃: in the vapour and in non-polar solvents exists as the **dimer Al₂Cl₆** (two bridging Cl, each Al tetrahedral); solid has a layer lattice with octahedral Al.
- Strong Lewis acid: AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → [AlCl₄]⁻ (basis of Friedel–Crafts catalysis).
- Hydrolysis: [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is acidic (pKa ≈ 5) — AlCl₃ fumes in moist air (HCl).

steps.title: Carbon allotropes
steps.body:
- **Diamond**: sp³, 3-D tetrahedral network, C–C 154 pm, hardest natural substance, insulator.
- **Graphite**: sp², hexagonal layers (C–C 142 pm), layers 335 pm apart held by van der Waals forces; conducts along planes; lubricant.
- **Fullerenes**: C₆₀ — truncated icosahedron of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons; soluble in toluene.
- **Graphene**: single graphite layer; very high electron mobility and strength. **Nanotubes**: rolled graphene.

steps.title: Solved: counting C₆₀
steps.body:
Euler for a polyhedron: V − E + F = 2.
- V = 60, F = 12 + 20 = 32
- E = V + F − 2 = 60 + 32 − 2 = **90 edges** (C–C bonds)
- Each carbon has 3 neighbours: 60 × 3/2 = 90 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing AlCl₃ as a planar monomer in the vapour at moderate temperatures (it is dimeric).
- Saying graphite conducts equally in all directions.
- Calling C₆₀ a 'nanotube'.

activity.prompt: Match each carbon allotrope to its structural feature.

quiz.q: In Al₂Cl₆, each Al is:
quiz.why: Each Al bonds to two terminal and two bridging chlorines, giving a tetrahedral environment.

quiz.q: Graphite conducts electricity because:
options: Each C has a delocalised π electron
quiz.why: Each sp² carbon contributes one p electron to a delocalised π system across the layer.

quiz.q: Number of hexagons in C₆₀:
quiz.why: Buckminsterfullerene has 20 hexagonal and 12 pentagonal faces.

scenes.text: Sand, clay, mica and asbestos are all silicates — built from the same SiO₄ tetrahedron.
Replace some oxygens with methyl groups and you get the silicone sealant around a bathtub.

steps.title: Classification of silicates
steps.body:
Based on how many O atoms each SiO₄⁴⁻ tetrahedron shares:
- 0 shared — **orthosilicates** SiO₄⁴⁻ (olivine, zircon ZrSiO₄)
- 1 — **pyrosilicates** Si₂O₇⁶⁻ (thortveitite)
- 2 — **cyclic** (SiO₃)ₙ²ⁿ⁻ (beryl Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈) and **single-chain pyroxenes** (SiO₃)ₙ²ⁿ⁻
