- 2.5 — **double chains** amphiboles (Si₄O₁₁)ₙ⁶ⁿ⁻ (asbestos)
- 3 — **sheets** (Si₂O₅)ₙ²ⁿ⁻ (mica, talc, clay)
- 4 — **3-D framework** SiO₂ (quartz); replacing Si by Al gives feldspars and zeolites.

steps.title: Solved: formula from sharing
steps.body: Each shared O counts ½ to each Si. For sheets: 3 shared (3 × ½ = 1.5) + 1 unshared = 2.5 O per Si → Si₂O₅, charge: 2(+4) + 5(−2) = −2 → **(Si₂O₅)²⁻** ✔

steps.title: Silicones
steps.body:
Polymers with –Si–O–Si– backbone and organic groups on Si.
- Synthesis: Rochow process Si + 2CH₃Cl → (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ (Cu catalyst, ≈ 300 °C); hydrolysis (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ + 2H₂O → (CH₃)₂Si(OH)₂ → condensation to –[(CH₃)₂SiO]ₙ–.
- (CH₃)₃SiCl ends chains (chain stopper); CH₃SiCl₃ gives cross-linking (resins).
- Properties: water-repellent, thermally stable, chemically inert, electrical insulators — used in sealants, greases, implants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that cyclic silicates and pyroxene chains share the same empirical formula SiO₃²⁻.
- Thinking (CH₃)₃SiCl gives long chains — it terminates them.
- Confusing silicones (–Si–O–) with silanes (Si–H).

activity.prompt: Match the silicate type to its repeating anion.

quiz.q: Mica is a:
quiz.why: Mica's tetrahedra share three oxygens each, forming sheets that cleave into thin flakes.

quiz.q: Cross-linked silicones are made using:
quiz.why: CH₃SiCl₃ forms three Si–OH groups on hydrolysis, so it can link chains together in three directions.

quiz.q: Silicate in which all four O are shared:
quiz.why: Quartz (SiO₂) is a 3-D framework where every oxygen bridges two silicon atoms.

questions.q: Bridging B–H bonds in diborane are:
questions.why: Each bridging bond shares two electrons over three atoms, so it is weaker and longer (≈133 pm vs 119 pm).

questions.q: Skeletal electron pairs in B₆H₁₀:
questions.why: Electrons = 18 + 10 = 28; subtract 12 for six B–H units to get 16 electrons, i.e. 8 SEP = n + 2 (nido).

questions.q: Borazine is isoelectronic with:
questions.why: B₃N₃H₆ has the same number of electrons and a similar planar ring as C₆H₆.

questions.q: Weakest Lewis acid:
questions.why: Strong pπ–pπ back-donation from fluorine partly fills boron's empty p orbital, making BF₃ the weakest acceptor.

questions.q: pKa of boric acid is about:
questions.why: Boric acid is very weak, with pKa ≈ 9.2, so it is titrated only after adding a diol.

questions.q: AlCl₃ fumes in moist air because:
questions.why: AlCl₃ reacts with moisture to form hydrated aluminium species and HCl gas, which appears as fumes.

questions.q: Interlayer spacing in graphite:
questions.why: Graphite layers are about 335 pm apart, held by weak van der Waals forces.

questions.q: Edges (bonds) in C₆₀:
questions.why: 60 carbons each with three bonds gives 60 × 3/2 = 90 bonds.

questions.q: Beryl contains:
questions.why: Beryl, Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈, contains six-membered rings of SiO₄ tetrahedra.

questions.q: Chain stopper in silicone synthesis:
questions.why: (CH₃)₃SiCl has only one hydrolysable Cl, so it can only cap a chain end.

questions.q: Zeolites are framework aluminosilicates used as:
questions.why: Their regular cages and channels trap molecules of specific size and exchange cations, e.g. in water softening and catalysis.

questions.q: Diborane reacts with excess NH₃ at low temperature to give:
questions.why: Ammonia unsymmetrically cleaves the bridges to form the ionic diammoniate, which gives borazine on heating.

courses.title: Unit 3 · p-Block II: groups 15–18
courses.summary: Hydrides and oxoacids of nitrogen and phosphorus, oxoacids of sulphur, halogens with interhalogens, pseudohalogens and chlorine oxoacids, and noble-gas chemistry with xenon fluorides and oxides.
outcomes: Predict basicity of phosphorus oxoacids from structure
Compare hydride properties down group 15 and 16
Draw structures of sulphur oxoacids and chlorine oxoacids and compare acid strengths
Predict shapes of interhalogens and xenon compounds with VSEPR

lessons.title: Group 15: hydrides and oxoacids of N and P

story.title: The acid that counts its OH groups

scenes.text: Ankit titrates H₃PO₃ with NaOH and finds it is dibasic, not tribasic, though it has three H atoms.
One H is bonded directly to P — and P–H hydrogens are not acidic.

steps.title: Hydrides MH₃
steps.body:
NH₃ > PH₃ > AsH₃ > SbH₃ in: basicity, bond angle (107° → 93.5° → 92° → 91°) and thermal stability.
Reducing power increases down the group (M–H bond weakens).
Boiling points: PH₃ (−88) < AsH₃ < SbH₃; NH₃ (−33 °C) anomalously high due to H-bonding.

steps.title: Oxoacids of phosphorus
steps.body:
Basicity = number of P–OH groups; P–H bonds are non-acidic and make the acid reducing.
- H₃PO₄ (orthophosphoric): 3 P–OH → tribasic
- H₃PO₃ (phosphorous/phosphonic): 2 P–OH + 1 P–H → **dibasic**, reducing
- H₃PO₂ (hypophosphorous/phosphinic): 1 P–OH + 2 P–H → **monobasic**, strong reducing agent
- H₄P₂O₇ (pyrophosphoric): tetrabasic, P–O–P bridge
All have tetrahedral P with one P=O.

steps.title: Oxoacids of nitrogen
steps.body:
- HNO₃: planar, strong acid, powerful oxidant; conc. HNO₃ passivates Fe, Al, Cr.
- HNO₂: weak acid (pKa ≈ 3.3), both oxidant and reductant; disproportionates 3HNO₂ → HNO₃ + 2NO + H₂O.
- Cu + 4HNO₃(conc) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O; 3Cu + 8HNO₃(dil) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O.

steps.title: Solved: titration of H₃PO₃
steps.body:
25.0 mL of 0.10 M H₃PO₃ requires how much 0.10 M NaOH?
- Dibasic: moles NaOH = 2 × 0.10 × 0.025 = 5.0 × 10⁻³
- V = 5.0 × 10⁻³/0.10 = **50 mL** (not 75 mL)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting all H atoms for basicity.
- Writing NO₂ as the product of copper with dilute nitric acid.
- Saying PH₃ is more basic than NH₃.

activity.prompt: Match each phosphorus oxoacid to its basicity.

quiz.q: H₃PO₂ is a strong reducing agent because it has:
quiz.why: Its two P–H bonds are readily oxidised, giving H₃PO₂ strong reducing power.

quiz.q: Bond angle in PH₃ is about:
quiz.why: In PH₃ the bonds use nearly pure p orbitals of the large P atom, so the angle is about 93.5°.

quiz.q: Conc. HNO₃ does not dissolve iron because:
options: It forms a passive oxide layer
quiz.why: Concentrated nitric acid oxidises the iron surface to a thin protective oxide film, stopping further attack.

scenes.text: A country's sulphuric acid output was long used as an index of its industrial strength.
From H₂SO₄ come relatives with S–S bonds and peroxide bridges — each with its own uses.

steps.title: Important oxoacids
steps.body:
- H₂SO₃ (sulphurous): exists only in solution; pyramidal S(IV); reducing.
- H₂SO₄: tetrahedral S(VI); dibasic, dehydrating, oxidising when hot and concentrated.
- H₂S₂O₇ (oleum, pyrosulphuric): S–O–S bridge.
- H₂S₂O₃ (thiosulphuric): one O replaced by S; S₂O₃²⁻ used in iodometry: 2S₂O₃²⁻ + I₂ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2I⁻.
- H₂SO₅ (Caro's acid, peroxomonosulphuric) and H₂S₂O₈ (Marshall's acid, peroxodisulphuric): contain –O–O–; strong oxidants.
- H₂S₂O₆ (dithionic): S–S bond.

steps.title: Solved: oxidation states in thiosulphate and tetrathionate
steps.body:
- S₂O₃²⁻: average S = (−2 + 6)/2 = **+2** (structurally central S +4/+6-like, terminal S −2/0 depending on convention).
- S₄O₆²⁻: average S = (−2 + 12)/4 = **+2.5**.
Iodine (0 → −1) oxidises thiosulphate, average S +2 → +2.5.

steps.title: Contact process (summary)
steps.body: S → SO₂ → (V₂O₅, ≈ 450 °C, 1–2 atm) 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (ΔH ≈ −197 kJ) → absorbed in conc. H₂SO₄ to form oleum → diluted. SO₃ is not absorbed directly in water because it forms a stable acid mist.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Marshall's acid has an S–S bond — it has S–O–O–S.
- Dissolving SO₃ directly in water industrially.
- Writing S₂O₃²⁻ with both S atoms equivalent.

activity.prompt: Match the oxoacid to its key structural feature.

quiz.q: Average oxidation state of S in S₄O₆²⁻:
Catalyst for SO₂ → SO₃ in the contact process:
quiz.why: Vanadium pentoxide is the industrial catalyst because it is efficient and resistant to poisoning.

quiz.q: Caro's acid is:
quiz.why: Peroxomonosulphuric acid H₂SO₅ is called Caro's acid.

scenes.text: Pool water is disinfected by hypochlorous acid, HOCl, formed when chlorine dissolves.
Add more oxygens and the acid gets stronger but, surprisingly, a weaker oxidant in practice.

steps.title: Interhalogens
steps.body:
Types XY, XY₃, XY₅, XY₇ (X larger, less electronegative halogen as central atom).
- ClF: linear; ClF₃, BrF₃: T-shaped; BrF₅, IF₅: square pyramidal; IF₇: pentagonal bipyramidal.
- More reactive than the halogens (except F₂) because X–Y bonds are weaker than X–X bonds; strong fluorinating agents (ClF₃ for UF₆ production).
- BrF₃ self-ionises: 2BrF₃ ⇌ BrF₂⁺ + BrF₄⁻.

steps.title: Pseudohalogens
steps.body:
Groups resembling halogens: (CN)₂ cyanogen, (SCN)₂ thiocyanogen, (OCN)₂.
They form HX-type acids (HCN, HSCN), insoluble Ag/Pb salts (AgCN, AgSCN), interhalogen-like compounds (ClCN) and disproportionate in alkali: (CN)₂ + 2OH⁻ → CN⁻ + OCN⁻ + H₂O.

steps.title: Oxoacids of chlorine
steps.body:
HOCl < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄ in **acid strength** (more O atoms delocalise the negative charge of the conjugate base; ClO₄⁻ is most stabilised).
Oxidising power (kinetically) roughly in the opposite order: HOCl is the most effective bleach.
Shapes (Cl central): ClO⁻ linear diatomic; ClO₂⁻ bent; ClO₃⁻ pyramidal; ClO₄⁻ tetrahedral.

steps.title: Solved: shapes by VSEPR
steps.body:
- BrF₅: Br 7 e⁻ − 5 = 2 → 1 lp; SN 6 → **square pyramidal**
- ICl₂⁻: I 8 e⁻ − 2 = 6 → 3 lp; SN 5 → **linear**
- ClO₃⁻: Cl with 3 O (one formal Cl–O⁻, two Cl=O) leaves 1 lp; SN 4 → **trigonal pyramidal**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the more electronegative halogen at the centre.
- Ranking HOCl as the strongest acid because it is the strongest bleach.
- Calling (CN)₂ a true halogen.

activity.prompt: Arrange the chlorine oxoacids by increasing acid strength.

quiz.q: Shape of IF₅:
quiz.why: Iodine has five bonds and one lone pair (SN 6), so the molecule is square pyramidal.

quiz.q: Strongest acid:
quiz.why: The perchlorate ion spreads its negative charge over four oxygens, making it the most stable conjugate base.

quiz.q: Interhalogens are more reactive than halogens (except F₂) because:
options: X–Y bonds are weaker than X–X
quiz.why: Polar X–Y bonds are weaker than the X–X bond of the parent halogen, so they break more easily.

quiz.q: Which is a pseudohalide ion?
quiz.why: Thiocyanate behaves like a halide, forming insoluble AgSCN and the dimer (SCN)₂.

scenes.text: In 1962 Neil Bartlett noticed O₂ and Xe have almost the same ionisation energy (≈ 1170 kJ mol⁻¹).
Since PtF₆ oxidised O₂, he tried Xe — and made the first noble-gas compound.

steps.title: Why xenon reacts
steps.body:
Xe has a lower IE (1170 kJ mol⁻¹) than lighter noble gases; it reacts with the most electronegative elements F and O.
- XeF₂: Xe + F₂ (2 : 1, heat or light)
- XeF₄: Xe + 2F₂ (1 : 5, 400 °C, 6 atm)
- XeF₆: Xe + 3F₂ (1 : 20, 300 °C, 60 atm)
- Hydrolysis: XeF₆ + 3H₂O → XeO₃ + 6HF (XeO₃ is explosive)
- XeF₆ + H₂O → XeOF₄ + 2HF (partial)

steps.title: Structures
steps.body:
| Compound | SN | Lone pairs | Shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| XeF₂ | 5 | 3 | Linear |
| XeF₄ | 6 | 2 | Square planar |
| XeF₆ | 7 | 1 | Distorted octahedral |
| XeO₃ | 4 | 1 | Trigonal pyramidal |
| XeOF₄ | 6 | 1 | Square pyramidal |
| XeO₄ | 4 | 0 | Tetrahedral |

steps.title: Solved: oxidation states
steps.body:
- XeF₂ +2; XeF₄ +4; XeF₆ +6; XeO₃ +6; XeOF₄: x − 2 − 4 = 0 → **+6**; XeO₄ **+8**.
In XeF₆ hydrolysis to XeO₃, Xe stays +6 — it is not a redox reaction.

steps.title: Uses of noble gases
steps.body: He: balloons, MRI magnet cooling, diving mixtures (less soluble in blood than N₂); Ne: signs; Ar: inert welding atmosphere, bulbs; Xe: high-intensity lamps and anaesthesia (research); Rn: radioactive, a health hazard in basements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling XeF₄ tetrahedral (it has two lone pairs → square planar).
- Assuming helium forms stable neutral compounds.
- Treating XeF₆ hydrolysis as redox.

activity.prompt: Match each xenon compound with its shape.

quiz.q: The first noble-gas compound was based on:
quiz.why: Bartlett reacted Xe with PtF₆ to give a compound formulated as Xe⁺[PtF₆]⁻ (later shown to be more complex).

quiz.q: Hydrolysis of XeF₆ gives:
quiz.why: Complete hydrolysis XeF₆ + 3H₂O → XeO₃ + 6HF keeps Xe in the +6 state.

quiz.q: Oxidation state of Xe in XeO₄:
quiz.why: Four oxide ligands at −2 each give Xe an oxidation state of +8.

questions.q: Basicity of H₃PO₃:
questions.why: H₃PO₃ has two P–OH groups and one non-acidic P–H bond.

questions.q: Volume of 0.1 M NaOH to neutralise 10 mL of 0.1 M H₃PO₂:
questions.why: H₃PO₂ is monobasic, so equal moles of NaOH are needed: 10 mL.

questions.q: Most basic hydride:
questions.why: The lone pair on small N is most available for protonation.

questions.q: Dilute HNO₃ with Cu mainly gives:
questions.why: 3Cu + 8HNO₃(dil) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O.

questions.q: Peroxodisulphuric acid contains:
questions.why: Marshall's acid H₂S₂O₈ has two SO₃H groups linked by a peroxide bridge.

questions.q: Thiosulphate reacts with I₂ to form:
questions.why: 2S₂O₃²⁻ + I₂ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2I⁻ is the basis of iodometric titrations.

questions.q: Shape of BrF₃:
questions.why: Br has three bonds and two equatorial lone pairs, giving a T-shaped molecule.

questions.q: Conjugate base most stabilised by resonance:
questions.why: ClO₄⁻ delocalises its negative charge over four equivalent oxygens.

questions.q: Cyanogen in alkali gives:
questions.why: Like Cl₂, cyanogen disproportionates in base to cyanide and cyanate.

questions.q: Lone pairs on Xe in XeF₂:
questions.why: Xe has 8 valence electrons, uses 2 in bonds and keeps 6, i.e. 3 lone pairs.

questions.q: Shape of XeOF₄:
questions.why: Five bonded atoms and one lone pair (SN 6) give a square pyramidal shape.

questions.q: Helium is preferred to N₂ in deep-sea diving mixtures because:
options: It is less soluble in blood
questions.why: Helium's low solubility in blood reduces the risk of decompression sickness and nitrogen narcosis.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Coordination chemistry: nomenclature, isomerism, VBT and CFT
courses.summary: Werner's theory, IUPAC nomenclature, the EAN rule, structural and stereoisomerism, valence bond theory of complexes, and crystal field splitting in octahedral and tetrahedral fields with CFSE and the spectrochemical series.
outcomes: Name complexes using IUPAC rules and write formulas from names
Identify and count geometrical and optical isomers
Predict hybridisation and magnetism of complexes with VBT
Calculate CFSE and decide high-spin versus low-spin configurations

scenes.text: Alfred Werner had a series of CoCl₃·nNH₃ salts: yellow, purple, green and violet. Silver nitrate precipitated different amounts of AgCl from each.
Explaining them with primary and secondary valencies won him the 1913 Nobel Prize.

steps.title: Werner's theory
steps.body:
- Primary valency = oxidation state (ionisable, satisfied by anions).
- Secondary valency = coordination number (non-ionisable, directed in space).
- CoCl₃·6NH₃ = [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ → 3 AgCl; CoCl₃·5NH₃ = [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ → 2 AgCl; CoCl₃·4NH₃ = [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl → 1 AgCl (green trans, violet cis).

steps.title: IUPAC naming rules
steps.body:
1. Cation first, then anion.
2. Inside the complex: ligands alphabetically (ignore prefixes di-, tri-), then metal.
3. Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido, oxalato; neutral: aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl; en = ethane-1,2-diamine.
4. Use bis-, tris- for ligands with numbers in their names.
5. Oxidation state in Roman numerals; anionic complexes end in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, plumbate, stannate).
Examples: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II); [Co(en)₂Cl₂]Cl dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) chloride; [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] diamminedichloridoplatinum(II).

steps.title: Solved: EAN rule
steps.body:
EAN = Z(metal) − oxidation state + 2 × (number of ligand donor pairs).
- [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: 26 − 2 + 12 = **36** (Kr) ✔
- [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: 27 − 3 + 12 = **36** ✔
- [Ni(CO)₄]: 28 − 0 + 8 = **36** ✔
- [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻: 26 − 3 + 12 = 35 — complexes need not obey EAN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Alphabetising by the prefix (tetraammine sorts under 'a').
- Writing 'ferrate' for cationic iron complexes.
- Counting a bidentate ligand as one donor pair in EAN (en gives two pairs).

activity.prompt: Match each complex with its IUPAC name.

quiz.q: Moles of AgCl precipitated by 1 mol [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ with excess AgNO₃:
quiz.why: Only the two chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are ionisable and precipitate as AgCl.

quiz.q: EAN of Cr in [Cr(CO)₆]:
quiz.why: 24 − 0 + 2 × 6 = 36, matching the krypton configuration.

quiz.q: Oxidation state of Fe in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]:
quiz.why: Three oxalate ligands contribute −6 and three K⁺ contribute +3, so Fe must be +3 for neutrality.

scenes.text: cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin) is a frontline anticancer drug; the trans isomer is clinically ineffective.
Same atoms, same bonds — only the arrangement differs.

steps.title: Structural isomerism
steps.body:
- **Ionisation**: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ (red-violet, gives BaSO₄) vs [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br (red, gives AgBr).
- **Hydrate**: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet), [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (light green), [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green).
- **Linkage**: ambidentate ligands, –NO₂ (nitrito-N) vs –ONO (nitrito-O); SCN⁻/NCS⁻.
- **Coordination**: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] vs [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆].

steps.title: Stereoisomerism
steps.body:
- Square planar MA₂B₂: cis and trans (tetrahedral MA₂B₂ has none).
- Octahedral MA₄B₂: cis, trans. MA₃B₃: fac (three B on one face) and mer (meridian).
- Optical isomers need no mirror plane/centre: [M(AA)₃] (e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺) and cis-[M(AA)₂B₂] are chiral; trans-[M(AA)₂B₂] has a mirror plane and is achiral.

steps.title: Solved: counting stereoisomers
steps.body:
- [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺: cis + trans = **2**, neither optically active
- [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺: trans (achiral) + cis pair (d, l) = **3**
- [Co(en)₃]³⁺: Δ and Λ = **2** (optical)
- [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃]: fac + mer = **2**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assigning cis/trans to tetrahedral complexes.
- Forgetting the optical pair of the cis isomer.
- Calling ionisation isomers 'hydrate' isomers when the exchanged species is not water.

activity.prompt: Match each pair to its type of isomerism.

quiz.q: Total stereoisomers of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺:
quiz.why: There is one achiral trans form and a pair of non-superimposable cis enantiomers, giving three.

quiz.q: Which shows linkage isomerism?
quiz.why: Thiocyanate can bind through S or through N, so it is ambidentate.

quiz.q: Tetrahedral [ZnCl₂Br₂]²⁻ has how many geometrical isomers?
quiz.why: All four tetrahedral positions are adjacent to each other, so only one arrangement of MA₂B₂ exists.

scenes.text: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is attracted to a magnet; [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is not.
VBT says cyanide forces electrons to pair, freeing inner d orbitals for hybridisation.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- Ligands donate lone pairs into empty hybrid orbitals of the metal.
- CN 4: sp³ (tetrahedral) or dsp² (square planar); CN 6: d²sp³ (inner-orbital, low spin) or sp³d² (outer-orbital, high spin).
- Strong ligands (CN⁻, CO) pair electrons; weak ligands (H₂O, F⁻) do not.
- Magnetism from unpaired electrons: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM.

steps.title: Solved: iron(II) complexes
steps.body:
Fe²⁺ = 3d⁶.
- [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺: no pairing → 4 unpaired → **sp³d², outer-orbital, 4.90 BM**
- [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: pair into three 3d orbitals → two 3d free → **d²sp³, inner-orbital, diamagnetic**

steps.title: Solved: nickel(II) complexes
steps.body:
Ni²⁺ = 3d⁸.
- [NiCl₄]²⁻: weak Cl⁻ → **sp³, tetrahedral, 2 unpaired (2.83 BM)**
- [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: CN⁻ pairs the electrons, freeing one 3d → **dsp², square planar, diamagnetic**
- [Ni(CO)₄]: Ni(0) 3d⁸4s² → 3d¹⁰ → **sp³, tetrahedral, diamagnetic**

steps.title: Limitations of VBT
steps.body: Cannot explain colours/spectra, gives no quantitative energies, cannot explain why some ligands are strong and others weak, and fails to account for temperature-dependent magnetism or the magnitude of orbital contributions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 4s electrons when forming M²⁺ ions.
- Assigning dsp² to [NiCl₄]²⁻.
- Forgetting that inner-orbital complexes use (n − 1)d orbitals.

activity.prompt: Match each complex to its VBT hybridisation.

quiz.q: Magnetic moment of [CoF₆]³⁻ (Co³⁺ d⁶, high spin):
quiz.why: Weak-field F⁻ leaves four unpaired electrons, so μ = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.

quiz.q: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar because:
options: CN⁻ pairs electrons, freeing a 3d orbital for dsp²
quiz.why: Strong-field cyanide forces pairing of the eight d electrons, leaving one 3d orbital for dsp² hybridisation.

quiz.q: VBT fails to explain:
quiz.why: VBT does not consider d-orbital splitting, so it cannot explain the absorption of visible light.

lessons.title: Crystal field theory: splitting, CFSE and spectrochemical series

story.title: The colour of ruby and emerald

scenes.text: Both ruby and emerald owe their colour to Cr³⁺ ions — red in one, green in the other.
A slightly different crystal field shifts which colour of light Cr³⁺ absorbs.

steps.title: Octahedral splitting
steps.body:
Six point-charge ligands along ±x, ±y, ±z raise d orbitals pointing at them.
- e_g (dx²−y², dz²): +0.6 Δo
- t₂g (dxy, dyz, dxz): −0.4 Δo
- CFSE = (−0.4 n_t₂g + 0.6 n_eg) Δo (+ pairing energy P for each extra pair)
- If Δo > P → low spin; if Δo < P → high spin (choice exists only for d⁴–d⁷).

steps.title: Tetrahedral and square planar
steps.body:
- Tetrahedral: inverted pattern; e (dz², dx²−y²) lower at −0.6 Δt, t₂ higher at +0.4 Δt; Δt ≈ (4/9) Δo → almost always high spin.
- Square planar: strong splitting with dx²−y² highest — favoured by d⁸ ions with strong fields (Ni²⁺ with CN⁻, Pd²⁺, Pt²⁺).

steps.title: Spectrochemical series
steps.body:
I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < NH₃ < en < bipy < NO₂⁻ < CN⁻ < CO
Δ also increases with oxidation state (Co³⁺ > Co²⁺) and down a group (3d < 4d < 5d).

steps.title: Solved: CFSE
steps.body:
- d⁴ high spin (t₂g³e_g¹): −1.2 + 0.6 = **−0.6 Δo**
- d⁴ low spin (t₂g⁴): **−1.6 Δo + P**
- d⁶ low spin [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ (t₂g⁶): **−2.4 Δo + 2P**
- d³ [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺: **−1.2 Δo**

steps.title: Solved: Δo from spectrum
steps.body:
[Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs at 20 300 cm⁻¹ (≈ 493 nm, green-yellow) and appears purple.
- Δo = 20 300 cm⁻¹ × 0.01196 kJ mol⁻¹ per cm⁻¹ = **243 kJ mol⁻¹**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying high/low-spin choice to d¹–d³ or d⁸–d¹⁰ octahedral ions.
- Using the octahedral splitting pattern for tetrahedral complexes.
- Saying a complex has the colour it absorbs (it shows the complementary colour).

activity.prompt: Arrange these ligands from weakest to strongest field.

quiz.q: CFSE of d⁶ high-spin octahedral:
Tetrahedral complexes are usually high spin because:
options: Δt is about 4/9 Δo, smaller than P
quiz.why: The small tetrahedral splitting rarely exceeds the pairing energy, so electrons stay unpaired.

quiz.q: Strongest-field ligand:
quiz.why: CO is a strong σ-donor and π-acceptor, placing it at the top of the spectrochemical series.

quiz.q: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ appears purple because it absorbs:
quiz.why: It absorbs around 493 nm, so the transmitted complementary colour looks purple.

questions.q: IUPAC name of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]:
questions.why: Ligands are listed alphabetically (ammine before chlorido) and a neutral complex keeps the metal name 'platinum'.

questions.q: EAN of Ni in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻:
questions.why: 28 − 2 + 8 = 34, so this complex does not follow the EAN rule.

questions.q: Ionisation isomers differ in:
questions.why: Ionisation isomers swap a coordinated anion with the counter-ion, giving different ions in solution.

questions.q: fac/mer isomerism is shown by:
questions.why: An octahedral MA₃B₃ complex can place the three B ligands on one face (fac) or along a meridian (mer).

questions.q: Optically active complex:
questions.why: The cis isomer lacks a mirror plane, so it exists as non-superimposable mirror images.

questions.q: Hybridisation of [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ (diamagnetic):
questions.why: Co³⁺ d⁶ is paired by NH₃, leaving two inner 3d orbitals for d²sp³ hybridisation.

questions.q: Spin-only moment of [NiCl₄]²⁻:
questions.why: Tetrahedral Ni²⁺ d⁸ with weak-field Cl⁻ has two unpaired electrons, so μ = √8 ≈ 2.83 BM.

questions.q: CFSE of d⁵ low spin octahedral (ignoring P):
questions.why: t₂g⁵ gives 5 × (−0.4) = −2.0 Δo.

questions.q: Δt in terms of Δo is about:
questions.why: With only four ligands not pointing directly at orbitals, Δt ≈ 4/9 of Δo for the same metal and ligand.

questions.q: Δo increases in the order:
questions.why: A higher oxidation state draws ligands closer and increases the crystal field splitting.

questions.q: Δo for an absorption at 25 000 cm⁻¹:
Which ligand is ambidentate?
questions.why: Nitrite can coordinate through N (nitro) or O (nitrito), giving linkage isomers.

courses.title: Unit 5 · CFT applications, revision & practicals
courses.summary: Applications of crystal field theory (Jahn–Teller distortion, colour, magnetism, spinels, chelate effect), complexometric EDTA titration for water hardness, semi-micro qualitative analysis of cations, and a full revision sheet with a paper-level exam.
outcomes: Predict Jahn–Teller distortions and explain the chelate effect
Use CFSE to explain hydration enthalpy trends and normal/inverse spinels
Determine water hardness by EDTA titration
Separate and identify cation groups in qualitative analysis

lessons.title: Jahn–Teller effect, chelate effect and spinels

scenes.text: X-ray data show [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has four short Cu–O bonds and two long ones.
An unevenly filled e_g set makes the octahedron distort to lower its energy.

steps.title: Jahn–Teller theorem
steps.body:
A non-linear molecule in a degenerate electronic state distorts to remove the degeneracy.
- Strong distortion when e_g is unevenly occupied: d⁹ (Cu²⁺), high-spin d⁴ (Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺), low-spin d⁷.
- Usually tetragonal elongation (z-out): dz² lowered, dx²−y² raised.
- Weak (t₂g) effects for d¹, d², low-spin d⁴, d⁵ — often not observed structurally.

steps.title: Chelate effect
steps.body:
Complexes of polydentate ligands are much more stable than those of equivalent monodentate ligands, largely for entropy reasons:
[Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 3en → [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ + 6NH₃ — 4 particles become 7, so ΔS > 0.
log β: [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ ≈ 8.6, [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ ≈ 18.3. Five-membered chelate rings are the most stable. EDTA⁴⁻ (hexadentate) forms very stable 1 : 1 complexes with most metal ions.

steps.title: CFSE applications
steps.body:
- **Hydration enthalpy** of M²⁺ (Ca to Zn) shows a double hump: d⁰, d⁵ (high spin) and d¹⁰ lie on a smooth line (CFSE = 0); others are more exothermic by their CFSE.
- **Spinels** AB₂O₄: normal (A²⁺ tetrahedral, B³⁺ octahedral), e.g. MgAl₂O₄, Mn₃O₄. Inverse when B³⁺ has no octahedral preference but A²⁺ does: **Fe₃O₄** is inverse because Fe²⁺ (d⁶) gains octahedral site preference energy while Fe³⁺ (d⁵) has none.

steps.title: Solved: will it distort?
steps.body:
- [Cr(H₂O)₆]²⁺: Cr²⁺ d⁴ high spin, t₂g³e_g¹ → **strong J–T**
- [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺: d⁸ t₂g⁶e_g² → e_g evenly filled → **no J–T**
- [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺: d⁹ → **elongated**
- [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺: d⁵ high spin → **none**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting Jahn–Teller distortion for d³, d⁸ or high-spin d⁵ ions.
- Explaining the chelate effect only by enthalpy.
- Calling Fe₃O₄ a normal spinel.

activity.prompt: Match each ion (octahedral, weak field) to its Jahn–Teller behaviour.

quiz.q: Main driving force of the chelate effect:
quiz.why: Replacing several monodentate ligands by one chelate releases more free molecules, increasing the entropy of the system.

quiz.q: Fe₃O₄ is an inverse spinel because:
options: Fe²⁺ gains octahedral site preference while Fe³⁺ d⁵ has none
quiz.why: High-spin Fe³⁺ has zero CFSE in any site, whereas Fe²⁺ d⁶ gains CFSE in octahedral sites, so Fe²⁺ takes octahedral positions.

quiz.q: Strong Jahn–Teller distortion is expected for:
quiz.why: d⁹ has an uneven e_g occupancy (e_g³), which is strongly stabilised by distortion.

lessons.title: Lab: Hardness of water by EDTA titration

scenes.text: White crust forms inside kettles in hard-water cities.
A 30-minute EDTA titration tells exactly how many ppm of CaCO₃ equivalent the tap water contains.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
M²⁺ + H₂Y²⁻ → MY²⁻ + 2H⁺ (1 : 1 for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺).
Buffer pH 10 (NH₃–NH₄Cl). Indicator Eriochrome Black T (EBT): wine-red with Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺, blue when free. End point: wine red → **blue**.
Hardness (ppm as CaCO₃) = (M_EDTA × V_EDTA × 100.09 × 1000)/V_sample (V in mL).

steps.title: Solved: total hardness
steps.body:
50.0 mL tap water needed 8.0 mL of 0.010 M EDTA.
- Moles EDTA = 0.010 × 0.0080 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ = moles of Ca + Mg
- Mass as CaCO₃ = 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 100.09 = 8.0 × 10⁻³ g = 8.0 mg in 50 mL
- Per litre: 8.0 × 20 = **160 mg L⁻¹ ≈ 160 ppm** (hard water)

steps.title: Solved: temporary vs permanent
steps.body:
After boiling and filtering, 50.0 mL needs 5.0 mL of 0.010 M EDTA → permanent hardness = **100 ppm**.
Temporary hardness = 160 − 100 = **60 ppm** (removed as CaCO₃/Mg(OH)₂ on boiling).

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body:
- Why pH 10? EBT shows the right colour change and Ca/Mg–EDTA complexes are stable there.
- Why is a little Mg–EDTA added when only Ca²⁺ is present? EBT gives a sharp end point with Mg²⁺.
- Disodium salt Na₂H₂Y·2H₂O (372.24 g mol⁻¹) is used because the free acid is poorly soluble. 0.01 M in 250 mL needs 0.931 g.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the buffer (end point drifts).
- Reporting mg per 50 mL instead of per litre.
- Titrating too fast near the end point — the colour change is slow.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the EDTA hardness determination.
items: Pipette 50.0 mL water sample into a conical flask
Add a pinch of EBT indicator (wine red)
Titrate with 0.01 M EDTA until the colour turns blue
Calculate hardness in ppm as CaCO₃

quiz.q: EBT colour at the end point:
quiz.why: When all Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ is bound to EDTA, EBT is released in its free blue form.

quiz.q: 100 mL water needs 12.0 mL of 0.01 M EDTA; hardness is:
quiz.why: 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 100.09 g mol⁻¹ = 12.0 mg in 100 mL, which is 120 mg L⁻¹.

quiz.q: Stoichiometry of EDTA with Ca²⁺:
quiz.why: EDTA is hexadentate and wraps one metal ion, forming 1 : 1 complexes.

scenes.text: In the practical exam Divya receives a pale green salt and 3 hours.
By systematic group separation she identifies Fe²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ — ferrous sulphate.

steps.title: Group separation scheme
steps.body:
| Group | Reagent | Cations | Precipitate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | NaOH, heat | NH₄⁺ | NH₃ gas |
| I | dil. HCl | Pb²⁺, Ag⁺, Hg₂²⁺ | Chlorides |
| II | H₂S in dil. HCl | Cu²⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺, Cd²⁺, As, Sb, Sn | Sulphides |
| III | NH₄Cl + NH₄OH | Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Cr³⁺ | Hydroxides |
| IV | H₂S in NH₄OH | Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, Co²⁺ | Sulphides |
| V | (NH₄)₂CO₃ in NH₄OH | Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ca²⁺ | Carbonates |
| VI | — | Mg²⁺, (Na⁺, K⁺) | Mg as MgNH₄PO₄ |

steps.title: Why the conditions matter
steps.body:
- Group II: low [S²⁻] in acid (common-ion effect of H⁺) precipitates only sulphides with very low Ksp.
- Group III: NH₄Cl suppresses NH₄OH ionisation so Mg(OH)₂ and group IV hydroxides stay dissolved; Fe²⁺ must be oxidised to Fe³⁺ with conc. HNO₃ first.
- Group IV: ammoniacal medium raises [S²⁻] for ZnS, MnS, NiS, CoS.

steps.title: Confirmatory tests
steps.body:
- Fe³⁺: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] → Prussian blue; KSCN → blood red
- Cu²⁺: NH₄OH excess → deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺; K₄[Fe(CN)₆] → chocolate brown
- Ni²⁺: dimethylglyoxime in NH₃ → rosy red
- Zn²⁺: white ZnS; with K₄[Fe(CN)₆] bluish-white
- Al³⁺: lake test (blue lake with litmus)
- Ba²⁺: K₂CrO₄ → yellow BaCrO₄; apple-green flame

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the oxidation of Fe²⁺ before group III.
- Adding too much HCl in group II (CdS may not precipitate).
- Not removing H₂S by boiling before group III.

activity.prompt: Order the group reagents in the standard cation analysis scheme.

quiz.q: Why is NH₄Cl added before NH₄OH in group III?
options: To suppress OH⁻ so only group III hydroxides precipitate
quiz.why: The common ion NH₄⁺ lowers [OH⁻] enough that only very insoluble Fe, Al and Cr hydroxides precipitate.

quiz.q: Rosy-red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime indicates:
quiz.why: Ni²⁺ forms the characteristic red bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II) chelate.

quiz.q: Blood-red colour with KSCN shows:
quiz.why: Fe³⁺ forms intensely red thiocyanato complexes such as [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺.

scenes.text: Varun has one evening to revise the whole Inorganic II paper.
A one-page sheet plus a set of typical long questions is his plan.

steps.title: Key-point sheet
steps.body:
- s-block: Li strongest reductant (hydration); oxides Li₂O/Na₂O₂/KO₂; group 2 carbonate stability ↑, sulphate solubility ↓, hydroxide solubility ↑
- Diborane: 4 terminal 2c–2e + 2 bridging 3c–2e; Wade: n+1 closo, n+2 nido, n+3 arachno
- BX₃ acidity BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ < BI₃ (back-bonding)
- Silicate formulas: SiO₄⁴⁻, Si₂O₇⁶⁻, (SiO₃)²⁻, (Si₄O₁₁)⁶⁻, (Si₂O₅)²⁻, SiO₂
- P oxoacid basicity = number of P–OH
- Xe compounds: XeF₂ linear, XeF₄ square planar, XeF₆ distorted octahedral, XeO₃ pyramidal
- EAN = Z − OS + 2 × donor pairs; CFSE = (−0.4 t + 0.6 e)Δo + nP; Δt = 4/9 Δo
- μ = √[n(n + 2)]; Δ(kJ mol⁻¹) = 0.01196 × wavenumber (cm⁻¹)

steps.title: Typical long questions (practise)
steps.body:
1. Describe the structure and bonding of diborane. How does it react with NH₃ and CO?
2. Classify silicates with one example each and draw their basic units.
3. Explain why BF₃ is a weaker Lewis acid than BCl₃.
4. Discuss the preparation, structure and hydrolysis of XeF₆.
5. Using CFT, explain why [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is diamagnetic while [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is paramagnetic. Calculate CFSE for both.
6. Explain the Jahn–Teller effect with Cu²⁺ complexes.

steps.title: Worked short answer
steps.body:
Q: Calculate CFSE of [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ and [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
- Low spin d⁶ (t₂g⁶): −2.4 Δo + 2P (two extra pairs vs high spin)
- High spin d⁶ (t₂g⁴e_g²): −0.4 Δo
The large Δo of CN⁻ exceeds P, so pairing is favoured and the complex is diamagnetic.

steps.title: Exam traps
steps.body:
- Name anionic complexes with -ate (ferrate, cuprate).
- Basicity of H₃PO₃ is 2, of H₃PO₂ is 1.
- KO₂ is paramagnetic; Na₂O₂ is diamagnetic.

activity.prompt: Match the formula to the correct fact.

quiz.q: Wade's n + 1 skeletal pairs gives:
quiz.why: n + 1 skeletal electron pairs correspond to a closed polyhedron, the closo type.

quiz.q: Which superoxide is commonly used in breathing sets?
quiz.why: KO₂ absorbs CO₂ and releases O₂, making it suitable for closed breathing systems.

quiz.q: CFSE of d⁸ octahedral:

questions.q: Strongest reducing agent in water:
questions.why: Li has the most negative E° because of the very high hydration enthalpy of Li⁺.

questions.q: Bridging hydrogens in B₂H₆:
questions.why: Diborane has two bridging H atoms forming two 3c–2e bonds.

questions.q: B₅H₁₁ is:
questions.why: B₅H₁₁ fits BₙHₙ₊₆, giving n + 3 skeletal pairs, i.e. arachno.

questions.q: Silicone resins are cross-linked using:
questions.why: CH₃SiCl₃ hydrolyses to three Si–OH groups that link chains in three directions.

questions.q: Shape of XeF₄:
questions.why: Two lone pairs trans to each other on an octahedron leave four F in a square plane.

questions.q: Total stereoisomers of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺:
questions.why: One achiral trans and two optically active cis forms make three.

questions.q: Hybridisation in [CoF₆]³⁻:
questions.why: Weak-field F⁻ does not pair electrons, so outer 4d orbitals are used: sp³d².

questions.q: CFSE of d³ octahedral:
questions.why: Three t₂g electrons give 3 × (−0.4) = −1.2 Δo.

questions.q: Jahn–Teller distortion is not expected for:
questions.why: Octahedral Ni²⁺ d⁸ has evenly filled e_g orbitals (e_g²), so there is no degeneracy to remove.

questions.q: [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is more stable than [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ mainly due to:
questions.why: Replacing six NH₃ with three en releases extra molecules, raising entropy and the stability constant.

questions.q: 50 mL water needs 6.0 mL of 0.01 M EDTA; hardness:
questions.why: 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 100.09 g mol⁻¹ = 6.0 mg in 50 mL, i.e. 120 mg L⁻¹ ≈ 120 ppm.

questions.q: Group II cations are precipitated with H₂S in acid because:
options: Low [S²⁻] precipitates only very insoluble sulphides
questions.why: H⁺ suppresses H₂S ionisation, so only sulphides with very small Ksp exceed their solubility product.

questions.q: Prussian blue forms when Fe³⁺ reacts with:
questions.why: Fe³⁺ with hexacyanidoferrate(II) gives the deep blue Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃.

questions.q: Fe₃O₄ is:
questions.why: Fe²⁺ prefers octahedral sites due to CFSE, so half the Fe³⁺ moves to tetrahedral sites.

questions.q: Most acidic chlorine oxoacid:
questions.why: Perchloric acid has the most stabilised conjugate base, ClO₄⁻.

uni-bsc-chem-organic-1.title: B.Sc Chemistry · Organic Chemistry I (basics, stereochemistry, hydrocarbons)
uni-bsc-chem-organic-1.description: Electronic effects, reactive intermediates and reaction types, stereochemistry (chirality, R/S, E/Z, conformations), alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, aromaticity and electrophilic aromatic substitution, with purification and melting-point practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Basics of organic chemistry
courses.summary: Hybridisation and bond properties, electronic displacement effects (inductive, electromeric, resonance, hyperconjugation), acidity and basicity, reactive intermediates (carbocations, carbanions, free radicals, carbenes) and types of organic reactions with curved-arrow notation.
outcomes: Use inductive, resonance and hyperconjugative effects to rank acidity, basicity and intermediate stability
Compare stabilities of carbocations, carbanions and radicals
Classify reactions as substitution, addition, elimination or rearrangement
Draw correct curved-arrow mechanisms showing homolytic and heterolytic fission

scenes.text: Acetic acid in vinegar is mild (pKa 4.76); trichloroacetic acid, used to remove warts, is about 10 000 times stronger.
Three chlorines pull electron density away and stabilise the carboxylate — the inductive effect at work.

steps.title: Inductive effect (I)
steps.body:
Permanent polarisation of σ bonds due to electronegativity differences; falls off rapidly with distance (negligible after ≈ 3 bonds).
- −I groups (withdraw): –NO₂ > –CN > –COOH > –F > –Cl > –Br > –I > –OCH₃ > –C₆H₅
- +I groups (donate): –C(CH₃)₃ > –CH(CH₃)₂ > –CH₂CH₃ > –CH₃; –COO⁻, –O⁻
**Electromeric effect (E)**: temporary, complete transfer of a π pair to one atom on demand of an attacking reagent (+E toward the reagent, −E away).

steps.title: Solved: acidity of chloroacetic acids
steps.body:
| Acid | pKa |
|---|---|
| CH₃COOH | 4.76 |
| ClCH₂COOH | 2.86 |
| Cl₂CHCOOH | 1.29 |
| Cl₃CCOOH | 0.65 |
More −I groups → more stable carboxylate → stronger acid.
Distance: CH₃CH₂CHClCOOH (pKa ≈ 2.8) ≫ ClCH₂CH₂CH₂COOH (≈ 4.5).

steps.title: Solved: basicity of amines in water
steps.body:
pKb: NH₃ 4.75; CH₃NH₂ 3.36; (CH₃)₂NH 3.27; (CH₃)₃N 4.20.
+I effect raises basicity, but in water the tertiary amine is weaker than expected because its protonated form is poorly solvated (fewer N–H for H-bonding) and is sterically crowded. In the gas phase the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the inductive effect transmits strongly over long chains.
- Calling electromeric effects permanent.
- Predicting 3° amines are the strongest bases in water.

activity.prompt: Arrange these acids from weakest to strongest.

quiz.q: Strongest acid:
quiz.why: Fluorine has the strongest −I effect of the halogens, so it best stabilises the carboxylate anion.

quiz.q: Most basic amine in water:
quiz.why: Dimethylamine balances +I donation with good solvation of its conjugate acid, giving the lowest pKb in water.

quiz.q: The electromeric effect is:
quiz.why: It occurs only when an attacking reagent demands electrons from a π bond and disappears when the reagent is removed.

story.title: Why phenol is acidic but ethanol is not

scenes.text: Phenol (pKa 10) was once used as the antiseptic carbolic acid; ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is barely acidic.
Phenoxide spreads its negative charge into the ring through resonance; ethoxide cannot.

steps.title: Resonance (mesomeric, M) effect
steps.body:
Delocalisation of π or lone-pair electrons through conjugation.
- +M (donate): –OH, –OR, –NH₂, –NHCOR, halogens (weak +M)
- −M (withdraw): –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH
Rules for contributors: same atom positions, same number of paired electrons; more covalent bonds, complete octets and negative charge on the more electronegative atom make a contributor more important. Resonance energy of benzene ≈ 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (from hydrogenation: 3 × 120 = 360 expected vs 208 observed).

steps.title: Hyperconjugation
steps.body:
Delocalisation of σ(C–H) electrons of an α-carbon into an adjacent empty p orbital or π system ('no-bond resonance').
- Number of hyperconjugative structures = number of α-H atoms.
- Explains: stability (CH₃)₃C⁺ (9 α-H) > (CH₃)₂CH⁺ (6) > CH₃CH₂⁺ (3) > CH₃⁺; alkene stability (more substituted more stable); shorter C–C bond in propene's CH₃–C.

steps.title: Solved: acidity of substituted phenols
steps.body:
pKa: phenol 10.0; p-nitrophenol 7.15; p-cresol 10.3; p-methoxyphenol ≈ 10.2.
- –NO₂ at para withdraws by −I and −M, delocalising the phenoxide charge onto the nitro oxygens → much more acidic.
- –CH₃ (+I, hyperconjugation) and –OCH₃ (+M at para) destabilise the anion → less acidic.
- m-Nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 8.4) is less acidic than para — only −I operates at meta.

steps.title: Solved: counting α-hydrogens
steps.body:
Stability of alkenes by hyperconjugation:
- (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂: 12 α-H (most stable)
- (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃: 9 α-H
- CH₃CH=CHCH₃: 6 α-H
- CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂: 2 α-H
Heats of hydrogenation decrease in the same order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating resonance structures as real, rapidly interconverting species — the molecule is a single hybrid.
- Moving atoms (not electrons) between contributors.
- Counting hydrogens on the carbocation carbon itself as α-H.

activity.prompt: Arrange carbocations from least to most stable.

quiz.q: Most acidic:
quiz.why: A para nitro group stabilises the phenoxide by both −I and −M effects, giving the lowest pKa.

quiz.q: Hyperconjugative structures for (CH₃)₂CH⁺:
quiz.why: Two methyl groups supply six α-hydrogens, each giving one hyperconjugative structure.

quiz.q: Halogens on benzene show:
quiz.why: Halogens withdraw through σ bonds (−I) but donate lone pairs into the ring (+M).

scenes.text: Most carbocations survive less than a microsecond in solution.
Yet knowing which intermediate forms tells you the product — and whether it will rearrange.

steps.title: Carbocations
steps.body:
- sp², planar, empty p orbital, 6 electrons.
- Stability: benzyl ≈ allyl > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (resonance, hyperconjugation, +I); vinyl and aryl cations are very unstable.
- Rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl shifts to more stable cations (e.g. 3,3-dimethyl-2-butyl cation → 2,3-dimethyl-2-butyl cation by methyl shift).

steps.title: Carbanions, radicals and carbenes
steps.body:
- **Carbanions**: sp³ pyramidal (or sp² if conjugated), 8 electrons. Stability: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3° (opposite to cations); stabilised by −I/−M groups and s-character (HC≡C⁻ more stable than CH₃CH₂⁻).
- **Free radicals**: 7 electrons, near-planar; stability benzyl ≈ allyl > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; formed by homolysis (light, peroxides).
- **Carbenes** (:CH₂): 6 electrons, neutral. Singlet (paired, sp², bent ≈ 103°) adds stereospecifically to alkenes; triplet (two unpaired, more stable for CH₂) adds non-stereospecifically. Dichlorocarbene from CHCl₃ + base (Reimer–Tiemann).

steps.title: Solved: predicting a rearrangement
steps.body:
Protonation of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene with HCl:
- H⁺ adds to C1 → 2° cation at C2 (next to C(CH₃)₃)
- 1,2-methyl shift from C3 → 3° cation at C3
- Cl⁻ attacks → **2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane** (major), not 3-chloro-2,2-dimethylbutane.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying carbocation stability order to carbanions.
- Forgetting possible hydride/alkyl shifts in SN1/E1 and HX additions.
- Calling carbenes charged species.

activity.prompt: Match the intermediate with its key feature.

quiz.q: Most stable carbanion:
quiz.why: Alkyl groups donate electrons (+I), destabilising a negative charge, so the methyl carbanion is the most stable.

quiz.q: Geometry of a carbocation:
quiz.why: The cationic carbon is sp² hybridised with an empty p orbital, so it is trigonal planar.

quiz.q: Dichlorocarbene is generated from:
quiz.why: Base removes H⁺ from CHCl₃ to give CCl₃⁻, which loses Cl⁻ to form :CCl₂.

lessons.title: Bond fission, reagents and reaction types

scenes.text: Priya's mechanism answers lose marks because her curved arrows start from atoms, not electron pairs.
Once she learns that arrows show electron movement, mechanisms become logical.

steps.title: Bond fission
steps.body:
- **Homolytic**: each atom takes one electron → radicals (fish-hook arrows); favoured by light, heat, non-polar solvents, peroxides.
- **Heterolytic**: one atom takes both → ions (full arrows); favoured by polar solvents and polar bonds.
Curved arrows start at a lone pair or bond and point to where the pair goes.

steps.title: Reagents
steps.body:
- **Electrophiles** (electron-seeking): H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br⁺, R⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, SO₃, carbonyl carbon.
- **Nucleophiles** (nucleus-seeking): OH⁻, CN⁻, RO⁻, NH₃, H₂O, ROH, RMgX carbon, alkenes toward strong electrophiles.
- Ambident nucleophiles: CN⁻ (C or N), NO₂⁻ (N or O).

steps.title: Reaction types
steps.body:
- **Substitution**: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻ (nucleophilic); C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ (electrophilic); CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl (free radical).
- **Addition**: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br; HCN to C=O (nucleophilic addition).
- **Elimination**: CH₃CH₂Br + alc. KOH → CH₂=CH₂ (β-elimination).
- **Rearrangement**: pinacol–pinacolone, Beckmann, carbocation shifts.
- Degree of unsaturation: DBE = C − H/2 − X/2 + N/2 + 1.

steps.title: Solved: degree of unsaturation
steps.body:
- C₆H₆: 6 − 3 + 1 = **4** (ring + 3 C=C)
- C₄H₈O: 4 − 4 + 1 = **1** (one ring or one π bond, e.g. butanal or THF)
- C₅H₅N: 5 − 2.5 + 0.5 + 1 = **4** (pyridine)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing arrows from a positive charge or from H⁺ toward a lone pair (arrows go from the nucleophile to the electrophile).
- Classifying NH₃ as an electrophile.
- Forgetting halogens count like H in the DBE formula.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction to its type.

quiz.q: Which is an electrophile?
quiz.why: The nitronium ion is electron-deficient and attacks electron-rich aromatic rings.

quiz.q: Degree of unsaturation of C₇H₈:
quiz.why: 7 − 8/2 + 1 = 4, consistent with toluene's ring plus three C=C bonds.

quiz.q: Homolytic fission produces:
quiz.why: In homolysis each fragment keeps one electron of the bond, giving radicals.

questions.q: Strongest −I group:
questions.why: The nitro group with its positive nitrogen is one of the strongest electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.q: pKa of ClCH₂COOH is about:
questions.why: One chlorine lowers the pKa of acetic acid from 4.76 to about 2.86 by −I stabilisation.

questions.q: Benzene's resonance energy from hydrogenation data (expected 360, observed 208 kJ mol⁻¹):
questions.why: 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ is the extra stability due to delocalisation.

questions.q: Most stable alkene:
questions.why: The tetrasubstituted alkene has 12 α-H atoms and the greatest hyperconjugative stabilisation.

questions.q: m-Nitrophenol is less acidic than p-nitrophenol because at meta:
questions.why: Resonance cannot delocalise the phenoxide charge onto a meta nitro group, so only the weaker −I effect helps.

questions.q: Hybridisation of carbon in a methyl free radical:
questions.why: The methyl radical is nearly planar with the odd electron in a p orbital, consistent with sp².

questions.q: Carbocation rearrangement in HCl addition to 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene occurs by:
questions.why: A methyl group migrates from the quaternary carbon to convert the 2° cation into a more stable 3° cation.

questions.q: Singlet carbene addition to cis-2-butene gives:
options: A mixture of cis and trans
questions.why: Singlet carbene adds in one concerted step, so the alkene geometry is retained (stereospecific).

questions.q: Ambident nucleophile:
questions.why: Cyanide can attack through carbon (giving nitriles) or nitrogen (giving isonitriles).

questions.q: Degree of unsaturation of C₄H₆:
questions.why: 4 − 3 + 1 = 2, e.g. but-2-yne or buta-1,3-diene.

questions.q: Free-radical stability order:
questions.why: More alkyl groups stabilise the radical by hyperconjugation, so 3° radicals are most stable.

questions.q: Basicity order of amines in the gas phase:
questions.why: Without solvation effects, basicity follows the +I effect, so tertiary amines are most basic in the gas phase.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Stereochemistry I: chirality and optical isomerism
courses.summary: Projection formulas (Fischer, Newman, sawhorse, wedge), chirality and symmetry elements, optical activity and specific rotation, enantiomers, diastereomers and meso compounds, CIP rules for R/S, D/L nomenclature, racemic mixtures and resolution.
outcomes: Interconvert wedge, Fischer, sawhorse and Newman projections
Identify chiral centres and decide chirality from symmetry elements
Assign R/S configurations using CIP priority rules
Count stereoisomers including meso forms
Calculate specific rotation and enantiomeric excess

scenes.text: Try placing your left glove on your right hand — mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
Many drug molecules are 'handed' too, and the body can tell the two hands apart.

steps.title: Projection formulas
steps.body:
- **Wedge–dash**: solid wedge toward viewer, dashed away.
- **Fischer**: vertical bonds go back, horizontal bonds come forward; main chain vertical, most oxidised carbon at top. Rotating by 180° in-plane keeps configuration; 90° rotation inverts it; one swap of two groups inverts it, two swaps restore it.
- **Sawhorse**: a C–C bond viewed at an angle.
- **Newman**: viewed down a C–C bond; front carbon is a point, rear carbon a circle.

steps.title: Chirality
steps.body:
A molecule is chiral if it is not superimposable on its mirror image. Practical test: it lacks a plane of symmetry (σ), a centre of symmetry (i) and an improper axis (Sₙ).
- A stereocentre (carbon with four different groups) usually makes a molecule chiral, but not always (meso compounds).
- Chirality without stereocentres: allenes with different end groups (abC=C=Cab), substituted biphenyls with bulky ortho groups (atropisomers), helicenes.

steps.title: Solved: is it chiral?
steps.body:
- Butan-2-ol: C2 bears H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅ → **chiral**
- Propan-2-ol: C2 has two CH₃ → achiral
- cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclopropane: has a mirror plane → **achiral (meso)**
- Penta-2,3-diene CH₃CH=C=CHCH₃: no plane of symmetry → **chiral** (axial chirality)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rotating a Fischer projection by 90° and assuming the same molecule.
- Deciding chirality only by counting stereocentres.
- Forgetting that horizontal Fischer bonds point toward the viewer.

activity.prompt: Match the projection operation to its effect on configuration.
pairs: Hold one group, rotate other three cyclically

quiz.q: Which is chiral?
quiz.why: C2 of 2-chlorobutane carries four different groups (H, Cl, CH₃, C₂H₅), and the molecule has no symmetry plane.

quiz.q: In a Fischer projection horizontal bonds point:
quiz.why: By convention the horizontal substituents project toward the viewer and vertical ones away.

quiz.q: A chiral allene requires:
options: Two different groups on each terminal carbon
quiz.why: The terminal substituent planes of an allene are perpendicular, so different groups on each end make the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image.

lessons.title: CIP rules: R/S and D/L configuration

scenes.text: (R)-Limonene smells of oranges; (S)-limonene smells more like turpentine and lemon.
The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules give each hand an unambiguous letter.

steps.title: CIP priority rules
steps.body:
1. Higher atomic number of the directly attached atom → higher priority (I > Br > Cl > S > F > O > N > C > H).
2. If tied, compare the sets of atoms at the next position, outward, at the first point of difference.
3. Multiple bonds are counted as duplicated atoms: –CH=O counts as C(O,O,H); –C≡N as C(N,N,N).
4. Isotopes: higher mass first (D > H).

steps.title: Assigning R/S
steps.body:
- Orient the lowest priority (4) away from you; trace 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise = **R**, anticlockwise = **S**.
- In a Fischer projection: if group 4 is on a vertical bond, read directly; if it is on a horizontal bond, read and then **reverse** the answer.
- R/S is unrelated to the sign of rotation (+/−).
- **D/L** (for sugars and amino acids): in the Fischer projection with the CHO/COOH at top, OH (or NH₂) on the lowest stereocentre on the right = D, left = L. Natural amino acids are L (mostly S); natural sugars are D.

steps.title: Solved: L-alanine
steps.body:
Fischer: COOH top, CH₃ bottom, NH₂ left, H right.
- Priorities: NH₂ (1) > COOH (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4)
- H is horizontal; 1 (left) → 2 (top) → 3 (bottom) traced: left → top → bottom = clockwise → reads R
- Reverse because H is horizontal → **S**. L-Alanine = (S)-alanine ✔

steps.title: Solved: glyceraldehyde
steps.body:
D-Glyceraldehyde: CHO top, CH₂OH bottom, OH right, H left.
- Priorities: OH > CHO (O,O,H) > CH₂OH (O,H,H) > H
- OH (right) → CHO (top) → CH₂OH (bottom): right → top → bottom = anticlockwise → S; reverse (H horizontal) → **R**. D-Glyceraldehyde = (R)-(+)-glyceraldehyde.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ranking by group size or mass of the whole group rather than atomic number at the first point of difference.
- Forgetting to reverse when the lowest priority is on a horizontal Fischer bond.
- Assuming R means dextrorotatory.

activity.prompt: Arrange these groups in decreasing CIP priority.

quiz.q: Higher priority between –CH₂OH and –CHO:
quiz.why: –CHO is treated as C(O,O,H) while –CH₂OH is C(O,H,H), so the aldehyde wins at the first difference.

quiz.q: If the lowest priority is on a horizontal Fischer bond and the sequence appears clockwise, the configuration is:
quiz.why: With group 4 pointing toward the viewer the apparent direction is reversed, so clockwise means S.

quiz.q: R/S notation and sign of rotation are:
quiz.why: R/S comes from a naming rule for 3-D arrangement, whereas the sign of rotation is measured experimentally; they do not correlate.

scenes.text: In 1848 Louis Pasteur separated mirror-image crystals of sodium ammonium tartrate by hand under a microscope.
Tartaric acid also has a third, optically inactive form — the meso isomer.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Enantiomers**: non-superimposable mirror images; identical physical properties except the direction of rotating plane-polarised light and interaction with other chiral species.
- **Diastereomers**: stereoisomers that are not mirror images; different physical properties (m.p., solubility).
- **Meso compound**: has stereocentres but an internal mirror plane → achiral, optically inactive.
- Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ (n stereocentres); fewer if meso forms exist.

steps.title: Solved: tartaric acid
steps.body:
HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH: two similar stereocentres.
- (2R,3R) and (2S,3S): enantiomers (m.p. 170 °C, [α] ±12°)
- (2R,3S): meso (m.p. ≈ 147 °C, [α] = 0)
- Total = **3** (not 4)

steps.title: Solved: 2,3-dihydroxybutanal (aldotetrose)
steps.body: OHC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH₂OH: two **different** stereocentres → no meso → 2² = **4** stereoisomers: D- and L-erythrose, D- and L-threose. Erythrose and threose are diastereomers.

steps.title: Erythro/threo and epimers
steps.body:
- Erythro: similar groups on the same side of a Fischer projection; threo: opposite sides.
- Epimers: diastereomers differing at only one stereocentre (D-glucose and D-mannose at C2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying 2ⁿ blindly to molecules with identical stereocentres.
- Calling a meso compound a racemic mixture (meso is one achiral compound; racemate is a 1 : 1 mixture of enantiomers).
- Thinking diastereomers must contain stereocentres (cis/trans alkenes are diastereomers).

activity.prompt: Match each pair to its relationship.

quiz.q: Number of stereoisomers of 2,3-dibromobutane:
quiz.why: Its two stereocentres are identical, so one (R,S) form is meso, giving three stereoisomers in total.

quiz.q: Meso compounds are optically inactive because:
options: They have an internal plane of symmetry
quiz.why: An internal mirror plane makes one half cancel the optical rotation of the other half.

quiz.q: Stereoisomers of CH₃CHBrCHClCH₃:
quiz.why: The two stereocentres are different (one Br, one Cl), so no meso form exists and 2² = 4.

scenes.text: Thalidomide's tragedy in the 1960s showed how differently enantiomers can act in the body.
Even a single enantiomer can racemise in vivo — which is why chiral analysis matters.

steps.title: Specific rotation
steps.body:
[α]ᵀ_λ = α/(l × c)
- α = observed rotation (degrees), l = path length (dm), c = concentration (g mL⁻¹)
- Usually measured at 589 nm (sodium D line), 20 or 25 °C.
- Dextrorotatory (+, d) or laevorotatory (−, l).

steps.title: Solved: specific rotation
steps.body:
A solution of 2.50 g sucrose in 50.0 mL (c = 0.0500 g mL⁻¹) in a 2.00 dm tube rotates light by +6.65°.
- [α] = 6.65/(2.00 × 0.0500) = **+66.5°** (literature +66.5°) ✔

steps.title: Racemisation and resolution
steps.body:
- **Racemisation**: conversion to a 1 : 1 mixture, e.g. via planar carbocations (SN1) or enolisation of α-chiral carbonyls.
- **Resolution**: (1) form diastereomeric salts with a chiral resolving agent (e.g. (+)-tartaric acid for amines, brucine/strychnine for acids), separate by crystallisation, regenerate; (2) enzymatic (kinetic) resolution; (3) chiral chromatography; (4) mechanical separation (Pasteur).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using path length in cm instead of dm.
- Confusing ee with the percentage of the major enantiomer.
- Trying to separate enantiomers by ordinary crystallisation or distillation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to resolve a racemic carboxylic acid.
items: React the racemic acid with a single enantiomer of a chiral amine
Separate the salts by fractional crystallisation
Treat each salt with mineral acid
Recover each pure enantiomer of the acid

quiz.q: Observed rotation −4.0°, l = 1 dm, c = 0.20 g mL⁻¹; [α] =
A mixture with 80% R and 20% S has ee:
quiz.why: ee = %major − %minor = 80 − 20 = 60%.

quiz.q: Enantiomers can be separated by:
options: Forming diastereomers with a chiral reagent
quiz.why: Diastereomers have different physical properties, so they can be separated by crystallisation and then converted back.

questions.q: Maximum stereoisomers for a molecule with 3 different stereocentres:
questions.why: With no meso possibilities the maximum is 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Which has a plane of symmetry?
questions.why: meso-Tartaric acid has an internal mirror plane between C2 and C3.

questions.q: Priority order:
questions.why: Directly attached atoms are ranked by atomic number: Cl (17) > O (8) > C (6).

questions.q: Natural amino acids are mostly:
questions.why: Natural amino acids are L, which corresponds to S for all except cysteine (R because of sulphur).

questions.q: Swapping two groups on a stereocentre once:
questions.why: A single interchange produces the mirror-image arrangement, inverting R to S.

questions.q: [α] of a compound giving α = +3.0° at c = 0.10 g mL⁻¹ in a 2 dm tube:
Sample with ee 90% contains the minor enantiomer at:
questions.why: Major = 50 + 45 = 95% and minor = 5%, since ee = 95 − 5 = 90%.

questions.q: Erythrose and threose are:
questions.why: They differ in configuration at only one of two stereocentres, so they are diastereomers (not mirror images).

questions.q: Atropisomerism is seen in:
questions.why: Bulky ortho groups prevent rotation around the aryl–aryl bond, so the twisted forms are isolable enantiomers.

questions.q: Racemic mixture is optically inactive because of:
questions.why: Equal amounts of the two enantiomers rotate light equally in opposite directions, which is external compensation.

questions.q: Resolving agent for a racemic amine:
questions.why: An enantiopure acid like (+)-tartaric acid forms separable diastereomeric salts with the amine.

questions.q: D-Glyceraldehyde has configuration:
questions.why: Applying CIP rules to the Fischer projection of D-glyceraldehyde gives the R configuration.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Stereochemistry II: geometrical isomerism and conformations
courses.summary: cis/trans and E/Z isomerism in alkenes, oximes and rings, physical property differences, conformational analysis of ethane and butane with energy profiles, Baeyer strain theory, and the chair conformations of mono- and disubstituted cyclohexanes.
outcomes: Assign E/Z and cis/trans descriptors and count geometrical isomers
Compare dipole moments, melting and boiling points of geometric isomers
Draw energy diagrams for ethane and butane rotation
Predict the preferred chair conformation of substituted cyclohexanes and estimate equilibrium ratios

scenes.text: Fumaric acid is found in many plants and used as a food acid; its isomer maleic acid is more toxic and forms an anhydride easily.
Both are HOOC–CH=CH–COOH — the C=C bond simply cannot rotate.

steps.title: Conditions and nomenclature
steps.body:
Geometrical isomerism arises from restricted rotation (C=C, C=N, rings) when each end carries two different groups.
- **cis/trans**: same/opposite sides — clear only when similar groups are present.
- **E/Z**: rank the two groups on each carbon by CIP rules; higher priorities on the same side = **Z** (zusammen), opposite = **E** (entgegen).
- Number of geometrical isomers for a polyene with n dissimilar-ended double bonds: 2ⁿ (fewer if the ends are identical).

steps.title: Solved: E/Z assignment
steps.body:
CH₃(Cl)C=C(Br)H:
- C1: Cl > CH₃; C2: Br > H
- If Cl and Br are on the same side → **Z**
Note: the same molecule could be called 'trans' if the methyl and H are... — cis/trans is ambiguous here, so E/Z is preferred.

steps.title: Physical properties
steps.body:
| Property | Maleic (cis) | Fumaric (trans) |
|---|---|---|
| m.p. | 135 °C | 287 °C |
| Water solubility | High | Low |
| pKa₁ | 1.9 | 3.0 |
| pKa₂ | 6.1 | 4.4 |
| Anhydride on heating | Yes | No |
- trans isomers pack better → higher m.p.; cis usually more polar → higher b.p. (cis-2-butene 3.7 °C vs trans 0.9 °C).
- Maleic acid's high pKa₂: the monoanion is stabilised by intramolecular H-bonding.

steps.title: Solved: oximes
steps.body: Aldoximes RCH=NOH show syn/anti (or E/Z) isomerism. Beckmann rearrangement of ketoximes is stereospecific — the group anti to OH migrates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming Z always equals cis.
- Expecting geometrical isomers for CH₂=CHCl (one carbon carries two identical H).
- Saying cis isomers always have higher melting points.

activity.prompt: Match each property with maleic or fumaric acid.

quiz.q: Which shows geometrical isomerism?
quiz.why: In but-2-ene each alkene carbon has two different groups (H and CH₃), allowing cis and trans forms.

quiz.q: In (Z)-alkenes the higher-priority groups are:
quiz.why: Z (zusammen, 'together') means the higher-priority groups lie on the same side of the double bond.

quiz.q: Geometrical isomers of hepta-2,5-diene CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH=CHCH₃:
quiz.why: The two double bonds have identical ends, so EE, ZZ and EZ (= ZE) give three isomers.

scenes.text: At room temperature ethane's C–C bond rotates about 10¹¹ times per second.
But not freely — there is a small energy hill every 120°.

steps.title: Ethane
steps.body:
- Staggered (dihedral 60°): minimum energy.
- Eclipsed (0°): maximum; torsional strain ≈ **12 kJ mol⁻¹** (≈ 4 kJ per H/H eclipsing).
- The barrier is small, so conformers interconvert rapidly and cannot be isolated.

steps.title: Butane (C2–C3 rotation)
steps.body:
Relative energies (kJ mol⁻¹, approximate):
- Anti (180°): **0** (most stable)
- Gauche (60°): **3.8** (CH₃/CH₃ steric strain)
- Eclipsed, CH₃/H (120°): ≈ 16
- Fully eclipsed, CH₃/CH₃ (0°): ≈ 19 (least stable)
At 298 K the anti : gauche ratio is about 70 : 30 (two gauche forms).

steps.title: Solved: gauche population
steps.body:
For each gauche form, K = exp(−ΔG/RT) = exp(−3800/(8.314 × 298)) = exp(−1.53) = 0.216.
Two gauche forms: anti : gauche = 1 : 0.43 → **≈ 70% anti, 30% gauche**.

steps.title: Intramolecular H-bonding exception
steps.body: In ethylene glycol (HOCH₂CH₂OH) and 2-fluoroethanol the **gauche** conformer is preferred because it allows an intramolecular O–H···O(F) interaction (and the gauche effect).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling conformers 'isomers' that can be separated at room temperature.
- Drawing Newman projections with the rear carbon's bonds touching the centre.
- Assuming anti is always preferred, even with H-bonding substituents.

activity.prompt: Arrange butane conformations from most stable to least stable.

quiz.q: Torsional barrier of ethane:
quiz.why: Three H/H eclipsing interactions of about 4 kJ mol⁻¹ each give a barrier of roughly 12 kJ mol⁻¹.

quiz.q: Gauche butane is less stable than anti by:
quiz.why: In the gauche form the two methyl groups are 60° apart, adding about 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹ of steric strain.

quiz.q: Preferred conformation of ethylene glycol:
quiz.why: The gauche form allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the two OH groups.

lessons.title: Cycloalkanes: Baeyer strain and cyclohexane chair

scenes.text: Baeyer assumed rings were planar and predicted cyclohexane to be strained. Experiment showed it is virtually strain-free.
Sachse and Mohr explained why: the ring puckers into a chair.

steps.title: Baeyer strain theory
steps.body:
Angle strain = deviation from 109.5°, calculated as ½(109.5° − internal planar angle):
- Cyclopropane: ½(109.5 − 60) = **24.75°**
- Cyclobutane: ½(109.5 − 90) = **9.75°**
- Cyclopentane: ½(109.5 − 108) = **0.75°**
- Cyclohexane (planar assumption): ½(109.5 − 120) = **−5.25°**
Limitation: rings larger than cyclopentane are not planar; heats of combustion per CH₂ show cyclohexane is strain-free (≈ 658.6 kJ mol⁻¹ per CH₂, the same as open-chain alkanes).

steps.title: Cyclohexane conformations
steps.body:
- **Chair**: all angles ≈ 111°, all C–H staggered → most stable.
- Each carbon has one **axial** (parallel to the ring axis) and one **equatorial** bond.
- Ring flip converts axial ⇄ equatorial; barrier ≈ 45 kJ mol⁻¹.
- Energies: chair 0 < twist-boat ≈ 23 < boat ≈ 29 < half-chair ≈ 45 kJ mol⁻¹. Boat suffers flagpole interactions and eclipsing.

steps.title: Solved: strain from heats of combustion
steps.body:
Cyclopropane ΔcH ≈ 2091 kJ mol⁻¹ → per CH₂ = 697 kJ.
Excess over strain-free 658.6: (697 − 658.6) × 3 = **≈ 115 kJ mol⁻¹** total ring strain (literature ≈ 115).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating cyclohexane as planar.
- Thinking axial and equatorial positions are fixed — ring flipping exchanges them.
- Saying the boat is a transition state (the half-chair is; the twist-boat is a local minimum).

activity.prompt: Arrange cyclohexane conformations from most to least stable.

quiz.q: Baeyer angle strain of cyclobutane:
quiz.why: ½(109.5° − 90°) = 9.75° deviation per bond.

quiz.q: Most stable conformation of cyclohexane:
quiz.why: The chair has near-tetrahedral angles and fully staggered C–H bonds, so it has almost no strain.

quiz.q: Ring flip of a chair converts:
quiz.why: In a ring flip every axial position becomes equatorial and vice versa, while cis/trans relationships are unchanged.

scenes.text: A tert-butyl group is so bulky that it locks a cyclohexane ring with itself equatorial over 99.9% of the time.
Chemists use it to 'freeze' rings and study axial versus equatorial reactivity.

steps.title: Monosubstituted rings
steps.body: Axial substituents suffer **1,3-diaxial interactions** with axial H atoms (each like a gauche-butane interaction). Equatorial preference (A-value, kJ mol⁻¹): CH₃ 7.3, C₂H₅ 7.5, i-Pr 9.2, t-Bu ≈ 20, OH ≈ 3.9, Cl ≈ 2.2, C₆H₅ ≈ 12.

steps.title: Solved: methylcyclohexane equilibrium
steps.body:
ΔG° = −7.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (axial → equatorial) at 298 K.
- K = exp(7300/(8.314 × 298)) = exp(2.95) ≈ **19**
- Equatorial = 19/20 = **95%**, axial = 5%

steps.title: Disubstituted rings
steps.body:
| Isomer | Positions | Best chair |
|---|---|---|
| cis-1,2 | a,e | a,e (either flip) |
| trans-1,2 | e,e or a,a | **e,e** |
| cis-1,3 | e,e or a,a | **e,e** |
| trans-1,3 | a,e | a,e |
| cis-1,4 | a,e | a,e |
| trans-1,4 | e,e or a,a | **e,e** |
So trans-1,2, cis-1,3 and trans-1,4 dimethylcyclohexanes are the more stable isomers of each pair. With two different groups (cis-1-t-Bu-4-methyl), the bulkier group goes equatorial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming 'cis' always means both equatorial (true only for 1,3).
- Forgetting that cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane interconverts between two equal-energy a,e chairs.
- Placing t-Bu axial in a locked system.

activity.prompt: Match each dimethylcyclohexane to its most stable chair.

quiz.q: More stable isomer of 1,3-dimethylcyclohexane:
quiz.why: cis-1,3 can adopt a chair with both methyl groups equatorial, whereas trans-1,3 always has one axial.

quiz.q: Destabilising interaction for an axial methyl group:
quiz.why: An axial methyl crowds the two axial hydrogens on the same face at C3 and C5.

quiz.q: If ΔG° = −11.4 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K, K for axial ⇌ equatorial is about:

questions.q: cis-But-2-ene has a higher boiling point than trans because it:
questions.why: In the cis isomer the bond dipoles add up to a small net dipole, increasing intermolecular attraction.

questions.q: Fumaric acid has a higher m.p. than maleic acid because:
options: It packs better and forms intermolecular H-bonds
questions.why: The symmetric trans structure packs efficiently in the crystal and forms an intermolecular H-bonded network.

questions.q: E/Z descriptor of (CH₃)(H)C=C(CH₃)(C₂H₅) with the two CH₃ groups cis:
questions.why: On C2, C₂H₅ outranks CH₃; on C1, CH₃ outranks H. With the two methyls cis, the higher-priority CH₃ (C1) and C₂H₅ (C2) are trans, so the isomer is E.

questions.q: Dihedral angle in the anti conformation of butane:
questions.why: In the anti form the two methyl groups are directly opposite, at 180°.

questions.q: Strain in planar cyclopropane (Baeyer):
Total ring strain of cyclobutane if ΔcH per CH₂ is 686 kJ mol⁻¹ (strain-free 658.6):
questions.why: (686 − 658.6) × 4 = 27.4 × 4 ≈ 110 kJ mol⁻¹, close to the literature value.

questions.q: Highest-energy conformer on the chair-to-chair pathway:
questions.why: The half-chair is the transition state for ring flipping, about 45 kJ mol⁻¹ above the chair.

questions.q: Percentage of equatorial methylcyclohexane at 298 K:
questions.why: K ≈ 19 for ΔG° = −7.3 kJ mol⁻¹, so about 19/20 = 95% equatorial.

questions.q: trans-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane prefers:
questions.why: The trans-1,4 isomer can place both methyl groups equatorial, avoiding 1,3-diaxial strain.

questions.q: The largest A-value among these:
questions.why: The bulky tert-butyl group has an A-value of about 20 kJ mol⁻¹, effectively locking it equatorial.

questions.q: Geometrical isomerism is not possible for:
questions.why: In 1,1-dichloroethene one carbon carries two identical Cl atoms, so no cis/trans pair exists.

questions.q: Conformers differ from configurational isomers because they:
options: Interconvert by rotation about single bonds
questions.why: Conformers interconvert by σ-bond rotation with low barriers, without breaking bonds.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Aliphatic hydrocarbons: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes
courses.summary: Preparation and free-radical halogenation of alkanes with selectivity calculations; electrophilic additions to alkenes (Markovnikov, peroxide effect, halogenation stereochemistry); hydroboration, oxidation and ozonolysis; and acidity and reactions of alkynes.
outcomes: Write chain mechanisms of radical halogenation and calculate product ratios from relative reactivities
Predict regio- and stereochemistry of HX, X₂, H₂O and BH₃ additions
Deduce alkene structures from ozonolysis products
Use the acidity of terminal alkynes in synthesis and distinguish them from internal alkynes

story.title: Chlorine, light and a chain reaction

scenes.text: A mixture of methane and chlorine is stable in the dark but reacts rapidly in sunlight.
One photon starts a chain that converts thousands of molecules.

steps.title: Preparation
steps.body:
- **Wurtz**: 2RX + 2Na (dry ether) → R–R + 2NaX (best for symmetric alkanes; mixed halides give mixtures).
- **Kolbe electrolysis**: 2RCOO⁻ → R–R + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (at anode).
- **Corey–House**: R₂CuLi + R′X → R–R′ (unsymmetrical alkanes).
- **Decarboxylation**: RCOONa + NaOH (CaO) → RH + Na₂CO₃.
- **Hydrogenation** of alkenes (Ni, Pd, Pt).

steps.title: Mechanism of chlorination
steps.body:
1. Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (hν)
2. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃; •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
3. Termination: 2Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; 2•CH₃ → C₂H₆ (ethane traces prove radicals)
Relative reactivity per H (25 °C): Cl• 1 : 3.8 : 5 (1° : 2° : 3°); Br• 1 : 82 : 1600 — bromination is far more selective (Hammond postulate: endothermic step, product-like transition state).

steps.title: Solved: monochlorination of propane
steps.body:
- 1°: 6 H × 1 = 6.0
- 2°: 2 H × 3.8 = 7.6
- Total 13.6 → 1-chloropropane **44%**, 2-chloropropane **56%** (experiment ≈ 45 : 55)

steps.title: Solved: isobutane, Cl vs Br
steps.body:
(CH₃)₃CH: 9 primary H, 1 tertiary H.
- Chlorination: 9 × 1 = 9; 1 × 5 = 5 → tert-butyl chloride **36%**
- Bromination: 9 × 1 = 9; 1 × 1600 = 1600 → tert-butyl bromide **99.4%**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply reactivity by the number of equivalent H atoms.
- Using Wurtz with two different halides to make one pure unsymmetrical alkane.
- Drawing ionic intermediates in radical halogenation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of methane chlorination.
items: Cl₂ absorbs light and splits into 2 Cl•
Cl• abstracts H from CH₄ giving HCl and •CH₃
•CH₃ reacts with Cl₂ giving CH₃Cl and Cl•
The new Cl• continues the chain
Two radicals combine and terminate the chain

quiz.q: Monochlorination of n-butane: % 2-chlorobutane (Cl 1 : 3.8 per H):
quiz.why: 1° gives 6 × 1 = 6 and 2° gives 4 × 3.8 = 15.2, so 2-chlorobutane = 15.2/21.2 ≈ 72%.

quiz.q: Bromination is more selective than chlorination because:
options: H-abstraction by Br• is endothermic with a late transition state
quiz.why: An endothermic step has a product-like transition state, so radical stability differences strongly affect the rate.

quiz.q: Unsymmetrical alkanes are best made by:
quiz.why: Corey–House couples a lithium dialkylcuprate with a different alkyl halide to give R–R′ cleanly.

story.title: The rule a Russian chemist wrote in 1870

scenes.text: Vladimir Markovnikov noticed HBr adds to propene to give mainly 2-bromopropane.
Decades later Kharasch found that peroxides flip the result — a radical pathway.

steps.title: Markovnikov addition of HX
steps.body:
H⁺ adds to the alkene carbon with more H atoms, forming the more stable carbocation; X⁻ then attacks.
CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃ (via 2° cation).
Reactivity HI > HBr > HCl. Carbocation rearrangements possible.

steps.title: Peroxide (Kharasch) effect
steps.body:
With HBr only, in presence of ROOR:
- ROOR → 2RO•; RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•
- Br• adds to the terminal carbon → more stable 2° radical
- Radical + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + Br•
Result: **anti-Markovnikov** 1-bromopropane. Not observed with HCl (H–Cl too strong) or HI (the I• addition step is endothermic).

steps.title: Halogenation and halohydrins
steps.body:
Br₂ adds via a cyclic **bromonium ion**; Br⁻ opens it from the back → **anti addition**.
- cis-But-2-ene + Br₂ → racemic (2R,3R) + (2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane
- trans-But-2-ene + Br₂ → meso-2,3-dibromobutane
In water (Br₂/H₂O), water opens the bromonium at the more substituted carbon → bromohydrin (OH on more substituted C). Decolourisation of Br₂ water is a test for unsaturation.

steps.title: Solved: acid-catalysed hydration
steps.body: 2-Methylpropene + H₂O (dil. H₂SO₄) → tertiary cation → **2-methylpropan-2-ol** (Markovnikov).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI.
- Drawing syn addition for Br₂.
- Forgetting that cis-alkene + Br₂ gives a racemate, trans gives meso.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with propene to the major product.

quiz.q: Peroxide effect is observed with:
quiz.why: Only HBr has both radical propagation steps exothermic, so the anti-Markovnikov radical chain works.

quiz.q: trans-But-2-ene with Br₂ gives:
quiz.why: Anti addition of Br across a trans alkene gives the (2R,3S) meso product.

quiz.q: Intermediate in Br₂ addition to alkenes:
quiz.why: The alkene attacks Br₂ to form a three-membered bromonium ion, which explains anti addition.

story.title: Reading a molecule by cutting it

scenes.text: Before NMR, chemists located double bonds by cutting them with ozone and identifying the pieces.
Put the fragments' C=O ends back together and you recover the alkene.

steps.title: Hydroboration–oxidation
steps.body:
R–CH=CH₂ + BH₃ (THF) → (RCH₂CH₂)₃B → H₂O₂/NaOH → RCH₂CH₂OH.
- **Anti-Markovnikov** OH, **syn** addition, no rearrangement.
- 1-Methylcyclopentene → trans-2-methylcyclopentanol (H and OH syn).

steps.title: Oxidation
steps.body:
- **Cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent)**: syn-diol; purple → brown MnO₂ (test for unsaturation). OsO₄ also gives syn-diols.
- **Hot acidic KMnO₄**: cleaves C=C: =CH₂ → CO₂; =CHR → RCOOH; =CR₂ → R₂C=O.
- **Epoxidation** with peracids (mCPBA), then acid hydrolysis → anti-diol.

steps.title: Ozonolysis
steps.body:
O₃ → molozonide → ozonide; then:
- Reductive work-up (Zn/H₂O or (CH₃)₂S) → aldehydes/ketones
- Oxidative work-up (H₂O₂) → carboxylic acids/ketones

steps.title: Solved: structure from ozonolysis
steps.body:
An alkene C₆H₁₂ gives acetone and propanal on reductive ozonolysis.
- Join the carbonyl carbons: (CH₃)₂C=O + O=CHCH₂CH₃ → (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₂CH₃
- Alkene = **2-methylpent-2-ene** ✔ (C₆H₁₂)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Markovnikov alcohol for hydroboration.
- Confusing cold dilute KMnO₄ (diol) with hot acidic KMnO₄ (cleavage).
- Forgetting formaldehyde from a terminal =CH₂ in reductive ozonolysis.

activity.prompt: Match reagent to product type from an alkene.

quiz.q: Hydroboration–oxidation of propene gives:
quiz.why: Boron adds to the less substituted carbon and is replaced by OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov primary alcohol.

quiz.q: Reductive ozonolysis of but-2-ene gives:
quiz.why: Cleaving CH₃CH=CHCH₃ at the double bond gives two molecules of CH₃CHO.

quiz.q: Baeyer's test for unsaturation uses:
quiz.why: Alkenes reduce purple permanganate to brown MnO₂ while forming diols.

scenes.text: Bubble propyne into ammoniacal silver nitrate and a white precipitate forms; but-2-yne gives nothing.
Only terminal alkynes have an acidic ≡C–H.

steps.title: Acidity of terminal alkynes
steps.body:
pKa: HC≡CH ≈ 25, CH₂=CH₂ ≈ 44, CH₄ ≈ 50. The sp carbon (50% s-character) holds the lone pair of the carbanion closer to the nucleus.
- NaNH₂ (pKa NH₃ ≈ 38) deprotonates alkynes; NaOH does not.
- Tests: ammoniacal AgNO₃ → white RC≡CAg; ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ → red RC≡CCu.
