- Acetylide alkylation: HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + CH₃CH₂Br → HC≡CCH₂CH₃ (with 1° halides only; 3° give elimination).

steps.title: Addition reactions
steps.body:
- **Hydrogenation**: H₂/Pd–C → alkane; **Lindlar** (Pd/CaCO₃, quinoline) → **cis-alkene**; **Na/liq. NH₃** → **trans-alkene**.
- **Hydration**: HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ → enol → ketone (Markovnikov); acetylene gives acetaldehyde; propyne gives acetone.
- **Hydroboration** of terminal alkynes (disiamylborane) → aldehyde.
- HX adds twice (Markovnikov) → gem-dihalide.

steps.title: Solved: a synthesis
steps.body:
Make cis-hex-3-ene from acetylene:
1. HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡C⁻ ; + C₂H₅Br → HC≡CC₂H₅
2. NaNH₂; + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅C≡CC₂H₅ (hex-3-yne)
3. H₂, Lindlar catalyst → **cis-hex-3-ene**
(Na/NH₃ in step 3 would give trans-hex-3-ene.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using NaOH to make acetylides.
- Alkylating acetylides with tertiary halides.
- Forgetting that alkyne hydration gives the ketone via keto–enol tautomerism, not an enol product.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with but-2-yne to its product.

quiz.q: Which gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃?
quiz.why: Only terminal alkynes have an acidic ≡C–H that is replaced by silver to form the insoluble acetylide.

quiz.q: Hydration of propyne gives:
quiz.why: Markovnikov hydration gives the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which tautomerises to acetone.

quiz.q: Na in liquid NH₃ reduces alkynes to:
quiz.why: Dissolving-metal reduction passes through a vinyl radical/anion that adopts the more stable trans geometry.

questions.q: Kolbe electrolysis of sodium propanoate gives:
questions.why: Two ethyl radicals from CH₃CH₂COO⁻ couple at the anode to give butane.

questions.q: Evidence for radicals in methane chlorination:
questions.why: Ethane can only form by two methyl radicals combining, proving radical intermediates.

questions.q: % tert-butyl chloride from isobutane (Cl 1 : 5 per H, 1° : 3°):
questions.why: 9 × 1 = 9 for primary and 1 × 5 = 5 for tertiary, so 5/14 ≈ 36%.

questions.q: Markovnikov product of HCl with 2-methylbut-2-ene:
questions.why: H adds to C3, giving a tertiary cation at C2 that captures Cl⁻.

questions.q: Peroxide effect proceeds through:
questions.why: Bromine atoms generated by peroxides add to the alkene to form the more stable carbon radical.

questions.q: cis-But-2-ene + Br₂ gives:
questions.why: Anti addition across a cis alkene produces a pair of enantiomers in equal amounts.

questions.q: Alkene giving only acetone on reductive ozonolysis:
questions.why: Cleaving (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ gives two molecules of (CH₃)₂C=O.

questions.q: Syn-dihydroxylation reagent:
questions.why: OsO₄ adds through a cyclic osmate ester, delivering both OH groups to the same face.

questions.q: pKa of acetylene is about:
questions.why: Acetylene's pKa is about 25, making it acidic enough to be deprotonated by NaNH₂.

questions.q: Lindlar catalyst converts alkynes to:
questions.why: The poisoned Pd surface delivers both H atoms from the same side and stops at the alkene.

questions.q: Hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclopentene gives:
questions.why: H and OH add syn and anti-Markovnikov, so OH sits on C2 trans to the methyl group.

questions.q: Acetylide alkylation works best with:
questions.why: Acetylides are strong bases; with 2° and 3° halides they cause E2 elimination instead of SN2.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Aromatic hydrocarbons, practicals & revision
courses.summary: Aromaticity and Hückel's rule, the mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel–Crafts), activating and directing effects of substituents, the practical skills of recrystallisation and melting-point determination, and a paper-level revision exam.
outcomes: Classify rings as aromatic, antiaromatic or non-aromatic using Hückel's rule
Write the arenium-ion mechanism for common EAS reactions
Predict the position and rate of substitution on substituted benzenes
Purify an organic solid by recrystallisation and judge purity by melting point

scenes.text: Kekulé said he dreamt of a snake biting its own tail and proposed a ring for benzene.
A century later, Hückel's 4n + 2 rule explained why that ring is so unusually stable.

steps.title: Criteria
steps.body:
A compound is **aromatic** if it is: (1) cyclic, (2) planar, (3) fully conjugated (every ring atom has a p orbital), and (4) has **(4n + 2) π electrons** (n = 0, 1, 2…: 2, 6, 10, 14).
- Cyclic, planar, conjugated with **4n** π electrons → **antiaromatic** (destabilised): cyclobutadiene.
- Fails planarity or conjugation → **non-aromatic**: cyclooctatetraene (tub-shaped), cyclohexa-1,3-diene.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- Benzene: 6 π → aromatic (n = 1)
- Cyclopentadienyl anion: 6 π → aromatic (why cyclopentadiene pKa ≈ 16 is so acidic)
- Cyclopentadienyl cation: 4 π → antiaromatic
- Cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation: 6 π → aromatic (tropylium bromide is ionic)
- Pyridine: 6 π (N lone pair in sp² orbital, not in ring) → aromatic
- Pyrrole, furan, thiophene: 6 π (heteroatom lone pair is part of the ring) → aromatic
- Naphthalene: 10 π → aromatic; cyclooctatetraene dianion: 10 π → aromatic

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
- Benzene's C–C bonds are all 139 pm (between 154 and 134 pm).
- Prefers substitution over addition (keeps aromaticity).
- Ring current: aromatic protons appear downfield in ¹H NMR (δ ≈ 7.3 for benzene).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting pyridine's N lone pair as a π electron.
- Calling cyclooctatetraene antiaromatic (it escapes by becoming non-planar).
- Forgetting that an sp³ carbon in the ring breaks conjugation (cyclopentadiene itself is non-aromatic).

activity.prompt: Classify each species.

quiz.q: Cyclopentadiene is unusually acidic because its conjugate base:
quiz.why: Losing H⁺ gives the planar cyclopentadienyl anion with 6 π electrons, which is aromatic and very stable.

quiz.q: π electrons counted for pyrrole aromaticity:
quiz.why: Four electrons from the two C=C bonds plus the nitrogen lone pair make a 6 π system.

quiz.q: Which is antiaromatic?
quiz.why: Cyclobutadiene is planar, cyclic and conjugated with 4 π electrons, which fits the 4n antiaromatic count.

lessons.title: Electrophilic aromatic substitution and directing effects

scenes.text: Paracetamol manufacture starts from phenol and relies on placing a nitro group para to OH.
Directing effects decide where each new group lands.

steps.title: General mechanism
steps.body:
1. Generate electrophile E⁺.
2. π electrons attack E⁺ → resonance-stabilised **arenium ion (σ-complex, Wheland intermediate)** — rate-determining.
3. Base removes H⁺ → aromaticity restored.
Electrophiles:
- Nitration: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻
- Halogenation: Br₂ + FeBr₃ → Br⁺[FeBr₄]⁻
- Sulphonation: SO₃ (fuming H₂SO₄), reversible
- Friedel–Crafts alkylation: RCl + AlCl₃ → R⁺ (rearranges; polyalkylation); acylation: RCOCl + AlCl₃ → RC≡O⁺ (no rearrangement, monosubstitution).

steps.title: Substituent effects
steps.body:
| Group | Effect | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| –NH₂, –OH, –OR, –NHCOR | Strong/moderate activating (+M) | o, p |
| –CH₃, alkyl | Weak activating (+I, hyperconjugation) | o, p |
| –F, –Cl, –Br, –I | Weak deactivating (−I > +M) | **o, p** |
| –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –CN, –SO₃H, –NO₂, –NR₃⁺ | Deactivating (−M/−I) | m |
o,p-Directors stabilise the arenium ion when E is ortho/para (a resonance form places + next to the donor). Meta-directors destabilise o/p attack most.

steps.title: Solved: planning a synthesis
steps.body:
Make m-bromonitrobenzene from benzene: **nitrate first** (–NO₂ is meta-directing), then brominate (Br₂/FeBr₃).
Make p-bromonitrobenzene: **brominate first** (–Br is o,p), then nitrate and separate p from o.
Make propylbenzene: Friedel–Crafts **acylation** with CH₃CH₂COCl, then Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) reduction — direct alkylation with n-PrCl rearranges to isopropylbenzene.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling halogens meta-directors because they deactivate.
- Running Friedel–Crafts on nitrobenzene or aniline (fails: ring too deactivated; NH₂ complexes AlCl₃).
- Forgetting carbocation rearrangement in FC alkylation.

activity.prompt: Match each substituent with its directing effect.

quiz.q: Electrophile in nitration:
quiz.why: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.

quiz.q: Benzene + n-propyl chloride/AlCl₃ gives mainly:
quiz.why: The primary carbocation-like species rearranges by hydride shift to the more stable isopropyl cation.

quiz.q: Chlorobenzene nitrates mainly at:
quiz.why: Chlorine deactivates the ring by −I but its lone pairs stabilise ortho/para arenium ions by +M.

quiz.q: Best route to m-bromonitrobenzene:
quiz.why: The nitro group directs the incoming bromine to the meta position.

scenes.text: Crude acetanilide from the class prep is brownish and melts from 106 to 110 °C.
One recrystallisation from hot water gives white plates melting sharply at 113–114 °C.

steps.title: Recrystallisation principle
steps.body:
Choose a solvent in which the compound is very soluble hot and sparingly soluble cold, while impurities are either very soluble (stay in mother liquor) or insoluble (removed by hot filtration).
Acetanilide in water: ≈ 5 g per 100 mL at 100 °C, ≈ 0.5 g per 100 mL at 25 °C.

steps.title: Solved: maximum recovery
steps.body:
5.0 g crude acetanilide dissolved in 100 mL boiling water, cooled to 25 °C.
- Remaining in solution ≈ 0.5 g
- Maximum recovery = 5.0 − 0.5 = 4.5 g → **90%** (before handling losses).
Using 200 mL would leave ≈ 1.0 g in solution → only 80% — use the minimum hot solvent.

steps.title: Melting point
steps.body:
- Pure compounds melt sharply (range ≤ 1–2 °C).
- Impurities lower and broaden the melting range (colligative effect).
- **Mixed melting point**: mix unknown with authentic sample; no depression → identical.
- Capillary method: pack 2–3 mm, heat in Thiele tube/apparatus at ≈ 1–2 °C min⁻¹ near the m.p.
Reference values: acetanilide 114 °C, benzoic acid 122 °C, urea 133 °C, salicylic acid 159 °C, naphthalene 80 °C.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body:
- Why add activated charcoal? Adsorbs coloured impurities (add to the slightly cooled solution to avoid bumping).
- Why cool slowly? Larger, purer crystals; rapid cooling traps impurities.
- Why scratch the flask? Provides nucleation sites.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using too much solvent (poor yield).
- Heating the m.p. apparatus too fast (reading too high).
- Recording one temperature instead of the melting range.

activity.prompt: Order the recrystallisation procedure.
items: Dissolve the crude solid in the minimum boiling solvent
Add a little activated charcoal if coloured, then reboil
Filter hot through a fluted filter paper
Allow the filtrate to cool slowly, then in ice
Collect crystals by suction filtration and wash with cold solvent
Dry and record the melting point range

quiz.q: An impure sample usually melts:
options: Lower and over a wider range
quiz.why: Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice and depress the melting point, while broadening the range.

quiz.q: Mixed melting point with no depression shows the compounds are:
quiz.why: If the unknown and authentic sample are the same compound, mixing them introduces no impurity, so the m.p. stays unchanged.

quiz.q: Recovery when 4.0 g is dissolved and 0.6 g remains in cold solvent:
quiz.why: Recovered 3.4 g out of 4.0 g gives 3.4/4.0 = 85% maximum recovery.

story.title: One page for the whole paper

scenes.text: Farah turns her notes on electronic effects, stereochemistry and hydrocarbons into one checklist.
She practises with typical long questions before the semester exam.

steps.title: Key-point sheet
steps.body:
- Stability: carbocation/radical 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃ (benzyl, allyl highest); carbanion opposite
- Acidity rises with −I/−M groups; pKa acetic 4.76, phenol 10, p-nitrophenol 7.15
- DBE = C − H/2 − X/2 + N/2 + 1
- Stereoisomers ≤ 2ⁿ; meso when identical halves mirror
- CIP: atomic number; Fischer horizontal-H → reverse
- [α] = α/(l · c), l in dm, c in g mL⁻¹; ee = (%major − %minor)
- Butane: anti 0, gauche 3.8, fully eclipsed ≈ 19 kJ mol⁻¹; cyclohexane chair; methyl A = 7.3 kJ mol⁻¹
- Radical halogenation per-H ratios: Cl 1 : 3.8 : 5, Br 1 : 82 : 1600
- HBr + ROOR → anti-Markovnikov; Br₂ anti; BH₃ syn anti-Markovnikov; Lindlar cis; Na/NH₃ trans
- Hückel 4n + 2; o,p-directors: –OH, –NH₂, –R, –X; meta: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH, –SO₃H

steps.title: Typical long questions (practise)
steps.body:
1. Explain hyperconjugation and use it to compare the stability of carbocations and alkenes.
2. Assign R/S to the stereocentres of (+)-tartaric acid and explain why meso-tartaric acid is inactive.
3. Draw the energy profile for rotation about C2–C3 of butane.
4. Discuss the conformations of cyclohexane and of cis- and trans-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane.
5. Explain the peroxide effect with mechanism.
6. Why are halogens deactivating yet ortho/para directing?

steps.title: Worked short answer
steps.body:
Q: Why does phenol undergo bromination without a catalyst while benzene needs FeBr₃?
A: –OH donates electrons by +M, strongly activating the ring; bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) instantly. Benzene needs a Lewis acid to polarise Br₂ into a stronger electrophile.

steps.title: Exam traps
steps.body:
- Peroxide effect: HBr only.
- Halogens: deactivating but o,p.
- cis/trans ≠ Z/E in every case.

activity.prompt: Match each rule to its application.

quiz.q: Bromine water with phenol gives:
quiz.why: Phenol's strongly activated ring is brominated at all free ortho and para positions without a catalyst.

quiz.q: Which is not aromatic?
quiz.why: Cyclopentadiene contains an sp³ CH₂ that breaks the cyclic conjugation.

quiz.q: Rotation α = +5.0°, l = 1 dm, c = 0.25 g mL⁻¹; [α] =

questions.q: Strongest acid:
questions.why: Three fluorines give the greatest −I stabilisation of the carboxylate, making trifluoroacetic acid strongest.

questions.q: Most stable carbocation:
questions.why: The benzyl cation delocalises its positive charge into the aromatic ring by resonance, so it is the most stable.

questions.q: Degree of unsaturation of C₆H₅NO₂:
questions.why: 6 − 5/2 + 1/2 + 1 = 5 (four from the benzene ring, one from N=O).

questions.q: Stereoisomers of 2,3-dichlorobutane:
questions.why: Two identical stereocentres give an (R,R)/(S,S) pair plus one meso form.

questions.q: (S)-2-butanol sample with ee 40% contains (S):
questions.why: %S = 50 + 40/2 = 70% and %R = 30%, which differ by 40%.

questions.q: Fully eclipsed butane is higher in energy than anti by about:
questions.why: The CH₃/CH₃ eclipsed form adds torsional and steric strain of about 19 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: More stable 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane:
questions.why: trans-1,2 can adopt a diequatorial chair, while cis-1,2 always has one axial methyl.

questions.q: % 2-bromopropane from propane bromination (1° : 2° = 1 : 82 per H):
HBr + propene with peroxide gives:
questions.why: Radical addition places Br on the terminal carbon to form the more stable secondary radical.

questions.q: Reductive ozonolysis giving HCHO and butanone comes from:
questions.why: Joining CH₂=O with (CH₃)(C₂H₅)C=O gives CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, 2-methylbut-1-ene.

questions.q: Reduction of but-2-yne with Na/NH₃ gives:
questions.why: Dissolving-metal reduction yields the trans alkene.

questions.q: Tropylium cation has π electrons:
questions.why: Seven sp² carbons with one empty p orbital hold six π electrons, an aromatic count.

questions.q: Friedel–Crafts reactions fail with:
questions.why: The strongly deactivating nitro group makes the ring too electron-poor to attack the electrophile.

questions.q: Halogens direct ortho/para because of:
questions.why: Halogen lone pairs stabilise the arenium ion formed by ortho/para attack, even though −I slows the overall rate.

questions.q: Pure acetanilide melts at about:
questions.why: Pure acetanilide melts sharply at about 113–114 °C.

uni-bsc-chem-organic-2.title: B.Sc Chemistry · Organic Chemistry II (functional groups)
uni-bsc-chem-organic-2.description: Alkyl and aryl halides with SN1/SN2/E1/E2 mechanisms, alcohols, phenols and ethers, aldehydes and ketones, carboxylic acids and their derivatives, amines and nitro compounds, with functional-group identification practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Alkyl and aryl halides: substitution and elimination
courses.summary: SN2 and SN1 mechanisms with kinetics, stereochemistry and the effects of substrate, nucleophile, leaving group and solvent; E2 and E1 eliminations with Saytzeff and Hofmann orientation; and nucleophilic aromatic substitution of aryl halides by addition–elimination and benzyne routes.
outcomes: Write rate laws and stereochemical outcomes of SN1 and SN2 reactions
Predict the dominant pathway (SN1, SN2, E1, E2) from substrate, base and solvent
Apply Saytzeff and Hofmann rules and the anti-periplanar requirement of E2
Explain the low reactivity of aryl halides and the SNAr and benzyne mechanisms

scenes.text: Walden noticed in 1896 that some substitutions turned (+) compounds into (−) ones.
The nucleophile attacks from the back and flips the carbon like an umbrella in a gust.

steps.title: Mechanism and kinetics
steps.body:
One concerted step: Nu⁻ attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (backside attack) through a trigonal bipyramidal transition state.
- Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order)
- **Walden inversion**: (R)-2-bromobutane + OH⁻ → (S)-butan-2-ol (if priorities are unchanged)
- Substrate order: CH₃X > 1° > 2° ≫ 3° (no reaction) — steric hindrance at the back face. Neopentyl halides are very slow despite being 1°.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body:
- **Nucleophile**: stronger is faster; in protic solvents I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ (small ions are heavily solvated); in polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF, acetone) F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻.
- **Leaving group**: weaker base leaves better: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; TsO⁻ is excellent; OH⁻ is poor (protonate first).
- **Solvent**: polar aprotic accelerates SN2 (anion not caged).

steps.title: Solved: rate changes
steps.body:
Rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻].
- Double [CH₃Br] only → rate × **2**
- Double both → rate × **4**
- Halve [OH⁻], triple [CH₃Br] → × 1.5

steps.title: Solved: Finkelstein reaction
steps.body:
CH₃CH₂Br + NaI (acetone) → CH₃CH₂I + NaBr↓
NaI is soluble in acetone but NaBr is not, so precipitation drives the SN2 equilibrium forward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting SN2 at tertiary carbons.
- Assuming inversion always changes R to S — the label can stay the same if the priorities change.
- Using protic solvent nucleophilicity order in DMSO.

activity.prompt: Arrange alkyl bromides from fastest to slowest SN2.

quiz.q: SN2 rate law:
quiz.why: Both the substrate and nucleophile are in the single rate-determining transition state, so the reaction is second order.

quiz.q: Best leaving group:
quiz.why: Iodide is the weakest base and most polarisable, so it departs most easily.

quiz.q: Best solvent for SN2 of CH₃Br with CN⁻:
quiz.why: Polar aprotic DMSO dissolves the salt but does not hydrogen-bond to CN⁻, keeping it highly nucleophilic.

scenes.text: tert-Butyl bromide in water reacts at the same speed whether you add a little or a lot of hydroxide.
The slow step is the C–Br bond breaking by itself — the nucleophile only joins afterwards.

steps.title: Mechanism and kinetics
steps.body:
1. Slow ionisation: R–X → R⁺ + X⁻ (rate-determining)
2. Fast capture: R⁺ + Nu → R–Nu
- Rate = k[RX] (first order; independent of [Nu])
- Substrate order: 3° > 2° > 1°; allylic and benzylic also good
- Planar carbocation → attack on both faces → **racemisation** (often with slight excess inversion, due to ion pairing)
- Rearrangements possible
- Favoured by polar protic solvents (stabilise ions) and weak nucleophiles (solvolysis).

steps.title: Solved: comparing conditions
steps.body:
| Substrate / conditions | Pathway |
|---|---|
| CH₃CH₂Br, NaOH, DMSO | SN2 |
| (CH₃)₃CBr, H₂O/EtOH, warm | SN1 (plus some E1) |
| (R)-CH₃CHBrC₂H₅, NaN₃, acetone | SN2, inversion |
| C₆H₅CH(CH₃)Cl, H₂O | SN1, racemisation |

steps.title: Solved: rate change
steps.body: Rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. Tripling [OH⁻] → rate **unchanged**; doubling [(CH₃)₃CBr] → rate × **2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the nucleophile in the SN1 rate law.
- Predicting complete inversion in SN1.
- Forgetting carbocation rearrangement (e.g. neopentyl → tert-amyl products under SN1 conditions).

activity.prompt: Match each feature to SN1 or SN2.

quiz.q: SN1 is favoured by:
quiz.why: A tertiary carbocation forms easily and is stabilised by a polar protic solvent.

quiz.q: An optically active 3° halide undergoing SN1 gives:
quiz.why: The planar carbocation can be attacked from either face, giving nearly equal amounts of both enantiomers.

quiz.q: Fastest SN1 rate:
quiz.why: Benzyl chloride ionises to a resonance-stabilised benzylic carbocation.

scenes.text: Treat 2-bromobutane with ethoxide and you get butenes as well as ethers.
Which alkene forms — and how much — depends on the base.

steps.title: E2
steps.body:
Concerted removal of β-H and leaving group; rate = k[RX][B⁻].
- Requires **anti-periplanar** H and X (dihedral 180°); in cyclohexanes both must be **axial**.
- **Saytzeff (Zaitsev)**: small bases (EtO⁻, OH⁻) give the more substituted alkene.
- **Hofmann**: bulky bases (t-BuO⁻), poor leaving groups (–NR₃⁺, F) give the less substituted alkene.
- Kinetic isotope effect (C–D slower) supports C–H cleavage in the rate-determining step.

steps.title: E1
steps.body: Via carbocation; rate = k[RX]; competes with SN1; heat favours elimination (ΔS > 0). Gives Saytzeff product; rearrangements possible. Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols is E1 for 2°/3° alcohols.

steps.title: Solved: 2-bromobutane
steps.body:
- NaOEt/EtOH, heat → **but-2-ene** major (trans > cis) — Saytzeff
- KOt-Bu/t-BuOH → **but-1-ene** major — Hofmann (bulky base removes the less hindered CH₃ hydrogen)

steps.title: Solved: menthyl vs neomenthyl chloride
steps.body:
Neomenthyl chloride (Cl axial in the stable chair, with axial H on both β-carbons) → E2 gives mainly the Saytzeff alkene (3-menthene ≈ 75%), fast.
Menthyl chloride must flip to put Cl axial; only one β-carbon then has an axial H → **100% 2-menthene** (non-Saytzeff), slow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the anti-periplanar requirement in rings.
- Predicting Saytzeff with t-BuO⁻.
- Forgetting that strong bulky bases favour E2 over SN2 even for 2° halides.

activity.prompt: Match conditions with the dominant pathway.

quiz.q: E2 in cyclohexanes requires H and leaving group to be:
quiz.why: Only trans-diaxial H and X are anti-periplanar on a cyclohexane chair.

quiz.q: Major product of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane with KOt-Bu:
quiz.why: The bulky tert-butoxide removes a less hindered CH₃ hydrogen, giving the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene.

quiz.q: Evidence that C–H breaks in the E2 rate step:
quiz.why: Replacing β-H by D slows the reaction several-fold, showing C–H cleavage in the rate-determining step.

scenes.text: Chlorobenzene ignores boiling NaOH, yet 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene reacts with water on warming.
And with NaNH₂, chlorobenzene reacts through one of chemistry's strangest intermediates — benzyne.

steps.title: Why aryl halides are unreactive
steps.body:
- C–Cl has partial double-bond character (resonance of Cl lone pair with the ring) → shorter, stronger bond (169 vs 177 pm).
- sp² carbon is more electronegative.
- Backside SN2 attack is blocked by the ring; aryl cations are very unstable (no SN1).
Industrial Dow process: C₆H₅Cl + NaOH, 350 °C, 300 atm → phenol.

steps.title: SNAr (addition–elimination)
steps.body:
Requires strong −M groups (–NO₂) ortho/para to the halogen.
1. Nu⁻ adds to the ipso carbon → resonance-stabilised **Meisenheimer complex** (charge delocalised onto NO₂).
2. Halide leaves.
Rate order: F > Cl > Br > I (addition is rate-determining; F's −I effect speeds it). More nitro groups → milder conditions (2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene hydrolyses in warm water).

steps.title: Benzyne (elimination–addition)
steps.body:
C₆H₅Cl + NaNH₂/liq. NH₃: NH₂⁻ removes the ortho H, Cl⁻ leaves → **benzyne** (strained 'triple bond' from sideways overlap of sp² orbitals) → NH₃ adds.
Labelling proof: ¹⁴C-1 chlorobenzene gives aniline with NH₂ at C1 and C2 in ≈ 1 : 1 ratio. p-Chlorotoluene gives a mixture of p- and m-toluidine.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying SN1/SN2 to aryl halides.
- Expecting I to be the best leaving group in SNAr.
- Placing nitro groups meta and expecting SNAr activation.

activity.prompt: Arrange the compounds by increasing ease of hydrolysis to the phenol.

quiz.q: Intermediate in SNAr:
quiz.why: Nucleophile addition gives a negatively charged σ-complex stabilised by ortho/para nitro groups.

quiz.q: Fastest SNAr with NaOMe:
quiz.why: Addition is rate-determining, and fluorine's strong −I effect makes the ipso carbon most electrophilic.

quiz.q: Benzyne is formed from chlorobenzene by:
quiz.why: The very strong base amide removes an ortho proton, and loss of chloride gives benzyne.

questions.q: Doubling [Nu⁻] in an SN1 reaction changes the rate by:
questions.why: The nucleophile is not involved in the rate-determining ionisation, so its concentration does not affect the rate.

questions.q: (R)-2-Iodooctane + NaN₃ (acetone) gives:
questions.why: SN2 backside attack inverts the stereocentre, and the priorities (N₃ replacing I) keep the label change to S.

questions.q: Nucleophilicity order in water:
questions.why: Small anions are tightly solvated by hydrogen bonds in water, so the large, polarisable iodide is most nucleophilic.

questions.q: Neopentyl bromide reacts slowly by SN2 because:
options: The bulky t-Bu group blocks backside attack
questions.why: Although primary, the adjacent tert-butyl group sterically shields the back of the reacting carbon.

questions.q: Finkelstein reaction is driven by:
questions.why: NaCl and NaBr are insoluble in acetone, so their precipitation pulls the equilibrium toward the iodide.

questions.q: Saytzeff product of 2-bromo-3-methylbutane with NaOEt:
questions.why: Removing H from C3 gives the trisubstituted alkene (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, the most substituted product.

questions.q: Hofmann orientation is favoured by:
questions.why: Bulky tert-butoxide abstracts the most accessible hydrogen, forming the less substituted alkene.

questions.q: Heat favours elimination over substitution because elimination:
questions.why: Elimination produces more molecules, so its positive ΔS makes −TΔS more favourable at high temperature.

questions.q: C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is shorter than in CH₃Cl because of:
questions.why: Resonance between the Cl lone pair and the ring gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character.

questions.q: ¹⁴C-labelled chlorobenzene with NaNH₂ gives aniline labelled at:
questions.why: The symmetrical benzyne intermediate lets NH₂⁻ add at either end of the 'triple bond'.

questions.q: SNAr needs nitro groups at:
questions.why: Only ortho/para nitro groups can delocalise the negative charge of the Meisenheimer complex by resonance.

questions.q: Rate law of E2 dehydrohalogenation:
questions.why: The base and substrate react in one concerted step, so E2 is second order.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Alcohols, phenols and ethers
courses.summary: Preparation and reactions of alcohols (Grignard routes, Lucas test, oxidation, dehydration), diols with pinacol rearrangement and periodate cleavage, acidity and named reactions of phenols, and the synthesis and cleavage of ethers and epoxides.
outcomes: Plan Grignard syntheses of 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols
Distinguish alcohol classes by the Lucas test and oxidation behaviour
Write mechanisms of pinacol–pinacolone, Reimer–Tiemann and Kolbe–Schmitt reactions
Predict products of Williamson synthesis, HI cleavage of ethers and epoxide ring opening

scenes.text: Early roadside breath tests used orange dichromate crystals that turned green with ethanol.
Cr(VI) is reduced to green Cr(III) as ethanol is oxidised — the same chemistry as in the lab.

steps.title: Preparation via Grignard reagents
steps.body:
RMgX + carbonyl, then H₃O⁺:
- HCHO → **1°** alcohol RCH₂OH
- R′CHO → **2°** alcohol RR′CHOH
- R′₂C=O → **3°** alcohol
- Ethylene oxide → 1° alcohol with two extra carbons (RCH₂CH₂OH)
- Ester (2 equiv. RMgX) → 3° alcohol with two identical R
Other routes: reduction of carbonyls (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄), hydration and hydroboration of alkenes.

steps.title: Key reactions
steps.body:
- **Lucas test** (ZnCl₂/conc. HCl): 3° turbid immediately; 2° in ≈ 5 min; 1° no turbidity at room temperature (SN1 via carbocation).
- **Oxidation**: 1° → aldehyde (PCC, CH₂Cl₂) or acid (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, KMnO₄); 2° → ketone; 3° resist.
- **Dehydration** (conc. H₂SO₄, 170 °C or H₃PO₄): E1 for 2°/3°, Saytzeff, rearrangements; ease 3° > 2° > 1°.
- **Esterification**: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O (H⁺); acyl–oxygen cleavage (¹⁸O stays in the ester).

steps.title: Solved: Grignard planning
steps.body:
Target 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃. Three disconnections:
- CH₃CH₂MgBr + acetone
- CH₃MgBr + butan-2-one
- 2 CH₃MgBr + ethyl propanoate

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using aqueous or protic solvents with Grignard reagents (destroyed by water/alcohols).
- Oxidising a 1° alcohol with acidified dichromate and expecting to stop at the aldehyde (distil it off as formed, or use PCC).
- Reporting 1° alcohols as positive in the Lucas test at room temperature.

activity.prompt: Match each carbonyl compound (with CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺) to the alcohol formed.

quiz.q: Immediate turbidity in the Lucas test indicates:
quiz.why: Tertiary alcohols form stable carbocations at once, giving the insoluble alkyl chloride immediately.

quiz.q: PCC oxidises propan-1-ol to:
quiz.why: PCC in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ stops at the aldehyde because no water is present to form the hydrate that oxidises further.

quiz.q: Grignard reagent + formaldehyde gives:
quiz.why: Formaldehyde carries two H atoms on the carbonyl carbon, so the product carbon has one R group: a primary alcohol.

lessons.title: Diols: pinacol rearrangement and periodate cleavage

scenes.text: Heat pinacol with acid and a methyl group jumps to the neighbouring carbon.
The driving force: forming a C=O stabilised oxocarbenium ion.

steps.title: Pinacol–pinacolone rearrangement
steps.body:
(CH₃)₂C(OH)–C(OH)(CH₃)₂ + H⁺ → (CH₃)₃C–CO–CH₃
1. Protonate one OH; lose H₂O → 3° carbocation.
2. 1,2-methyl shift to the cationic carbon → cation stabilised by the adjacent O lone pair (oxocarbenium).
3. Lose H⁺ → pinacolone (3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one).
Migratory aptitude (approximate): aryl (p-anisyl > phenyl) > H ≈ alkyl; the carbocation that forms is the more stable one.

steps.title: Periodic acid and lead tetraacetate
steps.body:
Vicinal diols are cleaved: R₂C(OH)–C(OH)R₂ + HIO₄ → 2 R₂C=O + HIO₃ + H₂O.
- Via a cyclic periodate ester — cis diols react faster.
- Malaprade reaction is used in carbohydrate structure determination: each C–C bond between OH-bearing carbons consumes one HIO₄; terminal CH₂OH gives HCHO, internal CHOH gives HCOOH.

steps.title: Solved: periodate count
steps.body:
Glycerol HOCH₂–CHOH–CH₂OH:
- Two C–C bonds between OH carbons → **2 mol HIO₄**
- Products: 2 HCHO (from terminal C) + 1 HCOOH (from the middle C)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the first-formed carbocation is the more stable one in unsymmetrical pinacols.
- Applying periodate cleavage to 1,3-diols (they are not cleaved).
- Writing CO₂ instead of HCOOH for the middle carbon of glycerol.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the pinacol rearrangement.
items: Lose water to form a tertiary carbocation
Oxygen lone pair stabilises the new cation
Lose a proton to give pinacolone

quiz.q: Product of pinacol rearrangement of pinacol:
quiz.why: Methyl migration followed by proton loss gives tert-butyl methyl ketone (pinacolone).

quiz.q: Moles of HIO₄ consumed by ethane-1,2-diol:
quiz.why: Ethylene glycol has one C–C bond between hydroxyl-bearing carbons, so it uses one mole and gives two HCHO.

quiz.q: Periodate does not cleave:
quiz.why: Periodate needs adjacent (vicinal) OH groups to form the cyclic ester; propane-1,3-diol has none.

scenes.text: Aspirin manufacture starts with Kolbe's 1860 reaction: sodium phenoxide plus CO₂ under pressure.
The product, salicylic acid, is then acetylated.

steps.title: Acidity
steps.body:
Phenol pKa 10.0 (ethanol ≈ 16, water 15.7, carbonic acid 6.4).
- Dissolves in NaOH but **not** in NaHCO₃ (carboxylic acids do) — a classic distinction.
- −M groups at o/p increase acidity: picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) pKa ≈ 0.4.
- +I/+M groups decrease acidity (p-cresol 10.3).

steps.title: Named reactions
steps.body:
- **Reimer–Tiemann**: phenol + CHCl₃ + NaOH → salicylaldehyde (o-CHO) via dichlorocarbene.
- **Kolbe–Schmitt**: sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (≈ 125 °C, 4–7 atm), then H⁺ → salicylic acid.
- **Bromination**: Br₂ water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt); Br₂ in CS₂ at low temperature → mainly p-bromophenol.
- **Nitration**: dilute HNO₃ → o- and p-nitrophenol (separate by steam distillation; ortho is volatile).
- **Fries rearrangement**: phenyl acetate + AlCl₃ → o-/p-hydroxyacetophenone.
- **FeCl₃ test**: violet colour with phenols (enol complex).

steps.title: Solved: separating a mixture
steps.body:
A mixture of benzoic acid, phenol and toluene in ether:
1. Shake with NaHCO₃(aq): benzoic acid → sodium benzoate (aqueous). Acidify → benzoic acid.
2. Shake ether layer with NaOH(aq): phenol → phenoxide (aqueous). Acidify → phenol.
3. Ether layer retains toluene.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming phenol liberates CO₂ from NaHCO₃.
- Placing the CHO para in Reimer–Tiemann (ortho is major).
- Forgetting that phenol needs no Lewis acid for bromination.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction with its product from phenol.

quiz.q: Phenol can be separated from benzoic acid using:
quiz.why: Only benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is acidic enough to react with bicarbonate and move into the aqueous layer.

quiz.q: Electrophile in Reimer–Tiemann reaction:
quiz.why: Base converts chloroform to dichlorocarbene, which attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring.

quiz.q: Most acidic:
quiz.why: Three nitro groups delocalise the phenoxide charge, making picric acid as strong as many mineral acids (pKa ≈ 0.4).

scenes.text: Diethyl ether was first demonstrated publicly as a surgical anaesthetic in 1846.
Its three-membered cousin, ethylene oxide, is so strained it is used to sterilise medical equipment.

steps.title: Williamson synthesis
steps.body:
RO⁻Na⁺ + R′X → ROR′ + NaX (SN2).
- Use the **less hindered halide** (1° or methyl) and the bulkier alkoxide.
- tert-Butyl methyl ether: (CH₃)₃CO⁻ + CH₃I ✔; CH₃O⁻ + (CH₃)₃CBr ✘ (gives isobutene by E2).
- Aryl ethers: ArO⁻ + RX (not ArX + RO⁻).

steps.title: Cleavage of ethers by HI
steps.body:
Protonation, then I⁻ attack:
- Methyl/1° groups: SN2 at the less hindered carbon → CH₃I + ROH
- 3° groups: SN1 → 3° iodide
- Anisole + HI → **phenol + CH₃I** (never iodobenzene — no SN at aryl C)
- Zeisel method: estimation of methoxy groups via CH₃I.

steps.title: Epoxides
steps.body:
Made by peracid epoxidation or from halohydrins + base.
- **Acidic opening**: nucleophile attacks the **more substituted** carbon (SN1-like, partial positive charge).
- **Basic/neutral opening** (RO⁻, RMgX, LiAlH₄): attack at the **less substituted** carbon (SN2).
- Both give anti (trans) products; cyclohexene oxide + H₃O⁺ → trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol.
- **Crown ethers** (see s-block) bind cations.

steps.title: Solved: 2,2-dimethyloxirane
steps.body:
- CH₃OH/H⁺ → (CH₃)₂C(OCH₃)CH₂OH (attack at the 3° carbon)
- CH₃O⁻/CH₃OH → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂OCH₃ (attack at the CH₂)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a tertiary halide in Williamson synthesis.
- Writing iodobenzene from anisole + HI.
- Swapping regiochemistry of acidic and basic epoxide opening.

activity.prompt: Match reaction to product.

quiz.q: Best Williamson route to ethyl phenyl ether:
quiz.why: Phenoxide attacks the primary ethyl bromide by SN2; aryl halides do not undergo SN2.

quiz.q: Under acidic conditions, nucleophiles open unsymmetrical epoxides at:
quiz.why: Protonation creates partial positive charge best supported on the more substituted carbon, which the nucleophile then attacks.

quiz.q: Anisole with excess HI gives:
quiz.why: Iodide attacks the methyl carbon by SN2 because substitution at an aromatic carbon is not possible.

questions.q: 3° alcohol from a Grignard reagent requires:
questions.why: A ketone's carbonyl carbon already carries two R groups, so adding a third gives a tertiary alcohol.

questions.q: Ethyl acetate + excess CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺:
questions.why: Two equivalents add: first forming acetone after loss of ethoxide, then a tertiary alkoxide giving (CH₃)₃COH.

questions.q: Lucas reagent is:
questions.why: Anhydrous ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl converts alcohols to alkyl chlorides at rates set by carbocation stability.

questions.q: Easiest to dehydrate:
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate via the most stable carbocation, so they react fastest by E1.

questions.q: Moles of HIO₄ consumed by glycerol:
questions.why: Glycerol has two C–C bonds between adjacent OH-bearing carbons, so it consumes two moles.

questions.q: Major migrating group in Ph₂C(OH)C(OH)(CH₃)₂ rearrangement:
questions.why: The more stable diphenyl carbocation forms first, so a group from the other carbon, methyl, must migrate to it.

questions.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
questions.why: The phenoxide negative charge is delocalised into the ring, stabilising the conjugate base.

questions.q: Kolbe–Schmitt reaction gives:
questions.why: Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂ under pressure at the ortho position to give sodium salicylate.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol are separated by:
questions.why: Intramolecular H-bonding makes o-nitrophenol volatile in steam, while the para isomer is not.

questions.q: Williamson synthesis fails with:
questions.why: Tertiary halides undergo E2 elimination with strongly basic alkoxides instead of SN2.

questions.q: Reaction of 2,2-dimethyloxirane with NaOCH₃/CH₃OH gives:
questions.why: Basic SN2 opening occurs at the less hindered CH₂ carbon, putting OCH₃ there.

questions.q: FeCl₃ gives violet colour with:
questions.why: Phenols form coloured iron(III) phenoxide complexes, a standard qualitative test.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Aldehydes and ketones
courses.summary: Structure and reactivity of the carbonyl group, nucleophilic additions (HCN, bisulphite, alcohols, ammonia derivatives), reactions via enolates (aldol, haloform), Cannizzaro, benzoin, Perkin and Wittig reactions, and oxidation–reduction methods with classical tests.
outcomes: Explain why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones toward nucleophiles
Write mechanisms for cyanohydrin, acetal and imine formation
Predict products of aldol, crossed aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions
Choose reagents for selective reduction (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄, Clemmensen, Wolff–Kishner) and use Tollens', Fehling's and 2,4-DNP tests

scenes.text: Bitter almonds contain amygdalin, a sugar derivative of benzaldehyde cyanohydrin.
Cyanide adding to a C=O is the textbook nucleophilic addition — and nature does it too.

steps.title: Reactivity
steps.body:
C=O is polar (Cδ⁺–Oδ⁻); nucleophiles attack the trigonal carbon (Bürgi–Dunitz angle ≈ 107°) → tetrahedral alkoxide.
Reactivity: HCHO > RCHO > R₂CO > ArCOR.
- Alkyl groups donate electrons (+I) and add steric bulk, so ketones are less reactive.
- Aryl groups conjugate with C=O, reducing electrophilicity.

steps.title: Important additions
steps.body:
- **HCN** (KCN, trace acid, pH ≈ 9–10): cyanohydrin; hydrolysis gives α-hydroxy acids.
- **NaHSO₃**: crystalline bisulphite adduct (aldehydes, methyl ketones, small cyclic ketones) — used for purification.
- **H₂O**: hydrates; HCHO is ≈ 99.9% hydrated; Cl₃CCHO forms stable chloral hydrate.
- **Alcohols** (dry HCl): hemiacetal → acetal; acetals are stable to base, used as protecting groups (ethylene glycol).
- **Ammonia derivatives** (pH ≈ 4.5): NH₂OH → oxime; NH₂NH₂ → hydrazone; 2,4-DNP → orange/yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (test for C=O); semicarbazide → semicarbazone.

steps.title: Solved: acetal protection
steps.body:
Reduce the ester of CH₃COCH₂CH₂COOC₂H₅ without touching the ketone:
1. Ethylene glycol, H⁺ → cyclic acetal of the ketone
2. LiAlH₄ → reduces ester to CH₂OH
3. H₃O⁺ → removes acetal
Product: **5-hydroxypentan-2-one**, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂OH.

steps.title: Why pH ≈ 4.5 for imine formation
steps.body: Too acidic: the amine nucleophile is protonated (inactive). Too basic: the OH of the carbinolamine is not protonated and cannot leave as water. The rate is highest at moderately acidic pH.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using aqueous acid during acetal formation (water reverses it).
- Saying ketones generally form bisulphite adducts (only unhindered ones do).
- Forgetting that acetals are cleaved by aqueous acid but stable to base and hydrides.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent to the product formed with acetone.

quiz.q: Most reactive toward nucleophilic addition:
quiz.why: Formaldehyde has no electron-donating or bulky groups on the carbonyl carbon.

quiz.q: Acetals are stable to:
quiz.why: Acetals lack an acidic proton or leaving group under basic conditions, so they survive bases and LiAlH₄.

quiz.q: Optimum pH for oxime formation is about:
quiz.why: Mild acidity protonates the leaving OH group while leaving enough free hydroxylamine to act as nucleophile.

scenes.text: Two molecules of acetaldehyde join in dilute alkali to form a four-carbon 'aldol'.
Your cells use the same chemistry in glycolysis (aldolase).

steps.title: Enols and enolates
steps.body:
α-H atoms of carbonyl compounds are acidic (acetone pKa ≈ 19–20; ethyl acetoacetate ≈ 11) because the enolate is resonance-stabilised.
Keto–enol tautomerism: acetone is > 99.99% keto; acetylacetone ≈ 80% enol (H-bonded and conjugated).

steps.title: Aldol condensation
steps.body:
2CH₃CHO (dil. NaOH) → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) → heat → CH₃CH=CHCHO (crotonaldehyde).
Mechanism: (1) enolate forms; (2) attacks second C=O; (3) protonation; (4) E1cB dehydration.
**Claisen–Schmidt** (crossed aldol): C₆H₅CHO + CH₃COCH₃ → C₆H₅CH=CHCOCH₃ (benzalacetone) — benzaldehyde has no α-H, so it acts only as acceptor.

steps.title: Haloform reaction
steps.body:
Methyl ketones (and CH₃CH(OH)– alcohols) + X₂/NaOH → CHX₃ + RCOO⁻.
- **Iodoform test**: yellow CHI₃ (m.p. 119 °C) — positive for ethanol, acetaldehyde, acetone, propan-2-ol, acetophenone; negative for methanol, propanal, pentan-3-one.

steps.title: Solved: which give iodoform?
steps.body:
- Butan-2-one CH₃COCH₂CH₃ → **yes** (CH₃CO–)
- Pentan-3-one → **no**
- Butan-2-ol → **yes** (oxidised to butan-2-one)
- Ethanol → **yes** (the only 1° alcohol that does)
- Benzophenone → **no**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing aldol products for aldehydes with no α-H (HCHO, PhCHO, (CH₃)₃CCHO) — they give Cannizzaro instead.
- Calling methanol iodoform-positive.
- Forgetting the dehydration step on heating.

activity.prompt: Match each compound to its iodoform result.

quiz.q: Aldol of propanal gives (before dehydration):
quiz.why: The enolate from C2 of propanal attacks another propanal, giving CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CHO.

quiz.q: Which cannot undergo aldol self-condensation?
quiz.why: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot form an enolate.

quiz.q: Iodoform test is positive for:
quiz.why: Propan-2-ol is oxidised to acetone, a methyl ketone, which gives yellow CHI₃.

lessons.title: Cannizzaro, benzoin, Perkin and Wittig reactions

scenes.text: Benzaldehyde in strong alkali becomes half benzyl alcohol, half benzoate.
With no α-H available, a hydride jumps from one molecule to another.

steps.title: Cannizzaro reaction
steps.body:
Aldehydes without α-H + conc. NaOH: 2RCHO → RCH₂OH + RCOO⁻.
Mechanism: OH⁻ adds to C=O; the tetrahedral anion transfers H⁻ (hydride) to a second aldehyde (rate-determining).
**Crossed Cannizzaro**: HCHO + ArCHO → HCOO⁻ + ArCH₂OH (formaldehyde is oxidised preferentially). Used to make pentaerythritol.

steps.title: Other named reactions
steps.body:
- **Benzoin condensation**: 2PhCHO (CN⁻ catalyst, aq. EtOH) → PhCH(OH)COPh; CN⁻ reverses carbonyl polarity (umpolung).
- **Perkin**: PhCHO + (CH₃CO)₂O + CH₃COONa, heat → cinnamic acid PhCH=CHCOOH.
- **Wittig**: R₂C=O + Ph₃P=CHR′ → R₂C=CHR′ + Ph₃P=O; double bond placed exactly where the C=O was.
- **Knoevenagel**: aldehyde + active methylene (CH₂(COOEt)₂), weak base (piperidine).

steps.title: Solved: deuterium labelling
steps.body: PhCDO + conc. NaOH in H₂O → PhCD₂OH + PhCOO⁻. The alcohol carries **two D atoms** and no H from water, proving direct hydride (deuteride) transfer between aldehyde molecules.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Cannizzaro for acetaldehyde (it has α-H → aldol).
- Thinking the Wittig reagent attacks like a Grignard to give an alcohol.
- Forgetting the catalyst in benzoin (cyanide, or a thiazolium salt).

activity.prompt: Match the reaction with its product.

quiz.q: Cannizzaro reaction requires an aldehyde:
quiz.why: If α-H were present, the base would form an enolate and aldol reactions would dominate.

quiz.q: Product of acetone with Ph₃P=CH₂:
quiz.why: The Wittig reaction replaces C=O with C=CH₂, giving (CH₃)₂C=CH₂.

quiz.q: In crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO, formaldehyde is:
quiz.why: Formaldehyde is most reactive toward OH⁻, so it forms the hydride donor and ends up as formate.

scenes.text: Warm glucose with Tollens' reagent and the test tube becomes a mirror.
Aldehydes reduce Ag⁺ to silver; ketones (with few exceptions) cannot.

steps.title: Oxidation tests
steps.body:
- **Tollens'** [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺: aldehydes → silver mirror (aliphatic and aromatic); α-hydroxy ketones (fructose) also positive.
- **Fehling's/Benedict's** (Cu²⁺ tartrate/citrate): aliphatic aldehydes → red Cu₂O; **aromatic aldehydes negative**.
- **Schiff's reagent**: pink with aldehydes.
- Strong oxidants (KMnO₄, HNO₃) cleave ketones; **Baeyer–Villiger** (peracid) converts ketones to esters (migration: 3° > 2° ≈ aryl > 1° > CH₃).

steps.title: Reductions
steps.body:
| Reagent | Result |
|---|---|
| NaBH₄ (EtOH) | C=O → CHOH (aldehydes, ketones; not esters) |
| LiAlH₄ (dry ether) | Also reduces esters, acids, amides |
| Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl) | C=O → CH₂ (acid-stable substrates) |
| Wolff–Kishner (NH₂NH₂, KOH, glycol, heat) | C=O → CH₂ (base-stable substrates) |
| MPV (Al(Oi-Pr)₃, i-PrOH) | Selective C=O → CHOH; C=C untouched |
| H₂/Ni | Reduces C=O and C=C |

steps.title: Solved: identify the unknown
steps.body:
Compound C₃H₆O: positive 2,4-DNP, negative Tollens', positive iodoform.
- C=O present; not an aldehyde; methyl ketone → **acetone**.
Isomer that is Tollens' positive and iodoform negative → **propanal**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling benzaldehyde Fehling-positive.
- Using Clemmensen on acid-sensitive molecules (use Wolff–Kishner).
- Expecting NaBH₄ to reduce esters at room temperature.

activity.prompt: Match test or reagent with its result.

quiz.q: Distinguishes acetaldehyde from benzaldehyde:
quiz.why: Fehling's solution is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes but not by benzaldehyde, while both give Tollens' and 2,4-DNP tests.

quiz.q: Reduce C=O to CH₂ in a base-stable, acid-sensitive compound:
quiz.why: Wolff–Kishner works in hot basic conditions, avoiding the strong acid of the Clemmensen method.

quiz.q: Reduces only the C=O of cinnamaldehyde, leaving C=C:
quiz.why: Hydride donors such as NaBH₄ and Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley reagents are selective for the carbonyl group.

questions.q: Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because of:
options: +I effect and steric hindrance of two R groups
questions.why: Two alkyl groups both reduce the carbonyl carbon's partial positive charge and block the approach of nucleophiles.

questions.q: Cyanohydrin of acetaldehyde on hydrolysis gives:
questions.why: CH₃CH(OH)CN hydrolyses to CH₃CH(OH)COOH, 2-hydroxypropanoic (lactic) acid.

questions.q: Test specific to carbonyl group:
questions.why: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine forms coloured hydrazones with aldehydes and ketones.

questions.q: Crotonaldehyde forms from acetaldehyde by:
questions.why: Aldol addition gives 3-hydroxybutanal, which loses water on heating to give but-2-enal.

questions.q: Claisen–Schmidt product of PhCHO + acetophenone:
questions.why: Acetophenone's enolate attacks benzaldehyde and dehydration gives the α,β-unsaturated ketone chalcone.

questions.q: Iodoform test is negative for:
questions.why: Methanol oxidises to formaldehyde, which has no CH₃CO– group.

questions.q: Products of Cannizzaro on 2 HCHO:
questions.why: One formaldehyde is reduced to methanol and the other oxidised to formate.

questions.q: Benzoin condensation catalyst:
questions.why: Cyanide adds to benzaldehyde and makes its carbon nucleophilic (umpolung) so it can attack a second aldehyde.

questions.q: Perkin reaction produces:
questions.why: Benzaldehyde condenses with acetic anhydride in the presence of sodium acetate to give PhCH=CHCOOH.

questions.q: Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of cyclohexanone gives:
questions.why: Oxygen inserts next to the carbonyl, expanding the ring to the seven-membered lactone.

questions.q: Reagent converting acetophenone into ethylbenzene:
questions.why: Clemmensen reduction converts the carbonyl directly to CH₂.

questions.q: C₄H₈O positive Tollens' and negative iodoform could be:
questions.why: Butanal is an aldehyde (Tollens' positive) without a CH₃CO– group (iodoform negative).

questions.q: Acetylacetone has high enol content because the enol is:
questions.why: The enol form gains conjugation with the second C=O and a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Carboxylic acids and their derivatives
courses.summary: Acidity of carboxylic acids and substituent effects, preparation and reactions (HVZ, decarboxylation, reduction), relative reactivity and interconversion of acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides, ester hydrolysis mechanism, and synthetic uses of malonic ester, acetoacetic ester and the Claisen condensation.
outcomes: Rank aliphatic and aromatic acids by strength using inductive, resonance and ortho effects
Write HVZ and decarboxylation reactions
Order acid derivatives by reactivity and convert one into another
Use malonic and acetoacetic ester syntheses to plan acids and ketones

scenes.text: Formic acid — from the Latin for ant — is about ten times stronger than acetic acid.
One methyl group's electron donation makes the difference.

steps.title: Why carboxylic acids are acidic
steps.body:
RCOO⁻ is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures (both C–O 127 pm). Acids are stronger than phenols and alcohols but weaker than mineral acids.
- Dissolve in NaHCO₃ with effervescence (CO₂) — distinguishes from phenols.
- Carboxylic acids exist as H-bonded dimers in non-polar solvents and the vapour (high boiling points).

steps.title: Substituent effects
steps.body:
| Acid | pKa |
|---|---|
| HCOOH | 3.75 |
| CH₃COOH | 4.76 |
| C₆H₅COOH | 4.20 |
| p-NO₂C₆H₄COOH | 3.44 |
| p-CH₃OC₆H₄COOH | 4.47 |
| o-CH₃C₆H₄COOH | 3.91 |
| (COOH)₂ (pKa₁) | 1.27 |
- −I/−M groups increase acidity; +I/+M groups decrease it.
- **Ortho effect**: almost any ortho substituent increases the acidity of benzoic acid (steric twist of COOH out of the ring plane reduces its conjugation with the ring).

steps.title: Solved: pH of 0.10 M acetic acid
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Predicting p-methoxybenzoic acid stronger than benzoic acid (+M of OCH₃ weakens it).
- Forgetting the ortho effect for o-toluic acid.
- Saying acids dissolve in NaHCO₃ without CO₂ evolution.

activity.prompt: Arrange from weakest to strongest acid.

quiz.q: Strongest acid:
quiz.why: The para nitro group withdraws electrons by −I and −M, stabilising the benzoate anion most.

quiz.q: Formic acid is stronger than acetic acid because:
quiz.why: The methyl group's +I effect increases negative charge density on acetate, making it a weaker acid.

quiz.q: pH of 0.010 M acetic acid (Ka 1.74 × 10⁻⁵) is about:

lessons.title: Preparation and reactions of carboxylic acids

scenes.text: Pour a Grignard reagent onto dry ice and you've made a carboxylic acid with one extra carbon.
Heat a malonic acid and it loses that carbon again as CO₂.

steps.title: Preparation
steps.body:
- Oxidation of 1° alcohols, aldehydes, alkylbenzenes (KMnO₄ → ArCOOH)
- RMgX + CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → RCOOH
- Hydrolysis of nitriles: RCN + 2H₂O (H⁺) → RCOOH + NH₄⁺ (RX + CN⁻ → RCN adds one carbon)
- Hydrolysis of esters, amides, acid chlorides

steps.title: Reactions
steps.body:
- **HVZ** (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky): RCH₂COOH + Br₂/P → RCHBrCOOH (α-bromination via acyl bromide enol).
- **Decarboxylation**: RCOONa + NaOH/CaO → RH; easy for β-keto acids and malonic acids (cyclic 6-membered TS) — CH₂(COOH)₂ → CH₃COOH + CO₂ at ≈ 150 °C.
- **Reduction**: LiAlH₄ → RCH₂OH (NaBH₄ does not reduce acids).
- **Hunsdiecker**: RCOOAg + Br₂ → RBr + CO₂ + AgBr.
- Conversion to derivatives: SOCl₂ → RCOCl; ROH/H⁺ → ester; NH₃, heat → amide.

steps.title: Solved: ascending the series
steps.body:
Convert CH₃COOH to CH₃CH₂COOH:
1. LiAlH₄ → CH₃CH₂OH
2. PBr₃ → CH₃CH₂Br
3. KCN → CH₃CH₂CN
4. H₃O⁺, heat → **CH₃CH₂COOH**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using NaBH₄ to reduce a carboxylic acid.
- Expecting HVZ at the β-carbon.
- Forgetting that the Grignard route needs dry conditions and no acidic groups in the substrate.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with the transformation.

quiz.q: Product of HVZ on propanoic acid:
quiz.why: HVZ brominates the α-carbon, giving CH₃CHBrCOOH.

quiz.q: Malonic acid on heating gives:
quiz.why: Malonic acid decarboxylates through a cyclic transition state to acetic acid and carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: Sodium propanoate + soda lime gives:
quiz.why: Decarboxylation removes the carboxyl carbon, leaving ethane.

scenes.text: Boiling coconut oil with lye produces soap and glycerol — saponification.
Base hydrolysis of esters is irreversible because the carboxylate cannot be attacked again.

steps.title: Reactivity order
steps.body:
Acid chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide (> carboxylate).
Reasons: leaving-group ability (Cl⁻ > RCOO⁻ > RO⁻ > NH₂⁻) and resonance donation into C=O (strongest for amide N, weakest for Cl).
A more reactive derivative can be converted to a less reactive one directly (RCOCl → anhydride → ester → amide), not the reverse.

steps.title: Nucleophilic acyl substitution
steps.body:
Addition–elimination via a tetrahedral intermediate.
- **Base hydrolysis (BAC2)**: OH⁻ adds → tetrahedral → RO⁻ leaves → RCOOH + RO⁻ → RCOO⁻ + ROH (irreversible).
- **Acid hydrolysis (AAC2)**: reversible; reverse of Fischer esterification.
- ¹⁸O labelling: ethyl propanoate-ethoxy-¹⁸O hydrolysis gives ethanol containing ¹⁸O → acyl–oxygen cleavage.
- tert-Butyl esters hydrolyse in acid via the 3° carbocation (AAL1, alkyl–oxygen cleavage).

steps.title: Solved: saponification value
steps.body:
Saponification value = mg KOH to saponify 1 g fat. For tristearin (M = 891.5 g mol⁻¹), 3 mol KOH (56.1 g mol⁻¹) per mol:
- 3 × 56.1 × 1000/891.5 = **189 mg KOH g⁻¹**

steps.title: Key reactions of derivatives
steps.body:
- RCOCl + R′₂CuLi → ketone; RCOCl + H₂/Pd–BaSO₄ (Rosenmund) → aldehyde
- Ester + 2 R′MgX → 3° alcohol; ester + DIBAL-H (−78 °C) → aldehyde
- Amide + LiAlH₄ → amine; amide + P₂O₅ → nitrile
- Amide + Br₂/NaOH → amine with one fewer carbon (Hofmann bromamide — see Unit 5)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling base hydrolysis of esters 'base-catalysed' (OH⁻ is consumed).
- Trying to make an acid chloride from an amide directly with water.
- Forgetting that amides are the least reactive because of strong N lone-pair resonance.

activity.prompt: Arrange derivatives from most to least reactive toward nucleophiles.

quiz.q: Ester hydrolysis in base is irreversible because:
options: The carboxylate formed is not electrophilic
quiz.why: The acid is deprotonated to a resonance-stabilised carboxylate that cannot be attacked by the alcohol.

quiz.q: ¹⁸O in the alcohol after hydrolysis of RCO–¹⁸OR′ shows:
quiz.why: The R′–¹⁸O bond stays intact, so the bond broken must be between the acyl carbon and oxygen.

quiz.q: Saponification value of a triglyceride of M = 806 g mol⁻¹:
quiz.why: 3 × 56.1 × 1000/806 ≈ 209 mg KOH g⁻¹ (this is about the value for tripalmitin).

lessons.title: Active methylene compounds and Claisen condensation

scenes.text: Diethyl malonate and ethyl acetoacetate are cheap, and their central CH₂ is easy to deprotonate.
Alkylate, hydrolyse, decarboxylate — and almost any acid or methyl ketone can be built.

steps.title: Claisen condensation
steps.body:
2CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOEt → CH₃COCH₂COOC₂H₅ (ethyl acetoacetate) + EtOH.
Mechanism: enolate of one ester attacks the C=O of another; ethoxide leaves; final deprotonation of the doubly activated CH₂ (pKa ≈ 11) drives the equilibrium. Intramolecular version: **Dieckmann** (diethyl adipate → cyclopentanone ester).

steps.title: Malonic ester synthesis
steps.body:
CH₂(COOEt)₂ + NaOEt → ⁻CH(COOEt)₂ → + RX → RCH(COOEt)₂ → H₃O⁺, heat → **RCH₂COOH** + CO₂.
Two alkylations → R(R′)CHCOOH.

steps.title: Acetoacetic ester synthesis
steps.body:
CH₃COCH₂COOEt + NaOEt → enolate → + RX → CH₃COCHRCOOEt
- Dilute acid/base, heat (ketonic hydrolysis) → **CH₃COCH₂R** (methyl ketone) + CO₂
- Concentrated alkali (acid hydrolysis) → RCH₂COOH + CH₃COOH
Ethyl acetoacetate shows keto–enol tautomerism (≈ 7–8% enol neat): gives FeCl₃ colour (enol) and 2,4-DNP (keto).

steps.title: Solved: plan syntheses
steps.body:
- Butanoic acid: malonic ester + C₂H₅Br → hydrolysis/decarboxylation → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH
- 2-Methylbutanoic acid: malonic ester + C₂H₅Br, then CH₃I → C₂H₅(CH₃)CHCOOH
- Hexan-2-one: acetoacetic ester + n-C₃H₇Br → ketonic hydrolysis → CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that decarboxylation removes one carbon of the malonate.
- Using aryl or 3° halides for alkylation (SN2 fails).
- Mixing up ketonic and acid hydrolysis of acetoacetic ester.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the malonic ester synthesis of butanoic acid.
items: Alkylate the enolate with ethyl bromide
Hydrolyse both esters with aqueous acid
Heat to decarboxylate the substituted malonic acid

quiz.q: Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate gives:
quiz.why: An ester enolate attacks another ester, displacing ethoxide to form the β-keto ester CH₃COCH₂COOEt.

quiz.q: Acetoacetic ester + CH₃I, then ketonic hydrolysis gives:
quiz.why: Methylation then hydrolysis and decarboxylation give CH₃COCH₂CH₃.

quiz.q: Malonic ester route to 3-phenylpropanoic acid uses:
quiz.why: Benzyl bromide alkylates the malonate by SN2 to give PhCH₂CH(COOEt)₂, which becomes PhCH₂CH₂COOH.

questions.q: Carboxylic acids, unlike phenols, react with:
questions.why: Carboxylic acids (pKa ≈ 4–5) are stronger than carbonic acid, so they liberate CO₂ from bicarbonate.

questions.q: o-Toluic acid is stronger than benzoic acid due to:
questions.why: The ortho methyl twists the COOH out of the ring plane, reducing destabilising ring–carboxylate conjugation and increasing acidity.

questions.q: Degree of ionisation of 0.10 M acetic acid:
RCN on acid hydrolysis gives:
questions.why: Nitriles hydrolyse through the amide to the carboxylic acid and ammonium ion.

questions.q: Hunsdiecker reaction converts RCOOAg into:
questions.why: Silver carboxylates with bromine lose CO₂ to give the alkyl bromide with one less carbon.

questions.q: Least reactive acid derivative:
questions.why: Strong resonance donation from nitrogen makes the amide carbonyl the least electrophilic.

questions.q: Rosenmund reduction converts acid chlorides into:
questions.why: H₂ over poisoned Pd/BaSO₄ stops at the aldehyde stage.

questions.q: tert-Butyl acetate in acid hydrolyses by:
questions.why: Protonated tert-butyl esters ionise to the stable tert-butyl cation (AAL1).

questions.q: Saponification value of tristearin (M 891.5):
questions.why: 3 × 56.1 × 1000/891.5 ≈ 189 mg KOH per gram of fat.

questions.q: Dieckmann condensation of diethyl adipate gives a:
questions.why: Intramolecular Claisen of the C6 diester closes a five-membered ring, ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate.

questions.q: Malonic ester + 2 CH₃I, then hydrolysis/decarboxylation:
questions.why: Two methyl groups on the central carbon give (CH₃)₂CHCOOH after losing one CO₂.

questions.q: Ethyl acetoacetate gives colour with FeCl₃ because of its:
questions.why: The enol tautomer's C=C–OH forms a coloured iron(III) complex, like phenols.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Nitro compounds, amines, diazonium salts, practicals & revision
courses.summary: Reduction of nitro compounds, preparation and basicity of amines (Gabriel, Hofmann bromamide), distinguishing tests (Hinsberg, carbylamine, nitrous acid), diazonium salts with Sandmeyer and coupling reactions, a systematic functional-group identification practical, and a paper-level revision exam.
outcomes: Predict products of nitrobenzene reduction under acidic, neutral and alkaline conditions
Rank aliphatic and aromatic amines by basicity
Distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° amines by Hinsberg and nitrous acid tests
Use diazonium salts to install –Cl, –Br, –CN, –OH, –F, –H and azo groups
Identify an unknown organic compound's functional group by standard tests

lessons.title: Nitro compounds and amines: preparation and basicity

scenes.text: In 1856, 18-year-old William Perkin oxidised impure aniline and made mauveine, the first synthetic dye.
Aniline itself is still made by reducing nitrobenzene.

steps.title: Reduction of nitrobenzene
steps.body:
| Conditions | Product |
|---|---|
| Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl (acidic) | Aniline |
| Zn/NH₄Cl (neutral) | N-Phenylhydroxylamine |
| Zn/NaOH (alkaline) | Hydrazobenzene (via azoxy, azobenzene) |
| H₂/Pd or Ni | Aniline |
| LiAlH₄ | Azobenzene |
Nitro groups are strongly deactivating, meta-directing; nitrobenzene is a useful high-boiling solvent.

steps.title: Preparation of amines
steps.body:
- **Gabriel phthalimide**: potassium phthalimide + RX → N-alkylphthalimide → hydrazine or KOH → **pure 1° RNH₂** (no over-alkylation; not for aryl amines).
- **Hofmann bromamide**: RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → RNH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O (one carbon fewer; via isocyanate).
- Reduction of nitriles (LiAlH₄ → RCH₂NH₂), amides (LiAlH₄), oximes, and reductive amination of carbonyls.
- Direct alkylation of NH₃ gives mixtures of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary salts.

steps.title: Basicity
steps.body:
pKb (water): (CH₃)₂NH 3.27 < CH₃NH₂ 3.36 < (CH₃)₃N 4.20 < NH₃ 4.75 < p-toluidine 8.9 < aniline 9.38 < p-nitroaniline ≈ 13.
- Aromatic amines are weak bases: the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
- Electron-donating ring substituents increase, withdrawing ones decrease basicity.

steps.title: Solved: Hofmann bromamide
steps.body:
Benzamide C₆H₅CONH₂ + Br₂/NaOH → **aniline**. Propanamide CH₃CH₂CONH₂ → **ethylamine**.
Mechanism: N-bromination → deprotonation → migration of R to N with loss of Br⁻ → isocyanate R–N=C=O → hydrolysis/decarboxylation → RNH₂. Migration occurs with retention of configuration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Gabriel synthesis for aniline (aryl halides do not undergo SN2).
- Forgetting the Hofmann product has one fewer carbon.
- Ranking aniline more basic than ammonia.

activity.prompt: Arrange from weakest to strongest base (in water).

quiz.q: Gabriel synthesis gives:
quiz.why: Phthalimide nitrogen can be alkylated only once, so hydrolysis releases a single primary amine.

quiz.q: Acetamide with Br₂/NaOH gives:
quiz.why: The Hofmann rearrangement removes the carbonyl carbon, giving CH₃NH₂.

quiz.q: Nitrobenzene with Zn/NH₄Cl gives:
quiz.why: Neutral reduction stops at the hydroxylamine stage, C₆H₅NHOH.

lessons.title: Reactions of amines and diazonium salts

scenes.text: Methyl orange, the titration indicator, is made by coupling a diazonium salt with N,N-dimethylaniline.
The key: keep the diazonium salt below 5 °C or it decomposes to phenol and N₂.

steps.title: Distinguishing tests
steps.body:
- **Hinsberg** (C₆H₅SO₂Cl, KOH): 1° → sulphonamide soluble in KOH (acidic N–H); 2° → insoluble sulphonamide; 3° → no reaction.
- **Carbylamine** (CHCl₃ + alc. KOH, heat): 1° amines only → foul-smelling isocyanide RNC.
- **Nitrous acid** (NaNO₂ + HCl, 0–5 °C): 1° aliphatic → N₂ bubbles + alcohol; 1° aromatic → diazonium salt; 2° → yellow oily N-nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → soluble salt; 3° aromatic → p-nitroso compound (green).
- Acetylation (Ac₂O) protects –NH₂ and moderates its activation (acetanilide → p-bromoacetanilide).

steps.title: Diazonium salt reactions
steps.body:
ArNH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl (0–5 °C) → ArN₂⁺Cl⁻ (stabilised by resonance with the ring).
- **Sandmeyer**: CuCl → ArCl; CuBr → ArBr; CuCN → ArCN
- **Gattermann**: Cu powder/HX → ArX
- KI → ArI (no catalyst)
- **Balz–Schiemann**: HBF₄, heat → ArF
- H₂O, warm → ArOH
- H₃PO₂ or EtOH → ArH (removes the amino group)
- **Coupling**: with phenol (pH ≈ 9–10) → p-hydroxyazobenzene (orange); with aniline (pH ≈ 4–5) → p-aminoazobenzene (yellow).

steps.title: Solved: 1,3,5-tribromobenzene
steps.body:
Direct bromination of benzene cannot give 1,3,5-substitution. Route:
1. Aniline + 3Br₂ (water) → 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (–NH₂ is o,p)
2. NaNO₂/HCl, 0–5 °C → diazonium salt
3. H₃PO₂ → **1,3,5-tribromobenzene** (amino group removed)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Warming diazonium salts during preparation.
- Running coupling with phenol in strong acid (phenoxide is the active coupler).
- Expecting a carbylamine result from 2° amines.

activity.prompt: Match the reagent with benzenediazonium chloride to the product.

quiz.q: Hinsberg product soluble in alkali comes from:
quiz.why: The sulphonamide of a primary amine still has an acidic N–H that dissolves in KOH.

quiz.q: Carbylamine test is given by:
quiz.why: Only primary amines react with dichlorocarbene to form isocyanides.

quiz.q: Balz–Schiemann reaction introduces:
quiz.why: Heating the diazonium tetrafluoroborate gives the aryl fluoride, BF₃ and N₂.

quiz.q: Diazotisation is done at 0–5 °C because:
quiz.why: Above about 5 °C aryl diazonium salts lose N₂ and react with water to give phenols.

lessons.title: Lab: Systematic identification of functional groups

scenes.text: In the practical exam Rahul gets a colourless liquid with a fruity smell and three hours.
Preliminary tests, then group tests, then a derivative with a melting point — the classic route.

steps.title: Order of tests
steps.body:
1. Physical state, colour, odour; ignition test (sooty flame → aromatic).
2. Solubility: water, 5% NaOH, 5% NaHCO₃, 5% HCl.
3. Elements (Lassaigne's sodium fusion): N (Prussian blue), S (violet with nitroprusside), halogens (AgNO₃).
4. Functional group tests.
5. Derivative preparation and melting point.

steps.title: Functional group tests
steps.body:
| Group | Test | Positive result |
|---|---|---|
| –COOH | NaHCO₃ | Effervescence (CO₂) |
| Phenol | Neutral FeCl₃ | Violet/blue/green colour |
| Alcohol | Ceric ammonium nitrate | Red colour |
| C=O | 2,4-DNP | Yellow/orange precipitate |
| –CHO | Tollens' / Fehling's | Silver mirror / red Cu₂O |
| Methyl ketone | I₂/NaOH | Yellow CHI₃ |
| Ester | Hydroxamic acid (NH₂OH, then FeCl₃) | Wine-red colour |
| 1° aromatic amine | Diazotisation + β-naphthol | Orange-red dye |
| –NO₂ | Mulliken–Barker (Zn/NH₄Cl, then Tollens') | Black/grey ppt |
| Amide | Boil with NaOH | NH₃ evolved |
| C=C | Br₂ water / Baeyer's | Decolourised |

steps.title: Solved: identify the unknown
steps.body:
Colourless liquid, fruity smell, insoluble in water, NaHCO₃ negative, 2,4-DNP negative, hydroxamic acid test wine red; no N, S or halogen; b.p. 77 °C.
→ **Ester**; b.p. matches **ethyl acetate**. Confirm by saponification and identifying ethanol (iodoform positive) and acetate.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body:
- Why fuse with sodium? Converts covalent N, S, X into ionic NaCN, Na₂S, NaX that can be tested in water.
- Why boil with HNO₃ before the AgNO₃ halogen test? Destroys CN⁻ and S²⁻, which would also precipitate with Ag⁺.
- Why is a derivative needed? Melting points of solid derivatives confirm identity more reliably than boiling points.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing FeCl₃ in acidic solution (colour fails).
- Skipping the HNO₃ boil in the halogen test.
- Reporting a functional group from a single test without confirmation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of systematic organic analysis.
items: Note physical state, colour and odour
Prepare a derivative and measure its melting point

quiz.q: Wine-red colour in the hydroxamic acid test indicates:
quiz.why: Esters react with hydroxylamine to form hydroxamic acids, which give a red iron(III) complex.

quiz.q: In Lassaigne's test, N is detected as:
quiz.why: NaCN from fusion forms ferrocyanide, which with Fe³⁺ gives Prussian blue.

quiz.q: An unknown dissolves in NaOH but not NaHCO₃ and gives violet with FeCl₃. It is likely a:
quiz.why: Phenols are acidic enough for NaOH but too weak for bicarbonate, and they give coloured FeCl₃ complexes.

scenes.text: Aisha draws one big map linking halides, alcohols, carbonyls, acids and amines.
Every arrow is a reagent she must know for the exam.

steps.title: Key-point sheet
steps.body:
- SN2: k[RX][Nu], inversion, CH₃ > 1° > 2°; SN1: k[RX], racemisation, 3° > 2°; E2 anti-periplanar; t-BuO⁻ → Hofmann
- SNAr needs o/p-NO₂; F fastest; benzyne with NaNH₂
- Grignard: HCHO → 1°, RCHO → 2°, ketone → 3°, ester (2 eq.) → 3°, CO₂ → acid
- Lucas: 3° instant, 2° ≈ 5 min, 1° none
- Pinacol: migrating group goes to the more stable cation; HIO₄ cleaves vicinal diols
- Phenol pKa 10; Reimer–Tiemann (o-CHO), Kolbe (salicylic acid)
- Epoxides: acid → more substituted C; base → less substituted C
- Aldehydes: Tollens' (all), Fehling's (aliphatic only); iodoform: CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–
- No α-H → Cannizzaro; α-H → aldol
- Reactivity: RCOCl > anhydride > ester > amide
- Malonic ester → RCH₂COOH; acetoacetic ester → CH₃COCH₂R
- Amine pKb: 2° < 1° < 3° < NH₃ ≪ aniline; Hinsberg, carbylamine (1° only)
- ArN₂⁺: CuCl/CuBr/CuCN (Sandmeyer), KI, HBF₄, H₂O, H₃PO₂, coupling

steps.title: Typical long questions (practise)
steps.body:
1. Compare SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with energy diagrams and stereochemistry.
2. Explain the mechanism of aldol condensation and Cannizzaro reaction. Why does benzaldehyde not give aldol?
3. How will you prepare butanoic acid and hexan-2-one using active methylene compounds?
4. Explain why aniline is a weaker base than methylamine. Arrange substituted anilines by basicity.
5. Give the synthesis of m-bromotoluene from toluene via a diazonium salt.

steps.title: Worked answer: m-bromotoluene
steps.body:
1. Toluene → nitrate → p-nitrotoluene (separate) → reduce → p-toluidine
2. Acetylate (moderate –NH₂) → brominate (ortho to NHAc, i.e. meta to CH₃) → hydrolyse → 2-bromo-4-methylaniline
3. NaNO₂/HCl, 0–5 °C, then H₃PO₂ → **m-bromotoluene**

steps.title: Exam traps
steps.body:
- Hofmann bromamide loses one carbon; nitrile reduction keeps all carbons.
- Fehling's test is negative for benzaldehyde.
- Basic epoxide opening at the less hindered carbon.

activity.prompt: Match each target with a suitable key reagent.

quiz.q: Which test distinguishes 1° from 2° amines?
quiz.why: Only primary amines form the foul-smelling isocyanide with chloroform and alcoholic KOH.

quiz.q: Ethyl bromide to propylamine (all carbons kept plus one):
quiz.why: Cyanide adds one carbon to give propanenitrile, and LiAlH₄ reduces it to CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.

quiz.q: Fehling's negative, Tollens' positive, 2,4-DNP positive compound C₇H₆O:
quiz.why: Benzaldehyde is an aromatic aldehyde, which reduces Tollens' reagent but not Fehling's solution.

questions.q: SN2 reaction of (S)-2-bromobutane with NaCN gives:
questions.why: Backside attack inverts the stereocentre; CN has the same priority rank as Br had (above ethyl), so S becomes R.

questions.q: Fastest SN1 solvolysis:
questions.why: The tertiary bromide ionises to the most stable carbocation.

questions.q: Major product of 2-bromobutane + NaOEt, heat:
questions.why: A small strong base gives E2 elimination following Saytzeff's rule, with the trans alkene favoured.

questions.q: Grignard + CO₂ then H₃O⁺ gives:
questions.why: RMgX adds to CO₂ to form a carboxylate, which acid converts to RCOOH.

questions.q: Picric acid is:
questions.why: Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, a strong phenolic acid.

questions.q: Anisole + HI gives:
questions.why: Iodide attacks the methyl carbon by SN2; aromatic C–O cleavage does not occur.

questions.q: Aldehyde without α-H in conc. NaOH undergoes:
questions.why: With no enolisable hydrogen, hydroxide adds and hydride transfer leads to disproportionation.

questions.q: Iodoform positive compound among:
questions.why: Butan-2-ol has the CH₃CH(OH)– unit, oxidised to a methyl ketone under the test conditions.

questions.q: pKa of p-nitrobenzoic acid vs benzoic acid:
questions.why: The nitro group stabilises the carboxylate, lowering the pKa from 4.20 to about 3.44.

questions.q: Acetoacetic ester + C₂H₅Br, then ketonic hydrolysis gives:
questions.why: Adding an ethyl group to CH₃COCH₂– gives CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃ after decarboxylation.

questions.q: Hofmann bromamide of benzamide gives:
questions.why: The phenyl group migrates to nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate.

questions.q: Least basic:
questions.why: The para nitro group pulls the nitrogen lone pair into the ring by −M, leaving it least available.

questions.q: Secondary amine with HNO₂ gives:
questions.why: Secondary amines form N-nitrosamines, R₂N–N=O, which separate as yellow oils.

questions.q: Benzenediazonium chloride + CuBr gives:
questions.why: The Sandmeyer reaction with CuBr replaces N₂⁺ by Br.

questions.q: Coupling of benzenediazonium with phenol is done at:
questions.why: Mildly alkaline conditions convert phenol to the more reactive phenoxide without destroying the diazonium ion.

uni-bsc-chem-organic-chemistry-3.title: Organic Chemistry III — Mechanisms, Heterocycles & Biomolecules
uni-bsc-chem-organic-chemistry-3.description: Reactive intermediates, SN1/SN2/E1/E2 mechanisms, carbonyl chemistry and molecular rearrangements, five- and six-membered heterocycles, and carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, with qualitative organic practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Reactive intermediates, substitution and elimination
courses.summary: Carbocations, carbanions, free radicals, carbenes, nitrenes and benzynes; kinetics, stereochemistry and energy profiles of SN1 and SN2; E1, E2 and E1cB eliminations with Saytzeff/Hofmann orientation; and the factors that decide substitution versus elimination.
outcomes: Rank stabilities of carbocations, carbanions and radicals and explain why
Distinguish SN1 and SN2 by kinetics, stereochemistry and substrate
Predict products of E2 using anti-periplanar geometry and Saytzeff/Hofmann rules
Choose conditions favouring substitution or elimination
Identify carbene, nitrene and benzyne reactions

scenes.text: Most organic reactions pass through species that live for less than a microsecond.
Knowing their stability lets you predict which path a reaction will take — and which product will dominate.

steps.title: Carbocations and carbanions
steps.body:
**Carbocation**: sp², planar, empty p orbital. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺, raised by hyperconjugation and +I alkyl groups; allyl and benzyl cations are resonance stabilised (benzyl ≈ 2° or better). Carbocations rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shifts to more stable ions.

**Carbanion**: sp³, pyramidal (lone pair). Stability: CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3° (opposite of cations); stabilised by −I/−M groups (C=O, NO₂, CN) and by more s-character (sp > sp² > sp³; HC≡C⁻ is fairly stable).

steps.title: Radicals, carbenes, nitrenes, benzyne
steps.body:
- **Free radicals**: nearly planar, one unpaired electron; stability 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃·; allyl/benzyl radicals resonance stabilised. Formed by homolysis (light, peroxides).
- **Carbenes** (:CH₂, :CCl₂): neutral, divalent carbon with 6 electrons. Singlet (paired, sp²) adds to alkenes stereospecifically; triplet (diradical) adds non-stereospecifically. :CCl₂ from CHCl₃ + base (Reimer–Tiemann).
- **Nitrenes** (R–N:): nitrogen analogues; intermediates in Hofmann and Curtius rearrangements.
- **Benzyne**: aryl halide + NaNH₂; strained 'triple bond' in a benzene ring; addition gives cine-substitution.

steps.title: Solved: predicting rearrangement
steps.body:
3-methylbut-2-yl cation (CH₃)₂CH–C⁺H–CH₃ (2°) undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift → (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃ (3°).

So HBr addition to 3-methylbut-1-ene gives mainly **2-bromo-2-methylbutane**, not the 'expected' 2-bromo-3-methylbutane.

steps.title: Solved: benzyne evidence
steps.body: Chlorobenzene with ¹⁴C at C-1 + NaNH₂/NH₃ gives aniline with NH₂ about 50% on C-1 and 50% on C-2. A direct substitution would put NH₂ only on C-1; the 50:50 split shows a symmetric benzyne intermediate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the cation stability order to carbanions.
- Drawing carbanions as planar (they are pyramidal unless conjugated).
- Forgetting carbocation rearrangements in SN1/E1 and HX additions.

activity.prompt: Match each intermediate to its feature.

quiz.q: Most stable carbocation:
quiz.why: The tertiary cation has three alkyl groups providing the most hyperconjugation and +I donation to the positive carbon.

quiz.q: Most stable carbanion:
quiz.why: Alkyl groups donate electrons and destabilise a negative charge, so the methyl carbanion is most stable of these.

quiz.q: Dichlorocarbene is generated from:
quiz.why: Base removes the acidic H of CHCl₃ to give CCl₃⁻, which loses Cl⁻ to form :CCl₂.

quiz.q: Radiolabelling showing 50:50 NH₂ at C-1 and C-2 supports:
quiz.why: Only a symmetric benzyne lets NH₂⁻ attack either end of the strained bond equally.

scenes.text: In an SN2 reaction the nucleophile attacks from the back and the three other groups flip like an umbrella in a gust.
Walden showed this inversion in the 1890s; SN1 reactions instead pass through a flat carbocation.

steps.title: SN2
steps.body:
- One step; rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] (second order).
- Backside attack, trigonal-bipyramidal transition state; **inversion of configuration** (Walden inversion): (R)-2-bromobutane + OH⁻ → (S)-butan-2-ol.
- Substrate: CH₃ > 1° > 2° ≫ 3° (steric hindrance); neopentyl halides are very slow.
- Favoured by strong nucleophiles and **polar aprotic solvents** (DMSO, DMF, acetone), which do not solvate anions strongly.
- Leaving group ability: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; tosylate is excellent.

steps.title: SN1
steps.body:
- Two steps: slow ionisation to R⁺, then fast attack; rate = k[RX] (first order).
- Planar carbocation → attack from both faces → **racemisation** (usually with slight excess inversion due to ion pairing).
- Substrate: 3° > 2° ≫ 1°; allyl and benzyl also good.
- Favoured by **polar protic solvents** (water, alcohols) that stabilise ions; weak nucleophiles (solvolysis).
- Rearrangements possible.

steps.title: Solved: which mechanism?
steps.body:
- CH₃CH₂Br + NaCN in DMSO → SN2 (1°, strong Nu, aprotic) → CH₃CH₂CN.
- (CH₃)₃CBr in aqueous ethanol → SN1 (3°, protic, weak Nu) → (CH₃)₃COH + (CH₃)₃COEt.
