- (S)-2-iodooctane + I⁻* (radioactive): rate of racemisation is twice the rate of isotope incorporation, because each SN2 inversion converts one S into one R.

steps.title: Neighbouring-group participation
steps.body: A neighbouring nucleophilic group (e.g. S in mustard gas, or an adjacent O⁻) can displace the leaving group internally, then be displaced by the external nucleophile: two inversions = **retention**, and often a large rate increase (anchimeric assistance).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Predicting SN2 on a tertiary halide.
- Saying SN1 always gives exactly 50:50 racemate.
- Using a protic solvent to speed an SN2 with an anionic nucleophile.

activity.prompt: Match each feature to SN1 or SN2.

quiz.q: (R)-2-bromobutane with NaOH in acetone mainly gives:
quiz.why: A secondary halide with strong nucleophile in aprotic solvent reacts by SN2, which inverts the configuration to S.

quiz.q: Rate of an SN1 reaction depends on:
quiz.why: The rate-determining step is ionisation of RX, so rate = k[RX], independent of the nucleophile.

quiz.q: Fastest SN2 reaction with NaI in acetone:
quiz.why: Primary unhindered CH₃CH₂Cl allows easy backside attack; tertiary and neopentyl substrates are sterically blocked.

quiz.q: Neighbouring-group participation usually leads to:
quiz.why: Two successive backside displacements (internal then external) give overall retention of configuration.

scenes.text: 2-bromobutane with ethoxide gives mostly but-2-ene; with bulky tert-butoxide, more but-1-ene.
The base and geometry steer elimination. That is Saytzeff versus Hofmann.

steps.title: E2
steps.body:
- One step; rate = k[RX][B⁻].
- H and leaving group must be **anti-periplanar** (dihedral 180°). In cyclohexanes both must be trans-diaxial.
- **Stereospecific**: e.g. meso-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane + base → (E)-1-bromostilbene.
- Kinetic isotope effect k_H/k_D ≈ 3–8 shows C–H breaks in the rate step.
- **Saytzeff (Zaitsev)**: small bases give the more substituted alkene. **Hofmann**: bulky bases (t-BuO⁻) or poor leaving groups (–NMe₃⁺, –F) give the less substituted alkene.

steps.title: E1 and E1cB
steps.body:
- **E1**: ionisation to R⁺ (slow), then loss of H⁺; rate = k[RX]; competes with SN1; Saytzeff product; rearrangement possible. Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols (3° > 2° > 1°).
- **E1cB**: base first removes an acidic H to form a carbanion (conjugate base), then the leaving group departs. Needs an acidifying group (C=O, NO₂) β to the leaving group and a poor leaving group (OH in aldol dehydration).

steps.title: Solved: menthyl vs neomenthyl chloride
steps.body:
- **Neomenthyl chloride**: Cl axial in the stable chair; two trans-diaxial H's → fast E2 giving mainly the Saytzeff alkene (3-menthene, ~75%).
- **Menthyl chloride**: Cl equatorial in the stable chair; must flip to an unfavourable conformer with Cl axial, where only one anti-H exists → slow E2 giving only 2-menthene (the less substituted, 'anti-Saytzeff' product).

Geometry outranks Saytzeff's rule.

steps.title: Solved: base controls orientation
steps.body:
2-bromo-2-methylbutane:
- KOEt/EtOH → 2-methylbut-2-ene (~70%, Saytzeff)
- KOt-Bu/t-BuOH → 2-methylbut-1-ene (~70%, Hofmann) because the bulky base reaches the less hindered CH₃ hydrogens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the trans-diaxial requirement in cyclohexyl E2.
- Expecting rearrangement in E2 (none — no carbocation).
- Calling E1cB a two-step E1; the order of events is reversed (H leaves first).

activity.prompt: Match each elimination fact with the mechanism.
pairs: Dehydration of aldol product with base

quiz.q: Bulky t-BuOK with 2-bromo-2-methylbutane mainly gives:
quiz.why: The bulky base removes the more accessible CH₃ hydrogen, giving the less substituted Hofmann alkene.

quiz.q: In cyclohexane E2 the H and leaving group must be:
quiz.why: Only trans-diaxial positions give the 180° anti-periplanar arrangement needed for E2 orbital overlap.

quiz.q: Hofmann elimination of quaternary ammonium hydroxides gives mainly:
quiz.why: The poor, bulky –NR₃⁺ leaving group gives a carbanion-like transition state, favouring removal of the most acidic, least hindered H.

quiz.q: E1 is favoured by:
options: 3° substrate, weak base, heat, protic solvent
quiz.why: E1 needs a stable carbocation (3°), ionising protic solvent and heat, with no strong base that would cause E2.

scenes.text: A student heats isopropyl bromide with ethoxide and gets mostly propene; at room temperature, more ether forms.
Substrate, nucleophile/base, solvent and temperature together decide the outcome.

steps.title: Decision guide
steps.body:
- **Methyl, 1°**: SN2 with most nucleophiles; E2 only with bulky strong bases (t-BuO⁻).
- **2°**: strong base (EtO⁻, OH⁻) → mainly E2; good nucleophile weak base (I⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, CH₃COO⁻) in aprotic solvent → SN2; weak Nu/protic solvent → SN1/E1 mix.
- **3°**: strong base → E2; weak Nu/protic solvent → SN1 (+ E1, more with heat); never SN2.
- Heat favours elimination (more molecules → +ΔS).

steps.title: Solved: predict the major product
steps.body:
1. CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOEt, 25 °C → **CH₃CH₂CH₂OEt** (SN2)
2. CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + KOt-Bu → **propene** (E2, bulky base)
3. (CH₃)₂CHBr + NaOEt/EtOH, 55 °C → **propene ~80%** (E2)
4. (CH₃)₂CHBr + NaN₃/DMF → **2-azidopropane** (SN2; N₃⁻ is a weak base)
5. (CH₃)₃CBr + H₂O, 25 °C → **t-butanol** (SN1), some isobutene

steps.title: Solved: Williamson ether design
steps.body: To make t-butyl methyl ether: use (CH₃)₃CO⁻Na⁺ + CH₃I (SN2 on methyl). The alternative CH₃O⁻ + (CH₃)₃CBr gives isobutene by E2. Always put the hindered part on the alkoxide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating all strong nucleophiles as weak bases — OH⁻ and RO⁻ are both.
- Forgetting temperature: heating shifts SN1/E1 mixtures toward alkene.
- Choosing a 3° halide for Williamson ether synthesis.

activity.prompt: Order the questions you ask to predict SN1/SN2/E1/E2.
items: Is the reagent a strong base, a good nucleophile, or both/neither?
Is the solvent protic or polar aprotic?

quiz.q: Best route to ethyl tert-butyl ether:
quiz.why: SN2 needs an unhindered halide; the tertiary alkoxide attacks EtBr, while EtO⁻ with a tertiary bromide would just eliminate.

quiz.q: (CH₃)₂CHBr + NaCN in DMSO gives mainly:
quiz.why: Cyanide is a good nucleophile but a weak base, and DMSO favours SN2, so substitution dominates.

quiz.q: Raising temperature in a SN1/E1 mixture increases:
quiz.why: Elimination produces more particles (higher ΔS), so the −TΔS term favours it more at higher temperature.

questions.q: Hybridisation of carbon in a carbocation:
questions.why: The cationic carbon has three σ bonds and an empty p orbital, so it is sp² and planar.

questions.q: Allyl cation is stabilised by:
questions.why: The positive charge is shared over the two terminal carbons through π resonance.

questions.q: SN2 rate when [Nu] is doubled and [RX] halved:
questions.why: Rate = k[RX][Nu] = k(½)(2) = unchanged.

questions.q: Solvolysis of (CH₃)₃CCl is faster in:
questions.why: Polar protic solvents stabilise the carbocation and chloride ion, speeding the ionisation step.

questions.q: Major product of 2-bromobutane + KOH/ethanol, heat:
questions.why: E2 with a small base follows Saytzeff's rule; the more stable trans-but-2-ene is the main product.

questions.q: Kinetic isotope effect in E2 indicates:
options: C–H bond breaks in rate step
questions.why: A large k_H/k_D shows the C–H (or C–D) bond is being broken in the rate-determining step.

questions.q: Which reacts by E1cB?
questions.why: The α-H next to C=O is acidic; base forms an enolate that expels OH⁻, the classic E1cB in aldol condensation.

questions.q: Carbene addition to cis-but-2-ene giving only cis-dimethylcyclopropane indicates:
questions.why: A singlet carbene adds in one concerted step, preserving alkene geometry; triplet adds stepwise and scrambles it.

questions.q: Best leaving group:
questions.why: Iodide is the weakest base of these (conjugate of strong HI), so it departs most easily.

questions.q: Hydride shift in carbocations converts:
questions.why: Shifts occur when they produce a more stable carbocation, e.g. secondary to tertiary.

questions.q: Menthyl chloride with ethoxide gives only 2-menthene because:
options: Only one trans-diaxial H is available in the reactive conformer
questions.why: In the conformer with Cl axial, only the H on C-2 is anti-periplanar, so E2 can give only 2-menthene.

questions.q: Polar aprotic solvents accelerate SN2 because they:
options: Leave the nucleophile poorly solvated and reactive
questions.why: DMSO and DMF solvate cations but not anions well, so the 'naked' nucleophile reacts faster.

questions.q: Reimer–Tiemann reaction involves which intermediate?
questions.why: CHCl₃ and NaOH generate :CCl₂, which attacks the phenoxide ring to give salicylaldehyde after hydrolysis.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Addition reactions, carbonyl chemistry and rearrangements
courses.summary: Electrophilic addition to alkenes with stereochemistry, nucleophilic addition to carbonyl groups, enolate condensations (aldol, Claisen, Perkin, Knoevenagel, Cannizzaro) and molecular rearrangements (pinacol, Beckmann, Hofmann, Curtius, benzilic acid).
outcomes: Predict regiochemistry and stereochemistry of additions to alkenes
Explain the relative reactivity of aldehydes and ketones
Write mechanisms of aldol, Claisen and Cannizzaro reactions
Draw mechanisms of the main 1,2-rearrangements and predict products
Use migratory aptitude and anti-migration in Beckmann rearrangement

scenes.text: Orange bromine water decolourises instantly when shaken with cyclohexene.
A three-membered bromonium ion forms and is opened from the back — giving only the trans dibromide.

steps.title: HX addition and Markovnikov's rule
steps.body:
- π electrons attack H⁺ to give the **more stable carbocation**; X⁻ then adds → Markovnikov product (H to the carbon with more H).
- Propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane.
- **Peroxide (Kharasch) effect**: with HBr only, ROOR initiates a radical chain; Br· adds first to give the more stable radical → **anti-Markovnikov** 1-bromopropane. Not seen with HCl or HI (unfavourable radical steps).
- Hydration: H₃O⁺ (Markovnikov, rearrangement possible); oxymercuration–demercuration (Markovnikov, no rearrangement); hydroboration–oxidation (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition).

steps.title: Halogen addition stereochemistry
steps.body:
Br₂ forms a cyclic **bromonium ion**; Br⁻ opens it from the opposite face → **anti addition**.

- cis-but-2-ene + Br₂ → racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane
- trans-but-2-ene + Br₂ → meso-2,3-dibromobutane
- In water, halohydrins form (OH on the more substituted carbon).

Syn additions: catalytic H₂, OsO₄ or cold dilute KMnO₄ (cis-diols), hydroboration.

steps.title: Solved: products
steps.body:
1. 2-methylpropene + HBr → **2-bromo-2-methylpropane**
2. 2-methylpropene + HBr/ROOR → **1-bromo-2-methylpropane**
3. 1-methylcyclohexene + BH₃ then H₂O₂/OH⁻ → **trans-2-methylcyclohexanol** (OH and H added syn, OH on less substituted C)
4. cyclohexene + cold dilute KMnO₄ → **cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI.
- Drawing a free carbocation in Br₂ addition (it would lose stereospecificity).
- Confusing syn with cis in products — check by drawing.

activity.prompt: Match each reagent with the regio/stereochemistry of addition to propene or a cyclic alkene.

quiz.q: trans-But-2-ene + Br₂ gives:
quiz.why: Anti addition to the trans alkene places the two Br atoms so that the product has a plane of symmetry: meso.

quiz.q: Peroxide effect is observed with:
quiz.why: Only for HBr are both radical propagation steps exothermic, so the anti-Markovnikov chain operates.

quiz.q: Hydroboration–oxidation of propene gives:
quiz.why: Boron adds to the less substituted carbon and is replaced by OH with retention, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

quiz.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene gives mainly 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol because:
options: Methyl shift to a tertiary carbocation
quiz.why: The initial secondary cation rearranges by a 1,2-methyl shift to a more stable tertiary cation before water adds.

scenes.text: Bitter almonds contain amygdalin, a natural cyanohydrin derivative of benzaldehyde.
Nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbon of C=O — the key step in almost all carbonyl chemistry.

steps.title: Reactivity
steps.body:
C=O is polar (Cδ+). Nucleophiles add to the carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide.

**HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ > PhCOPh**: aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because (1) alkyl groups donate electrons (+I) and reduce δ+, and (2) two groups crowd the tetrahedral intermediate more.

Acid catalysis protonates O and makes C more electrophilic (for weak nucleophiles like H₂O, ROH).

steps.title: Key additions
steps.body:
- **HCN** (base catalysed, CN⁻ attacks) → cyanohydrin
- **NaHSO₃** → crystalline bisulphite adduct (aldehydes, methyl ketones) — used for purification
- **ROH/H⁺** → hemiacetal → acetal (protecting group; stable to base)
- **Grignard RMgX** → alcohols (HCHO → 1°, RCHO → 2°, ketone → 3°)
- **NH₂–Z** (addition–elimination) → imines/oximes/hydrazones/semicarbazones; optimum pH ≈ 4.5
- **NaBH₄/LiAlH₄** → alcohols (hydride addition)

steps.title: Solved: Grignard synthesis
steps.body:
Prepare 2-phenylbutan-2-ol (PhC(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃):

- Route A: acetophenone (PhCOCH₃) + CH₃CH₂MgBr, then H₃O⁺
- Route B: butan-2-one + PhMgBr, then H₃O⁺

Both give the tertiary alcohol; choose by availability. Water must be excluded (Grignard + H₂O → RH).

steps.title: Solved: 2,4-DNP test
steps.body: Acetone + 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (H⁺) → orange-yellow acetone 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate. The melting point of the purified derivative identifies the carbonyl compound — a classic qualitative test.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing imine formation in strong acid (amine fully protonated, not nucleophilic) or strong base (no activation of C=O).
- Using a Grignard reagent with an unprotected –OH or –COOH in the same molecule.
- Forgetting acetals are cleaved by aqueous acid.

activity.prompt: Match each carbonyl + reagent with the product type.

quiz.q: Most reactive towards nucleophilic addition:
quiz.why: Formaldehyde has no electron-donating or bulky groups on the carbonyl carbon, so it is most electrophilic and least hindered.

quiz.q: Acetone + CH₃MgBr then H₃O⁺ gives:
quiz.why: The methyl group adds to the ketone carbon, giving tertiary (CH₃)₃COH after protonation.

quiz.q: Acetals are used as protecting groups because they are stable to:
quiz.why: Acetals resist bases, hydrides and Grignard reagents but are hydrolysed by aqueous acid, allowing later removal.

quiz.q: Optimum pH for oxime formation is about:
quiz.why: Mild acid activates C=O and assists water loss while leaving enough free amine to act as nucleophile.

scenes.text: Industrial chemists make butanol and cinnamic acid from small aldehydes by joining them together.
The trick: make an enolate from one carbonyl and let it attack another.

steps.title: Aldol and Claisen
steps.body:
- α-H of aldehydes/ketones are acidic (pKa ≈ 19–20) because the enolate is resonance stabilised.
- **Aldol**: enolate + C=O → β-hydroxy carbonyl; heating → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (E1cB). 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO → crotonaldehyde.
- **Crossed aldol (Claisen–Schmidt)**: PhCHO (no α-H) + CH₃COCH₃/NaOH → benzalacetone.
- **Claisen condensation**: 2 ester + NaOEt → β-keto ester (2CH₃COOEt → CH₃COCH₂COOEt, ethyl acetoacetate). Driven by deprotonation of the acidic product.
- **Dieckmann**: intramolecular Claisen → cyclic β-keto ester (5- or 6-membered).

steps.title: Perkin, Knoevenagel, Cannizzaro
steps.body:
- **Perkin**: ArCHO + (CH₃CO)₂O + CH₃COONa, heat → cinnamic acid (ArCH=CHCOOH).
- **Knoevenagel**: aldehyde + active methylene compound (malonic ester, CH₂(COOH)₂) + weak base (piperidine/pyridine) → α,β-unsaturated product.
- **Cannizzaro**: aldehyde **without α-H** + conc. NaOH → alcohol + carboxylate (disproportionation via hydride transfer). 2HCHO → CH₃OH + HCOO⁻. Crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO: HCHO is oxidised, the other aldehyde reduced.
- **Benzoin condensation**: 2PhCHO + CN⁻ → PhCH(OH)COPh.

steps.title: Solved: identify the reaction
steps.body:
1. PhCHO + conc. NaOH → PhCH₂OH + PhCOONa (**Cannizzaro**)
2. PhCHO + HCHO + conc. NaOH → PhCH₂OH + HCOONa (**crossed Cannizzaro**)
3. PhCHO + CH₂(COOH)₂ / pyridine, heat → PhCH=CHCOOH + CO₂ (**Knoevenagel–Doebner**)
4. Diethyl adipate + NaOEt → ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate (**Dieckmann**)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying Cannizzaro on acetaldehyde (it has α-H and undergoes aldol).
- Using NaOH for a Claisen condensation (it hydrolyses esters); use the matching alkoxide.
- Forgetting that the Claisen product is deprotonated and needs acid work-up.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction to its typical substrate/reagent.
pairs: Aldehyde + active methylene + weak amine base

quiz.q: Which aldehyde undergoes Cannizzaro reaction?
quiz.why: Pivaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot form an enolate and instead disproportionates in conc. NaOH.

quiz.q: Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate gives:
quiz.why: The ester enolate attacks a second ester and expels EtO⁻, forming the β-keto ester CH₃COCH₂COOEt.

quiz.q: Perkin reaction of benzaldehyde gives:
quiz.why: Condensation with acetic anhydride/acetate followed by hydrolysis gives PhCH=CHCOOH.

quiz.q: In crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO, formaldehyde is:
quiz.why: Formaldehyde is the more reactive hydride donor after OH⁻ attack, so it is oxidised to formate and the other aldehyde is reduced.

scenes.text: Every nylon-6 thread starts with cyclohexanone oxime rearranged by acid into caprolactam.
In a 1,2-shift, a group migrates to an electron-deficient neighbour. Many famous reactions share this one idea.

steps.title: Rearrangements to electron-deficient carbon and nitrogen
steps.body:
- **Pinacol–pinacolone**: 1,2-diol + H⁺ → carbocation → 1,2-shift → ketone. (CH₃)₂C(OH)C(OH)(CH₃)₂ → (CH₃)₃CCOCH₃. Migratory aptitude roughly aryl (p-MeO-C₆H₄ > Ph) > H ≈ alkyl, and the more stable carbocation forms first.
- **Beckmann**: ketoxime + H₂SO₄/PCl₅ → amide; the group **anti** to the OH migrates. Cyclohexanone oxime → ε-caprolactam.
- **Hofmann bromamide**: RCONH₂ + Br₂/NaOH → RNH₂ (one carbon less) via isocyanate; migration with retention.
- **Curtius**: RCON₃ (acyl azide), heat → RNCO → RNH₂.
- **Benzilic acid**: benzil + KOH → benzilic acid (Ph₂C(OH)COOH); aryl migrates to carbonyl carbon.

steps.title: Solved: Hofmann bromamide
steps.body:
Benzamide + Br₂ + 4NaOH → aniline + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O.

Steps: N-bromination → N-bromoamide anion → loss of Br⁻ with Ph migrating to N → phenyl isocyanate → hydrolysis → aniline + CO₂ (as carbonate).

Use: making amines with one carbon fewer, e.g. acetamide → methylamine.

steps.title: Solved: Beckmann stereochemistry
steps.body:
(E)-acetophenone oxime (OH anti to phenyl) + H₂SO₄ → phenyl migrates → **acetanilide** (CH₃CONHPh).

If the OH were anti to methyl, N-methylbenzamide (PhCONHCH₃) would form. The product reveals the oxime geometry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting the group syn to OH migrate in Beckmann.
- Forgetting Hofmann bromamide loses one carbon.
- Ionising the wrong OH in unsymmetrical pinacols — the one giving the more stable carbocation leaves.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the pinacol–pinacolone rearrangement.
items: Lose water to form a tertiary carbocation
Oxygen lone pair stabilises the new cation (oxocarbenium)

quiz.q: Hofmann bromamide reaction of propanamide gives:
quiz.why: The alkyl group migrates from C to N and the carbonyl carbon is lost as CO₂, so CH₃CH₂CONH₂ gives CH₃CH₂NH₂.

quiz.q: In the Beckmann rearrangement, the group that migrates is:
quiz.why: Migration is concerted with departure of the protonated OH, so the group anti-periplanar to it migrates.

quiz.q: Beckmann rearrangement of cyclohexanone oxime gives:
quiz.why: Ring expansion inserts NH into the ring, giving the seven-membered lactam used to make nylon-6.

quiz.q: Benzil + KOH, then H₃O⁺ gives:
quiz.why: OH⁻ adds to one carbonyl and a phenyl migrates to the adjacent carbonyl carbon, giving Ph₂C(OH)COOH.

questions.q: Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene gives:
questions.why: H⁺ adds to C-1 to give the more stable secondary cation, and Br⁻ attacks C-2.

questions.q: cis-But-2-ene + Br₂ gives:
questions.why: Anti addition to the cis alkene gives (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) in equal amounts — a racemate.

questions.q: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ converts cyclopentene to:
questions.why: A cyclic manganate ester forms on one face, so both OH groups end up cis (syn dihydroxylation).

questions.q: Benzaldehyde does not undergo aldol self-condensation because:
questions.why: Without an α-H no enolate can form from benzaldehyde, so it can only act as the acceptor.

questions.q: Grignard reagent + CO₂ followed by H₃O⁺ gives:
questions.why: RMgX adds to CO₂ to give RCOOMgX, which is protonated to the carboxylic acid RCOOH.

questions.q: Semicarbazone formation is an example of:
questions.why: The NH₂ group adds to C=O and water is then eliminated to form the C=N bond.

questions.q: Product of Dieckmann condensation of diethyl hexanedioate:
questions.why: Intramolecular Claisen of the C6 diester closes a five-membered ring, giving ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate.

questions.q: Curtius rearrangement proceeds via:
questions.why: The acyl azide loses N₂ and the R group migrates to N, giving an isocyanate R–N=C=O.

questions.q: In pinacol rearrangement of Ph₂C(OH)C(OH)Me₂, the OH that leaves first is:
questions.why: Loss of OH from CPh₂ gives the diphenyl-stabilised carbocation, which is more stable than the dimethyl one.

questions.q: Oxymercuration–demercuration of an alkene gives:
questions.why: A bridged mercurinium ion prevents carbocation rearrangement while water attacks the more substituted carbon.

questions.q: Reagent for converting a ketone to an acetal-protected ketone:
questions.why: A diol with acid catalyst forms a cyclic acetal (dioxolane), protecting the ketone from bases and nucleophiles.

questions.q: Benzoin condensation is catalysed by:
questions.why: Cyanide adds to one benzaldehyde and makes the former carbonyl carbon nucleophilic (umpolung), which attacks a second aldehyde.

questions.q: Hofmann bromamide reaction reduces the carbon chain by:
questions.why: The carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, so the amine has one carbon fewer than the amide.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Heterocyclic compounds
courses.summary: Structure, aromaticity, basicity, syntheses and reactions of pyrrole, furan, thiophene and pyridine, and of the fused heterocycles indole, quinoline and isoquinoline, with their importance in drugs and natural products.
outcomes: Explain aromaticity and electron density in five- and six-membered heterocycles
Compare basicities of pyrrole, pyridine, piperidine and related amines
Predict the position of electrophilic and nucleophilic substitution
Write Paal–Knorr, Hantzsch, Fischer indole, Skraup and Bischler–Napieralski syntheses
Recognise heterocyclic cores in drugs and biomolecules

scenes.text: The haem in your blood is built from four pyrrole rings; chlorophyll in a neem leaf is similar.
Replace one CH of a ring with N, O or S and you get a heterocycle with its own personality.

steps.title: Structure and aromaticity
steps.body:
Each is a planar five-membered ring with four sp² carbons and one heteroatom whose **lone pair is part of the 6π aromatic sextet** (Hückel 4n + 2, n = 1).

- The ring is **π-excessive**: 6 electrons over 5 atoms, so carbons are electron-rich.
- Aromaticity (resonance energy): benzene > thiophene > pyrrole > furan. O is most electronegative and holds its lone pair tightly, so furan is least aromatic (it even does Diels–Alder reactions).
- **Pyrrole is an extremely weak base** (conjugate acid pKa ≈ −3.8) because protonating N destroys aromaticity; its N–H is weakly acidic (pKa ≈ 17).

steps.title: Reactions and syntheses
steps.body:
**Electrophilic substitution** occurs at **C-2** (α): the intermediate cation has three resonance forms vs two for C-3 attack. Reactivity: pyrrole > furan > thiophene > benzene.

- Mild reagents are needed (pyrrole polymerises in strong acid): nitration with HNO₃/acetic anhydride, sulphonation with pyridine–SO₃, Vilsmeier formylation, coupling with diazonium salts.
- **Paal–Knorr synthesis**: 1,4-dicarbonyl + NH₃ (or RNH₂) → pyrrole; + P₂O₅/acid → furan; + P₂S₅ → thiophene.
- Furan from pentosans: furfural by acid treatment of bran or corncobs.
- Thiophene + Ni (Raney) → desulphurisation to butane chain.

steps.title: Solved: products
steps.body:
1. Hexane-2,5-dione + NH₃, heat → **2,5-dimethylpyrrole** (Paal–Knorr)
2. Thiophene + Ac₂O/SnCl₄ → **2-acetylthiophene**
3. Pyrrole + PhN₂⁺Cl⁻ → **2-(phenylazo)pyrrole**
4. Furan + maleic anhydride → **Diels–Alder adduct** (furan acts as a diene)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling pyrrole basic like amines — its lone pair is tied up in the aromatic ring.
- Predicting C-3 substitution for pyrrole/furan/thiophene.
- Using concentrated H₂SO₄/HNO₃ with pyrrole or furan — they resinify.

activity.prompt: Match each statement to the heterocycle.
pairs: N–H weakly acidic, very weakly basic
Building block of haem and chlorophyll
Made from bran or corncobs via furfural

quiz.q: Electrophilic substitution in pyrrole occurs mainly at:
quiz.why: Attack at C-2 gives a cation stabilised by three resonance structures, more than the two for C-3 attack.

quiz.q: Order of reactivity towards electrophiles:
quiz.why: Nitrogen donates its lone pair best and sulphur least among the heteroatoms, and all are more reactive than benzene.

quiz.q: Pyrrole is a very weak base because:
options: Its lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet
quiz.why: Protonation would remove the N lone pair from the π system and destroy aromaticity, so it is strongly disfavoured.

quiz.q: Paal–Knorr synthesis of thiophene uses a 1,4-dicarbonyl compound with:
quiz.why: Phosphorus pentasulphide supplies sulphur and dehydrates the 1,4-diketone to close the thiophene ring.

story.title: The smell of a fish market

scenes.text: Pyridine has a fishy, unpleasant smell. It is also a common solvent and base in organic labs.
It looks like benzene with one CH replaced by N, but its chemistry is very different.

steps.title: Structure and basicity
steps.body:
Six-membered, aromatic, isoelectronic with benzene. N contributes one electron to the π sextet; its **lone pair is in an sp² orbital in the ring plane** and not part of the aromatic system.

- So pyridine is a moderate base: pKa (pyridinium) = **5.2**, weaker than aliphatic amines (piperidine ≈ 11.1) because sp² lone pairs have more s-character.
- The ring is **π-deficient**: N withdraws electrons, especially from C-2, C-4, C-6.
- Dipole moment ≈ 2.2 D, towards N.

steps.title: Reactions
steps.body:
- **Electrophilic substitution**: very difficult (≈ nitrobenzene) and at **C-3**; conditions are harsh because N is protonated/complexed. E.g. nitration needs KNO₃/H₂SO₄ at ~300 °C (low yield).
- **Nucleophilic substitution** at **C-2/C-4**: Chichibabin reaction — pyridine + NaNH₂ → 2-aminopyridine. 2-chloropyridine + NaOMe → 2-methoxypyridine.
- N-reactions: forms salts, N-oxides (with peracid; N-oxide activates C-4 for electrophiles), and quaternary salts with RX.
- **Hantzsch synthesis**: 2 β-keto ester + aldehyde + NH₃ → 1,4-dihydropyridine → oxidise to pyridine. (Drugs like nifedipine are 1,4-dihydropyridines.)

steps.title: Solved: basicity order
steps.body:
Conjugate-acid pKa values:
- Piperidine (sp³ N) ≈ 11.1
- Pyridine (sp² N) ≈ 5.2
- Aniline (lone pair delocalised into ring) ≈ 4.6
- Pyrrole (lone pair in aromatic sextet) ≈ −3.8

Order of basicity: **piperidine > pyridine > aniline > pyrrole**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking pyridine's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet (that's pyrrole).
- Predicting EAS at C-2 for pyridine — it is C-3.
- Forgetting that NaNH₂ attacks C-2 (Chichibabin), not C-3.

activity.prompt: Match each reaction of pyridine with its position.

quiz.q: Pyridine is less basic than piperidine because:
options: Its N lone pair is in an sp² orbital
Its lone pair is in the aromatic sextet
quiz.why: An sp² lone pair has more s-character and is held closer to N, making it less available than piperidine's sp³ lone pair.

quiz.q: Chichibabin reaction converts pyridine to:
quiz.why: Amide ion attacks the electron-poor C-2 and hydride is lost, giving 2-aminopyridine.

quiz.q: Electrophilic substitution of pyridine is slow because:
options: N withdraws electrons and is protonated under acidic conditions
quiz.why: The electronegative N, and especially the pyridinium ion formed in acid, strongly deactivates the ring toward electrophiles.

quiz.q: Hantzsch synthesis first gives a:
quiz.why: Condensation of two β-keto esters, an aldehyde and ammonia forms a 1,4-dihydropyridine, which can be oxidised to pyridine.

scenes.text: Indigo, the dye in denim, is an indole derivative; so is the amino acid tryptophan.
Quinine, the old anti-malarial from cinchona bark, contains a quinoline ring.

steps.title: Indole
steps.body:
Benzene fused to pyrrole (benzopyrrole). π-excessive; **electrophilic substitution at C-3** (attack at C-3 keeps the benzene ring intact in the intermediate).

**Fischer indole synthesis**: phenylhydrazine + aldehyde/ketone (with α-CH₂) → phenylhydrazone → acid (ZnCl₂, PPA), heat → [3,3]-sigmatropic shift, loss of NH₃ → indole. E.g. phenylhydrazine + acetone → 2-methylindole.

Indoles in nature: tryptophan, serotonin, indole-3-acetic acid (plant hormone), reserpine.

steps.title: Quinoline and isoquinoline
steps.body:
Benzene fused to pyridine. Basic (pKa ≈ 4.9 and 5.4). Electrophiles attack the **benzene ring (C-5, C-8)**; nucleophiles attack the pyridine ring (quinoline C-2/C-4; isoquinoline C-1).

- **Skraup synthesis**: aniline + glycerol + conc. H₂SO₄ + nitrobenzene (oxidant) → quinoline. Glycerol dehydrates to acrolein, aniline adds (Michael), cyclises and is oxidised.
- **Bischler–Napieralski**: β-phenylethylamide + POCl₃ → 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline → dehydrogenate (Pd) → isoquinoline.
- Quinoline core: quinine, chloroquine; isoquinoline core: papaverine, morphine skeleton (partly).

steps.title: Solved: name the synthesis and product
steps.body:
1. PhNHNH₂ + cyclohexanone, H⁺/heat → **tetrahydrocarbazole** (Fischer indole)
2. Aniline + glycerol + H₂SO₄ + PhNO₂ → **quinoline** (Skraup)
3. N-acetyl-2-phenylethylamine + POCl₃ → **1-methyl-3,4-dihydroisoquinoline** (Bischler–Napieralski)
4. Indole + Me₂NH + HCHO → **gramine** (3-substituted, Mannich)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing EAS of indole at C-2 (it is C-3).
- Forgetting the oxidant in the Skraup reaction.
- Using a ketone without an α-CH₂ in Fischer synthesis (it must tautomerise to an ene-hydrazine).

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the Fischer indole synthesis.
items: Condense phenylhydrazine with a ketone to form the phenylhydrazone
[3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement forms a new C–C bond
Eliminate NH₃ to give the aromatic indole

quiz.q: Electrophilic substitution in indole occurs at:
quiz.why: Attack at C-3 gives an intermediate where the positive charge is stabilised by N without disrupting the benzene ring.

quiz.q: Skraup synthesis uses glycerol because it forms:
quiz.why: Concentrated H₂SO₄ dehydrates glycerol to acrolein, which undergoes conjugate addition with aniline.

quiz.q: In quinoline, electrophiles attack:
quiz.why: The pyridine ring is electron-poor, so electrophiles prefer the carbocyclic ring, at C-5 and C-8.

quiz.q: Bischler–Napieralski reaction gives:
quiz.why: POCl₃ cyclises the β-arylethylamide onto the aromatic ring, forming the dihydroisoquinoline ring.

scenes.text: Rashmi lines up paracetamol, omeprazole, ciprofloxacin and caffeine tablets for a class presentation.
All except paracetamol contain a heterocyclic ring — the most common structural unit in drugs.

steps.title: Heterocycles in biology
steps.body:
- **Purines** (adenine, guanine) and **pyrimidines** (cytosine, thymine, uracil) in DNA and RNA.
- **Imidazole** in histidine — acts as a proton shuttle in enzymes (pKa ≈ 6).
- **Porphyrin** (four pyrroles) in haem and chlorophyll; **corrin** in vitamin B₁₂.
- **Thiazole** in thiamine (vitamin B₁); **pyridine** in NAD⁺ (nicotinamide) and vitamin B₆.
- **Indole** in tryptophan and serotonin.

steps.title: Heterocycles in drugs
steps.body:
- Caffeine, theophylline — purines
- Ciprofloxacin — a fluoroquinolone (quinoline-type core)
- Chloroquine — quinoline
- Omeprazole — benzimidazole + pyridine
- Nifedipine — 1,4-dihydropyridine
- Penicillins — β-lactam fused to a thiazolidine
- Sildenafil — pyrazolopyrimidine

steps.title: Solved: aromatic or not?
steps.body:
Apply Hückel (planar, cyclic, conjugated, 4n + 2 π electrons):
- Imidazole: 6π (one N lone pair in sextet, the other in plane) → **aromatic**, basic at the 'pyridine-like' N.
- 2H-pyran: sp³ carbon breaks conjugation → **not aromatic**.
- Pyrylium ion (C₅H₅O⁺): 6π → **aromatic**.
- Pyrimidine: 6π, two pyridine-like N → aromatic, less basic than pyridine (pKa ≈ 1.3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting both N lone pairs of imidazole in the π sextet.
- Calling any ring with a heteroatom aromatic without checking conjugation.
- Assuming more N atoms make a ring more basic — extra ring N withdraws electrons.

activity.prompt: Match each heterocycle to where it is found.

quiz.q: Which ring is present in histidine?
quiz.why: Histidine's side chain is an imidazole ring, whose near-neutral pKa lets it act as acid or base in enzymes.

quiz.q: Number of π electrons in the aromatic ring of imidazole:
quiz.why: Four from the two C=C/C=N bonds and two from the pyrrole-like N lone pair give a 6π aromatic system.

quiz.q: Caffeine is a derivative of:
quiz.why: Caffeine is 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine, and xanthine is a purine (fused pyrimidine–imidazole).

quiz.q: Pyrimidine is less basic than pyridine because:
options: The second ring N withdraws electrons
quiz.why: The extra electronegative nitrogen pulls electron density from the ring, making each lone pair less available for protonation.

questions.q: Number of π electrons in pyrrole's aromatic system:
questions.why: Four from two C=C bonds plus two from the nitrogen lone pair make a 6π Hückel aromatic system.

questions.q: Most basic compound:
questions.why: Piperidine has an sp³ N lone pair not delocalised anywhere, giving conjugate-acid pKa ≈ 11.

questions.q: Furan undergoes Diels–Alder reactions because:
options: It has the lowest aromatic stabilisation of the three five-membered heterocycles
questions.why: Low resonance energy means little is lost when furan reacts as a diene.

questions.q: Pyridine + NaNH₂, heat gives:
questions.why: This is the Chichibabin reaction, nucleophilic attack at the electron-poor C-2.

questions.q: Paal–Knorr synthesis of pyrrole requires:
questions.why: A 1,4-dicarbonyl condenses with ammonia or a primary amine at both carbonyls to close the five-membered ring.

questions.q: Position of electrophilic substitution in pyridine:
questions.why: Attack at C-3 avoids putting positive charge on the electronegative nitrogen in the intermediate.

questions.q: Fischer indole synthesis from phenylhydrazine and acetone gives:
questions.why: The methyl of acetone that is not used to form the ring ends up at C-2 of the indole.

questions.q: Skraup synthesis product:
questions.why: Aniline, glycerol, sulphuric acid and an oxidant together build the pyridine ring onto benzene to give quinoline.

questions.q: Which statement about pyridine N-oxide is correct?
options: It is less polar than pyridine
It activates C-4 towards electrophilic substitution
questions.why: The N-oxide oxygen donates electrons into the ring, so nitration occurs readily at C-4.

questions.q: Thiophene can be removed from benzene by shaking with conc. H₂SO₄ because:
options: Thiophene sulphonates much faster than benzene
questions.why: Thiophene is more reactive to electrophiles, so it forms a water-soluble sulphonic acid at room temperature while benzene does not.

questions.q: Heterocycle in nicotinamide (NAD⁺):
questions.why: Nicotinamide is pyridine-3-carboxamide; in NAD⁺ the pyridine N is quaternised.

questions.q: Isoquinoline undergoes nucleophilic attack at:
questions.why: C-1 is adjacent to N and most electron-deficient in isoquinoline.

questions.q: Imidazole's basic nitrogen is the one:
questions.why: The pyridine-like N has an in-plane sp² lone pair free for protonation; the N–H lone pair is in the aromatic sextet.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Biomolecules: carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids
courses.summary: Open-chain and cyclic structures of glucose and fructose, mutarotation, chain lengthening and shortening, disaccharides and polysaccharides; amino acids, zwitterions and isoelectric point, peptide synthesis and sequencing, levels of protein structure; nucleosides, nucleotides and DNA structure; fats, oils, saponification and iodine values.
outcomes: Draw Fischer and Haworth structures of glucose and explain mutarotation
Distinguish reducing and non-reducing sugars
Calculate isoelectric points and describe peptide synthesis and sequencing
Describe the Watson–Crick model and base pairing
Calculate saponification and iodine values of fats

scenes.text: A freshly made solution of α-D-glucose rotates plane-polarised light by +112°, but the reading slowly falls to +52.7°.
The ring opens and closes, interconverting α and β forms until they reach equilibrium — mutarotation.

steps.title: Structure of glucose
steps.body:
- C₆H₁₂O₆, an aldohexose. Open-chain evidence: forms a pentaacetate (5 OH), oxime and cyanohydrin (C=O), oxidised by Br₂ water to gluconic acid (CHO), reduced by HI/P to n-hexane (straight chain).
- But glucose does not give Schiff's test or a bisulphite adduct, and forms two methyl glucosides — evidence for a **cyclic hemiacetal** (C-5 OH adds to C-1 CHO).
- Six-membered **pyranose** ring (Haworth); C-1 is the **anomeric carbon**. α: OH on C-1 trans to CH₂OH (down in Haworth for D-sugars); β: OH up.
- D-configuration: OH on C-5 on the right in the Fischer projection.

steps.title: Solved: equilibrium composition from mutarotation
steps.body:
[α] values: α-D-glucose +112°, β-D-glucose +18.7°, equilibrium +52.7°. Let x = fraction β.

- 112(1 − x) + 18.7x = 52.7
- 112 − 93.3x = 52.7 → x = 59.3/93.3 = **0.636**
- Equilibrium: **≈ 64% β, 36% α** (open chain < 0.1%). β predominates because all bulky groups are equatorial.

steps.title: Fructose and interconversions
steps.body:
- Fructose: ketohexose; forms a five-membered **furanose** ring (C-5 OH to C-2) in sucrose; levorotatory.
- **Osazone** formation: glucose, fructose and mannose give the same osazone (C-1 and C-2 react with 3 PhNHNH₂), proving the same configuration at C-3, C-4, C-5.
- **Kiliani–Fischer** (chain lengthening): HCN, hydrolyse, lactonise, reduce → aldose with one more C (two epimers).
- **Ruff degradation** (chain shortening): oxidise to aldonic acid, Ca salt + H₂O₂/Fe³⁺ → aldose with one less C.
- Glucose → fructose: via osazone → osone → reduction (Zn/AcOH).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling α and β enantiomers — they are anomers (diastereomers differing at C-1).
- Saying fructose is not a reducing sugar — it reduces Fehling's and Tollens' in alkaline solution.
- Drawing the Haworth CH₂OH down for D-sugars (it is up).

activity.prompt: Match each observation with what it proves about glucose.
pairs: Aldehyde is mostly tied up in a ring
Same configuration at C-3, C-4, C-5

quiz.q: α- and β-D-glucopyranose are:
quiz.why: They differ only in configuration at C-1, the anomeric carbon formed on ring closure, so they are anomers.

quiz.q: Which reagent converts an aldose to an aldose with one carbon more?
quiz.why: Kiliani–Fischer adds HCN to the aldehyde, adding a carbon that becomes the new C-1 after hydrolysis and reduction.

quiz.q: Glucose, mannose and fructose give the same osazone because:
options: They differ only at C-1 and/or C-2
They have the same molecular formula only
quiz.why: Osazone formation involves C-1 and C-2 only; sugars identical at C-3 to C-6 give the same osazone.

quiz.q: Equilibrium [α] of a sugar is +80°; pure α is +150° and pure β is +10°. Fraction of β:

story.title: Why sugar does not reduce Fehling's

scenes.text: Table sugar gives no red precipitate with Fehling's solution; milk sugar and malt sugar do.
It all depends on whether the anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond.

steps.title: Disaccharides
steps.body:
- **Sucrose**: α-D-glucopyranose (C-1) linked to β-D-fructofuranose (C-2) — both anomeric carbons used → **non-reducing**, no mutarotation. Hydrolysis gives invert sugar ([α] changes from +66.5° to about −20°, since fructose is strongly laevorotatory).
- **Maltose**: glucose α(1→4) glucose → reducing.
- **Lactose**: galactose β(1→4) glucose → reducing (milk sugar).
- **Cellobiose**: glucose β(1→4) glucose → reducing.

steps.title: Polysaccharides
steps.body:
- **Starch**: amylose (α-1,4, unbranched, helical, blue with I₂, ~20%) + amylopectin (α-1,4 with α-1,6 branches every ~24–30 units, ~80%).
- **Glycogen**: animal starch, more highly branched (every 8–12 units).
- **Cellulose**: β-1,4 glucose, straight chains with extensive H-bonding → fibres; humans lack cellulase.
- **Chitin**: β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine (insect exoskeletons).

steps.title: Solved: identifying sugars
steps.body:
An unknown disaccharide reduces Tollens', mutarotates, and gives only glucose on hydrolysis by maltase (an α-glucosidase) → **maltose**.

Another gives glucose + galactose with β-galactosidase → **lactose**. A third does not reduce Tollens' and gives glucose + fructose → **sucrose**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sucrose is reducing because its components are.
- Confusing α-1,4 (starch, digestible) with β-1,4 (cellulose, not digestible by humans).
- Saying amylopectin gives a deep blue colour with iodine — it gives red-violet; amylose gives blue.

activity.prompt: Match each carbohydrate to its linkage.

quiz.q: Which is a non-reducing sugar?
quiz.why: In sucrose both anomeric carbons form the glycosidic bond, so no free hemiacetal can open to an aldehyde.

quiz.q: Invert sugar is so called because:
options: Hydrolysis changes the sign of optical rotation
quiz.why: Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the glucose + fructose mixture is laevorotatory because fructose rotates strongly to the left.

quiz.q: Humans cannot digest cellulose because:
options: They lack enzymes that hydrolyse β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
quiz.why: Human amylases attack α-linkages; the β-1,4 bonds of cellulose need cellulase, which humans do not produce.

quiz.q: Amylose gives a blue colour with iodine because:
options: I₃⁻/I₅⁻ chains fit inside the amylose helix
quiz.why: Polyiodide ions are trapped inside the helical amylose chain, forming a deep blue complex.

story.title: A protein's address on a gel

scenes.text: In isoelectric focusing, each protein migrates through a pH gradient until it stops at its isoelectric point.
At that pH its positive and negative charges exactly cancel.

steps.title: Amino acids
steps.body:
- α-amino acids RCH(NH₂)COOH; 20 standard; all chiral except glycine; natural ones are L (mostly S).
- In water they exist as **zwitterions** ⁺H₃N–CHR–COO⁻ (high m.p., water-soluble, insoluble in ether).
- **Isoelectric point**: pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2 for neutral amino acids; for acidic/basic side chains, average the two pKa values on either side of the neutral form.
- Ninhydrin gives purple (Ruhemann's purple) with α-amino acids (yellow with proline).

steps.title: Solved: isoelectric points
steps.body:
- Glycine: pKa₁ (COOH) = 2.34, pKa₂ (NH₃⁺) = 9.60 → pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = **5.97**
- Aspartic acid: pKa 2.09 (α-COOH), 3.86 (side chain), 9.82 → neutral form between 2.09 and 3.86 → pI = (2.09 + 3.86)/2 = **2.98**
- Lysine: pKa 2.18, 8.95 (α-NH₃⁺), 10.53 (side chain) → pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = **9.74**

steps.title: Peptides: synthesis and sequencing
steps.body:
- Peptide bond –CO–NH– is planar (partial double-bond character), usually trans.
- **Synthesis**: protect N (Boc, Cbz, Fmoc) and C (ester); activate COOH with DCC; couple; deprotect. **Merrifield solid-phase**: C-terminal residue anchored on polystyrene resin; repeat deprotect–couple cycles; cleave with HF/TFA.
- **N-terminal analysis**: Sanger's reagent (FDNB) → DNP-amino acid; **Edman degradation** (PhNCS) removes one residue at a time as a PTH derivative.
- **C-terminal**: carboxypeptidase.
- Structure levels: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix, β-sheet; H-bonds), tertiary (3-D fold; disulphide, ionic, hydrophobic), quaternary (subunits, e.g. haemoglobin α₂β₂). Denaturation destroys 2°–4° structure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging all three pKa values for acidic or basic amino acids.
- Forgetting to protect the amine of the acylating amino acid (you get random oligomers).
- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds (primary structure survives).

activity.prompt: Order one cycle of Merrifield solid-phase peptide synthesis.
items: Attach the Boc-protected C-terminal amino acid to the resin
Couple the next Boc-amino acid using DCC
Repeat deprotection and coupling for each residue
Cleave the peptide from the resin with HF

quiz.q: pI of alanine (pKa 2.34 and 9.69):
Edman degradation identifies:
options: Residues one by one from the N-terminus
quiz.why: Phenyl isothiocyanate reacts with the free N-terminal NH₂ and cleaves off just that residue each cycle.

quiz.q: At pH 7, lysine (pI 9.74) carries a net charge that is:
quiz.why: Below its pI an amino acid is protonated overall, so lysine at pH 7 is net positive.

quiz.q: An α-helix is an example of:
quiz.why: The α-helix is a regular local folding held by C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds four residues apart — secondary structure.

scenes.text: In a Kerala village soap unit, coconut oil is boiled with lye to make bars of soap.
How much lye is needed? The saponification value of the oil tells them.

steps.title: Nucleic acids
steps.body:
- **Nucleoside** = base + pentose (β-N-glycosidic bond at C-1′); **nucleotide** = nucleoside + phosphate (at C-5′).
- DNA: 2′-deoxyribose; bases A, G (purines), C, T (pyrimidines). RNA: ribose; U replaces T.
- Chain: 3′,5′-phosphodiester links; written 5′ → 3′.
- **Watson–Crick double helix** (B-DNA): antiparallel strands, right-handed, ~10 base pairs per turn, 3.4 Å rise, 20 Å diameter; **A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds)**.
- **Chargaff's rules**: A = T, G = C, so purines = pyrimidines.

steps.title: Solved: Chargaff's rules
steps.body:
A DNA sample has 22% adenine.

- T = 22%; A + T = 44%
- G + C = 56% → G = C = **28%**

Complementary strand of 5′-ATGCCA-3′ is 3′-TACGGT-5′, written 5′-TGGCAT-3′.

steps.title: Lipids
steps.body:
- Fats and oils are **triglycerides** (glycerol triesters of fatty acids). Oils have more unsaturated (cis) chains, lower m.p.
- **Saponification value** (SV): mg KOH to saponify 1 g fat; SV = 3 × 56.1 × 1000/M — higher SV means shorter chains.
- **Iodine value** (IV): g I₂ absorbed per 100 g fat — measures unsaturation.
- **Acid value**: mg KOH to neutralise free fatty acids in 1 g (rancidity).
- Phospholipids (lecithin) form bilayers; steroids (cholesterol) have the four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton.

steps.title: Solved: triolein
steps.body:
Triolein (glyceryl trioleate), M = 885.4 g mol⁻¹; three C=C bonds.

- SV = 3 × 56.1 × 1000/885.4 = **190 mg KOH g⁻¹**
- IV = 3 × 253.8 × 100/885.4 = **86.0 g I₂ per 100 g**

Coconut oil (rich in lauric acid, C12) has a higher SV (≈ 250) and a low IV (≈ 10).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ribose for DNA.
- Pairing A with C or G with T.
- Thinking a high iodine value means a saturated fat — it means more unsaturation.

activity.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: mg KOH per g of fat
g I₂ per 100 g of fat

quiz.q: DNA with 30% guanine contains thymine:
quiz.why: G = C = 30% makes 60%, so A + T = 40% and T = 20%.

quiz.q: Sugar in RNA:
quiz.why: RNA contains D-ribose with a 2′-OH; DNA lacks this OH (2′-deoxyribose).

quiz.q: Saponification value of tristearin (M = 891.5):
Higher iodine value indicates:
quiz.why: Each C=C adds one I₂ (as ICl in Wijs' method), so more double bonds absorb more iodine.

questions.q: Number of chiral centres in open-chain D-glucose:
questions.why: C-2, C-3, C-4 and C-5 each carry four different groups, giving four stereocentres (2⁴ = 16 aldohexoses).

questions.q: Glucose on oxidation with HNO₃ gives:
questions.why: Nitric acid oxidises both the CHO and the terminal CH₂OH to COOH, giving the dicarboxylic glucaric acid.

questions.q: Anomeric carbon in fructofuranose is:
questions.why: Fructose is a 2-ketose; ring closure creates the hemiketal at C-2, which is the anomeric carbon.

questions.q: Glycosidic linkage in cellulose:

courses.title: Unit 5 · Revision, practicals & exam
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Organic Chemistry III practicals)
courses.summary: A one-page review of mechanisms, named reactions, heterocycles and biomolecules; standard practicals — functional-group analysis, preparation and yield of acetanilide, and colour tests for carbohydrates and proteins — with viva questions and a full practice exam.
outcomes: Recall mechanisms and named reactions at a glance
Identify functional groups in an unknown organic compound
Prepare and recrystallise acetanilide and calculate percentage yield
Distinguish sugars and proteins by colour tests
Handle viva and long-answer questions

scenes.text: Aman writes every named reaction on a card: reagents on the front, product and key step on the back.
By the exam he can recall forty reactions in ten minutes. Here is the condensed version.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- Cation stability 3° > 2° > 1°; carbanion opposite; radicals like cations.
- SN2: 2nd order, inversion, 1° > 2°, aprotic solvent. SN1: 1st order, racemisation, 3°, protic solvent.
- E2: anti-periplanar, Saytzeff (small base) / Hofmann (bulky base, –NR₃⁺). E1: via R⁺. E1cB: via carbanion.
- Br₂ addition anti; OsO₄ syn; hydroboration anti-Markovnikov syn; HBr/ROOR anti-Markovnikov.

steps.title: Named reactions and heterocycles
steps.body:
- Aldol, Claisen, Dieckmann, Perkin, Knoevenagel, Cannizzaro (no α-H), benzoin (CN⁻)
- Pinacol, Beckmann (anti group), Hofmann bromamide (−1 C), Curtius (acyl azide), benzilic acid
- Pyrrole/furan/thiophene: EAS at C-2; pyridine EAS at C-3, NAS at C-2/4 (Chichibabin); indole EAS at C-3
- Paal–Knorr, Hantzsch, Fischer indole, Skraup, Bischler–Napieralski
- pI = average of flanking pKa; A=T, G≡C; SV = 168 300/M (triglyceride)

steps.title: Long-answer practice
steps.body:
Q1. Compare SN1 and SN2 reactions with respect to kinetics, stereochemistry, substrate, nucleophile and solvent. Give one example of each.

Q2. Discuss the structure of pyridine. Why is it more basic than pyrrole but less basic than piperidine? Give its electrophilic and nucleophilic substitution reactions.

Q3. Establish the cyclic structure of D-glucose. Explain mutarotation with a calculation of the equilibrium composition.

Q4. Write the mechanism of the Beckmann rearrangement and explain how it reveals oxime stereochemistry.

steps.title: Answer-writing tips
steps.body: Draw curly arrows from electron-rich to electron-poor sites and show all charges. For stereochemistry questions, draw wedge–dash or Newman projections; for heterocycle questions, draw resonance forms of the σ-complex to justify the position of attack.

activity.prompt: Match each named reaction to its product type.

quiz.q: Which reaction shortens a carbon chain by one carbon?
quiz.why: In the Hofmann bromamide reaction the carbonyl carbon of the amide is lost as carbonate.

quiz.q: Hofmann orientation in E2 is favoured by:
quiz.why: A bulky base removes the most accessible hydrogen, giving the less substituted alkene.

quiz.q: EAS in pyridine occurs at:
quiz.why: Attack at C-3 avoids placing a positive charge on the electronegative ring nitrogen in the intermediate.

lessons.title: Lab: Functional-group analysis of an unknown

scenes.text: Each student receives an unlabelled organic compound and three hours.
A logical sequence of tests — elements, solubility, functional groups, derivative — reveals its identity.

steps.title: Systematic scheme
steps.body:
1. Physical state, colour, odour; ignition test (sooty flame → aromatic).
2. **Lassaigne's test** (sodium fusion) for N, S, halogens: N → Prussian blue; S → violet with nitroprusside; halogen → AgX precipitate.
3. **Solubility**: water, 5% NaOH, 5% NaHCO₃, 5% HCl.
4. **Functional group tests** (below).
5. Prepare a derivative and determine its melting point.

steps.title: Functional-group tests
steps.body:
- **Carboxylic acid**: effervescence with NaHCO₃.
- **Phenol**: violet/blue with neutral FeCl₃; dissolves in NaOH but not NaHCO₃.
- **Aldehyde**: silver mirror with Tollens'; red Cu₂O with Fehling's (aliphatic); pink with Schiff's.
- **Ketone**: 2,4-DNP positive but Tollens' negative; methyl ketones give iodoform (yellow CHI₃).
- **Primary aromatic amine**: diazotisation + β-naphthol → orange-red azo dye; carbylamine test (foul smell).
- **Ester**: fruity smell; hydroxamic acid test → wine-red with FeCl₃.
- **Amide**: NH₃ evolved on boiling with NaOH.
- **Nitro**: Mulliken's test (Zn/NH₄Cl, then Tollens' → black/grey).

steps.title: Solved: identify the compound
steps.body:
White solid, m.p. 121–122 °C. Lassaigne: no N, S or halogen. Soluble in NaHCO₃ with effervescence. Neutral FeCl₃ → buff precipitate. Sooty flame.

→ Aromatic carboxylic acid; m.p. matches **benzoic acid** (122 °C). Confirm with a derivative such as benzamide (m.p. 128 °C).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing with FeCl₃ in acidic solution — neutralise first.
- Not fusing long enough in Lassaigne's test (false negatives for N).
- Concluding 'ketone' only from a 2,4-DNP precipitate without checking Tollens'.

activity.prompt: Match each test result to the functional group.
pairs: Wine-red colour in hydroxamic acid test

quiz.q: A compound dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO₃ and gives violet FeCl₃ colour. It is likely:
quiz.why: Phenols are acidic enough to dissolve in NaOH but too weak to release CO₂ from bicarbonate, and give coloured complexes with Fe³⁺.

quiz.q: Prussian blue in Lassaigne's test indicates:
quiz.why: Nitrogen forms NaCN during fusion, which gives ferric ferrocyanide (Prussian blue) with FeSO₄ and Fe³⁺.

quiz.q: Acetone gives which of these?
quiz.why: Acetone is a methyl ketone, so it is iodinated and cleaved by I₂/NaOH to give yellow iodoform.

lessons.title: Lab: Preparation of acetanilide and percentage yield

scenes.text: Pouring the warm reaction mixture into ice water, Divya watches white flakes of acetanilide appear.
After recrystallisation she weighs the dry crystals and calculates her yield.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
C₆H₅NH₂ + (CH₃CO)₂O → C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ + CH₃COOH (acetylation, nucleophilic acyl substitution).

Acetylation protects the amine — used before nitration to make p-nitroacetanilide (the bulky, less activating –NHCOCH₃ group gives mainly para product and prevents oxidation).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. In a fume hood, mix 5.0 mL aniline with 5 mL glacial acetic acid and 5.5 mL acetic anhydride in a dry flask.
2. Warm gently (reflux 10–15 min).
3. Pour into about 100 mL ice-cold water with stirring.
4. Filter the crude solid; wash with cold water.
5. Recrystallise from hot water (add a little activated charcoal if coloured).
6. Dry, weigh and take the melting point (lit. 114 °C).

steps.title: Solved: yield calculation
steps.body:
Aniline: 5.0 mL × 1.02 g mL⁻¹ = 5.10 g; M = 93.13 → 0.0548 mol (limiting; anhydride is in excess).

- Theoretical acetanilide (M = 135.17) = 0.0548 × 135.17 = **7.40 g**
- Obtained after recrystallisation: 5.90 g
- % yield = 5.90/7.40 × 100 = **79.7%**

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why acetic anhydride rather than acetyl chloride? — Less violent, no HCl fumes, cheaper.
- Why pour into ice water? — Acetanilide is poorly soluble in cold water; excess anhydride hydrolyses.
- Why recrystallise from water? — Acetanilide is much more soluble in hot water than cold.
- What does a sharp m.p. show? — Purity; impurities lower and broaden the melting range.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating yield from the anhydride (not the limiting reagent).
- Weighing the product while still damp.
- Adding charcoal to a boiling solution (it froths over); cool slightly first.

activity.prompt: Order the steps in the preparation of acetanilide.
items: Mix aniline, glacial acetic acid and acetic anhydride
Pour into ice-cold water with stirring
Filter and wash the crude product
Dry, weigh and record the melting point

quiz.q: 4.65 g aniline (M 93) gives 5.40 g acetanilide (M 135). % yield:
Melting point of pure acetanilide is about:
quiz.why: Pure acetanilide melts sharply near 114 °C; a lower, broad range indicates impurities.

quiz.q: Aniline is acetylated before nitration to:
options: Moderate activation, protect from oxidation and favour para substitution
quiz.why: The acetamido group is less activating than NH₂, resists oxidation by HNO₃, and its bulk directs mainly to the para position.

lessons.title: Lab: Tests for carbohydrates and proteins

scenes.text: A biochemistry practical gives students glucose, sucrose, fructose, starch and egg albumin in unlabelled tubes.
A handful of colour reactions sorts them out in under an hour.

steps.title: Carbohydrate tests
steps.body:
- **Molisch** (α-naphthol + conc. H₂SO₄ layered): violet ring — all carbohydrates.
- **Benedict's/Fehling's**: brick-red Cu₂O — reducing sugars (glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose); sucrose negative.
- **Barfoed's**: red precipitate within ~2 min — monosaccharides; disaccharides take longer.
- **Seliwanoff's** (resorcinol/HCl): cherry red quickly — ketoses (fructose, and sucrose after hydrolysis).
- **Iodine**: blue-black — starch.
- **Osazone**: needle-shaped crystals (glucose/fructose), sunflower (maltose), powder-puff (lactose).

steps.title: Protein tests
steps.body:
- **Biuret** (CuSO₄ + NaOH): violet — two or more peptide bonds.
- **Ninhydrin**: purple — free α-amino groups.
- **Xanthoproteic** (conc. HNO₃, heat, then NH₃): yellow → orange — aromatic amino acids (Tyr, Trp).
- **Millon's**: red — tyrosine (phenol group).
- **Lead acetate** (after boiling with NaOH): black PbS — sulphur amino acids (Cys).

steps.title: Solved: identifying the tubes
steps.body:
| Tube | Molisch | Benedict | Seliwanoff | Iodine | Biuret |
| A | + | + | + (fast) | − | − | → fructose
| B | + | − | + (slow, after hydrolysis) | − | − | → sucrose
| C | + | + | − | − | − | → glucose
| D | + | − | − | blue-black | − | → starch
| E | − | − | − | − | violet | → albumin

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shaking during the Molisch test — the ring must form at the interface.
- Heating Seliwanoff's too long (glucose also turns red slowly).
- Using excess CuSO₄ in the biuret test, masking the violet colour with blue.

activity.prompt: Match each test with what it detects.

quiz.q: A sugar gives positive Molisch and negative Benedict's tests. It could be:
quiz.why: Sucrose is a carbohydrate (Molisch positive) but non-reducing, so Benedict's reagent is not reduced.

quiz.q: Seliwanoff's test distinguishes:
quiz.why: Ketoses dehydrate faster in HCl to hydroxymethylfurfural, giving a quick cherry-red colour with resorcinol.

quiz.q: Biuret test requires at least:
quiz.why: Cu²⁺ forms the violet complex with nitrogen atoms of at least two adjacent peptide bonds.

questions.q: SN1 reaction of an optically active halide gives:
questions.why: The planar carbocation is attacked from both faces, giving largely racemic product.

questions.q: Most stable free radical:
questions.why: Tertiary radicals are stabilised most by hyperconjugation with nine C–H bonds.

questions.q: Major product of HBr + propene with benzoyl peroxide:
questions.why: Peroxide starts a radical chain in which Br· adds to C-1 to give the more stable secondary radical, yielding the anti-Markovnikov product.

questions.q: Reagent for converting acetophenone oxime to acetanilide:
questions.why: Acid promotes the Beckmann rearrangement, in which the phenyl anti to OH migrates to N.

questions.q: Aldol condensation requires:
questions.why: An α-H must be removed to form the enolate nucleophile.

questions.q: Basicity order:
questions.why: sp³ N lone pair (piperidine) > sp² lone pair (pyridine) > lone pair in aromatic sextet (pyrrole).

questions.q: Furfural is obtained from:
options: Pentosans in bran or corncobs with acid
questions.why: Acid hydrolysis and dehydration of pentose sugars in agricultural waste give furfural.

questions.q: Skraup synthesis uses nitrobenzene as:
questions.why: Nitrobenzene oxidises the dihydroquinoline intermediate to aromatic quinoline.

questions.q: Fehling's test is negative for:
questions.why: Sucrose has no free anomeric carbon, so it cannot reduce Cu²⁺.

questions.q: Equilibrium mixture of D-glucose in water is mainly:
questions.why: About 64% is β-pyranose because all its substituents can be equatorial.

questions.q: pI of an amino acid with pKa values 2.0 and 9.0 (neutral side chain):
Hydrogen bonds between G and C:
questions.why: Guanine and cytosine form three hydrogen bonds, making GC-rich DNA more thermally stable.

questions.q: Theoretical yield of acetanilide (M 135) from 0.040 mol aniline:
questions.why: One mole of aniline gives one mole of acetanilide: 0.040 × 135 = 5.40 g.

questions.q: Lassaigne's test for sulphur gives violet colour with:
questions.why: Sulphide ions from fusion form a violet complex with sodium nitroprusside.

questions.q: Methyl glucoside does not mutarotate because:
options: The anomeric OH is converted to OCH₃, blocking ring opening
questions.why: As an acetal the glycoside cannot open to the aldehyde in neutral water, so α and β cannot interconvert.

uni-bsc-chem-physical-chemistry-1.title: Physical Chemistry I — States of Matter & Thermodynamics
uni-bsc-chem-physical-chemistry-1.description: Gaseous state, kinetic theory, real gases, liquids and crystalline solids, and the first, second and third laws of thermodynamics with thermochemistry and free energy. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Chemistry programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Gaseous state
courses.summary: Postulates of kinetic theory, derivation of PV = ⅓mNu², molecular speeds and the Maxwell distribution, collision parameters, real-gas behaviour, the van der Waals equation and critical constants.
outcomes: Derive the kinetic gas equation and obtain the ideal gas laws from it
Calculate rms, average and most probable speeds
Compute compressibility factor and van der Waals pressure
Relate a and b to Tc, Pc, Vc and the Boyle temperature
Explain the law of corresponding states

lessons.title: Kinetic theory and the kinetic gas equation

story.title: The tyre on a summer afternoon

scenes.text: Ravi fills his scooter tyre to 30 psi in the cool morning; by 3 pm the gauge reads higher.
Faster molecules hit the tyre wall harder and more often. Kinetic theory turns that picture into an equation.

steps.title: Postulates
steps.body:
- A gas is made of a very large number of molecules whose own volume is negligible compared with the container.
- Molecules move randomly in straight lines and collide elastically with each other and the walls.
- No attractive or repulsive forces act between molecules except during collisions.
- Pressure is due to wall collisions.
- Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.

steps.title: Derivation of PV = ⅓ m N u²
steps.body:
Take a cube of edge l with N molecules of mass m. A molecule with x-velocity uₓ hits the wall and reverses: momentum change = 2muₓ. Time between hits on the same wall = 2l/uₓ, so force = 2muₓ ÷ (2l/uₓ) = muₓ²/l.

Summing over all molecules: Fₓ = (m/l) Σuₓ². Pressure = F/l² = (m/V) Σuₓ². Since motion is random, Σuₓ² = ⅓ Σu² = ⅓ N u²(rms).

So **PV = ⅓ m N u²rms**. Writing ½mu² as kinetic energy: PV = ⅔ N (½mu²) = ⅔ E. For one mole, E = 3/2 RT, giving **PV = RT** — Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws all follow.

steps.title: Solved: rms speed of N₂ at 300 K
steps.body:
u_rms = √(3RT/M), M in kg/mol.

- 3RT = 3 × 8.314 × 300 = 7482.6 J/mol
- ÷ M = 7482.6 ÷ 0.028 = 2.672 × 10⁵ m²/s²
- u_rms = √(2.672 × 10⁵) ≈ **517 m/s**

Kinetic energy per mole = 3/2 RT = 1.5 × 8.314 × 300 = **3741 J/mol**, the same for every gas at 300 K.

steps.title: Solved: Graham's law from kinetic theory
steps.body:
At the same T, ½m₁u₁² = ½m₂u₂², so u₁/u₂ = √(M₂/M₁). Rates of effusion follow the same ratio.

H₂ vs O₂: rate ratio = √(32/2) = √16 = **4**. Hydrogen effuses four times faster.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M in g/mol in √(3RT/M) — the answer comes out √1000 ≈ 31.6 times too small. Use kg/mol.
- Using °C instead of kelvin.
- Thinking average KE depends on molar mass — it depends on T only; speed depends on M.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of the kinetic gas equation derivation.
items: Collision frequency on one wall = uₓ/2l
Sum over N molecules and divide by area to get pressure
Use Σuₓ² = ⅓Σu² to get PV = ⅓mNu²

quiz.q: The rms speed of a gas becomes double when its absolute temperature is:
quiz.why: Since u_rms ∝ √T, doubling the speed requires T to increase by a factor of 2² = 4.

quiz.q: At the same temperature, which has the greatest average kinetic energy per molecule?
quiz.why: Average kinetic energy per molecule is 3/2 kT, which depends only on temperature, not on the identity or mass of the gas.

quiz.q: Ratio of effusion rates of He to CH₄ at the same T and P:
quiz.why: Rate ∝ 1/√M, so rate(He)/rate(CH₄) = √(16/4) = 2, giving 2 : 1.

quiz.q: In PV = ⅔E, E stands for:
options: Total translational kinetic energy of the gas
quiz.why: The derivation only considers translational motion, so E is the total translational kinetic energy ½mNu².

scenes.text: In a marathon a few runners sprint ahead and a few lag; most cluster near the middle.
Gas molecules behave the same way. Maxwell's curve shows how many molecules have each speed.

steps.title: The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve
steps.body:
The fraction of molecules with speed between u and u + du rises from zero, passes a maximum and falls off with a long tail.

- Most probable speed **u_mp = √(2RT/M)** (peak)
- Average speed **u_avg = √(8RT/πM)**
- rms speed **u_rms = √(3RT/M)**
- Ratio u_mp : u_avg : u_rms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224

Raising T flattens the curve and shifts the peak to higher speed; the area (total molecules) stays the same. A heavier gas has a narrower curve at lower speeds.

steps.title: Collision diameter, number and mean free path
steps.body:
- Collision diameter σ: distance between centres at closest approach.
- Collision number (one molecule): Z₁ = √2 π σ² u_avg N*, where N* = molecules per unit volume.
- Collision frequency (per unit volume): Z₁₁ = (1/√2) π σ² u_avg N*².
- Mean free path **λ = u_avg/Z₁ = 1/(√2 π σ² N*) = kT/(√2 π σ² P)**.

λ increases with T at constant P and decreases as pressure rises.

steps.title: Solved: speeds of O₂ at 300 K
Solved: effect of pressure on λ
steps.body: If λ of a gas is 66 nm at 1 bar, at 0.5 bar and the same T: λ ∝ 1/P, so λ = 66 × 2 = **132 nm**. In a high-vacuum line at 10⁻⁶ bar it would be about 66 mm, longer than many tube diameters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the speeds in the wrong order — it is always u_mp < u_avg < u_rms.
- Thinking the peak height increases with T; it decreases because the curve spreads.
- Forgetting the √2 that accounts for relative motion of molecules.

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its expression.

quiz.q: When temperature rises, the Maxwell curve:
options: Becomes flatter and broader, peak moving to higher speed
quiz.why: Higher T gives more molecules high speeds, so the distribution spreads out, the peak moves right and its height drops while total area is constant.

quiz.q: Mean free path at constant temperature is:
quiz.why: λ = kT/(√2πσ²P); at fixed T a higher pressure packs more molecules per volume, so the distance between collisions falls as 1/P.

quiz.q: u_rms/u_mp equals:
Collision diameter is:
options: Distance between centres of two molecules at closest approach
quiz.why: Two molecules collide when their centres come within σ of each other, so σ is defined as that closest centre-to-centre distance.

lessons.title: Real gases and the van der Waals equation

scenes.text: A lab assistant calculates that a CO₂ cylinder should be at 25 bar using PV = nRT, but the gauge reads lower.
CO₂ molecules attract one another and take up space. Real gases need a corrected equation.

steps.title: Compressibility factor
steps.body:
Z = PV/(nRT). Ideal gas: Z = 1 at all P.

- Z < 1: attractions dominate (gas more compressible) — CO₂, NH₃ at moderate P.
- Z > 1: repulsion/excluded volume dominates — H₂ and He at room temperature, and all gases at very high P.

Deviations are largest at low T and high P. Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low P and high T.

steps.title: Deriving van der Waals corrections
steps.body:
- **Volume correction**: molecules exclude volume b per mole, so free volume = V − nb. For spheres of diameter σ, b = 4 × (Avogadro's number × volume of one molecule).
- **Pressure correction**: molecules striking the wall are pulled back by neighbours. The pull ∝ (n/V) for the striking molecules and ∝ (n/V) for the pulling ones, so the observed pressure is lower by an²/V².

**(P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT**. Units: a in L² bar mol⁻² (or Pa m⁶ mol⁻²), b in L mol⁻¹.

steps.title: Solved: pressure of 1 mol CO₂ in 1.00 L at 300 K
Solved: limiting forms
steps.body:
- Low pressure (V large): V − b ≈ V, so PV = RT − a/V → Z < 1 (attraction).
- High pressure: a/V² is small compared with P, so P(V − b) = RT → PV = RT + Pb → Z = 1 + Pb/RT > 1.
- H₂ and He: a is very small, so Z > 1 at all pressures at room temperature.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding an²/V² to the observed pressure when calculating P — it must be subtracted.
- Mixing R units: with a in L² bar mol⁻² use R = 0.08314 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
- Saying b equals the actual volume of the molecules — it is four times that volume.

activity.prompt: Match the condition to the behaviour of a real gas.

quiz.q: A gas with Z < 1 is:
quiz.why: Z < 1 means the actual volume is smaller than the ideal volume, so the gas is easier to compress because attractions pull molecules together.

quiz.q: At very high pressure the vdW equation reduces to:
quiz.why: At high P the a/V² term is negligible relative to P, leaving P(V − b) = RT, i.e. PV = RT + Pb.

quiz.q: The units of a in the vdW equation are:
quiz.why: an²/V² must have pressure units, so a = pressure × V²/n², giving L² bar mol⁻².

quiz.q: Using a = 3.64 L² bar mol⁻² for 1 mol in 1 L, the pressure correction term is:
quiz.why: an²/V² = 3.64 × 1²/1² = 3.64 bar, which is the amount by which attractions reduce the observed pressure.

scenes.text: In 1869 Thomas Andrews compressed CO₂ in a sealed glass tube and watched the liquid–gas boundary.
Above about 31 °C the meniscus vanished — no amount of pressure made a separate liquid. That temperature is the critical temperature.

steps.title: Andrews isotherms
steps.body: Isotherms of CO₂ below Tc show a horizontal section where liquid and vapour coexist. As T rises this section shortens and at Tc (≈ 304 K) it shrinks to a point of inflection — the **critical point** (Tc, Pc, Vc). Above Tc the gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone. Beyond the critical point the fluid is called **supercritical** (used in supercritical CO₂ decaffeination).

steps.title: Critical constants from a and b
steps.body:
At the critical point (∂P/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0. Solving with the vdW equation gives:

- **Vc = 3b**
- **Pc = a/(27b²)**
- **Tc = 8a/(27Rb)**
- Critical compressibility Zc = PcVc/RTc = 3/8 = 0.375 (real gases ≈ 0.27–0.30)
- **Boyle temperature T_B = a/(Rb)**, where the gas behaves ideally over a range of low pressures; T_B = 27/8 Tc.

steps.title: Solved: Tc and Pc of CO₂ from vdW constants
Solved: reduced variables
steps.body:
Reduced variables: Pr = P/Pc, Tr = T/Tc, Vr = V/Vc. Law of corresponding states: gases at the same Pr and Tr have about the same Vr and Z.

CO₂ at 456 K and 148 bar: Tr = 456/304 = 1.5, Pr = 148/74 = 2.0. Any other gas at Tr = 1.5, Pr = 2 (e.g. N₂ at 1.5 × 126 = 189 K and 2 × 33.9 = 67.8 bar) has nearly the same Z.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Tc = 8a/27b without R.
- Expecting vdW Zc = 0.375 to match experiment — real gases are lower, showing the equation's limits.
- Confusing Boyle temperature with critical temperature; T_B is higher (≈ 3.4 Tc).

activity.prompt: Order what you observe as CO₂ is compressed at 20 °C (below Tc).
items: Gas volume falls as pressure rises (Boyle-like)
Liquid first appears at the vapour pressure
Volume falls at constant pressure as more gas condenses
Steep rise in pressure as the liquid is compressed

quiz.q: In terms of vdW constants, Tc equals:
quiz.why: Applying the inflection conditions to the vdW equation gives Tc = 8a/(27Rb); a/Rb is the Boyle temperature.

quiz.q: The vdW critical compressibility factor is:
