courses.title: Unit 2 · Liquid and solid states
courses.summary: Surface tension and viscosity with their measurement, laws of crystallography, unit cells and Miller indices, cubic lattices and density, Bragg's law and X-ray diffraction, and defects in crystals.
outcomes: Measure relative surface tension and viscosity with a stalagmometer and Ostwald viscometer
Assign Miller indices and compute interplanar spacing in cubic crystals
Calculate density and packing fraction of sc, bcc and fcc lattices
Apply Bragg's equation to X-ray data
Distinguish Schottky and Frenkel defects

scenes.text: Meera notices honey crawls off a spoon while water splashes off. Water forms beads on a waxed leaf.
Two liquid properties explain this: viscosity (resistance to flow) and surface tension (energy of the surface).

steps.title: Surface tension
steps.body:
Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally on all sides; surface molecules feel a net inward pull. **Surface tension γ** is the force per unit length acting along the surface (N m⁻¹), equal to the work needed to create unit new area (J m⁻²).

- Water at 25 °C: γ ≈ 72 mN m⁻¹
- γ decreases with rising temperature and becomes zero at Tc.
- Soaps and detergents (surfactants) lower γ.

**Stalagmometer (drop-number method):** γ₁/γ₂ = (ρ₁ n₂)/(ρ₂ n₁), where n is the number of drops for the same volume.

steps.title: Viscosity
steps.body:
Viscosity η is resistance to flow between layers. Newton: F = η A (dv/dx). SI unit Pa s (1 poise = 0.1 Pa s); water at 25 °C ≈ 0.89 mPa s.

- η of liquids falls with rising temperature (η = A e^(E/RT)); for gases it rises.
- **Ostwald viscometer** (from Poiseuille's law): η₁/η₂ = (ρ₁ t₁)/(ρ₂ t₂), where t is the flow time between two marks.

steps.title: Solved: surface tension by drop number
steps.body:
Water (ρ = 1.00, γ = 72.0 mN m⁻¹) gives 25 drops; a liquid of ρ = 0.80 gives 50 drops from the same volume.

- γ = 72.0 × (0.80 × 25)/(1.00 × 50) = 72.0 × 20/50 = **28.8 mN m⁻¹**

More drops means smaller drops, i.e. lower surface tension.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inverting the drop ratio: more drops means lower γ, so n of the reference goes on top.
- Not keeping temperature constant — η and γ are both temperature-sensitive.
- Forgetting to rinse the viscometer with the test liquid before timing.

activity.prompt: Order the Ostwald viscometer procedure.
items: Clean and dry the viscometer, clamp it vertically in a thermostat
Fill a fixed volume of water and suck it above the upper mark
Time the flow from upper to lower mark (repeat three times)
Rinse with the test liquid and fill the same volume
Time the liquid flow and find densities

quiz.q: When temperature rises, the viscosity of a liquid:
quiz.why: Higher temperature gives molecules more energy to overcome intermolecular attraction, so liquid viscosity falls exponentially.

quiz.q: The SI unit of surface tension is:
quiz.why: Surface tension is force per unit length, so its SI unit is N m⁻¹ (equivalently J m⁻²).

quiz.q: In a stalagmometer a liquid gives more drops than water of the same density. Its surface tension is:
quiz.why: Drop size is held by surface tension; more, smaller drops for the same volume means the liquid has lower surface tension.

quiz.q: Ostwald viscometer measurements rely on:
quiz.why: Poiseuille's equation relates flow time through a capillary to viscosity, giving η ∝ ρt for the same apparatus.

lessons.title: Crystal lattices, unit cells and Miller indices

scenes.text: Under a hand lens every grain of rock salt is a tiny cube with flat faces.
The faces reflect an internal repeating unit — the unit cell — stacked in three dimensions.

steps.title: Laws of crystallography and lattices
steps.body:
- **Constancy of interfacial angles**: angles between corresponding faces are constant for a substance.
- **Rationality of indices**: intercepts of faces are small whole-number multiples of unit distances.
- **Symmetry**: crystals show planes, axes and a centre of symmetry (a cube has 23 elements of symmetry: 9 planes, 13 axes, 1 centre).

There are **7 crystal systems** and **14 Bravais lattices**. Cubic: a = b = c, α = β = γ = 90°, with simple (sc), body-centred (bcc) and face-centred (fcc) lattices.

steps.title: Miller indices
steps.body:
1. Find intercepts on a, b, c axes in unit-cell lengths.
2. Take reciprocals.
3. Clear fractions to smallest integers → (hkl).

A plane parallel to an axis has intercept ∞ → index 0. Negative intercepts are written with a bar.

Cubic interplanar spacing: **d(hkl) = a/√(h² + k² + l²)**.

steps.title: Solved: atoms per cell and packing
steps.body:
- sc: 8 × ⅛ = 1 atom; a = 2r; packing fraction 52.4%; coordination 6
- bcc: 1 + 1 = 2 atoms; √3a = 4r; 68%; coordination 8
- fcc (ccp): 8 × ⅛ + 6 × ½ = 4 atoms; √2a = 4r; 74%; coordination 12

bcc packing check: 2 × (4/3)πr³ ÷ a³ with a = 4r/√3 → 2 × 4.189 r³ / 12.32 r³ = 0.680.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using intercepts directly instead of their reciprocals.
- Writing (2 3 ∞) — infinity becomes 0 after taking the reciprocal.
- Counting a face atom as one full atom; it is shared by two cells (½).

activity.prompt: Match each cubic lattice to its property.

quiz.q: Miller indices of a plane with intercepts a, 2b, 3c:
quiz.why: Reciprocals are 1, 1/2, 1/3; multiplying by 6 gives (632).

quiz.q: Number of Bravais lattices:
quiz.why: Bravais showed there are only 14 distinct 3-D lattices spread across the 7 crystal systems.

quiz.q: d(111) for a cubic cell of edge 346 pm:
Coordination number in an fcc metal:
quiz.why: In cubic close packing each atom touches 6 neighbours in its layer and 3 above and 3 below, giving 12.

lessons.title: Density of cubic crystals and X-ray diffraction

scenes.text: In 1913 W. H. and W. L. Bragg shone X-rays on rock salt and saw sharp reflections at particular angles.
From those angles they measured the spacing between planes of ions — the first look at atomic arrangement.

steps.title: Density from the unit cell
steps.body:
**ρ = Z M/(N_A a³)**, where Z = formula units per cell, M = molar mass (g mol⁻¹), a = edge (cm), N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

1 pm = 10⁻¹⁰ cm, so a in pm must be multiplied by 10⁻¹⁰ before cubing. NaCl (rock-salt) has Z = 4; CsCl has Z = 1.

steps.title: Bragg's law
steps.body:
X-rays reflected from successive parallel planes interfere constructively when the extra path 2d sin θ equals a whole number of wavelengths:

**nλ = 2d sin θ**

- θ = glancing angle between the beam and the planes
- n = order of reflection
- Cu Kα radiation: λ = 154 pm

For cubic crystals, combine with d = a/√(h² + k² + l²): sin²θ ∝ (h² + k² + l²). The allowed ratios identify the lattice (sc: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8…; bcc: 2, 4, 6, 8…; fcc: 3, 4, 8, 11, 12…).

steps.title: Solved: Bragg spacing
steps.body:
First-order reflection at θ = 15.0° with λ = 154 pm:

- d = nλ/(2 sin θ) = 154/(2 × 0.2588) = **297.5 pm**
- Second-order reflection from the same planes: sin θ = 2 × 154/(2 × 297.5) = 0.5176 → θ ≈ **31.2°**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 2θ (the diffractometer angle) in Bragg's law instead of θ.
- Cubing a in pm and forgetting the 10⁻³⁰ factor.
- Taking Z = 1 for NaCl; the rock-salt cell contains 4 NaCl units.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the density of a metal from XRD data.
items: Index the reflections and identify the lattice type
Obtain d for a known (hkl) from nλ = 2d sin θ

lessons.title: Defects in crystals and liquid crystals

story.title: The perfect crystal does not exist

scenes.text: A jeweller explains that the colour of some gems comes from tiny flaws in an otherwise regular lattice.
Meanwhile the display on her phone uses molecules that are partly liquid and partly crystal.

steps.title: Point defects
steps.body:
- **Schottky defect**: equal numbers of cation and anion vacancies; density decreases. Found in highly ionic compounds with similar ion sizes (NaCl, KCl, CsCl).
- **Frenkel defect**: an ion (usually the smaller cation) leaves its site and sits in an interstitial position; density unchanged. Found when ions differ greatly in size (AgCl, AgBr, ZnS).
- AgBr shows both types.
- **Non-stoichiometric / F-centres**: heating NaCl in Na vapour traps electrons in anion vacancies, giving a yellow colour.

steps.title: Liquid crystals
steps.body:
Some substances (e.g. cholesteryl benzoate) melt first to a turbid fluid that is anisotropic, then at a higher temperature to a clear liquid. This mesophase is a liquid crystal.

- **Nematic**: molecules parallel but not in layers (used in LCD displays)
- **Smectic**: molecules parallel and arranged in layers
- **Cholesteric**: nematic layers twisted progressively; colour changes with temperature (thermometers)

steps.title: Solved: effect of Schottky defects on density
steps.body:
KCl: ideal density calculated from X-ray data = 1.989 g cm⁻³; measured density = 1.984 g cm⁻³.

- Fraction of sites vacant = (1.989 − 1.984)/1.989 = 0.005/1.989 ≈ **2.5 × 10⁻³** (0.25%)

A measured density lower than the X-ray density indicates vacancies (Schottky).

steps.title: Solved: doping and vacancies
steps.body:
Adding SrCl₂ to NaCl: each Sr²⁺ replaces two Na⁺ to keep neutrality, creating one cation vacancy.

If 10⁻³ mol SrCl₂ is added per mole of NaCl, the cation vacancies = 10⁻³ × 6.022 × 10²³ = **6.02 × 10²⁰ per mol** of NaCl.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a Frenkel defect lowers density — the ion only moves; mass and volume are unchanged.
- Confusing nematic (no layers) with smectic (layers).
- Thinking defects are always undesirable; they enable ionic conductivity and colour.

pairs: Yellow NaCl heated in Na vapour

quiz.q: Which defect lowers the density of a crystal?
quiz.why: A Schottky defect removes cation–anion pairs from the lattice, so mass per unit volume decreases.

quiz.q: AgBr shows:
quiz.why: AgBr is known to show both defects: Ag⁺ ions can be missing in pairs with Br⁻ or move to interstitial sites.

quiz.why: In an F-centre an electron occupies a vacant anion site; it absorbs visible light, colouring the crystal.

quiz.why: Smectic phases have molecules aligned parallel and also organised into layers, unlike nematic phases.

questions.why: For fcc only all-odd or all-even hkl reflect, giving (111), (200), (220), (311) → 3, 4, 8, 11.

courses.title: Unit 3 · First law of thermodynamics and thermochemistry
courses.summary: Systems and state functions, work and heat, the first law, reversible isothermal and adiabatic processes, heat capacities, enthalpy, Hess's law, bond enthalpies, Kirchhoff's equation and the Joule–Thomson effect.
outcomes: Calculate q, w, ΔU and ΔH for isothermal and adiabatic ideal-gas processes
Use Cp − Cv = R and adiabatic relations
Apply Hess's law and bond enthalpies to find reaction enthalpies
Convert between ΔH and ΔU with Δn_g RT
Use Kirchhoff's equation and explain Joule–Thomson cooling

lessons.title: System, work, heat and the first law

scenes.text: Anita's pressure cooker hisses: heat flows in from the flame and steam pushes the weight up.
Energy in as heat equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done on the weight. That bookkeeping is the first law.

steps.title: Basic terms
steps.body:
- **System / surroundings**; open (matter + energy exchange), closed (energy only), isolated (neither).
- **State functions** depend only on the state: U, H, S, G, P, V, T. **Path functions**: q and w.
- **Intensive** (T, P, density) vs **extensive** (V, U, mass).
- Processes: isothermal (ΔT = 0), adiabatic (q = 0), isobaric, isochoric, cyclic (ΔU = 0), reversible (infinitesimally slow, always near equilibrium).

steps.title: First law and work
steps.body:
IUPAC sign convention: **ΔU = q + w**, with q and w positive when energy enters the system.

- Expansion work: w = −∫P_ext dV
- Against constant external pressure: w = −P_ext ΔV
- Free expansion (P_ext = 0): w = 0
- **Reversible isothermal, ideal gas**: ΔU = 0, w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = −nRT ln(P₁/P₂), q = −w

Reversible work is the maximum work an expanding gas can do.

steps.title: Solved: reversible isothermal expansion
steps.body:
1 mol ideal gas, 300 K, from 10 L to 20 L reversibly.

- w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = −1 × 8.314 × 300 × ln 2
- = −2494.2 × 0.6931 = **−1729 J**
- ΔU = 0 (ideal gas, isothermal) → q = **+1729 J**
- ΔH = 0

steps.title: Solved: irreversible expansion against 1 bar
steps.body:
Same gas, 10 L → 20 L against P_ext = 1.00 bar = 10⁵ Pa.

- ΔV = 10 L = 0.010 m³
- w = −10⁵ × 0.010 = **−1000 J**, q = +1000 J

Less work is obtained than in the reversible path (1729 J), showing work is a path function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions (some older books write ΔU = q − w). State which you use.
- Using L bar with R = 8.314 J; convert: 1 L bar = 100 J.
- Assuming ΔU = 0 for every isothermal process — only for ideal gases (no phase change).

activity.prompt: Match each process to what is zero.

quiz.q: Which is a path function?
quiz.why: Work depends on how a change is carried out (reversible vs irreversible), so it is a path function; U, H and S are state functions.

quiz.q: An isolated system exchanges:
quiz.why: By definition an isolated system has walls that allow neither matter nor energy to pass.

quiz.q: 2 mol ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 5 L to 50 L. w is about:
For an ideal gas in a reversible isothermal expansion, q equals:
quiz.why: ΔU = 0 for an isothermal ideal gas, so q + w = 0 and q = −w; all heat absorbed is converted to work.

story.title: Why a bicycle pump gets hot

scenes.text: Kabir pumps his cycle tyre quickly and the pump barrel warms up.
Fast compression leaves no time for heat to escape, so the work done goes into internal energy — an adiabatic process.

steps.title: Cv, Cp and enthalpy
steps.body:
- Cv = (∂U/∂T)_V; Cp = (∂H/∂T)_P; H = U + PV.
- For an ideal gas: **Cp − Cv = R** (per mole); ΔU = nCvΔT and ΔH = nCpΔT for any process.
- Monatomic: Cv = 3/2 R, Cp = 5/2 R, γ = Cp/Cv = 1.67
- Diatomic (room T): Cv = 5/2 R, Cp = 7/2 R, γ = 1.40

steps.title: Reversible adiabatic relations
steps.body:
With q = 0: dU = −P dV → nCv dT = −(nRT/V)dV. Integrating:

- **TV^(γ−1) = constant**
- **PV^γ = constant**
- T^γ P^(1−γ) = constant
- w = ΔU = nCv(T₂ − T₁) = (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(γ − 1)

An adiabat on a P–V diagram is steeper than an isotherm through the same point.

steps.title: Solved: adiabatic expansion of a monatomic gas
steps.body:
1 mol monatomic ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and adiabatically to twice its volume.

- γ − 1 = 2/3; T₂ = 300 × (1/2)^(2/3) = 300 × 0.630 = **189 K**
- w = ΔU = nCvΔT = 1 × 12.47 × (189 − 300) = **−1384 J**
- ΔH = nCpΔT = 20.79 × (−111) = −2308 J; q = 0

steps.title: Solved: adiabatic compression of air
steps.body:
Air (γ = 1.40) at 1 bar is compressed reversibly and adiabatically to 1/10 of its volume.

- P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^γ = 1 × 10^1.4 = **25.1 bar**
- From 300 K: T₂ = 300 × 10^0.4 = 300 × 2.512 = **754 K**

This is why diesel engines ignite fuel without a spark.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using PV = constant (isotherm) for an adiabatic change.
- Taking γ = 1.67 for air; air is diatomic (γ ≈ 1.40).
- Forgetting that ΔU = nCvΔT holds even when the volume changes (ideal gas).

activity.prompt: Order the steps for solving a reversible adiabatic expansion problem.
items: Identify γ from the type of gas

quiz.q: For one mole of an ideal gas, Cp − Cv equals:
quiz.why: At constant pressure extra heat is needed for expansion work P dV = R dT per mole, so Cp − Cv = R.

quiz.q: γ for a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature:
In a reversible adiabatic expansion the gas:
quiz.why: With q = 0, the work done by the gas comes from its internal energy, so U and T fall.

quiz.q: An adiabat compared with an isotherm through the same point on a P–V plot is:
quiz.why: Slope of adiabat = −γP/V and of isotherm = −P/V; since γ > 1 the adiabat is steeper.

lessons.title: Thermochemistry: Hess's law and bond enthalpies

scenes.text: In the lab, Priya burns a sample in a bomb calorimeter and records a temperature rise.
Combining her result with tabulated data through Hess's law, she gets an enthalpy no one can measure directly.

steps.title: Enthalpy changes
steps.body:
- Standard enthalpy of formation ΔfH°: 1 mol of compound from elements in standard states (ΔfH° of elements = 0).
- **ΔrH° = Σ ΔfH°(products) − Σ ΔfH°(reactants)**
- Enthalpy of combustion, neutralisation (strong acid + strong base ≈ −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹), solution, atomisation.
- **Hess's law**: ΔH is independent of path, so thermochemical equations add like algebra.
- Bomb calorimeter measures ΔU (constant V); **ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT**.

steps.title: Solved: Hess's law and bond enthalpy
steps.body:
Find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂ → CO(g).
- C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ
- CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ
- Subtract: ΔH = −393.5 − (−283.0) = **−110.5 kJ mol⁻¹**

Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432.
- H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = (436 + 243) − 2 × 432 = **−185 kJ**

steps.title: Bond enthalpy limits
steps.body: Average bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds and apply to gases only. Estimates are usually within about 5–10% of calorimetric values; use ΔfH° data when available.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing products minus reactants for bond enthalpies — it is broken (reactants) minus formed (products).
- Counting liquid water in Δn_g.
- Forgetting to convert R to kJ (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find ΔfH° of a compound from combustion data.
items: Write combustion equations for the compound and each element
Reverse the compound's combustion equation (change the sign of ΔH)
Add equations and their ΔH values

quiz.q: ΔfH° of O₂(g) at 298 K is:
quiz.why: By convention the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.

quiz.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH − ΔU equals:
quiz.why: Δn_g = 2 − 4 = −2, so ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT = −2RT.

quiz.q: Enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is about:
quiz.why: Both are fully ionised, so the reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, releasing about 57.1 kJ per mole of water.

quiz.q: Bond enthalpies: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 463 kJ/mol. ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g) is:

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's equation and the Joule–Thomson effect

scenes.text: At a gas plant, compressed air passes through a throttle valve and comes out colder.
Repeat the cycle enough times and air liquefies. This is the Joule–Thomson effect at work (Linde process).

steps.title: Kirchhoff's equation
steps.body:
Reaction enthalpy changes with temperature because products and reactants have different heat capacities:

**(∂ΔH/∂T)_P = ΔCp**, so ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔCp (T₂ − T₁) (if ΔCp is constant).

Similarly (∂ΔU/∂T)_V = ΔCv. ΔCp = ΣCp(products) − ΣCp(reactants).

steps.title: Joule–Thomson expansion
steps.body:
A gas flows through a porous plug from high to low pressure in an insulated tube. The process is **isenthalpic** (ΔH = 0).

- **μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H**
- μ > 0: gas cools on expansion (most gases at room T)
- μ < 0: gas warms (H₂, He at room T)
- Ideal gas: μ = 0
- **Inversion temperature** (vdW): Ti = 2a/(Rb). A gas cools on throttling only below Ti.

steps.title: Solved: inversion temperature of N₂
steps.body:
For N₂, a = 1.37 L² bar mol⁻², b = 0.0387 L mol⁻¹.

- Ti = 2a/(Rb) = 2.74/(0.08314 × 0.0387) = 2.74/0.003218 ≈ **852 K**

Room temperature is well below this, so N₂ cools on throttling. The simple vdW estimate is higher than the experimental value (≈ 620 K) but shows the trend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving ΔCp in J while ΔH is in kJ.
- Thinking JT expansion is adiabatic reversible — it is adiabatic but irreversible and isenthalpic.
- Expecting H₂ to cool when throttled at room temperature; it must first be pre-cooled below its inversion temperature (≈ 200 K).

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

quiz.q: Joule–Thomson expansion occurs at constant:
quiz.why: For a throttling process with no heat exchange, the work done on and by the gas balances so that H₁ = H₂.

quiz.q: If ΔCp is positive, ΔH of a reaction with rising temperature becomes:
quiz.why: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔCp(T₂ − T₁); with ΔCp > 0 and T₂ > T₁ the second term adds a positive amount.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas μ_JT is:

courses.title: Unit 4 · Second and third laws, entropy and free energy
courses.summary: Statements of the second law, the Carnot cycle and efficiency, entropy changes in physical processes, Gibbs and Helmholtz free energies and spontaneity, the Gibbs–Helmholtz and Clausius–Clapeyron equations, and the third law with residual entropy.
outcomes: Calculate Carnot efficiency and work from heat engines

lessons.title: Second law and the Carnot cycle

scenes.text: A plant engineer tells interns that even a perfect steam turbine cannot turn all the heat from coal into electricity.
Some heat must always be dumped into the river or cooling tower. Sadi Carnot worked out the limit in 1824.

steps.title: Statements of the second law
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic engine can convert heat from a single reservoir completely into work.
- **Clausius**: heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body without external work.
- **Entropy form**: for any spontaneous process ΔS(universe) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) > 0; = 0 at equilibrium.

steps.title: The Carnot cycle
steps.body:
An ideal gas engine undergoes four reversible steps:
1. Isothermal expansion at T_h (absorbs q_h)
2. Adiabatic expansion (T_h → T_c)
3. Isothermal compression at T_c (rejects q_c)
4. Adiabatic compression (T_c → T_h)

Using w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁) and the adiabatic relation V₃/V₄ = V₂/V₁:

**η = −w/q_h = 1 − T_c/T_h**. Also q_h/T_h + q_c/T_c = 0, which defines entropy as dS = dq_rev/T.

steps.title: Solved: engine efficiency
steps.body:
A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J per cycle.

- η = 1 − 300/500 = **0.40 (40%)**
- Work = 0.40 × 1000 = **400 J**
- Heat rejected = 1000 − 400 = **600 J**

To reach 60% with T_c = 300 K: T_h = 300/0.4 = 750 K.

steps.title: Solved: refrigerator
steps.body:
Coefficient of performance (Carnot refrigerator) = T_c/(T_h − T_c).

Freezer at 255 K, kitchen at 300 K: COP = 255/45 = **5.67**, so 1 J of work removes up to 5.67 J of heat from the freezer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in η = 1 − T_c/T_h (always kelvin).
- Thinking a real engine can reach Carnot efficiency — irreversibility lowers it.
- Confusing the efficiency of an engine with the COP of a refrigerator.

activity.prompt: Order the four steps of the Carnot cycle starting from the hot reservoir.
items: Adiabatic reversible compression back to T_h

quiz.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine between 400 K and 300 K:
quiz.why: η = 1 − 300/400 = 0.25, so 25% of the heat absorbed can become work.

quiz.q: The Kelvin–Planck statement forbids:
options: A cyclic engine converting all heat from one reservoir to work
Heat flow from hot to cold
quiz.why: Kelvin–Planck says no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and turn it entirely into work; some heat must be rejected.

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency can be increased by:
quiz.why: η = 1 − T_c/T_h, so a colder sink (lower T_c) increases efficiency; the working substance does not matter.

quiz.q: For a reversible Carnot cycle, Σ q/T is:
quiz.why: q_h/T_h + q_c/T_c = 0 for the reversible cycle, which shows q_rev/T is a state function (entropy).

scenes.text: An ice cube in a glass of water melts on its own; the reverse never happens unaided.
Entropy measures how many ways energy and matter can be arranged. The melted state has far more.

steps.title: Formulae for ideal gases and phases
steps.body:
dS = dq_rev/T.

- Isothermal expansion: **ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = nR ln(P₁/P₂)**
- Heating at constant P: **ΔS = nCp ln(T₂/T₁)**; at constant V: nCv ln(T₂/T₁)
- General ideal-gas change: ΔS = nCv ln(T₂/T₁) + nR ln(V₂/V₁)
- Phase change at T_tr: **ΔS = ΔH_tr/T_tr**
- Mixing ideal gases: **ΔS_mix = −nR Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ**
- Reversible adiabatic: ΔS = 0 (isentropic)

steps.title: Solved: expansion and vaporisation
steps.body:
- 1 mol ideal gas doubles its volume isothermally: ΔS = 8.314 × ln 2 = **5.76 J K⁻¹**
- Water vaporises at 373 K, ΔvapH = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹: ΔS = 40 700/373 = **109.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**

Trouton's rule: many non-polar liquids have ΔvapS ≈ 85–88 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; water is higher due to hydrogen bonding.

steps.title: Solved: heating and mixing
steps.body:
- 1 mol water (Cp = 75.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) heated from 298 K to 348 K: ΔS = 75.3 × ln(348/298) = 75.3 × 0.1551 = **11.7 J K⁻¹**
- 1 mol N₂ mixed with 1 mol O₂ (x = 0.5 each): ΔS_mix = −2 × 8.314 × ln 0.5 = **+11.5 J K⁻¹**

steps.title: Solved: spontaneity of freezing
steps.body: Water freezing at 263 K (−10 °C). Approximate ΔS(sys) ≈ −ΔfusH/273 = −6010/273 = −22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Heat released to surroundings at 263 K: ΔS(surr) ≈ +6010/263 = +22.9 J K⁻¹. ΔS(universe) ≈ +0.9 J K⁻¹ > 0, so supercooled water freezes spontaneously. (A full treatment corrects ΔH for temperature; the sign is the same.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ΔS = q/T for an irreversible heat flow — always use a reversible path between the same states.
- Writing ln(T₁/T₂) and getting the wrong sign.
- Thinking ΔS(system) < 0 means non-spontaneous; check ΔS(universe).

activity.prompt: Match each process to its ΔS expression.
pairs: Melting at the normal melting point

quiz.q: ΔS when 2 mol ideal gas expand isothermally from 1 L to 10 L:
ΔfusH of ice is 6.01 kJ/mol at 273 K. ΔfusS is:
quiz.why: ΔS = ΔH/T = 6010/273 ≈ 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, positive because the liquid is more disordered.

quiz.q: Entropy change in a reversible adiabatic process is:
quiz.why: No heat is exchanged reversibly (dq_rev = 0), so dS = 0; the process is isentropic.

quiz.q: Trouton's rule gives ΔvapS approximately:
quiz.why: For many non-associated liquids the entropy of vaporisation at the normal boiling point is close to 85–88 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

scenes.text: In a lime kiln near Katni, limestone is roasted to make quicklime. At room temperature nothing happens.
Above about 1100 K the reaction goes. Free energy tells you exactly where the switch happens.

steps.title: Definitions and criteria
steps.body:
- **Helmholtz**: A = U − TS; at constant T, V: ΔA ≤ 0 for spontaneity; −ΔA = maximum total work.
- **Gibbs**: G = H − TS; at constant T, P: **ΔG = ΔH − TΔS**, ΔG < 0 spontaneous, = 0 equilibrium; −ΔG = maximum non-PV (e.g. electrical) work.
- Fundamental equations: dG = V dP − S dT; dA = −P dV − S dT.
- Maxwell relation from dG: (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P.
- Ideal gas, isothermal: ΔG = nRT ln(P₂/P₁).

steps.title: Four sign cases
steps.body:
- ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous at all T
- ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0: never spontaneous
- ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0: spontaneous at low T (below ΔH/ΔS)
- ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous at high T (above ΔH/ΔS)

**Gibbs–Helmholtz**: [∂(ΔG/T)/∂T]_P = −ΔH/T².

steps.title: Solved: compressing a gas
steps.body:
1 mol ideal gas compressed isothermally at 300 K from 1 bar to 10 bar:

- ΔG = RT ln(P₂/P₁) = 8.314 × 300 × 2.303 = **+5.74 kJ**

The positive ΔG reflects that compression does not happen spontaneously.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ΔS in J and ΔH in kJ without converting.
- Treating ΔG° as ΔG; ΔG depends on actual concentrations/pressures.
- Assuming ΔH and ΔS stay constant over very wide ranges; it is an approximation.

activity.prompt: Match the sign combination with when the reaction is spontaneous.

quiz.q: ΔH = −10 kJ and ΔS = −50 J/K. Reaction is spontaneous below:
quiz.why: T = ΔH/ΔS = 10 000/50 = 200 K; below this the −TΔS penalty is smaller than |ΔH| so ΔG < 0.

quiz.q: Spontaneity criterion at constant T and V:
quiz.why: At constant temperature and volume the Helmholtz energy decreases in a spontaneous change.

quiz.q: −ΔG equals the maximum:
quiz.why: At constant T and P, the decrease in G is the maximum work other than expansion work, such as electrical work in a cell.

quiz.q: (∂G/∂T)_P equals:
quiz.why: From dG = V dP − S dT, the temperature derivative at constant pressure is −S.

lessons.title: Clausius–Clapeyron equation and the third law

scenes.text: At 3500 m in Leh, water boils at about 88 °C and dal takes forever to cook.
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation links lower air pressure to a lower boiling point.

steps.title: Clapeyron and Clausius–Clapeyron
steps.body:
At equilibrium between two phases, dG₁ = dG₂, giving the **Clapeyron equation**: dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV).

For liquid ⇌ vapour, neglect liquid volume and treat vapour as ideal:

**ln(P₂/P₁) = (ΔvapH/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)**

For ice ⇌ water, ΔV < 0, so dP/dT < 0: higher pressure lowers the melting point of ice.

steps.title: Solved: vapour pressure of water at 90 °C
Third law
steps.body:
**The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at 0 K.** This gives absolute entropies:

S(T) = ∫₀^T (Cp/T) dT + Σ ΔH_tr/T_tr. Near 0 K the Debye T³ law (Cp = aT³) is used.

**Residual entropy**: crystals that are not perfectly ordered at 0 K. CO can sit as CO or OC (two orientations), so S₀ ≈ R ln 2 = **5.76 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹** (measured ≈ 4.6, since disorder is not completely random).

steps.title: Solved: boiling point from Trouton-type data
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping T₁ and T₂ so the sign of the answer is wrong — check that lower T gives lower P.
- Applying Clausius–Clapeyron to solid–liquid equilibrium (vapour is not involved; use Clapeyron).
- Saying the third law makes all entropies zero at 0 K; it is for perfect crystals only.

quiz.q: Pressure lowers the melting point of ice because:
quiz.why: Water occupies less volume than ice, so ΔV of melting is negative and the Clapeyron slope dP/dT is negative.

CO is a gas at 0 K

questions.why: Clausius stated that heat cannot by itself flow from a colder body to a hotter one.

curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Physical Chemistry I practicals)
courses.summary: A formula and key-point sheet for gases, solids and thermodynamics, standard calorimetry practicals (water equivalent, enthalpy of neutralisation, enthalpy of hydration by Hess's law), viva questions and a full-length practice exam.
outcomes: Recall the key formulae of the paper quickly
Determine the water equivalent of a calorimeter
Measure the enthalpy of neutralisation of HCl by NaOH

scenes.text: Rohit has one evening left and five chapters of notes.
He condenses them to one page of formulae and practises a few long questions. Here is that page.

steps.title: Gases and solids
steps.body:
- PV = ⅓mNu²; u_rms = √(3RT/M); u_avg = √(8RT/πM); u_mp = √(2RT/M)
- λ = kT/(√2πσ²P); Z = PV/nRT
- (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT; Vc = 3b, Pc = a/27b², Tc = 8a/27Rb, T_B = a/Rb, Ti = 2a/Rb
- ρ = ZM/(N_A a³); nλ = 2d sin θ; d = a/√(h² + k² + l²)
- η₁/η₂ = ρ₁t₁/ρ₂t₂; γ₁/γ₂ = ρ₁n₂/ρ₂n₁

steps.title: Thermodynamics
steps.body:
- ΔU = q + w; w(rev, isothermal) = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁); Cp − Cv = R
- Adiabatic: TV^(γ−1) = const, PV^γ = const, w = nCvΔT
- ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT; ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔCpΔT
- η = 1 − T_c/T_h; ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁), nCp ln(T₂/T₁), ΔH_tr/T_tr, −nRΣx ln x
- ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG = nRT ln(P₂/P₁)
- ln(P₂/P₁) = (ΔH/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂); dP/dT = ΔH/TΔV

steps.title: Long-answer practice (10 marks style)
steps.body:
Q. Derive Tc, Pc and Vc in terms of van der Waals constants and show that Zc = 3/8.

Outline: write P = RT/(V − b) − a/V²; set (∂P/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0; divide the two equations to get Vc = 3b; substitute to get Tc = 8a/27Rb and Pc = a/27b²; compute PcVc/RTc = (a/27b² × 3b)/(8a/27b) = 3/8.

Q. Show that for a reversible adiabatic process PV^γ = constant. Start from nCv dT = −P dV with P = nRT/V and integrate.

steps.title: Short numericals
steps.body:
1. Density of a bcc metal, a = 287 pm, M = 55.85: a³ = 2.364 × 10⁻²³ cm³; ρ = 111.7/(6.022 × 2.364) = **7.85 g cm⁻³** (iron).
2. ΔS for melting 36 g of ice (ΔH = 6.01 kJ/mol): 2 mol × 22.0 = **44.0 J K⁻¹**.
3. Efficiency of an engine between 127 °C and 27 °C: 1 − 300/400 = **25%**.

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: Always write the formula, substitute with units, and box the answer with units. For derivations, list assumptions first (ideal gas, reversible, constant Cp). Draw P–V diagrams for Carnot and Andrews questions; a labelled sketch often earns marks by itself.

quiz.why: Substituting Pc, Vc and Tc gives PcVc/RTc = 3/8 = 0.375 for any vdW gas.

An engine works between 127 °C and 27 °C. Maximum efficiency:

lessons.title: Lab: Water equivalent of a calorimeter

scenes.text: Neha mixes hot and cold water in a polystyrene-insulated beaker and the final temperature is a little lower than expected.
The vessel, stirrer and thermometer absorbed some heat. She measures how much as a 'water equivalent'.

steps.title: Aim and principle
steps.body:
Aim: determine the water equivalent W of a calorimeter (the mass of water that would absorb the same heat per degree as the calorimeter, stirrer and thermometer).

Principle: heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water + calorimeter:

m_h s (T_h − T_f) = (m_c + W) s (T_f − T_c), with s = 4.184 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Put 50 mL water in the calorimeter; record its steady temperature T_c every 30 s for 2 min.
2. Heat another 50 mL water to about 20 K above room temperature; record T_h just before mixing.
3. Pour the hot water in quickly, stir and record temperature every 30 s for 5 min.
4. Plot temperature vs time and extrapolate back to the mixing time to get T_f (corrects for heat loss).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body:
- Heat loss during transfer (pour quickly, use a lid).
- Not extrapolating the cooling curve to the mixing time.
- Thermometer read to only 1 °C — use a 0.1 °C thermometer or a digital probe.

activity.prompt: Order the procedure for finding the water equivalent.
items: Take 50 mL water in the calorimeter and record its steady temperature
Heat 50 mL water about 20 K above room temperature and note T_h
Record temperature every 30 s for 5 minutes
Extrapolate the curve to find T_f
Calculate W from the heat balance

quiz.q: Water equivalent is expressed in:
quiz.why: It is the mass of water whose heat capacity equals that of the calorimeter, so it is expressed in grams.

quiz.q: Why is the temperature–time graph extrapolated?
options: To correct for heat lost during mixing
To make the graph look neat
quiz.why: Extrapolating back to the instant of mixing estimates the temperature that would have been reached without heat loss to the surroundings.

quiz.q: If W is ignored, a calculated enthalpy of neutralisation will be:
quiz.why: Ignoring the heat absorbed by the calorimeter underestimates the total heat released, so |ΔH| comes out too small.

lessons.title: Lab: Enthalpy of neutralisation of HCl and NaOH

story.title: A constant for every strong acid

scenes.text: Three groups use HCl, HNO₃ and HClO₄ with NaOH and all get about −57 kJ mol⁻¹.
The reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. With acetic acid the value is smaller, because some energy is used to ionise the weak acid.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Take 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH in the calorimeter; record temperature for 2 min.
2. Take 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl in a beaker at the same temperature.
3. Add the acid, stir, and record temperature every 30 s for 5 min.
4. Extrapolate to find ΔT.
5. Calculate using total heat capacity = (100 g + W) × 4.184 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (assume density and specific heat equal to water).

steps.title: Solved: observation table
steps.body:
W = 20 g; ΔT = 5.7 K; moles of water formed = 0.050 mol.

- Heat capacity = (100 + 20) × 4.184 = 502 J K⁻¹
- q = 502 × 5.7 = 2862 J
- ΔH_neut = −2862/0.050 = **−57.2 kJ mol⁻¹**

steps.title: Weak acids and bases
steps.body: With CH₃COOH + NaOH the value is about −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹. The difference (≈ 2 kJ mol⁻¹) is the enthalpy of ionisation of acetic acid, absorbed when it dissociates. The limiting reagent sets the moles of water formed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the volume of only one solution for the mass of liquid.
- Taking moles from the excess reagent instead of the limiting one.
- Starting with acid and base at different temperatures; use their average initial temperature.

activity.prompt: Match the acid–base pair with its approximate enthalpy of neutralisation.
pairs: Enthalpy of ionisation of the weak acid

quiz.q: 100 mL of 0.5 M HCl + 100 mL of 0.5 M NaOH; total heat capacity 900 J/K; ΔT = 3.2 K. ΔH_neut:
Why is ΔH_neut less negative for acetic acid?
options: Energy is absorbed to ionise the weak acid
quiz.why: Part of the heat released by H⁺ + OH⁻ is used to dissociate the weak acid, so the net heat released is smaller.

quiz.q: In this experiment the limiting reagent decides:
quiz.why: Only as much water forms as the reagent in shorter supply allows, and ΔH is calculated per mole of water formed.

lessons.title: Lab: Enthalpy of hydration of CuSO₄ and viva

scenes.text: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; it turns blue and warm when a drop of water is added.
You cannot measure the hydration heat directly, but two solution experiments and Hess's law give it.

steps.title: Hess cycle
steps.body:
- (1) CuSO₄(s) + aq → CuSO₄(aq), ΔH₁
- (2) CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) + aq → CuSO₄(aq), ΔH₂
- Target: CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s), **ΔH_hyd = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂**

steps.title: Solved: calculation
steps.body:
Literature-type values: ΔH₁ = −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (anhydrous, exothermic); ΔH₂ = +11.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (pentahydrate, endothermic).

- ΔH_hyd = −66.5 − (+11.7) = **−78.2 kJ mol⁻¹**

In the lab, dissolve about 0.02 mol of each solid in 100 mL water, measure ΔT, and use q = (m + W) × 4.184 × ΔT.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why is a polystyrene cup used? — It is a poor conductor and has low heat capacity.
- Is enthalpy of solution always negative? — No; e.g. KNO₃, NH₄Cl and CuSO₄·5H₂O dissolve endothermically.
- Why is the enthalpy of neutralisation constant for strong acids? — The net reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
- What is a state function? — A property depending only on the state, e.g. H, which is why Hess's law works.
- Why does viscosity decrease with temperature? — Molecules gain energy to overcome attraction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting anhydrous CuSO₄ absorb moisture before weighing — keep it in a desiccator.
- Using the mass of solution only and ignoring W.
- Writing ΔH_hyd = ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ (sign reversed).

activity.prompt: Order the procedure for the hydration-enthalpy experiment.
items: Weigh about 0.02 mol anhydrous CuSO₄ quickly from a desiccator
